methods.mergeable_reason: \(W_0S(P_r,T_r)\) is again a weight matrix, equal to \(W_0+W_0P_r^{\top}(T_r-I_r)P_r\).
methods.identity_at_init: \(E=0\) gives \(T_r=I_r\) and \(S=I\), so the model is unchanged. The support \(P_r\) is computed once before training: from the SVD of \(W_0\) (principal), or from the gradient \(G\) of the downstream loss at \(W_0\) estimated on a small calibration set (GradSVD, SkewGrad), then frozen.
methods.key_idea: Separate where an orthogonal update acts (the support \(P_r\)) from how it acts (the in-subspace transform \(T_r\)), and choose the support from the task: the first-order training signal of a right-subspace rotation is \(P_r\operatorname{skew}(W_0^{\top}G)P_r^{\top}\), whose norm is largest when \(P_r\) spans the top invariant subspace of \(\operatorname{skew}(W_0^{\top}G)\).
methods.results_note: With SkewGrad support at \(r=46\), the GLUE average on DeBERTaV3-base is 88.73 against 88.04 for PSOFT, and the VTAB-1K average on ViT-B/16 is 73.8 against 73.4, with 0.07M trainable parameters; principal-support LOFT matches PSOFT (88.06).

relations.note: Principal-support LOFT is PSOFT with both scaling vectors frozen at 1, when both use the same exactly orthogonal transform.
HRA is an instance of the paper's multi-factor primitive with learnable width-one supports, not of fixed-support LOFT; LOFT's image is one leaf of HRA's image.
Block OFT is an instance of the paper's multi-factor primitive with coordinate-block supports; single-factor LOFT maps into full-block exact-Cayley OFT.
GOFT is a depth-L composition of width-2 coordinate-pair supports in the paper's multi-factor primitive.
BOFT is a multi-stage composition of butterfly-block supports in the paper's multi-factor primitive.
Both choose a starting frame from the gradient at W_0: LoRA-GA for an additive low-rank update, LOFT (GradSVD, SkewGrad) for an orthogonal support.

methods.verification_notes: Added 2026-10-02 after a reader reported it missing. Title, authors and date checked against the arXiv API; formula, supports, parameter count and results read from the paper (Sections 2-3, Tables 1-4, Appendix C.1). Two independent referees checked the entry and the site text the same day. The released code (github.com/Kris-camp/loft) defaults to a 5-term Cayley–Neumann transform with R^T R = (I - X^6)^2, which is not exactly orthogonal; per the referee's inspection the gradient-based supports are not in the code release. Not in the Hugging Face PEFT tuners list at the pinned commit.
corrections: Relation types corrected after review (PSOFT: special-case-of; HRA, OFT, GOFT, BOFT: competes-with; GaLore relation dropped).

methods.name: PreFT
methods.full_name: Prefill-only Finetuning (prefill-only LoRA, \( \text{LoRA}_P \), and prefill-only DiReFT, \( \text{DiReFT}_P \))
methods.paper_title: PreFT: Prefill-only finetuning for efficient inference
methods.formula_latex: h_i=W_0x_i+m_i\,\tfrac{\alpha}{r}BAx_i\ \ (\text{LoRA}_P),\qquad h^{(l)}_i\leftarrow h^{(l)}_i+m_i\,s_r\,W_2^{\top}\big(W_1h^{(l)}_i+b\big)\ \ (\text{DiReFT}_P),\qquad m_i=\mathbf{1}[\,i\le\ell\,];\ \ B\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r},\ A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}},\ W_1,W_2\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d},\ b\in\mathbb{R}^{r},\ s_r=1/\sqrt{r},\ \alpha=32;\ \ \text{decode positions } i>\ell \text{ run the frozen model and see the adapter only through the KV cache of positions } \le\ell;\ \ W_0\ \text{frozen},\ (A,B)\ \text{or}\ (W_1,W_2,b)\ \text{trained}
methods.trainable_params: r(d_{in}+d_{out})\ \text{per adapted matrix for LoRA}_P\ (\text{same as LoRA});\ \ L\,(2rd+r)\ \text{per model for DiReFT}_P\ (\text{one residual-stream intervention per layer})
methods.locus: Token-time locus: only the prompt positions \( i\le\ell \) processed at prefill, never the generated tokens. \( \text{LoRA}_P \) targets \( W_q,W_k,W_v,W_o,W_{gate},W_{up},W_{down} \) at every layer; \( \text{DiReFT}_P \) edits the residual stream after every block (post-MLP). Generated tokens reach the adapter only through the keys and values cached at prompt positions.
methods.structure: A position mask placed on an existing adapter. Writing an adapter as \( \langle\Phi_\phi,\mathcal F,\mathcal P\rangle \) (intervention, target modules, target positions), PreFT keeps \( \Phi_\phi \) and \( \mathcal F \) and shrinks \( \mathcal P=\{1,\dots,\ell+T\} \) to \( \mathcal P=\{1,\dots,\ell\} \). For \( \text{LoRA}_P \) the per-token update is the rank-\( r \) matrix \( m_i\tfrac{\alpha}{r}BA \), so the effective weight depends on the token: \( W_0+\tfrac{\alpha}{r}BA \) on prompt tokens and \( W_0 \) on generated tokens. For \( \text{DiReFT}_P \) the per-token update is a rank-\( r \) affine edit \( s_rW_2^{\top}(W_1h+b) \) of the residual stream at prompt positions. Attention is causal, so the whole effect on token \( i>\ell \) is carried by the adapted \( (K,V) \) entries of positions \( \le\ell \) at every layer. No KV entries are added, unlike prefix or KV-cache tuning.
methods.mergeable_reason: The update is gated by position, so no single matrix \( W' \) reproduces it: prompt tokens need \( W_0+\tfrac{\alpha}{r}BA \) and generated tokens need \( W_0 \). A single-adapter deployment could prefill with a merged copy and decode with \( W_0 \), but that doubles weight memory and defeats multi-adapter batching. The design goal is that decode runs the bare base model, so no adapter weights are touched at decode.
methods.identity_at_init: Yes. \( \text{LoRA}_P \) keeps LoRA's init (Kaiming-uniform \( A \), \( B=0 \), scaling \( \alpha/r \)). \( \text{DiReFT}_P \) uses the paper's zero-delta init \( W_1=0 \), \( b=0 \), \( W_2 \) with orthonormal rows (App. C.1 and the released preft/adapters/direft.py), so \( \Phi(h)=h \) at step 0. App. A.2 states the roles the other way round (orthonormal down-projection, zero up-projection and bias); either assignment gives a zero delta at init.
methods.key_idea: Multi-adapter serving is throughput-bound at decode, where each request's adapter matmul is memory-bound, so PreFT applies the adapter only to the \( \ell \) prompt tokens processed at prefill and runs every decode step on the frozen base model. The adapter steers generation only through the KV cache it shaped during prefill, and the method optimises accuracy per unit of serving throughput rather than per parameter.
methods.results_note: Serving 512 adapters on Llama 3.1 70B (4 H100s, Punica workload, vLLM fork), prefill-only DiReFT reaches 1.9x and prefill-only LoRA 1.87x the throughput of all-position multi-LoRA, while on RLVR (GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval) prefill-only adapters trail all-position ones by a mean of about 2 points.

relations.note: \( \text{LoRA}_P \) is LoRA with its parametrisation and init unchanged, restricted to prompt positions

\( \text{DiReFT}_P \) is ReFT's DiReFT variant applied to all prompt positions (ReFT uses a few prefix/suffix positions), with a new zero-delta init and a \( 1/\sqrt r \) prefactor for learning-rate transfer across ranks

mirror-image position masks on the same LoRA update: aLoRA is off for the prompt and on from the invocation sequence onward (to reuse the base model's prompt KV cache), PreFT is on for the prompt and off for generation (to drop adapter cost at decode); PreFT cites aLoRA as prior position-masked LoRA

S-LoRA amortises per-request adapter cost with batched gather kernels and CPU-GPU paging; PreFT removes the adapter cost at decode instead, reuses S-LoRA-style paging (as implemented in vLLM) for multi-ReFT serving, and states that it composes with such paging and kernels at prefill
throughput is benchmarked on the Punica workload against vLLM's Punica-style multi-LoRA kernels

both adapt a model through the KV cache seen at decode; Cartridges adds trained KV entries (extra attention work at every decode step), PreFT adds none and only reshapes the prompt's own cache; the paper calls KV-cache methods complementary and does not benchmark them
soft prompts also act at decode only through extra KV entries; the paper expects their throughput to fall between PEFTs and PreFTs but does not benchmark them

corrections: s-lora relation: type changed from competes-with to combines. The paper says PreFT 'composes naturally' with S-LoRA/Punica-style paging and kernels at prefill and replicates vLLM's S-LoRA-derived paging for multi-ReFT (Sec. 4.1).

full_name, locus, structure, identity_at_init and relation notes: wrapped the subscripted names LoRA_P / DiReFT_P and 1/sqrt(r) in \( \).

methods.name: OrthoMerge
methods.paper_title: Orthogonal Model Merging
methods.formula_latex: \text{OFT experts: } W_i=W_0R_i^{\top},\ R_i=(I+Q_i)(I-Q_i)^{-1},\ Q_i^{\top}=-Q_i;\ \ \text{other experts: } R_i^{\top}=U_iV_i^{\top},\ U_i\Sigma_iV_i^{\top}=\mathrm{SVD}\big(W_0^{\top}W_i^{\mathrm{tgt}}\big)\ \big(\text{Procrustes } \min_{R^{\top}R=I}\|W_i^{\mathrm{tgt}}-W_0R^{\top}\|_F\big),\ Q_i=(R_i-I)(R_i+I)^{-1};\ \ Q_m=\frac{\sum_i\|Q_i\|_F}{\|\sum_iQ_i\|_F}\cdot\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}Q_i,\ \ R_m=(I+Q_m)(I-Q_m)^{-1};\ \ W_m=W_0R_m^{\top}+\mathrm{EuclidMerge}\big(\{\rho_i\}\big),\ \rho_i=W_i-W_0R_i^{\top}\ (\rho_i=0\ \text{for OFT experts});\ \ W_i^{\mathrm{tgt}}\in\{W_i,\ W_0+\tau_i^{\mathrm{conf}}\};\ \text{training-free, all weights frozen}
methods.trainable_params: 0\ (\text{training-free});\ \text{merge state per matrix: } N \text{ generators } Q_i\in\mathfrak{so}(d_{in})\ (\text{block-diagonal for OFT experts}) \text{ and, for non-OFT experts, residuals } \rho_i\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times d_{in}}
methods.locus: Weights of every linear layer of the merged experts: the input-side rotation of OFT-adapted layers, or, through orthogonal-residual decoupling, every layer of LoRA or fully fine-tuned experts (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-3B, Llama-3.2-3B MergeBench experts, Qwen2.5-VL-7B). Post hoc, no training.
methods.structure: Merging in the Cayley chart of the orthogonal group. Each expert contributes a rotation \( R_i\in O(d_{in}) \), read off an OFT checkpoint or obtained by orthogonal Procrustes from \( W_0 \) to a target weight. The inverse Cayley map sends it to a skew-symmetric generator \( Q_i\in\mathfrak{so}(d_{in}) \); the generators are averaged linearly and rescaled by \( c=\sum_i\|Q_i\|_F/\|\sum_iQ_i\|_F\ge1 \) to undo norm loss from cancellation, then mapped back by the Cayley map. The merged multiplicative factor is exactly orthogonal, so \( W_0R_m^{\top} \) keeps the singular values of \( W_0 \) (hence its spectral norm and hyperspherical energy) for any number of experts. For non-OFT experts each weight is split as \( W_i=W_0R_i^{\top}+\rho_i \) (orthogonal plus residual), and the residuals are merged by a Euclidean rule (TA, TIES or TSV-M). The Procrustes target is \( W_i \) (OrthoMerge-G) or \( W_0+\tau_i^{\mathrm{conf}} \), where \( \tau_i^{\mathrm{conf}} \) keeps only the output-neuron rows of \( \tau_i=W_i-W_0 \) whose cosine with the mean task vector is negative (OrthoMerge-C). The Cayley chart covers only orthogonal matrices without eigenvalue \( -1 \), so a reflection returned by Procrustes would fall outside it; the paper does not discuss this case.
methods.mergeable_reason: The output is an ordinary weight matrix \( W_m=W_0R_m^{\top}+\rho_m \) in the base architecture (the merged OFT rotation can be multiplied into \( W_0 \)), so the merged model has no inference overhead.
methods.identity_at_init: Not applicable (training-free merge). Trivially consistent: if every expert equals \( W_0 \) then \( Q_i=0 \), \( R_m=I \), \( \rho_i=0 \) and \( W_m=W_0 \) (taking \( c=1 \) when \( \sum_iQ_i=0 \)).
methods.key_idea: Average OFT rotations in their Lie algebra rather than in weight space: map each \( R_i \) to \( Q_i\in\mathfrak{so}(d_{in}) \) with the inverse Cayley transform, average with a norm-restoring factor, and map back, so the merge stays on \( O(d_{in}) \) and preserves the spectrum of \( W_0 \). An orthogonal-plus-residual split by Procrustes extends the rule to LoRA and fully fine-tuned experts.
methods.results_note: Merging five OFT-finetuned Llama-3.1-8B experts (math, code, ScienceQA, CommonsenseQA, Social-IQA), OrthoMerge reaches 46.25% average task accuracy, above the experts' own 44.71% and every Euclidean baseline (TA, TIES, DARE, TSV-M), with the best out-of-domain average (41.80% on M-ARC and AGIEval).

relations.note: merges OFT's Cayley-parameterised rotations through their skew-symmetric generators; the merged factor is again an OFT-type rotation of \( W_0 \)
task arithmetic is the default Euclidean rule for the residuals \( \rho_i \) after orthogonal-residual decoupling
TIES can be used as the residual-merging rule; TIES+OrthoMerge-C is best on the VLM merge

TSV-M can be used as the residual-merging rule; TSV-M+OrthoMerge-C gives the best task average (42.07%) on the Llama-3.2-3B MergeBench merge and TSV-M+OrthoMerge-G the best IFEval retention among TSV variants on the VLM merge; also a Euclidean baseline
Euclidean merging baseline applied in weight space to both LoRA and OFT experts

corrections: tsv-merge relation note: the best Llama-3.2-3B MergeBench result is TSV-M+OrthoMerge-C (42.07%, Sec. 5.2.2), not only the -G variant; the note now names both.
oft and task-arithmetic relation notes: wrapped W_0 and rho_i in \( \).
methods.verification_notes: arXiv 2602.05943 v1 2026-02-05, first author Sihan Yang; arXiv API confirms. ICML 2026 'Accept (regular)' poster 61531 (OpenReview pCaeMsqpCa); arXiv comment still says 'Technical report'. Formula converted from the paper's W = R W_0 with W_0 in R^{d_in x d_out}: transposing gives W = W_0 R^T in catalogue notation, and SVD(W_ft W_0^T) in the paper becomes R^T = U V^T with U Sigma V^T = SVD(W_0^T W^tgt) (checked by transposing the SVD). Magnitude correction c (Eq. 7-8), Cayley and inverse Cayley maps (Eqs. 2, 5), residual rho_i = W_i - R_i W_0 (Eq. 13) and conflict-aware target (Eq. 10-11, columns in the paper = output-neuron rows here) all match. The Cayley-chart caveat holds: Procrustes can return det = -1, which forces an eigenvalue -1 and makes R + I singular. Training-free, so trainable_params = 0 is correct. Code repo exists. methods.name: PRISM
methods.full_name: Projected Riemannian Invariant Subspace Mechanism (gauge-invariant tangent-space DP-LoRA)
methods.paper_title: PRISM: Gauge-Invariant Tangent-Space Differentially Private LoRA
methods.formula_latex: W=W_0+BA,\ B\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r},\ A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}};\ \ \mathcal{P}_{B,A}(G)=G-(I-\Pi_B)\,G\,(I-\Pi_A),\ \ \Pi_B=B(B^{\top}B)^{\dagger}B^{\top},\ \Pi_A=A^{\top}(AA^{\top})^{\dagger}A;\ \ \widehat{\Delta Z}=\frac{1}{b}\sum_{i=1}^{b}\min\!\Big(1,\frac{C}{s_i}\Big)\mathcal{P}_{B,A}(G_i)+\frac{\sigma C}{b}\,\mathcal{P}_{B,A}(\Xi),\ \ G_i=\nabla_{\Delta W}\ell_i,\ s_i=\Big(\sum_{\text{modules}}\|\mathcal{P}_{B,A}(G_i)\|_F^2\Big)^{1/2},\ \Xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d_{out}\times d_{in}});\ \ BA\leftarrow\mathrm{Retr}_r\big(BA-\eta\,\mathcal{A}(\widehat{\Delta Z})\big),\ \mathrm{Retr}_r=\text{truncated rank-}r\text{ SVD},\ \mathcal{A}=\text{Adam-style first moments of the noisy factor lifts, preconditioned by }(V+\lambda I_r)^{-1/2}\text{ from }r\times r\text{ second moments, with DP-aware floors }\lambda;\ \ W_0\ \text{frozen},\ (A,B)\ \text{trained}
methods.trainable_params: r(d_{in}+d_{out})\ \text{per adapted matrix (as LoRA)};\ \text{optimizer state: first moments of size } r(d_{in}+d_{out}) \text{ and two } r\times r \text{ second-moment matrices per module}
methods.locus: Any LoRA-adapted linear layer (experiments: \( W_q,W_k,W_v,W_{up},W_{down} \) of Gemma-3-4B-pt, Gemma-2-9B, Gemma-3-12B-pt). The method changes how per-example gradients are clipped and noised and how the factors are updated, not the adapter shape.
methods.structure: Plain LoRA on the fixed-rank manifold \( \mathcal M_r \), with DP-SGD moved from the factors to the base of the gauge bundle \( (B,A)\mapsto BA \), whose fibres are the orbits \( (B,A)\sim(BR,R^{-1}A) \), \( R\in GL(r) \). Per-example gradients are projected onto the tangent space \( T_{BA}\mathcal M_r=\{\delta B\,A+B\,\delta A\} \) (dimension \( r(d_{in}+d_{out}-r) \)) by \( \mathcal P_{B,A} \), which depends only on \( \mathrm{col}(B) \) and \( \mathrm{row}(A) \) and is therefore gauge invariant. The projection is lifted to the factors canonically as \( \Delta B=g_B(AA^{\top})^{\dagger}-\tfrac12\Pi_Bg_B(AA^{\top})^{\dagger} \), \( \Delta A=(B^{\top}B)^{\dagger}g_A-\tfrac12(B^{\top}B)^{\dagger}g_A\Pi_A \) with \( g_B=GA^{\top} \), \( g_A=B^{\top}G \), so that \( \Delta B\,A+B\,\Delta A=\mathcal P_{B,A}(G) \). Clipping uses the intrinsic Frobenius norm summed over all modules. The noise is the tangent projection of an isotropic Gaussian, sampled through factor lifts \( \Xi_B=(I-\Pi_B)\Omega_B(AA^{\top})^{-1/2} \), \( \Xi_A=(B^{\top}B)^{-1/2}\Omega_A^{\top} \); it is isotropic on \( T_{BA}\mathcal M_r \) with \( \mathbb E\|\mathcal P(\Xi)\|_F^2=r(d_{in}+d_{out}-r) \), independent of \( \|A\|_F,\|B\|_F \). The noisy step is post-processed by right/left rank-space preconditioners \( (V+\lambda I_r)^{-1/2} \) built from \( r\times r \) second moments, with floors \( \lambda\asymp(\sigma C/b)^2\,\mathrm{tr}(\cdot^{-1})/r \), and then retracted to rank \( r \) by truncated SVD. Because the step is additive in the tangent space, the bilinear noise term \( \eta^2\xi_B\xi_A \) of factor-space DP never appears, and the retraction error is \( O(\eta^2) \).
methods.mergeable_reason: The released adapter is an ordinary low-rank product and merges like LoRA; privacy follows from post-processing. Because the official code trains on a spectrally re-based base \( W_{res}=W_0-U_r\Sigma_rV_r^{\top} \), it saves the adapter re-expressed against the original \( W_0 \) as the rank-\( 2r \) pair \( [B,\,B_0]\,[A;\,-A_0] \) (PiSSA-style conversion in spectral_rebase_adapter_inplace), which merges into \( W_0 \) the same way.
methods.identity_at_init: The paper does not state an init. The tangent projectors and noise sampler need full-column-rank \( B \) and full-row-rank \( A \), which rules out LoRA's \( B=0 \). The official code uses a PiSSA-style spectral residual init, \( W_0\leftarrow W_0-U_r\Sigma_rV_r^{\top} \), \( B=U_r(\Sigma_r/s)^{1/2} \), \( A=(\Sigma_r/s)^{1/2}V_r^{\top} \) with LoRA scale \( s \), so \( W_{res}+sBA \) equals the original \( W_0 \) at step 0 (function-preserving with non-degenerate factors).
methods.key_idea: LoRA factors are defined only up to \( (B,A)\mapsto(BR,R^{-1}A) \), so DP-SGD on the factors clips and noises a gauge-dependent quantity and injects a bilinear \( \eta^2\xi_B\xi_A \) term whose energy can be made arbitrarily large without changing \( BA \). PRISM clips and noises the projection of per-example gradients onto the tangent space of the rank-\( r \) manifold at \( BA \), which gives gauge-invariant updates with closed-form intrinsic noise \( \tfrac{\sigma C}{b}\sqrt{r(d_{in}+d_{out}-r)} \).
methods.results_note: On GLUE8 and Math-10K with Gemma-3-4B-pt, PRISM has the best average utility under DP (0.690 at epsilon=6 and 0.680 at epsilon=3, delta=1e-5) against FFA-LoRA, LoRA-RITE, AdamW, LoRA+ and LAMB, while LoRA-RITE is best without DP.

relations.note: same adapter; only the private optimisation of the factors changes
FFA-LoRA freezes \( A \) so DP noise enters as \( \xi_BA_0 \) with no bilinear term, but its size still depends on the frozen factor's norm; PRISM removes that dependence; DP baseline

LoRA-RITE makes a deterministic optimizer transformation-invariant; PRISM argues this does not make the randomized clip-and-noise step invariant and extends invariance to it, while also using \( r\times r \) rank-space second moments; baseline (best without DP)

structural kinship, not cited: PRISM's canonical lift starts from the scaled gradients \( g_B(AA^{\top})^{\dagger} \) and \( (B^{\top}B)^{\dagger}g_A \) of Riemannian-preconditioned LoRA and subtracts half the overlap term; both rest on the quotient geometry of fixed-rank matrices (PRISM cites Mishra et al. 2014, not Zhang and Pilanci)
optimizer baseline under DP

corrections: mergeable_reason: added that the official code saves the adapter re-based to the original W_0 as a rank-2r pair [B, B_0][A; -A_0] (src/prism_cli/trainers.py, _rebase_prism_for_save -> spectral_rebase_adapter_inplace), because training runs on the spectral residual base; mergeability is unchanged.

formula_latex: spelled out the adaptive post-processing (Eqs. 24-26: first moments of the noisy lifts, right/left (V + lambda I)^{-1/2} with r x r second moments, DP-aware floors) instead of an opaque operator name.
relation notes (ffa-lora, lora-rite, riemannian-preconditioned-lora): wrapped math in \( \).
methods.verification_notes: arXiv 2606.00944 v1 2026-05-31, authors Shihao Wang and Xueru Zhang; arXiv API confirms. ICML 2026 'Accept (spotlight)' with both a poster (63899) and an oral event (71157), OpenReview SiCjKmArjQ. Conversion from the paper's Z = A B^T (A in R^{m x r}, B in R^{n x r}) checked symbol by symbol: Pi_A, Pi_B swap roles, g_A = G B and g_B = G^T A become g_B = G A^T and g_A = B^T G, M = A^T A and N = B^T B become B^T B and A A^T, and the lift (Eq. 14) and noise sampler (Eq. 19) map to the entry's expressions. Verified algebraically that Delta B A + B Delta A = G Pi_A + Pi_B G - Pi_B G Pi_A = P(G), and that the sampled noise has the law of P(Xi) (independent projections onto col(B) and onto col(B)^perp x row(A)). E||P(Xi)||^2 = r(m+n-r) (Thm. 3.1), retraction error <= eta^2 ||Delta A Delta B^T|| (Prop. 3.2), floors (Eq. 26) match. Target modules q,k,v,up,down (App. table). The paper states no init; the code's spectral_init_peft_model matches identity_at_init (randomized SVD, W_res + s B A = W_0). Results match Table 2 (0.690 / 0.680 under DP; LoRA-RITE 0.782 best non-DP). trainable_params re-derived (same as LoRA; optimizer state r(d_in+d_out) first moments + two r x r matrices). Not in HF PEFT (optimizers/ has lorafa, loraplus, riemannian only).

methods.name: KeepLoRA
methods.full_name: KeepLoRA: residual-subspace gradient adaptation for continual learning
methods.paper_title: KeepLoRA: Continual Learning with Residual Gradient Adaptation
methods.formula_latex: W_0=U_0\Sigma_0V_0^{\top},\ P_W=V_{0,[:,1:p]}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{in}\times p}\ \big(\text{smallest }p\text{ with }\|\Sigma_{0,[1:p]}\|_F^2\ge\epsilon_w\|W_0\|_F^2\big);\ \ \hat G_t=G_t\big(I-P_WP_W^{\top}-M_{t-1}M_{t-1}^{\top}\big),\ G_t=\nabla_W\mathcal{L}(W;\mathcal{D}^t)\ \text{at the first step};\ \ \hat G_t=USV^{\top}:\ A_t=V_{[:,1:r]}^{\top}\ (\text{frozen}),\ B_t^{(0)}=U_{[:,1:r]}S_{[1:r]};\ \ W=W'+\tfrac{\alpha}{r}B_tA_t,\ W'=W-\tfrac{\alpha}{r}B_t^{(0)}A_t\ \text{frozen},\ B_t\ \text{trained}\ \Rightarrow\ \Delta W=-\tfrac{\eta\alpha^2}{r^2}\,G\,A_t^{\top}A_t;\ \ \text{after task }t:\ W\leftarrow W'+\tfrac{\alpha}{r}B_tA_t,\ M_t=[M_{t-1},\ \text{top-}m\ \text{directions in }\mathbb{R}^{d_{in}}\text{ of }(I-P_WP_W^{\top}-M_{t-1}M_{t-1}^{\top})X_t]\ (m\text{ set by energy threshold }\epsilon_f)
methods.trainable_params: r\,d_{out}\ \text{per adapted matrix per task (only }B_t\text{; }A_t\text{ frozen)}
methods.locus: Linear (attention) weight matrices of CLIP ViT-B/16 image and text encoders and of LLaVA's language model; the constraint acts on the input side \( \mathbb R^{d_{in}} \) of each adapted matrix.
methods.structure: Per task, a LoRA with frozen down-projection \( A_t \) whose rows span a subspace of the residual space \( \{P_W,M_{t-1}\}^{\perp}\subset\mathbb R^{d_{in}} \). \( P_W \) holds the principal input-side singular vectors of the pre-trained weight (general knowledge) and \( M_{t-1} \) the dominant input-feature directions of past tasks. \( A_t \) is the top-\( r \) right singular subspace of the first-step gradient after projecting out \( [P_W,M_{t-1}] \), and \( B_t \) starts at \( U_{[:,1:r]}S_{[1:r]} \) with \( W'=W-\tfrac{\alpha}{r}B_t^{(0)}A_t \) absorbing the offset. Training only \( B_t \) makes every step a projected gradient step \( \Delta W\propto-GA_t^{\top}A_t \) (Prop. 3.1), so \( \Delta W\,[P_W,M_{t-1}]=0 \): outputs on old-task feature directions and on the principal input subspace of the pre-trained weight are untouched. After each task the adapter is merged and \( M \) grows, with \( p+k\le d_{in} \) bounding the stored memory. KeepLoRA+ adds trainable class prototypes for CLIP classification.
methods.mergeable_reason: Each task's \( \tfrac{\alpha}{r}B_tA_t \) is merged into \( W \) after training (Algorithm 1), so inference uses a single dense matrix with no task identity and no extra modules (KeepLoRA+ keeps its class prototypes).
methods.identity_at_init: Yes, by re-basing: \( B_t^{(0)}A_t\ne0 \), but the frozen weight is replaced by \( W'=W-\tfrac{\alpha}{r}B_t^{(0)}A_t \), so \( W'+\tfrac{\alpha}{r}B_t^{(0)}A_t=W \) at the start of every task.
methods.key_idea: General knowledge sits in the principal singular subspace of the pre-trained weights and task knowledge in the residual subspace, so KeepLoRA initialises each task's LoRA from the SVD of the first-step gradient projected away from both that principal subspace and past-task feature directions, then freezes \( A_t \). Training only \( B_t \) turns every update into gradient descent confined to the residual subspace, which balances retention of pre-trained knowledge, retention of past tasks and plasticity.
methods.results_note: On the MTIL benchmark with CLIP ViT-B/16 (order I, no extra architecture), KeepLoRA reaches Transfer/Average/Last of 69.0/77.5/86.1 versus 67.4/76.3/85.2 for InfLoRA and 67.1/72.5/79.2 for SD-LoRA.

methods.name: LoRA-Pre
methods.full_name: LoRA-Pre: low-rank online-linear-regression compression of optimizer momenta
methods.paper_title: Taming Momentum: Rethinking Optimizer States Through Low-Rank Approximation
methods.formula_latex: G_t=\nabla_W\mathcal{L}(W_{t-1})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times d_{in}};\ \ m\approx m_Bm_A,\ m_B\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r},\ m_A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}}:\ \ m_B\leftarrow(1-\gamma_1)m_B+\gamma_1G_tm_A^{\top}(m_Am_A^{\top})^{-1},\ \ m_A\leftarrow(1-\gamma_1)m_A+\gamma_1(m_B^{\top}m_B)^{-1}m_B^{\top}G_t,\ \ 1-\gamma_1=\sqrt{\beta_1}\ (\text{both factors updated simultaneously from their previous values; App. C damps the inverses as }(m_Am_A^{\top}+\lambda_{d}I)^{-1},\ (m_B^{\top}m_B+\lambda_{d}I)^{-1},\ \lambda_{d}>0);\ \ v\approx(v_Bv_A)^{\circ2}\ \text{updated the same way with }|G_t|\ \text{in place of }G_t,\ 1-\gamma_2=\beta_2^{1/4};\ \ M_t=\beta_1m_Bm_A+(1-\beta_1)G_t,\ V_t=\beta_2(v_Bv_A)^{\circ2}+(1-\beta_2)G_t^{\circ2},\ \ W_t=W_{t-1}-\gamma\Big(\frac{\hat M_t}{\sqrt{\hat V_t+\epsilon}}+\lambda W_{t-1}\Big);\ \ \text{Muon variant: } O_t=\mathrm{NS}_5\big(\mu\,m_Bm_A+G_t\big)\ (\text{factor steps use }\tfrac{\gamma_1}{1-\mu}G_t\text{ in place of }\gamma_1G_t,\ 1-\gamma_1=\sqrt{\mu}),\ W_t=W_{t-1}-\gamma(O_t+\lambda W_{t-1});\ \ \text{all of }W\text{ trained, only the momenta are factored}
methods.trainable_params: d_{out}d_{in}\ \text{per matrix (full-parameter training)};\ \text{optimizer state } 2r(d_{in}+d_{out})\ \text{(Adam) or } r(d_{in}+d_{out})\ \text{(Muon) instead of } 2d_{out}d_{in}\ \text{or } d_{out}d_{in}
methods.locus: Optimizer states of all attention and MLP weight matrices (other parameters use standard Adam): Llama pre-training from 60M to 1B parameters on C4, and full fine-tuning of Llama-2-7B and Llama-3.1-8B on MetaMath100k.
methods.structure: No adapter: the weight step is the usual full-rank Adam (or Muon) step, but the EMA momenta are stored as rank-\( r \) factors. The EMA update \( m\leftarrow\beta m+(1-\beta)g \) is one gradient step with learning rate \( 1-\beta \) on \( \tfrac12\|m-g\|_F^2 \), so momentum is the weight of an online linear regressor. LoRA-Pre replaces \( m \) by \( m_Bm_A \) and takes one exact Newton step per factor on \( \tfrac12\|m_Bm_A-g\|_F^2 \) (Hessians \( m_Am_A^{\top}\otimes I \) and \( I\otimes m_B^{\top}m_B \)). The result is a simultaneous (Jacobi-style) EMA of each factor toward the least-squares fit of the new gradient given the other factor's previous value, with \( 1-\gamma_1=\sqrt{\beta_1} \) so that the product decays at Adam's rate \( \beta_1 \). The second moment stays positive through the Hadamard-square parametrisation \( v=(v_Bv_A)^{\circ2} \), with \( v_Bv_A \) regressed onto \( |g| \). For Muon the regression target is \( \tfrac12\|m-g\|_F^2-\tfrac{\mu}{1-\mu}\langle m,g\rangle \). Since the Adam ratio \( \hat M_t/\sqrt{\hat V_t} \) is elementwise, the weight update is full-rank even though the state is rank-\( r \). LoRA's update is rank-\( r \), and GaLore's step lies in a rank-\( r \) projected subspace. Adafactor's rank-1 factored second moment is an earlier instance of factoring optimizer state.
methods.mergeable_reason: There is no auxiliary module: updates are written straight into W, so the result is an ordinary dense checkpoint with the original architecture and unchanged inference cost.
methods.identity_at_init: Trivial: no reparametrisation, training starts at \( W_0 \) (random init for pre-training). The factored states start at \( m_B=v_B=0 \), \( m_A,v_A\sim\mathcal N(0,0.02) \), so the reconstructed momenta start at 0 as in Adam. Theorem 3.1 assumes full-rank factors and Algorithm 1 writes plain inverses, which are singular at the first step because \( m_{B,0}=0 \). Appendix C.1 defines the update with Tikhonov-damped pseudo-inverses \( (m_B^{\top}m_B+\lambda_d I)^{-1}m_B^{\top} \) and \( m_A^{\top}(m_Am_A^{\top}+\lambda_d I)^{-1} \), \( \lambda_d>0 \), which are well defined at \( m_B=0 \); the value of \( \lambda_d \) used in experiments is not reported and the code is not released.
methods.key_idea: An EMA momentum update is one step of online gradient descent on \( \tfrac12\|m-g\|_F^2 \), so momentum is an online linear regressor and can be compressed like any model. LoRA-Pre factors \( m \) (and \( v=(v_Bv_A)^{\circ2} \)) into rank-\( r \) matrices updated by closed-form Newton steps, which cuts optimizer memory for Adam and Muon in both pre-training and fine-tuning.
methods.results_note: Pre-training Llama-1B on C4 at rank 512, LoRA-Pre Adam reaches 13.53 validation perplexity versus 15.64 for GaLore and 15.56 for full-state Adam, and fine-tuning on MetaMath100k at rank 8 it beats LoRA by 3.14 points on Llama-3.1-8B and 6.17 points on Llama-2-7B (GSM8K/MATH-500 average).

methods.name: StructLoRA
methods.full_name: StructLoRA: information-bottleneck direction filtering with graph-based layer coordination
methods.paper_title: Not All Directions Matter: Towards Structured and Task-Aware Low-Rank Model Adaptation
methods.formula_latex: \Delta\tilde W_l=\tfrac{\alpha}{r}B_l\,\mathrm{diag}(m_l)\,A_l,\ \ m_l\in[0,1]^{r}\ (\text{IB gate: variational-IB KL penalty; paper: Gumbel-Softmax relaxation with a Gaussian or Bernoulli/Beta choice; code: Bernoulli logits, Gumbel-sigmoid relaxation, KL to a Bernoulli prior});\ \ u_l^{(0)}=\mathrm{vec}(\Delta\tilde W_l),\ \ u_l^{(t+1)}=u_l^{(t)}+\sigma\Big(\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}(l)\cup\{l\}}\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{d_ld_j}}\,u_j^{(t)}\Theta^{(t)}\Big),\ \ \Delta\tilde W_l^{\mathrm{final}}=\mathrm{reshape}\big(W_ou_l^{(T)}\big);\ \ \min\ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{task}}\big(f(X;W_0+\Delta\tilde W^{\mathrm{final}})\big)+\lambda_{\mathrm{IB}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{IB}}(m);\ \ W_0\ \text{frozen};\ A_l,B_l,m_l,\Theta,W_o\ \text{trained};\ \text{gate and GNN discarded after the final update is merged}
methods.trainable_params: r(d_{in}+d_{out})+r\ \text{per adapted matrix, plus a shared training-only coordinator } (\Theta^{(t)},W_o)\ \text{(stated as}<0.05\%\ \text{of model parameters)}
methods.locus: \( W_q \) and \( W_v \) of every Transformer layer (LLaMA-7B/13B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, ViT-B/16, LLaVA-1.5-7B; RoBERTa-base on GLUE). The coordinator acts across depth on the stack of per-layer updates.
methods.structure: LoRA with a learned diagonal gate between the factors, \( B\,\mathrm{diag}(m)\,A \): a sparsifying selector over the \( r \) rank-one directions, like SoRA's gate but trained with a variational-IB KL to a Bernoulli prior. A training-time map across layers is added on top: the vectorised filtered updates \( U=[u_1;\dots;u_L] \) pass through a shallow residual GCN on a depth graph (adjacent layers plus semantic edges between layers with highly aligned updates or gradients). To first order this is a Laplacian smoothing step \( U\leftarrow U-\eta(\mathbf L\otimes I)U \), which lowers the drift energy \( \sum_l\|u_{l+1}-u_l\|^2 \). Section 3.3 and the released code merge the coordinated \( \Delta\tilde W_l^{\mathrm{final}} \), which in general no longer has rank \( \le r \) because the GCN mixes and nonlinearly maps updates from several layers. Appendix E.7 says instead that the gated \( \Delta\tilde W \) is merged. The released code's coordinator is a dense linear encoder on \( \mathrm{vec}(\Delta\tilde W_l) \) of width \( d_{out}d_{in} \), which does not match the stated \( <0.05\% \) overhead at LLaMA scale.
methods.mergeable_reason: Whichever update is deployed, the gated \( \tfrac{\alpha}{r}B\,\mathrm{diag}(m)\,A \) (Appendix E.7) or the coordinator output \( \Delta\tilde W^{\mathrm{final}} \) (Sec. 3.3 and the code's merge_structlora), it is a fixed matrix added to \( W_0 \), so inference cost equals the base model's.
methods.identity_at_init: The gated LoRA path is the identity at init (\( B=0 \), Kaiming-uniform \( A \), gate logits 2.0 in the code). The coordinated update is not guaranteed to be: in the released code the coordinator returns \( u+\mathrm{dec}(\mathrm{enc}(u)) \) with default nn.Linear biases, so \( \Delta\tilde W^{\mathrm{final}}\ne0 \) at step 0 whenever it is active. The paper does not discuss this.
methods.key_idea: Not all \( r \) LoRA directions carry task signal, and layers adapted independently drift apart. StructLoRA gates the rank-one directions with an information-bottleneck filter and, during training only, smooths the per-layer updates across depth with a shallow GCN (a Laplacian smoother), then merges the result so inference costs the same as LoRA.
methods.results_note: On GLUE with RoBERTa-base, StructLoRA reports an 86.5 average, 0.5 points above Sensitivity-LoRA, the strongest dynamic-rank baseline.

methods.name: FedRot-LoRA
methods.full_name: Federated LoRA with rotational alignment of client factors
methods.paper_title: FedRot-LoRA: Mitigating Rotational Misalignment in Federated LoRA
methods.formula_latex: h=(W_0+\bar B^{t}\bar A^{t})x,\ \ \bar B^{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r},\ \bar A^{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}};\quad \text{client } i \text{ trains } (B_i^t,A_i^t) \text{ starting from } (\bar B^{t-1},\bar A^{t-1});\quad R_i^{t,*}=\arg\min_{R^\top R=I_r,\ \det R>0}\begin{cases}\|R^\top A_i^t-\bar A^{t-1}\|_F^2, & t\ \text{odd}\\ \|B_i^tR-\bar B^{t-1}\|_F^2, & t\ \text{even}\end{cases}\ \ (\text{orthogonal Procrustes, closed form via the SVD of an } r\times r \text{ correlation matrix});\quad R_{i,\mathrm{soft}}^t=\Pi_{SO(r)}\big((1-\lambda)I_r+\lambda R_i^{t,*}\big);\quad \tilde A_i^t=R_{i,\mathrm{soft}}^{t\top}A_i^t,\ \ \tilde B_i^t=B_i^tR_{i,\mathrm{soft}}^t\ \ (\tilde B_i^t\tilde A_i^t=B_i^tA_i^t);\quad \bar A^t=\tfrac1N\textstyle\sum_i\tilde A_i^t,\ \ \bar B^t=\tfrac1N\sum_i\tilde B_i^t;\ \ W_0\ \text{frozen},\ A,B\ \text{trained on clients},\ R\ \text{computed in closed form}
methods.trainable_params: r(d_{in}+d_{out})\ \text{per adapted matrix (per client; same communication as FedIT); } R_i^t\in SO(r)\ \text{is computed, not trained}
methods.locus: LoRA-adapted linear layers in federated fine-tuning (RoBERTa-Large on GLUE; Llama 3-8B on GSM8K and HumanEval), implemented in FederatedScope-LLM
methods.structure: Each client trains a rank-\(r\) LoRA \(\Delta W=BA\). The contribution is the aggregation map: before uploading, each client picks a representative of its factor pair's orbit under the \(SO(r)\) subgroup of the \(GL(r)\) gauge action \((B,A)\mapsto(BR,R^{-1}A)\). The representative is chosen by orthogonal Procrustes against last round's global factors, aligning \(A\) and \(B\) in alternate rounds. The server then averages factors, so the global adapter stays rank \(r\) and \(\bar B\bar A\) approximates \(\tfrac1N\sum_iB_iA_i\) up to the aggregation error \(E^t=\bar B\bar A-\tfrac1N\sum_iB_iA_i\).
methods.mergeable_reason: The global adapter \(\bar B^t\bar A^t\) is an ordinary rank-\(r\) LoRA product and folds into \(W_0\).
methods.identity_at_init: \(\Delta W_0=\bar B^0\bar A^0=0\) (Algorithm 1, line 2; the scalar example in Fig. 2 starts from \(\bar B^0=0\)), so training starts at \(W_0\). Each alignment preserves every client's update exactly, since \(\tilde B_i\tilde A_i=B_iRR^\top A_i=B_iA_i\).
methods.key_idea: Because \((BR)(R^\top A)=BA\) for every rotation \(R\), clients can reach equivalent but rotated factors, and averaging them gives a \(\bar B\bar A\) far from \(\tfrac1N\sum_iB_iA_i\). Fixing this gauge with a closed-form Procrustes rotation toward last round's global factors (softened by \(\lambda\); \(\lambda=0\) is plain FedIT averaging) shrinks the aggregation-error term in the nonconvex convergence bound. It costs \(O(dr^2+r^3)\) per client and adds no communication.
methods.results_note: On GLUE with RoBERTa-Large (\(r=4\), Dirichlet \(h=0.5\), \(N=50\) clients; Table 1), FedRot-LoRA averages 87.34% accuracy versus 82.44% for RoLoRA and 76.80% for FedIT.

relations.note: Plain LoRA factors on each client; only the aggregation changes.
With rotation strength \(\lambda=0\), FedRot-LoRA reduces to FedIT's naive factor-wise averaging (Section 3, after Eq. 6).

FFA-LoRA makes aggregation exact by freezing \(A\) (losing expressivity). FedRot keeps both factors trainable and instead reduces the error by aligning the rotation gauge. FFA-LoRA is a baseline in Table 1.
FLoRA stacks client factors for exact aggregation at rank \(Nr\) and higher communication. FedRot keeps rank \(r\) and communication unchanged (cited in related work; not a Table 1 baseline).

Structural analogue, not a baseline: KnOTS aligns several task LoRAs in a shared SVD basis before merging, FedRot aligns each client's factors to the previous global adapter by a Procrustes rotation before averaging. FedRot does not cite KnOTS.

Formula checked against Section 3 (Eqs. 3-6) and Algorithm 1 of arXiv v3: odd rounds align \(A\), even rounds align \(B\), reference is the previous global adapter, aggregation is uniform \(1/N\) averaging. Eq. 4, \(R^*=V\,\mathrm{diag}(1,\dots,\det(UV^\top))\,U^\top\) with \(M=A_{ref}A_i^\top=U\Sigma V^\top\), is the correct Procrustes solution. The soft-rotation projection reuses the same formula for \(R'=U\Sigma V^\top\), which gives the transpose of the nearest rotation; the released rotation_alignment_tools.py builds \(M=A_iA_{ref}^\top\), takes \(R=UV^\top\) and projects \(R'\) by \(U'V'^\top\), the nearest-rotation projection, so the entry's generic \(\Pi_{SO(r)}\) is right. methods.name: LoRA-RLPO / LoRA-RLMO
methods.full_name: Geometry-preserving orthonormal LoRA initialization for RLVR (principal / minor variants)
methods.paper_title: Geometry-Preserving Orthonormal Initialization for Low-Rank Adaptation in RLVR
methods.formula_latex: W_0=U\Sigma V^\top;\quad h=\big(W_0+\tfrac{\alpha}{r}BA\big)x,\quad B_0=0_{d_{out}\times r},\quad A_0=V_{[:,1:r]}^\top\ (\text{LoRA-RLPO, top-}r)\ \ \text{or}\ \ A_0=V_{[:,-r:]}^\top\ (\text{LoRA-RLMO, bottom-}r),\ \ A_0A_0^\top=I_r;\quad \max_{A,B}\ \mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_\theta}[R(x,y)]-\beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi_\theta\|\pi_{ref})\ \ (\text{general RLVR objective, Eq. 9; the main DAPO runs drop the explicit KL term; GRPO for Qwen2.5-7B});\ \ W_0\ \text{frozen and not modified (no residual)},\ A,B\ \text{trained};\quad \tfrac1T\|W_T^{LoRA}-W_T^{full}\|_F\le M\eta\,\Gamma_T(\eta)\,\|I_{d_{in}}-A_0^\top A_0\|_2+O(\eta^2),\ \ \|I_{d_{in}}-A_0^\top A_0\|_2=\max\big(1,\max_i|1-s_i(A_0)^2|\big)\ge1\ \text{for } r<d_{in},\ \text{with equality iff every singular value } s_i(A_0)\le\sqrt2\ (\text{in particular if } A_0A_0^\top=I_r)
methods.trainable_params: r(d_{in}+d_{out})\ \text{per adapted matrix (}r=16\text{ in the main experiments)}
methods.locus: all linear layers (attention and MLP projections). Main runs: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B with DAPO on DAPO-Math-17k (\(r=16\), \(\alpha=32\)). Appendix: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with GRPO (\(r=32\)), Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct on MBPP-style code generation, and an SFT check on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (GLUE CoLA and MRPC, GSM8K)
methods.structure: Plain rank-\(r\) LoRA \(\Delta W=\tfrac{\alpha}{r}BA\); only the starting point changes. \(A_0\) is the transpose of \(r\) right singular vectors of \(W_0\) (top \(r\) for RLPO, bottom \(r\) for RLMO), so it has orthonormal rows and no singular-value scaling, and \(B_0=0\). PiSSA and MiLoRA use \(B_0=U_r\Sigma_r^{1/2}\), \(A_0=\Sigma_r^{1/2}V_r^\top\) and a residual base \(W_0-B_0A_0\).
methods.mergeable_reason: After training, \(\tfrac{\alpha}{r}BA\) is an ordinary rank-\(r\) matrix added to the untouched \(W_0\).
methods.identity_at_init: Exact: \(B_0=0\) gives \(\Delta W=0\), and \(W_0\) is left untouched, unlike PiSSA, MiLoRA and OLoRA, which subtract \(B_0A_0\) from \(W_0\).
methods.key_idea: In RLVR with \(B_0=0\), Theorem 5.2 bounds the gap between LoRA and full fine-tuning after \(T\) steps by a term proportional to \(\|I-A_0^\top A_0\|_2\ge1\). A row-orthonormal \(A_0\) attains this minimum and also caps the first update at full fine-tuning's (\(\|\Delta W_1\|_F\le\eta\|G_0\|_F\), Proposition 5.3). The minimum is not unique: any \(A_0\) whose singular values are at most \(\sqrt2\) attains it, including, with high probability, the \(\mathcal N(0,1/n)\) LoRA baseline in Table 1, so the bound alone does not separate orthonormal from Gaussian \(A_0\). Taking \(A_0\) from \(W_0\)'s principal or minor right singular vectors keeps PiSSA's and MiLoRA's subspaces but drops their singular-value scaling, which inflates the first update by at least \(\sigma_r\) (Theorem 4.1), and their nonzero \(B_0\). The authors argue this scaling explains the KL blow-up and reward collapse of PiSSA and MiLoRA in RL.
methods.results_note: With DAPO on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (\(r=16\), cosine LR, Table 1), LoRA-RLPO averages 65.03% over GSM8K, MATH500 and AIME22-24, versus 63.76% for LoRA-RLMO, 62.40% for LoRA, 51.71% for MiLoRA and 4.57% for PiSSA.

relations.note: Keeps LoRA's \(B_0=0\) and replaces the Gaussian \(A_0\) with an orthonormal, SVD-derived one.

RLPO uses the same top-\(r\) singular subspace without \(\Sigma^{1/2}\) scaling, without a nonzero \(B_0\) and without a residual base; PiSSA collapses under RLVR in the paper's runs (4.57% average in Table 1).

RLMO is the minor-subspace counterpart with orthonormal \(A_0\) and \(B_0=0\); the paper attributes MiLoRA's RLVR instability to singular-value scaling, not to near-zero tail initialization (Appendix D.1).

The paper uses an 'OLoRA' control with \(B_0=U_r\), \(A_0=V_r^\top\) and a residual base (Eq. 7), and proves PiSSA's first update is at least \(\sigma_r\) times that control's (Theorem 4.1). Published OLoRA (and HF PEFT init_lora_weights='olora') instead uses the QR factors \(B_0=Q_{[:,1:r]}\), \(A_0=R_{[1:r,:]}\), so the control is an SVD-orthonormal variant, not OLoRA as published. RLPO goes further and sets \(B_0=0\).
Cites the asymmetry result that a fixed random orthonormal \(A\) works well, and gives an RLVR-specific reason to prefer an orthonormal \(A_0\).

Both target the minor singular subspace of \(W_0\). MiCA freezes \(B=U_{[:,-r:]}\) and zero-initializes \(A\); RLMO sets \(A_0=V_{[:,-r:]}^\top\), \(B_0=0\) and trains both factors. MiCA is not cited.

Gives a theoretical account of that benchmark's finding that PiSSA and MiLoRA underperform LoRA and become unstable under RLVR, and disputes its near-zero-initialization explanation for MiLoRA (Appendix D.1).

methods.name: NaRA
methods.paper_title: NaRA: Noise-Aware LoRA for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning of Diffusion LLMs
methods.formula_latex: h=W_0x+B\,C(\lambda)\,A\,x,\quad C(\lambda)=I_r+\eta\,\mathcal{F}_\phi(e_\lambda),\quad e_\lambda=\cos(2\pi k\lambda)\oplus\sin(2\pi k\lambda),\ k\in\mathbb{R}^{32},\ k\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2I)\ \text{fixed};\quad \lambda=m/L_s\in[0,1]\ (\text{fraction of masked response tokens});\quad \Delta W_{l,m}(\lambda)=B_{l,m}\,C(\lambda)\,A_{l,m},\ \ B_{l,m}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r},\ A_{l,m}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}};\ \ W_0\ \text{frozen};\ A,B\ (\text{per module})\ \text{and one globally shared MLP}\ \mathcal{F}_\phi:\mathbb{R}^{64}\to\mathbb{R}^{r\times r}\ \text{trained};\ \eta=0.1
methods.trainable_params: r(d_{in}+d_{out})\ \text{per adapted matrix} + |\phi|\ \text{once per model (shared MLP } 64\to256\to512\to r^2;\ \approx6.7\times10^{5}\ \text{for } r=32)
methods.locus: q, k, v, o attention projections of masked-diffusion LLMs (LLaDA-8B-Base and LLaDA-8B-Instruct); one image-diffusion experiment (SDXL, DreamBooth) in Section 6.6
methods.structure: \(\Delta W(\lambda)=BC(\lambda)A\). Static per-module factors \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r}\) and \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}}\) sandwich a dynamic \(r\times r\) core that is a smooth function of the scalar noise level \(\lambda\). One Fourier-feature MLP, shared by every adapted module, produces the core once per denoising step. The update therefore moves continuously along the denoising trajectory inside fixed rank-\(r\) column and row spaces.
methods.mergeable_reason: For a fixed \(\lambda\), \(W_0+BC(\lambda)A\) is a dense matrix. But \(\lambda\) changes at every denoising step (and can differ across sequences in a batch), so no single merged weight exists. The paper lists non-mergeability as a limitation (Appendix, Table 10); re-merging at every step is possible in principle (catalogue's inference, not the paper's).
methods.identity_at_init: \(B=0\) gives \(\Delta W(\lambda)=0\) for every \(\lambda\). The hypernetwork's last layer is zero-initialized, so \(C(\lambda)=I_r\) and the initial gradients equal LoRA's.
methods.key_idea: Masked-diffusion LLMs see very different inputs at different noise levels, so a static \(\Delta W\) helps mostly at mid noise. NaRA sandwiches a noise-conditioned core \(C(\lambda)=I_r+\eta\mathcal F_\phi(e_\lambda)\) between static LoRA factors, giving a continuous family \(\Delta W(\lambda)\). Theorem 4.1 shows this family can represent any finite set of updates whose combined column and row spaces have dimension \(\le r\); the extra parameters are under 0.01% of the model. Timestep-conditioned LoRAs already existed for image diffusion (TC-LoRA, TimeStep Master); NaRA is the first noise-aware PEFT for diffusion LLMs.
methods.results_note: On LLaDA-8B-Instruct commonsense reasoning (\(r=32\), Table 1), NaRA averages 84.09% versus 80.18% for LoRA and 82.73% for HiRA, with 0.425% versus 0.417% trainable parameters.

relations.note: \(\eta=0\) (so \(C=I_r\)) recovers LoRA exactly.

Structural comparison (MoSLoRA is not cited). A \(\lambda\)-independent hypernetwork output gives a static \(r\times r\) core between \(B\) and \(A\), but NaRA's core is shared by every adapted module, whereas MoSLoRA learns one mixer per module, so neither method contains the other. Only the module-specific hypernetwork ablation (Section 6.3) would contain MoSLoRA.
Strongest baseline on commonsense reasoning (82.73% vs NaRA's 84.09%, Table 1). On mathematical reasoning (Table 2) plain LoRA and P-Tuning beat HiRA.
Appendix M applies the same noise-conditioned core inside DoRA.

methods.name: LiME
methods.paper_title: LiME: Lightweight Mixture of Experts for Efficient Multimodal Multi-task Learning
methods.formula_latex: h=W_0x+\hat z\odot\mathcal{P}(x)+\gamma\,(\hat z\odot p_s),\quad \hat z=\delta_\phi(x)\ (\text{e.g. } \tfrac{\alpha}{r}BAx,\ r=2,\ \alpha=4),\quad \mathcal{P}(x)=\sum_{i\in S_\theta(x)}\tilde w_i(x)\,p_i,\ \ p_i\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}};\quad w(x)=\mathrm{softmax}\!\Big(\tfrac{(1-\gamma_r)\,z_{1:E}/\|z_{1:E}\|_\infty+\gamma_r\,\hat z_{1:E}/\|\hat z_{1:E}\|_\infty}{\tau}\Big),\ \ z=W_0x;\quad S_\theta(x)=\{i:w_i(x)\ge\theta\max_jw_j(x)\},\ \ \tilde w_i=w_i\big/\textstyle\sum_{j\in S_\theta}w_j;\ \ W_0\ \text{frozen};\ \phi,\{p_i\},p_s,\gamma\ \text{trained};\ \text{router has no parameters};\ \ \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{task}+\alpha\mathcal{L}_{imp}+\beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\bar p\,\|\,\mathcal{U});\ \ \text{defaults: } E=4,\ \gamma_r=0.7,\ \tau=0.5,\ \theta=0.7,\ n\text{-gram window }3
methods.trainable_params: |\phi|+E\,d_{out}+d_{out}+1\ \text{per adapted layer (LoRA: } |\phi|=r(d_{in}+d_{out})\text{), versus } E|\phi|\ \text{plus a } d\times E \text{ router for MoE-LoRA}
methods.locus: q, k, v, o attention projections in both the SigLIP vision encoder and the Qwen2 LLM of LLaVA-OneVision-Qwen2-7B (216 target layers; 0.5B model for ablations; also Molmo2-8B); wraps LoRA, DoRA, LoRA-FA, SliceFine (\(r=2\), \(\alpha=4\)) or prompt tuning (10 virtual tokens); \(E=4\) experts, n-gram routing window 3
methods.structure: The output \(\hat z\) of one shared PEFT module is rescaled element-wise by a convex combination of \(E\) expert vectors. A parameter-free softmax router chooses the combination from normalized slices of \(W_0x\) and \(\hat z\), with confidence-adaptive top-\(k\) and one decision per n-gram window. For LoRA this is \(\Delta W(x)=\mathrm{diag}(\mathcal P(x)+\gamma p_s)\,BA\): a token-dependent diagonal rescaling of the rows of one rank-\(r\) update.
methods.mergeable_reason: \(\mathcal P(x)\) depends on each token (or n-gram window) through the router, so \(\Delta W(x)=\mathrm{diag}(\mathcal P(x)+\gamma p_s)BA\) varies per token. Only with \(E=1\) does it collapse to a static, mergeable \(\mathrm{diag}(p_1+\gamma p_s)BA\).
methods.identity_at_init: With LoRA, the released code zero-initializes \(B\), so \(\hat z=0\) and \(h=W_0x\) exactly. Initialization is \(p_i\sim\mathcal U(0.9,1.1)\), \(p_s\sim\mathcal N(0,0.1^2)\), \(\gamma=0\), so LiME also starts close to the plain shared PEFT module.
methods.key_idea: MoE-PEFT methods normally keep \(E\) adapter copies plus a learned router. LiME keeps one PEFT module and lets \(E\) vectors \(p_i\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}}\) rescale its output, so expert cost becomes \(E\,d_{out}\) and works with any PEFT method. Routing logits come for free from the first \(E\) coordinates of the frozen output and the PEFT output. Theorem 2 states that the optimal-risk gap to expert-specific PEFT is \(O(\bar\varepsilon)\) if the modulation approximates it within \(\bar\varepsilon\); the approximation error itself is assumed, not bounded.
methods.results_note: On MMT-47 with LLaVA-OneVision-Qwen2-7B (Table 2), LiME-LoRA has the best commonsense-reasoning average (84.98%), with 3.49M trainable parameters versus 10.79M for MoELoRA. In the GLUE efficiency study (one epoch on one H100, about 894M total parameters), LiME-LoRA trains 0.52M parameters versus 1.97M for MoELoRA and runs 23% faster.

relations.note: Structural competitor: MOELoRA (2310.18339) replicates LoRA experts under a task-id gate. LiME does not cite it; LiME's 'MoELoRA' baseline is a different paper, Luo et al. 2024 (arXiv 2402.12851), which the catalogue does not list. Against that baseline LiME uses 3-4 times fewer trainable parameters.
HydraLoRA shares \(A\) and routes among several \(B\) heads. LiME shares the whole adapter and routes among diagonal output scalings. HydraLoRA is a Table 2 baseline.
MoE-PEFT baseline with replicated LoRA experts and a learned router.
Cited as an adapter-replicating MoE-PEFT design.
MoV already mixes routed (IA)\(^3\) scaling vectors with a learned router. LiME applies routed scaling vectors to a shared PEFT output and removes the router. LiME does not cite MoV.

methods.locus: all parameters (full-parameter zeroth-order fine-tuning); activation-guided perturbations on linear layers (attention and FFN projections), dense Gaussian perturbations elsewhere; Qwen3-0.6B/4B and openPangu-Embedded-1B, plus Qwen3-8B in the appendix
methods.structure: A randomized finite-difference (SPSA) gradient estimate with rank-\(r\) perturbations \(R_\ell U_\ell^\top\). Their row space is the top-\(r\) left singular subspace of the layer's current input activations. In expectation the estimate is \(\nabla_{W_\ell}F_{\mu,U}(W)\,U_\ell U_\ell^\top\): the gradient of a subspace-smoothed objective, projected onto the activation subspace.
methods.mergeable_reason: AGZO edits the model's own weights in place; there is no adapter to merge.
methods.identity_at_init: Trivial: there is no reparameterization, and training starts at \(W_0\).
methods.key_idea: A linear layer's gradient \(Q_\ell H_\ell^\top\) has its row space inside the span of the layer's input activations, and that span is spectrally concentrated. AGZO therefore perturbs only along \(R_\ell U_\ell^\top\), with \(U_\ell\) the top activation directions found by power iteration in the same forward pass. The expected cosine with the true gradient is \(\beta_{d_{out}r}\|GU\|_F/\|G\|_F\), versus \(\beta_{d_{out}d_{in}}\) for MeZO (Theorem 5.4, Corollary 5.5). Theorem 5.6 makes the gain strict when the activations are rank-deficient and the average upstream-gradient energy along the top-\(r\) activation directions is at least the average over all of them.
methods.results_note: On Qwen3-0.6B, AGZO beats MeZO and LOZO on most SuperGLUE-style tasks, e.g. CB 0.892 versus 0.803 (MeZO) and 0.760 (LOZO), against 0.946 for first-order fine-tuning, with almost the same peak memory as MeZO.

relations.note: With \(U_\ell=I\) (full activation space) the estimator has MeZO's dense Gaussian form (Corollary 5.5), up to AGZO's one-sided versus MeZO's two-sided finite difference.

Both confine updates to a data-derived low-rank subspace. GaLore uses the gradient's top singular vectors (first-order); AGZO uses the activations', which contain the gradient's row space (zeroth-order). AGZO does not cite GaLore.

Both use low-rank ZO perturbations. AGZO's subspace is activation-informed on the input side; ZO-Muon's is random on the output side and adds Muon-style orthogonalization. Neither paper cites the other.
The released code is built on the ZO-LLM benchmark codebase.

methods.name: ZO-Muon
methods.full_name: Zeroth-order Muon via subspace gradient orthogonalization
methods.paper_title: Powering Up Zeroth-Order Training via Subspace Gradient Orthogonalization
methods.formula_latex: \text{for each weight } W_\ell\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times d_{in}}:\ P_\ell\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r},\ P_\ell^\top P_\ell=I_r\ (\text{QR of a Gaussian, resampled every } v=100 \text{ steps});\quad \widehat G_{Z,\ell}=\frac{1}{N_q}\sum_{i=1}^{N_q}\frac{f(W+\mu P\Psi_i)-f(W)}{\mu}\,\Psi_{i,\ell},\ \ \Psi_{i,\ell}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{r\times d_{in}});\quad O_\ell=P_\ell\,\mathrm{msign}(\widehat G_{Z,\ell}),\ \ \mathrm{msign}(G)=(GG^\top)^{-1/2}G=U_kV_k^\top\ \text{for } G\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}}\ (\text{the paper's } G(G^\top G)^{-1/2} \text{ needs a pseudo-inverse here; computed by Newton--Schulz});\quad W_\ell\leftarrow W_\ell-\eta\,O_\ell;\ \ \text{first-order analogue } O=P\,\mathrm{msign}(P^\top\nabla_Wf),\ \text{equal to } \mathrm{msign}(\nabla_Wf) \text{ when } P \text{ spans the gradient's column space};\ \text{all weights trained, no backpropagation; 1-D parameters (biases, norms) use dense Gaussian RGE};\ N_q=4,\ r\in\{64,128\}\ \text{for LLMs};\ N_q=16,\ r=64\ \text{for ViTs}
methods.trainable_params: \text{all } d_{out}d_{in} \text{ entries of each weight matrix (full-parameter ZO); each step's update has rank} \le r;\ \text{state: } P_\ell\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r}
methods.locus: all weight matrices (full-parameter zeroth-order fine-tuning) of OPT-1.3B/13B, LLaMA3-8B and Gemma2-2B (SuperGLUE, SQuAD) and ViT-B/16, ViT-L/16 (CIFAR-10/100)
methods.structure: A multi-query forward-difference gradient estimate (RGE) is taken in a random rank-\(r\) left subspace \(\mathrm{col}(P)\), which is lazily resampled. The \(r\times d_{in}\) estimate is orthogonalized by the matrix sign function and lifted back by \(P\). With an exact matrix sign each update \(P\,\mathrm{msign}(\widehat G_Z)\) is a rank-\(\le r\) partial isometry whose nonzero singular values equal 1; the Newton–Schulz iteration used in practice makes them only approximately 1.
methods.mergeable_reason: ZO-Muon edits the model's own weights in place; there is no adapter to merge.
methods.identity_at_init: Trivial: there is no reparameterization, and training starts at \(W_0\).
methods.key_idea: Estimate the ZO gradient of the projected variable \(Z\) (\(W\approx PZ\), with \(P\) random and column-orthonormal) by multi-query RGE. This cuts the dimension behind the estimator's variance from \(d_{out}d_{in}\) to \(rd_{in}\). Then orthogonalize the estimate Muon-style and lift it back with \(P\). Orthogonalizing full-space MeZO estimates (ZO-Muon-V0) does not help, but inside the subspace the matrix sign acts as a spectral noise filter, making ZO-Muon a zeroth-order approximation of low-rank Muon.
methods.results_note: Versus MeZO, ZO-Muon needs 24.7% of the queries to reach 0.90 on SST-2 (OPT-1.3B, Fig. 2a) and reaches 72.4% versus 47.3% on CIFAR-100 with ViT-L (Table 1). The abstract attributes this +25.1-point gain to ViT-B, but Table 1 shows it is ViT-L.

relations.note: Same seed-regenerated, forward-only RGE. ZO-Muon adds a random orthonormal subspace, multiple queries and Muon-style orthogonalization; applying \(\mathrm{msign}\) to MeZO directly (ZO-Muon-V0) fails.

methods.name: FlexLoRA
methods.paper_title: FlexLoRA: Entropy-Guided Flexible Low-Rank Adaptation
methods.formula_latex: h=W_0x+s\,P_\ell\Lambda_\ell Q_\ell\,x,\ \ s=\alpha/r_{init}\ \text{(released code)},\quad P_\ell\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r_\ell},\ \Lambda_\ell=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_{r_\ell}),\ Q_\ell\in\mathbb{R}^{r_\ell\times d_{in}};\quad \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{task}+\gamma\textstyle\sum_\ell\big(\|P_\ell^{\top}P_\ell-I\|_F^2+\|Q_\ell Q_\ell^{\top}-I\|_F^2\big);\quad I(\Lambda_\ell)=-\frac{1}{\log r_\ell}\sum_{i=1}^{r_\ell}s_i\log(s_i+\epsilon),\ \ s_i=\frac{\lambda_i^2}{\sum_j\lambda_j^2};\quad \text{every }\Delta_T\text{ steps: the }b(t)\text{ lowest-}I\text{ matrices with }r_\ell>1\text{ drop their smallest-}\lambda\text{ triplet; the }b(t)\text{ highest-}I\text{ matrices append }(p,\lambda{=}0,q),\ p,q\sim\mathcal{N};\ \ b(t)=\mathrm{round}\big(b_0(1-\tfrac{t-t_{warmup}}{T-t_{final}})^3\big);\quad W_0\ \text{frozen};\ P_\ell,\Lambda_\ell,Q_\ell\ \text{trained}
methods.trainable_params: r_\ell(d_{in}+d_{out}+1)\ \text{per adapted matrix, with } r_\ell \text{ changing during training. Each reallocation removes one triplet from each of } b(t) \text{ matrices and adds one to each of } b(t) \text{ others, so } \textstyle\sum_\ell r_\ell \text{ stays at the initial budget; the parameter count itself can drift when the adapted matrices differ in } d_{in}+d_{out}
methods.locus: DeBERTaV3-base for GLUE (the paper's rank-allocation figure shows query, key, value, attention-output, intermediate and output dense matrices), the Q, K, V, Up and Down projections of LLaMA3-8B for commonsense reasoning, and ViT-B/16 (ImageNet-22K) for VTAB-1K, whose target modules the paper does not list
methods.structure: An SVD-form additive update \(\Delta W_\ell=P_\ell\Lambda_\ell Q_\ell\) of rank \(r_\ell\). It uses the AdaLoRA parameterization, with a soft orthogonality penalty on \(P_\ell\) and \(Q_\ell\), and it moves rank between matrices during training. Allocation uses one score per matrix, the Shannon entropy of the normalized spectral energies \(s_i=\lambda_i^2/\sum_j\lambda_j^2\) divided by \(\log r_\ell\), which lies in \([0,1]\). Low entropy means the energy sits in a few directions, so the matrix can give up rank. High entropy means the energy is spread out, so the matrix should gain rank. Pruning removes the triplet with the smallest \(\lambda\) from each of the \(b(t)\) lowest-entropy matrices. Expansion appends a Gaussian pair \((p,q)\) with \(\lambda=0\) to each of the \(b(t)\) highest-entropy matrices, so insertion leaves the function unchanged. \(b(t)\) follows a cubic decay schedule between a warm-up and a final freeze phase. The released code differs from the paper in three details: its schedule is \(b_0(1-p^3)\) rather than \(b_0(1-p)^3\), with \(p\) the elapsed fraction of the allocation phase; pruning removes the triplet with the smallest signed \(\lambda\) rather than the smallest magnitude; and the orthogonality penalty uses the unsquared Frobenius norm, averaged over factors.
methods.mergeable_reason: \(P_\ell\Lambda_\ell Q_\ell\) is a dense \(d_{out}\times d_{in}\) matrix that folds into \(W_0\). Ranks change only during training.
methods.identity_at_init: Exact. \(\Lambda=0\) at initialization: in the released flexlora.py the singular-value vector is zero-initialized and \(P,Q\sim\mathcal{N}(0,0.02^2)\), so \(\Delta W=0\). Every expanded direction also starts at \(\lambda=0\) (the paper's zero-impact initialization), so growing a rank does not change the current output.
methods.key_idea: FlexLoRA replaces per-direction sensitivity scores with a matrix-level score, the normalized entropy of each matrix's learned singular values \(\Lambda_\ell\). Under a fixed global budget it moves rank from low-entropy to high-entropy matrices, and new directions enter with \(\lambda=0\) so that expansion is function-preserving.
methods.results_note: With DeBERTaV3-base FlexLoRA averages 89.1 on GLUE against 88.1 for AdaLoRA at the same 1.9M parameters; with LLaMA3-8B on eight commonsense tasks it scores 85.2 at rank 8 (AdaLoRA 85.1) and 85.5 at rank 32.

relations.note: Same \(P\Lambda Q\) parameterization, orthogonality penalty and \(\Lambda=0\) initialization. FlexLoRA replaces AdaLoRA's per-triplet sensitivity scores with a matrix-level spectral-entropy score and adds rank expansion. AdaLoRA is its main baseline.
Not compared in the paper. Both prune and expand ranks during training. ElaLoRA scores individual directions by gradient-based importance, while FlexLoRA scores whole matrices by spectral entropy.
Not compared in the paper. IncreLoRA only grows rank. FlexLoRA moves rank in both directions and keeps the total fixed.
DyLoRA (\(r=8\), 0.9M parameters) is a dynamic-rank baseline in FlexLoRA's GLUE table.
Fixed-rank baseline at the same parameter budget.

methods.name: FourierMoE
methods.paper_title: FourierMoE: Fourier Mixture-of-Experts Adaptation of Large Language Models
methods.formula_latex: h=W_0x+\eta\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}(x)}g_i(x)\,\Delta W_i\,x,\quad g(x)=\mathrm{softmax}\big(\mathcal{G}_\Phi(x)\big),\ \ \mathcal{S}(x)=\mathrm{TopK}_k\,g(x);\quad \Delta W_i=\mathcal{F}^{-1}(E_i)=\frac{1}{d_{out}d_{in}}\sum_{u,v}E_i(u,v)\,f_ug_v^{\top},\ \ (f_u)_q=e^{j2\pi uq/d_{out}},\ (g_v)_y=e^{j2\pi vy/d_{in}};\quad E_i(u,v)=c_{i,uv}\in\mathbb{C}\ \text{for }(u,v)\in\Omega_i,\ \ E_i(\langle-u\rangle,\langle-v\rangle)=\overline{c_{i,uv}},\ \ 0\ \text{elsewhere};\quad \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{task}+\lambda\,Z\sum_{i=1}^{Z}f_iP_i;\quad W_0\ \text{frozen};\ \{c_{i,uv}\}\ \text{and router }\Phi\ \text{trained};\ \Omega_i\ (|\Omega_i|=n)\ \text{fixed, sampled from a Gaussian band-pass around centre frequency }\mathcal{D}_{c,i}
methods.trainable_params: \mathcal{O}(Zn+Z\,d_{in})\ \text{per adapted matrix (App. G, Eq. 15). Read literally (}n\text{ complex coefficients, i.e. }2n\text{ reals, per expert, plus one }Z\times d_{in}\text{ router per adapted matrix), this is }Z(2n+d_{in})\text{. For the LLaMA-2 7B setting (}Z=8,\ n=8192\text{, six projections, 32 layers) that is about 33M parameters (0.49\%), far above the reported 0.06\%, so the paper's actual accounting is unresolved}
methods.locus: The Q, K, V, Up, Down and Gate projections (plus O for math) of LLaMA-2 7B, Gemma 7B, LLaMA-3 8B and Qwen2.5-14B; Q and V only for RoBERTa-large (GLUE) and CLIP ViT-B/32 (image classification). \(Z=8\) experts throughout, with top-4 routing for commonsense reasoning and top-2 elsewhere
methods.structure: A token-routed mixture of \(Z\) dense spectral experts. Each expert update \(\Delta W_i\) is the inverse 2-D DFT of a sparse, Hermitian-symmetric spectrum supported on a fixed set \(\Omega_i\) of \(n\) frequencies. \(\Omega_i\) is drawn from a Gaussian band-pass around a per-expert centre frequency, so each expert is band-limited. \(\Delta W_i\) is therefore a real sum of 2-D sinusoids \(2|c|\cos(2\pi(uq/d_{out}+vy/d_{in})+\angle c)\), and each conjugate pair contributes rank at most 2. The router keeps the top \(k\) experts per token and mixes their spatial updates linearly, so the applied update \(\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}(x)}g_i(x)\Delta W_i\) depends on the input, with rank at most the number of non-zero spectral entries of the selected experts (App. H), which with conjugate partners counted is at most \(2kn\). Unlike FourierFT, the coefficients are complex, so the experts learn phase as well as amplitude. Catalogue observation, not from the paper: \(\mathrm{Re}\,\mathcal{F}^{-1}(F)=\mathcal{F}^{-1}\big(\tfrac12(F+\bar F^{\sharp})\big)\) with \(\bar F^{\sharp}(u,v)=\overline{F(\langle-u\rangle,\langle-v\rangle)}\) for every \(F\). Taking the real part of an unsymmetrized complex spectrum therefore reaches the same set of updates, and the substantive change from FourierFT is the learned phase rather than the symmetry constraint.
methods.mergeable_reason: The gate values \(g_i(x)\) and the active set \(\mathcal{S}(x)\) change from token to token. Each \(\Delta W_i\) can be computed once per forward pass and cached, but no single static matrix reproduces the layer unless the routing is frozen.
methods.identity_at_init: Not specified. The paper's algorithm only says that the complex coefficients are initialized and that the router starts random. \(\Delta W=0\) at the start would require zero coefficients (the FourierFT paper draws its coefficients from \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\)), and no code is public.
methods.key_idea: FourierMoE moves MoE-LoRA into the frequency domain. Each expert owns a band of 2-D Fourier frequencies with learnable complex coefficients (amplitude and phase), and a token-level top-\(k\) router decides which bands, and therefore how much rank, each token's weight update receives.
methods.results_note: In the multi-task commonsense setting on LLaMA-2 7B FourierMoE averages 83.95 against 82.73 for GOAT, the strongest mixture-of-PEFT baseline, using 0.06% trainable parameters; on seven GLUE tasks with RoBERTa-large it averages 91.40 against 86.73 for FourierFT.

relations.note: Each expert is a FourierFT-style IDFT of a sparse spectrum. FourierMoE adds complex coefficients with conjugate symmetry, band-limited per-expert supports and token routing; FourierFT is a baseline.
Uses MoLoRA-style token-level top-\(k\) routing with a load-balancing loss, with spectral experts in place of LoRA experts. MoLoRA is a baseline.
GOAT is the strongest mixture-of-PEFT baseline. FourierMoE reports +1.22 points on LLaMA-2 7B commonsense with about 16x fewer trainable parameters (0.06% vs 0.96%).
Mixture-of-PEFT baseline in the multi-task commonsense and math experiments.

methods.name: SMoA
methods.paper_title: SMoA: Spectrum Modulation Adapter for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
methods.formula_latex: \widetilde W_0=P_{out}W_0P_{in}^{\top},\quad M_k=\widetilde W_0[\mathcal{O}_k,\mathcal{I}_k]\in\mathbb{R}^{\frac{d_{out}}{K}\times\frac{d_{in}}{K}};\quad \Delta W=P_{out}^{\top}\,\mathrm{blkdiag}\big((B_1A_1)\odot M_1,\dots,(B_KA_K)\odot M_K\big)\,P_{in},\quad B_k\in\mathbb{R}^{\frac{d_{out}}{K}\times\rho},\ A_k\in\mathbb{R}^{\rho\times\frac{d_{in}}{K}},\ \rho=\tfrac{r}{K};\quad h=(W_0+\Delta W)x;\quad W_0\ \text{frozen};\ \text{permutations }P_{out},P_{in}\ \text{(fixed once from the SVD of }W_0\text{) and anchors }M_k\ \text{frozen};\ \{A_k,B_k\}_{k=1}^{K}\ \text{trained}
methods.trainable_params: \tfrac{r}{K}(d_{in}+d_{out})\ \text{per adapted matrix, i.e. }1/K\text{ of rank-}r\text{ LoRA}
methods.locus: Query, key, value and projection layers (the paper's wording, App. D) of Llama-2-7B and Llama-3-8B; \(K=2\) by default, with reference ranks \(r\in\{16,32\}\)
methods.structure: A block-diagonal HiRA in permuted coordinates. Write \(\tilde B=\mathrm{blkdiag}(B_1,\dots,B_K)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r}\) and \(\tilde A=\mathrm{blkdiag}(A_1,\dots,A_K)\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}}\). Because \(\mathrm{blkdiag}(B_kA_k)\odot\widetilde W_0=\mathrm{blkdiag}((B_kA_k)\odot M_k)\), the update equals \(\Delta W=(P_{out}^{\top}\tilde B\tilde AP_{in})\odot W_0\) (catalogue rewriting). This is a Hadamard modulation of the frozen weight by a rank-\(r\) matrix whose factors are block-sparse in a coordinate order fixed once from the SVD of \(W_0\). The paper does not spell out the rule beyond grouping coordinates with similar spectral roles. Off-diagonal blocks of \(\widetilde W_0\) are never modulated. Proposition 1 bounds the rank by \(\sum_k\min(s_k,\rho\,\mathrm{rank}\,M_k)\) with \(s_k=\min(d_{out},d_{in})/K\), against \(r\) for LoRA. With \(K=1\) the permutations are absorbed into the factors and SMoA is exactly HiRA. Without the Hadamard factor it becomes block-diagonal mini-LoRAs (MELoRA's shape) in permuted coordinates. A second catalogue observation follows. \(\tilde B\tilde A\) has rank at most \(r\), so at budget \(r\) SMoA's update set lies inside rank-\(r\) HiRA's set \(\{W_0\odot(BA)\}\), reached with \(1/K\) of HiRA's parameters. The rank-ceiling gain of Proposition 1 is over LoRA, not over HiRA.
methods.mergeable_reason: \(\Delta W\) is a dense matrix once it is scattered back with \(P_{out}^{\top}\) and \(P_{in}\). It is added to \(W_0\) after training, so inference has no extra branch.
methods.identity_at_init: Not stated. The paper follows HiRA's training setup; if one factor of each block is zero-initialized as in HiRA, \(\Delta W=0\) at the start. The SVD-based reordering does not change the layer.
methods.key_idea: Pretrained weights carry information in their long spectral tails, so one global low-rank branch under-covers them. SMoA reorders \(W_0\) by its spectral structure, cuts it into \(K\) aligned diagonal blocks, and attaches a rank-\(r/K\) HiRA-style (Hadamard-modulated) branch to each block. This raises the rank ceiling while using \(1/K\) of LoRA's parameters.
methods.results_note: With \(r=32\) and \(K=2\) (half of rank-32 LoRA's parameters) SMoA averages 81.85% on eight commonsense tasks with Llama-2-7B (HiRA at \(r=32\): 81.42%) and 87.39% with Llama-3-8B (HiRA: 86.73%), and reaches 72.33% on GSM8K with Llama-3-8B against 65.89% for LoRA.

relations.note: With \(K=1\) the permutations are absorbed into the factors and the update is exactly HiRA's \(W_0\odot(BA)\). For \(K>1\) at the same \(r\), SMoA's update set is a subset of HiRA's. HiRA is the strongest baseline.
Takes MELoRA's block-diagonal direct sum of small branches, in spectrum-permuted coordinates, and modulates each block entrywise by the matching diagonal block of \(W_0\). MELoRA is a baseline.
Another high-rank-at-low-budget design (square matrix with fixed compression); a baseline.
The rank ceiling exceeds \(r\) at \(r(d_{in}+d_{out})/K\) parameters.

The results were checked against the text of Secs. 4.1 and 4.3, because the tables are images in the HTML. The Hadamard rewriting was re-derived: \(\mathrm{blkdiag}(B_kA_k)=\tilde B\tilde A\), and permutations applied on both sides commute with the Hadamard product, so \(\Delta W=(P_{out}^{\top}\tilde B\tilde AP_{in})\odot W_0\). No public code was found. The paper does not state the initialization; it follows HiRA's setup. methods.name: Bayesian-LoRA
methods.full_name: Bayesian-LoRA (sparse-GP inducing-variable posterior over both LoRA factors)
methods.paper_title: Bayesian-LoRA: Probabilistic Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
methods.formula_latex: h=\big(W_0+\tfrac{\alpha}{r}BA\big)x,\quad A\mid U^A\sim\mathcal{N}\big(T_r^AU^AT_c^A,\ \lambda^2\Sigma_A\big),\ \ B\mid U^B\sim\mathcal{N}\big(T_r^BU^BT_c^B,\ \lambda^2\Sigma_B\big);\quad T_r=Z_r^{\top}K_r^{-1},\ T_c=K_c^{-1}Z_c,\ K_r=Z_rZ_r^{\top}+D_r^2,\ K_c=Z_cZ_c^{\top}+D_c^2;\quad U=T_\phi(U_0),\ U_0\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{m},\mathrm{diag}\,\boldsymbol{\sigma}^2)\ \text{(masked autoregressive flow)},\ \ p(U)=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},K_c\otimes K_r);\quad \max\ \mathbb{E}_{q}\big[\log p(\mathcal{D}\mid W)\big]-\mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(U)\,\|\,p(U)\big)-\tfrac{D}{2}\big(\lambda^2-1-2\log\lambda\big);\quad W_0\ \text{frozen};\ Z_r,Z_c,D_r,D_c,\mathbf{m},\boldsymbol{\sigma},\phi,\lambda\ \text{trained (per factor and layer)}
methods.trainable_params: \approx c\,d_{in}+r\,d_{out}+r_L(r+c)+O(rc)\ \text{per adapted matrix, with an } r\times c \text{ inducing matrix per factor and LoRA rank } r_L\text{. The inducing locations } Z_c^A\in\mathbb{R}^{c\times d_{in}} \text{ and } Z_r^B\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{out}} \text{ dominate; the variational means and standard deviations, diagonal noise, flow and } \lambda \text{ add } O(rc) \text{ (derived from Eqs. 6, 13 and 14 and the released code). Paper total: 4.9M, against 4.48M for LoRA on Q, K and the LM head of Llama-2-7B with } r=c=9\text{; 4.48M is LoRA at rank 8, the rank used in the released configs}
methods.locus: Q, K and LM-head weights of Llama-2-7B for commonsense reasoning (inducing size \(r=c=9\)); also Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 for MATH (App. Table 22)
methods.structure: A stochastic rank-\(r\) additive update. Both LoRA factors are random matrices generated from small \(r\times c\) inducing matrices through a Kronecker-structured sparse-GP conditional: a bilinear projection \(T_rUT_c\) plus Gaussian noise of scale \(\lambda\). The posterior over each inducing matrix is a diagonal Gaussian pushed through a masked autoregressive flow. The ELBO's KL over \(U\) is estimated from base samples (Prop. 4.1), and its conditional-KL term is in closed form. Every sample has rank at most \(r\), and the posterior mean \(\tfrac{\alpha}{r}\bar B\bar A\) has exactly LoRA's shape. A point-mass \(q(U)\) with \(\lambda\to0\) recovers a deterministic LoRA update in the reparameterization \(A=T_r^AU^AT_c^A\), \(B=T_r^BU^BT_c^B\) (Corollary 4.2).
methods.mergeable_reason: In deterministic mode the posterior mean \(W_0+\tfrac{\alpha}{r}\bar B\bar A\) is merged with no added latency. Calibrated predictions need \(N\) Monte Carlo samples of \((A,B)\) at test time. Latency is \(1.52\times\) LoRA's with \(N=2\) and \(2.79\times\) with \(N=4\), the setting used in the accuracy and calibration tables.
methods.identity_at_init: Not exact, and the paper does not state it. The released training script first applies PEFT LoRA, then replaces both LoRA factor layers on each key layer with InducingLinear modules. Their inducing means are drawn from \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) and their inducing locations are random, so both sampled factors are non-zero at step 0 and \(\tfrac{\alpha}{r}BA\neq0\). The update is small because the prior scale is divided by the square root of the fan-in. The repository also has an InducingAdapter wrapper whose learnable output scale starts at 0, but the training script never uses it.
methods.key_idea: The Kronecker-factored sparse-GP conditional mean \(T_rUT_c\) has the same bilinear shape as LoRA's \(BA\). Bayesian-LoRA puts a flow-enriched variational posterior on small inducing matrices that generate both LoRA factors, giving end-to-end calibrated Bayesian LoRA with plain LoRA as the zero-uncertainty limit.
methods.results_note: On six commonsense benchmarks with Llama-2-7B Bayesian-LoRA has the best accuracy on five and cuts ECE by 84% relative to MAP LoRA on WinoGrande-S, at 1.23x LoRA's training time and 0.42M extra parameters.

relations.note: LoRA is the point-mass, \(\lambda\to0\) limit (Corollary 4.2), up to the bilinear reparameterization of the factors through inducing variables.
Laplace-LoRA fits a posterior after training, while Bayesian-LoRA learns a variational posterior end to end. The Laplace variants (LA, LLLA) are baselines.
BLoB puts a mean-field Gaussian on \(A\) only. Bayesian-LoRA makes both factors stochastic through sparse-GP inducing variables with a flow posterior. BLoB is a baseline.
Also learns a distribution over LoRA parameters during training (a Gaussian mixture on \(A\)); not compared in the paper.

methods.verification_notes: arXiv 2601.21003 v1 (28 Jan 2026; v4 27 Sep 2026) by Moule Lin, Shuhao Guan, Andrea Patane, David Gregg and Goetz Botterweck, with the arXiv comment 'accepted by ICML 2026'.
