methods.name: FLoRG
methods.paper_title: FLoRG: Federated Fine-tuning with Low-rank Gram Matrices and Procrustes Alignment
methods.formula_latex: W^{t}=W_0+L\,(A^{t})^{\top}A^{t}R,\quad L\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times k},\ R\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times d_{in}}\ \text{fixed semi-orthogonal},\ A^{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times k},\ k=\min(d_{in},d_{out});\quad \text{client } n:\ A_n^{t+\frac12}=A^{t}-\eta\,A^{t}\big(H_n^{t}+H_n^{t\top}\big),\ \ H_n^{t}=L^{\top}\nabla_WF_n(W^{t})R^{\top};\quad \text{server: } Q^{t+1}=\tfrac1N\sum_n(A_n^{t+\frac12})^{\top}A_n^{t+\frac12}=(P^{t+1})^{\top}\Lambda^{t+1}P^{t+1},\ \ \tilde A^{t+1}=(\Lambda^{t+1})^{1/2}P^{t+1},\ \ A^{t+1}=S^{\star}\tilde A^{t+1},\ \ S^{\star}=UV^{\top}\ \text{where } A^{t}(\tilde A^{t+1})^{\top}=U\Sigma V^{\top};\quad W_0,L,R\ \text{frozen};\ A\ \text{trained};\quad \text{experiments use a LoRA scaling factor of 16 and AdamW (App. A.6)}
methods.trainable_params: r\,k=r\min(d_{in},d_{out})\ \text{per adapted matrix (a single factor); per round each client uploads } A_n \text{ and downloads } A^{t}\text{, } rk \text{ numbers each way}
methods.locus: LoRA-adapted weight matrices of OPT-125M, RoBERTa-large and Llama-3.2-3B (the paper does not list the modules); \(r=4\), \(N=20\) clients
methods.structure: A rank-\(\le r\) additive update confined to the cone \(\{LQR:\ Q\succeq0,\ \mathrm{rank}\,Q\le r\}\): a PSD Gram core \(Q=A^{\top}A\) between two fixed semi-orthogonal frames (the paper says only that they are initialized with orthogonal columns). The core is invariant under the gauge \(A\mapsto OA\), \(O\in O(r)\), and is linear to average, so the server aggregates \(Q\) exactly (no \(B_iA_j\) cross terms) from one factor per client. Re-factoring the aggregate is ambiguous up to that gauge, and \(\mathrm{rank}\,Q^{t+1}\le\min(k,Nr)\) can exceed \(r\). Orthogonal Procrustes picks the rank-\(r\) factor closest to the previous round's \(A^{t}\), which removes the drift term from the convergence bound. Two catalogue observations, not from the paper: because \(Q\succeq0\), \(-\Delta W\) is never reachable for \(\Delta W\neq0\); and when \(\mathrm{rank}\,Q^{t+1}>r\), the \(r\times r'\) map \(S^{\star}\) projects the aggregate, so the broadcast update is no longer exactly the client average. The paper's constraint \((S^{t})^{\top}S^{t}=I_{r'}\) cannot hold when \(r'>r\); in that case the solution \(S^{\star}=UV^{\top}\) has orthonormal rows.
methods.mergeable_reason: \(L(A^{t})^{\top}A^{t}R\) is a dense \(d_{out}\times d_{in}\) matrix that is added to \(W_0\).
methods.identity_at_init: Not exact. \(W^{1}=W_0+L(A^{1})^{\top}A^{1}R\), and \(A^{1}=0\) cannot be used because \(\nabla_AF=A(H+H^{\top})\) vanishes there. The paper does not specify how \(A^{1}\) is initialized; \(L\) and \(R\) get semi-orthogonal initialization, which beats Kaiming and SVD initialization in its ablation.
methods.key_idea: FLoRG trains a single factor \(A\) of a symmetric update \(LA^{\top}AR\) and aggregates its Gram matrix \(A^{\top}A\), which is gauge-invariant. Federated averaging becomes exact and uplink traffic halves. The server then re-factors the average and fixes the \(O(r)\) gauge by Procrustes alignment to the previous round.
methods.results_note: With 20 clients, Dirichlet non-IID GLUE splits and rank 4 FLoRG beats FedIT, FeDeRA, FFA-LoRA, FedSA-LoRA and FedEx-LoRA in most cases, and it transmits up to 2041x fewer parameters than FedEx-LoRA to reach a target QNLI accuracy.

relations.note: Both make aggregation exact with one trained factor. FFA-LoRA freezes \(A\) and averages \(B\), which is linear. FLoRG averages the Gram matrix of a single trained factor, which is quadratic but gauge-invariant. FFA-LoRA is a baseline.

Cited in FLoRG's related work (stacking-based aggregation) but not a baseline. FLoRA makes aggregation exact by stacking client factors, so its rank grows with the number of clients. FLoRG keeps rank \(r\) by re-factoring.
Replaces the two LoRA factors \(BA\) with the tied symmetric form \(LA^{\top}AR\).

FLoRG cites SingLoRA as reformulating LoRA with a single matrix. SingLoRA's centralized update \(AA^{\top}\) has the same single-factor Gram form. FLoRG places it between fixed frames \(L,R\) to handle rectangular weights and exploits its linearity for exact federated averaging. On a square weight with \(L=R^{\top}=I\), FLoRG's update is SingLoRA's without the ramp \(u(t)\).
FedIT, which averages \(B\) and \(A\) separately, is the first of FLoRG's five baselines.

methods.verification_notes: arXiv 2602.17095 v1 (19 Feb 2026; v2 6 Mar 2026) by Chuiyang Meng, Ming Tang and Vincent W. S. Wong. methods.name: LoDA
methods.paper_title: Task-Driven Subspace Decomposition for Knowledge Sharing and Isolation in LoRA-based Continual Learning
methods.formula_latex: h=\big(W^{t-1}+w_GB_GA_G+B_IA_I\big)x;\quad S^{i}=X^{i\top}X^{i},\ S^{1:t-1}=\textstyle\sum_{i<t}S^{i};\quad A_G=U_G^{\top},\ U_G=\text{top-}r\ \text{eigenvectors of } S^{1:t-1}+S^{t};\quad A_I=\mathrm{QR}(U_I^{\top}),\ U_I=\text{top-}r\ \text{generalized eigenvectors of } S^{t}u=\mu\,S^{1:t-1}u\ \ (\text{via } S^{1:t-1}=LL^{\top},\ U_I=L^{-\top}\,\mathrm{top}_r\,\mathrm{eig}(L^{-1}S^{t}L^{-\top}));\quad A_G,A_I\ \text{frozen};\ B_G,B_I\ \text{trained from }0\text{ with GAO};\quad \text{after task } t:\ W^{t}=W^{t-1}+w_GB_G\Lambda_GA_G+B_IA_I,\ \ \Lambda_G=\mathrm{diag}(\gamma_j),\ \ \gamma_j=\frac{\lambda\,a_jS^{t}a_j^{\top}}{a_j(\lambda S^{t}+S^{1:t-1})a_j^{\top}}\in[0,1],\ a_j=A_G^{(j)}
methods.trainable_params: 2r\,d_{out}\ \text{per adapted matrix per task (}B_G,B_I\text{), or } r\,d_{out} \text{ on task 1, where the isolated branch is disabled. } A_G,A_I \text{ are designed, not trained, and both branches are merged after each task, so inference adds no parameters}
methods.locus: All attention blocks of an ImageNet-21K ViT-B/16 at rank 32; also CLIP and self-supervised ViT backbones
methods.structure: Each task adds two rank-\(r\) additive branches whose down-projections are frozen and designed from second moments of the layer inputs. The shared branch spans the top-\(r\) eigenspace of the accumulated old-plus-new statistics, for knowledge sharing. The isolated branch spans the top-\(r\) generalized eigenvectors of the pencil \((S^{t},S^{1:t-1})\), the directions with the largest ratio of new-task to old-task projection energy, instead of an approximate null space of old tasks. Training only \(B\) is gradient descent restricted to \(\mathrm{row}(A)\), with output change scaled by the projection energy \(\|Ax\|^2\) (Thm 3.1). The up-projections are trained with GAO, a two-subset look-ahead update that favors gradients agreeing across label-disjoint halves of a batch. Before merging, each rank-1 unit of the shared branch is shrunk by a closed-form ridge-type factor \(\gamma_j\in[0,1]\) that trades new-task fit against drift on old-task features. Both branches are then folded into the backbone.
methods.mergeable_reason: After each task \(w_GB_G\Lambda_GA_G+B_IA_I\) is added to the backbone and the LoRA matrices are discarded, so inference uses a single weight matrix and needs no task identity.
methods.identity_at_init: Exact for each task. \(B_G=B_I=0\) when a task starts, and on task 1 the isolated branch is disabled, so the layer equals \(W^{t-1}\). \(A_G\) and \(A_I\) are set beforehand from cached layer inputs.
methods.key_idea: With a frozen down-projection, LoRA learns only along directions the inputs excite (projection energy \(\|Ax\|^2\)). LoDA therefore builds one subspace that old and new tasks both excite, for transfer, and one that the new task excites far more than old tasks, for isolation. Null-space designs instead use old-task null spaces, which the new task may barely use.
methods.results_note: Without feature replay LoDA beats the strongest baseline, CoSO, by 0.80-1.70 points in final accuracy on its class-incremental benchmarks with a ViT-B/16, and the classifier-aligned LoDA+CA beats the replay-based MACIL by 0.15-5.11 points.

relations.note: InfLoRA's frozen down-projection spans new-task directions inside the approximate null space of old tasks. LoDA replaces it with a generalized-eigenvector (energy-ratio) subspace, adds a shared branch, and beats InfLoRA in the paper's subspace-isolation comparison (Table 4).
Cited in related work but not a baseline (O-LoRA is a language-model method). O-LoRA uses soft orthogonality between task subspaces; LoDA uses hard subspaces designed from data.
LoRA-based class-incremental baseline.

Not cited by LoDA; the link is structural. On each task the two branches together form one LoRA-FA-style update \([w_GB_G,\ B_I][A_G;A_I]\), whose frozen rank-\(2r\) down-projection is designed from data rather than drawn at random.

methods.verification_notes: arXiv 2603.00191 v1 (27 Feb 2026; v4 24 May 2026) by Lingfeng He, De Cheng, Huaijie Wang, Xi Yang, Nannan Wang and Xinbo Gao, with the arXiv comment 'Accepted by ICML 2026'. The icml.cc accepted-paper JSON lists it as Accept (regular), event 63718, OpenReview UJJfkcJ7K9. The formula was checked against Eqs. 3-14, Theorems 3.1-3.3 and Algorithm 1 (App. A); on task 1 the isolated branch is disabled. The setup (ViT-B/16 pretrained on ImageNet-21K, all attention blocks, rank 32, \(w_G=0.5\), \(\lambda=3\)) and the results were checked against Sec. 4. The code repository HHHLF/LoDA_ICML2026 exists and was created 2026-05-02. One caveat about the paper itself: the ratio objective in Eq. 6 is maximized by putting every column on the top generalized eigenvector. The orthonormality imposed in the proof of Theorem 3.2 is therefore a design choice, not 'without loss of optimality'. The method uses the top-\(r\) generalized eigenspace, as the entry states. methods.name: LRAgent
methods.full_name: LRAgent: KV cache sharing for multi-LoRA agents (BaseShared / BaseLRShared with Flash-LoRA-Attention)
methods.paper_title: LRAgent: Efficient KV Cache Sharing for Multi-LoRA LLM Agents
methods.formula_latex: W_v^{(i)}=W_0+B_iA_i,\ \ A_i\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}},\ B_i\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r}\ (i=1,\dots,N),\ \ A_i=A\ \text{for all }i\ \text{(shared-}A\text{; used in the main experiments and required by BaseLRShared)};\ \ \text{value cache for context token }t:\ v^{base}_t=W_0x_t\ \text{(computed once by the agent that first processes }t\text{ and reused by every agent; the key cache is shared the same way)};\ \ \text{LR cache: }c_t=Ax_t\in\mathbb{R}^{r}\ \text{(one shared cache, BaseLRShared) or }c^{(i)}_t=A_ix^{(i)}_t\ \text{(per agent, recomputed from agent }i\text{'s own hidden states over context it has not yet processed, BaseShared)};\ \ o^{(i)}=\sum_t p_t\big(v^{base}_t+B_ic_t\big)=\sum_t p_t\,v^{base}_t+B_i\Big(\sum_t p_t\,c_t\Big)\ \text{(Flash-LoRA-Attention evaluates the right-hand form)};\ \ W_0\ \text{frozen};\ A,\{B_i\}\ \text{trained as LoRA on }W_q,W_v\ (r=8)
methods.trainable_params: r\,d_{in}+N\,r\,d_{out}\ \text{per adapted matrix for }N\text{ agents with shared }A\ \ (N\,r(d_{in}+d_{out})\text{ for independent multi-LoRA})
methods.locus: LoRA (\(r=8\)) on the query and value projections of every attention layer, one up-projection per agent role (plan, action, reflect) on a shared down-projection; cache sharing acts on the value cache, and the key cache is shared outright
methods.structure: Serving-time decomposition of each agent's value cache into a shared full-width part \(W_0x_t\) and an \(r\)-dimensional part \(Ax_t\) that is expanded by the agent's own \(B_i\). With a shared \(A\) the agents differ only in the output map \(B_i\) (HydraLoRA's asymmetric layout with a fixed one-hot assignment of heads to agent roles), so the \(r\)-dimensional cache is common to all agents as well. Associativity \(P(V_{base}+V_{lr}B_i^{\top})=PV_{base}+(PV_{lr})B_i^{\top}\) moves the expansion after the attention weighting, so the expansion cost per decoding step is \(\Theta(Lr+r\,d_{out})\) instead of \(\Theta(L\,r\,d_{out})\) for context length \(L\). In BaseShared each agent still rebuilds its own LR cache over context it has not processed (the paper's 'LR prefill'), so compute stays \(O(NL^2d_{model})\) and only memory falls to about \(1/N\); BaseLRShared also skips that prefill. Reusing a base cache that another agent computed is an approximation, because \(x_t\) depends on that agent's adapters.
methods.mergeable_reason: For one agent alone, \(W_0+B_iA\) folds into a plain matrix, but the cache-sharing scheme needs the unmerged form: it stores \(W_0x_t\) and \(Ax_t\) separately so that every agent can reuse them.
methods.identity_at_init: The paper does not state the LoRA initialization (training follows AutoAct). With the usual \(B_i=0\), every agent starts at \(W_0\); all agents then coincide, so the shared caches are exact at that point. Once the \(B_i\) differ, cache sharing is approximate: agents reuse base caches (and, in BaseLRShared, LR caches) built from other agents' hidden states.
methods.key_idea: On a shared context, agents' base value caches \(W_0x_t\) are nearly identical (average cosine similarity 0.95 to 0.97 across agent pairs) while their adapter outputs are nearly uncorrelated (0.02 to 0.05). LRAgent therefore shares the base cache, stores the adapter part in its native rank-\(r\) form \(Ax_t\), shares that too once all agents use one \(A\), and applies \(B_i\) only after attention has summed over tokens.
methods.results_note: On multi-hop HotpotQA and ScienceQA agents built on LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct and Ministral-8B-Instruct, BaseLRShared with Flash-LoRA-Attention reaches up to 2.46x the throughput and up to 4.44x lower time-to-first-token than non-shared caching (measured on an emulated trace of 2k to 66k tokens), with an average accuracy drop of at most 1.5 points (at most 0.7 points for BaseShared).

relations.note: Adopts HydraLoRA's shared-\(A\), per-head-\(B\) layout (cited as Tian et al. 2024, with MTL-LoRA), replacing the token-wise router by a fixed agent-to-head assignment. Sharing \(A\) is what lets the low-rank cache \(Ax\) be shared across agents (BaseLRShared).

Both cut the cost of serving many LoRAs on one backbone by keeping the shared base term \(W_0x\) separate from the per-adapter low-rank terms: S-LoRA for batching and adapter memory, LRAgent for the KV cache of agents that share a context. The paper does not cite S-LoRA (its multi-LoRA serving reference is Xia et al. 2024, LoRA-Inlaid), so no lineage is claimed.

Both cut the cost of running many LoRAs on one backbone: Punica batches the low-rank matmuls across adapters, while LRAgent removes redundant prefill and KV memory across adapters that share a context. The paper does not cite Punica.

methods.verification_notes: Checked 2026-10-02. arXiv abs page: title matches; first author Hyesung Jeon (with Hyeongju Ha, Jae-Joon Kim); v1 1 Feb 2026, v2 31 May 2026; journal-ref 'ICML 2026 Poster'. methods.name: GeoRA
methods.paper_title: GeoRA: Geometry-Aware Low-Rank Adaptation for RLVR
methods.formula_latex: h=W_{res}\,x+s\,BA\,x,\ \ s=\alpha/r;\ \ W_{Geo}=W_0\odot(M_{Spec}\lor M_{Euc}),\ \ (M_{Euc})_{ij}=\mathbb{I}\big(|(W_0)_{ij}|\le\tau_\rho(|W_0|)\big),\ \ (M_{Spec})_{ij}=\mathbb{I}\big(|(\hat W_r)_{ij}|\le\tau_\rho(|\hat W_r|)\big),\ \hat W_r=\mathrm{SVD}_r(W_0),\ \tau_\rho=\rho\text{-quantile};\ \ W_{Geo}=U\Sigma V^{\top},\ B_0=U_{:,1:r}\Sigma_{1:r,1:r}^{1/2},\ A_0=\Sigma_{1:r,1:r}^{1/2}V_{:,1:r}^{\top};\ \ W_{res}=W_0-s\,B_0A_0\ \text{(frozen)};\ B\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r},A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}}\ \text{trained from }(B_0,A_0)\ \text{with an RLVR objective (GRPO)}
methods.trainable_params: r(d_{in}+d_{out})
methods.locus: all linear layers ('all-linear'), \(r=16\), \(\alpha=32\), \(\rho=0.2\) in the experiments
methods.structure: PiSSA's residual-anchored rank-\(r\) reparametrization (base point moved to a frozen \(W_{res}\), \(\Delta W\) factors through \(r\) dimensions), with the starting factors taken from the top-\(r\) SVD of a sparse masked copy \(W_{Geo}\) of \(W_0\) instead of \(W_0\) itself. The mask keeps the entries that are small either in \(W_0\) or in its rank-\(r\) principal reconstruction \(\hat W_r\). With \(\rho=0.2\) each mask keeps 20% of entries and they overlap on 4.55% (Qwen3-8B), so \(W_{Geo}\) keeps about 35% of the entries. The construction is data-free: no RL gradient or update enters the initialization.
methods.mergeable_reason: \(W_{res}+s\,BA\) is a plain matrix. As a delta on the original weights the update is \(s(BA-B_0A_0)\), as for PiSSA.
methods.identity_at_init: Exact: \(W_{res}x+s\,B_0A_0x=W_0x\) by construction of \(W_{res}\).
methods.key_idea: RLVR updates avoid the principal and large-magnitude weights. GeoRA builds a data-free proxy for that region by masking \(W_0\) to its low-magnitude entries, in weight space and in the rank-\(r\) principal reconstruction, and starts a dense rank-\(r\) adapter on the top-\(r\) SVD of the masked matrix, with the remainder frozen as an anchor. RLVR then trains in this region at the hardware cost of dense LoRA, not sparse fine-tuning.
methods.results_note: With GRPO on DeepMath-103K and \(r=16\), Qwen3-8B-Base trained with GeoRA scores 23.75 on AIME24, against 19.58 for LoRA, 22.50 for PiSSA, 20.42 for MiLoRA and 23.33 for full fine-tuning.

relations.note: Same frozen-residual parametrization \(W=W_{res}+sBA\) with an SVD start; the SVD is of the masked \(W_{Geo}\), not of \(W_0\). Under RLVR at an aggressive learning rate (\(5\times10^{-5}\), Qwen3-4B), PiSSA's reward collapses late in training while GeoRA's does not.
MiLoRA starts on \(W_0\)'s minor singular directions. GeoRA takes the top directions of a low-magnitude masked copy of \(W_0\), and its ablation finds tail-\(r\) initialization worst.

LIFT tunes the largest-magnitude entries of the rank-\(r\) truncation \(\mathrm{SVD}_r(W_0)\) ('principal weights'). GeoRA's spectral mask keeps the smallest \(\rho\)-fraction of the same truncation, unions it with \(W_0\)'s smallest entries, and compresses the result into a dense rank-\(r\) adapter. GeoRA cites LIFT.
Motivated by the finding that RLVR updates stay off the principal directions, in low-magnitude, low-curvature regions; GeoRA's masks are a weight-only proxy for that region.
RL fine-tuning touches a small subnetwork. GeoRA replaces sparse fine-tuning of such a subnetwork, which modern hardware runs poorly, with a dense low-rank adapter.

methods.name: MatryoshkaLoRA
methods.full_name: MatryoshkaLoRA (nested-rank LoRA trained through a fixed diagonal rank weighting)
methods.paper_title: MatryoshkaLoRA: Learning Accurate Hierarchical Low-Rank Representations for LLM Fine-Tuning
methods.formula_latex: \text{train: }h=\big(W_0+B\,\mathrm{diag}(p)\,A\big)x,\ \ B\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times R},\ A\in\mathbb{R}^{R\times d_{in}},\ \ p=\sum_{r\in S}s_r\,\mathbf{1}_{[1,r]}\ (\mathbf{1}_{[1,r]}\in\{0,1\}^R\text{ has ones in its first }r\text{ entries}),\ \text{i.e. }p_j=\sum_{r\in S,\ r\ge j}s_r,\ \ \text{so }B\,\mathrm{diag}(p)\,A=\sum_{r\in S}s_r\,B_{:,1:r}A_{1:r,:};\ \ S=\{1,2,4,\dots,R\},\ s_r\in\{1,\,1/r,\,1/\sqrt{r}\};\ \ \text{deploy at any }k\in S:\ h=\big(W_0+s_k\,B_{:,1:k}A_{1:k,:}\big)x;\ \ W_0,\ p\ \text{frozen (one }p\text{ for all layers)};\ A,B\ \text{trained}\ (A\ \text{Kaiming},\ B=0)
methods.trainable_params: R(d_{in}+d_{out})
methods.locus: same placement as LoRA; the released run scripts wrap all seven linear projections of every Llama block (query, key, value, output, gate, up and down) of Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct (\(R=32\)) and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (\(R=256\))
methods.structure: A rank-\(R\) LoRA with a frozen, non-increasing diagonal \(\mathrm{diag}(p)\) inserted between the factors, so the training update is the sum of all nested prefix adapters \(\sum_{r\in S}s_rB_{:,1:r}A_{1:r,:}\). The diagonal multiplies the gradient of the \(j\)-th column of \(B\) and row of \(A\) by \(p_j\), so leading rank-1 components get the most signal. The train-time adapter, weighted by \(p\), is never deployed: inference drops \(p\) and uses a single prefix \(s_kB_{:,1:k}A_{1:k,:}\). The paper (Appendix B) justifies this as a first-order surrogate of the multi-rank objective that DyLoRA samples one rank at a time: for convex weights \(\lambda_r\), \(\sum_r\lambda_r\ell(W_0+\Delta_r)=\ell\big(W_0+\sum_r\lambda_r\Delta_r\big)+O\big(\sum_r\lambda_r\|\Delta_r\|_F^2\big)\) with \(\Delta_r=s_rB_{:,1:r}A_{1:r,:}\), which gives \(p=\sum_r\lambda_rs_r\mathbf{1}_{[1,r]}\). The main-text \(p\) takes every \(\lambda_r=1\), which is \(|S|\) times the uniform-weight surrogate.
methods.mergeable_reason: After choosing the deployment rank \(k\), \(s_kB_{:,1:k}A_{1:k,:}\) is a plain rank-\(k\) matrix that folds into \(W_0\).
methods.identity_at_init: Yes: the released code initializes \(B=0\) (with \(A\) Kaiming-uniform), so \(B\,\mathrm{diag}(p)\,A=0\) and every prefix adapter is zero.
methods.key_idea: Train every nested rank at once in a single forward pass: a fixed diagonal \(p_j=\sum_{r\in S,\,r\ge j}s_r\) between \(B\) and \(A\) turns the sum of all prefix adapters into one rank-\(R\) product. Every prefix then receives gradient at every step, unlike DyLoRA, whose sampled rank \(b\) gives components beyond \(b\) no gradient at that step. LoRA is \(p=s_R\mathbf{1}\), and DyLoRA is a per-step random truncation \(p=s_b\mathbf{1}_{[1,b]}\).
methods.results_note: Fine-tuning Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct on GSM8K (8-shot) with maximum rank \(R=32\), MatryoshkaLoRA reaches an area under the rank-accuracy curve (AURAC) of 38.4%, against 34.5% for LoRA and 34.9% for DyLoRA, and its sub-rank \(r=1\) (35.8%) already beats every sub-rank of either baseline. The pre-trained model scores 34.7%, so LoRA and DyLoRA barely move it in this setting.

relations.note: In the paper's framework DyLoRA is the per-step random choice \(p=s_b\mathbf{1}_{[1,b]}\). MatryoshkaLoRA replaces the sampled rank with the deterministic \(p=\sum_r s_r\mathbf{1}_{[1,r]}\), a first-order surrogate of the same multi-rank objective, so every prefix gets gradient at every step.
\(p=s_R\mathbf{1}_R\) recovers standard rank-\(R\) LoRA.

Same \(B\,\mathrm{diag}(g)\,A\) shape. SoRA learns a sparse gate \(g\) to prune ranks; MatryoshkaLoRA freezes a non-increasing \(g=p\) to order the rank-1 components so that every prefix is usable. The paper does not cite SoRA.

methods.name: LoCO
methods.paper_title: LoCO: Low-rank Compositional Rotation Fine-tuning
methods.formula_latex: h=W_0\tilde R\,x,\ \ \tilde R=I_{d_{in}}+2\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i\big(I_{2r}-Y_i^{\top}X_i\big)^{-1}Y_i^{\top},\ \ X_i=[U_i\mid -V_i],\ Y_i=[V_i\mid U_i],\ U_i,V_i\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{in}\times r};\ \ \text{each summand is }R_i-I\text{ for the Cayley rotation }R_i=(I-\mathcal{A}_i)^{-1}(I+\mathcal{A}_i),\ \mathcal{A}_i=U_iV_i^{\top}-V_iU_i^{\top}\in\mathfrak{so}(d_{in})\ \text{(Woodbury form)},\ \text{and }\tilde R\text{ is the first-order (parallel) approximation of }R_1R_2\cdots R_n;\ \ \text{inference temperature }t:\ \mathcal{A}_i\mapsto t\,\mathcal{A}_i\ (t=1\text{ in training});\ \ W_0\ \text{frozen};\ \{U_i,V_i\}_{i=1}^{n}\ \text{trained}
methods.locus: input side of the adapted linear layers: all linear modules of DeBERTa-V3-base (GLUE), \(W_q\) and \(W_v\) of LLaMA-2-7B (math), the FLUX.1 diffusion transformer (OminiControl setup) and ViT-B/16 (VTAB-1k)
methods.structure: Right action on \(W_0\) of rotations generated by low-rank skew-symmetric matrices. One component is a Cayley rotation that maps the learned subspace \(\mathrm{span}(U_i,V_i)\) (dimension at most \(2r\)) into itself and fixes its orthogonal complement pointwise, computed through a \(2r\times 2r\) inverse in \(O(d_{in}r^2+r^3)\). Several components are combined by summing their deviations from \(I\) rather than multiplying them. Equivalently, \(\tilde R\) is the Cayley formula for \(\sum_i\mathcal{A}_i\) with the off-diagonal blocks \(Y_i^{\top}X_j\) (\(i\ne j\)) of the \(2nr\times 2nr\) core dropped. \(\tilde R\) is exactly orthogonal only for \(n=1\); in general \(\|I-\tilde R^{\top}\tilde R\|_F\le n(n-1)\gamma^2\) when \(\|R_i-I\|_F\le\gamma\). The induced additive update \(W_0(\tilde R-I)\) has rank at most \(2nr\). The LLaMA-2-7B math result uses \(n=1\), so it exercises the exact Cayley rotation, not the parallel approximation.
methods.mergeable_reason: For a fixed temperature, \(W_0\tilde R\) is a dense \(d_{out}\times d_{in}\) matrix and replaces \(W_0\) at no inference cost.
methods.identity_at_init: Approximate. The paper only says parameters start near zero, so \(\tilde R=I+O(\|U_i\|\|V_i\|)\); \(\tilde R=I\) holds exactly if, for example, every \(V_i=0\). At inference \(t=0\) recovers \(W_0\) exactly.
methods.key_idea: The tangent space \(\mathfrak{so}(d)\) of the rotation group admits a low-rank parametrization \(UV^{\top}-VU^{\top}\). Woodbury then makes its Cayley rotation cost \(O(dr^2)\) instead of \(O(d^3)\), and a first-order sum of several such rotations gives a richer, nearly orthogonal transform that can be computed in parallel. Scaling the generator by a temperature \(t\) at test time interpolates the adaptation strength.
methods.results_note: Fine-tuning \(W_q\) and \(W_v\) of LLaMA-2-7B on MetaMathQA-40K with 0.12% trainable parameters and a single component (\(n=1\), \(r=16\)), LoCO reaches 50.19 on GSM8K and 8.40 on MATH, against 49.35 and 8.39 for OFT, 50.04 and 7.45 for HRA (Table 2; the paper's text quotes 49.65 for HRA) and 45.58 and 6.85 for BOFT.

relations.note: Same Cayley-parametrized right multiplication \(W_0R\). The skew generator is low-rank (\(UV^{\top}-VU^{\top}\)) rather than block-diagonal, and its inverse is computed through Woodbury.

Both are input-side orthogonal transforms equal to \(I\) plus a low-rank term (rank at most \(r\) for HRA, at most \(2nr\) for LoCO). HRA composes \(r\) reflections sequentially; LoCO sums \(n\) Cayley rotations in parallel.
Both compose several orthogonal factors into a dense rotation: BOFT multiplies butterfly factors exactly and in sequence, while LoCO sums low-rank Cayley factors to first order.

A LoCO component with \(r=1\), \(U=a\,e_i\) and \(V=e_j\) is the Givens rotation by angle \(2\arctan a\) in plane \((i,j)\). LoCO learns the planes and combines them additively rather than as an exact product.
LOFT fixes an \(r\)-dimensional input support and trains \(T\in SO(r)\) on it. A single LoCO component instead rotates a learned subspace \(\mathrm{span}(U,V)\) of dimension at most \(2r\).
Both are input-centric and never form the \(d\times d\) rotation. OFTv2 keeps a block-diagonal generator with a Neumann-series inverse; LoCO uses a low-rank generator with an exact Woodbury inverse.

methods.name: Compress-then-Merge (CtM)
methods.full_name: Compress-then-Merge: merging several LoRAs into one low-rank LoRA inside learned shared subspaces
methods.paper_title: Compress then Merge: From Multiple LoRAs into One Low-Rank Adapter
methods.formula_latex: \Delta W^{(t)}=B^{(t)}A^{(t)}\ (t=1,\dots,T);\ \ \Delta W^{(t)}_{tgt}=\lambda^{(t)}\frac{\Delta W^{(t)}}{\|\Delta W^{(t)}\|_F},\ \ \lambda^{(t)}=\beta\|\Delta W^{(t)}\|_F+(1-\beta)\frac{1}{T}\sum_{s=1}^{T}\|\Delta W^{(s)}\|_F;\ \ (U,V)=\arg\min_{U^{\top}U=V^{\top}V=I_r,\ \{C^{(t)}\}}\sum_{t}\big\|\Delta W^{(t)}_{tgt}-UC^{(t)}V^{\top}\big\|_F^2\ \ \text{(Tucker-2 by HOSVD+HOOI, solved in Core Space: }U=U_BU_{core},\ V=V_AV_{core});\ \ O^{(t)}=U^{\top}\Delta W^{(t)}V\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r},\ O_{merged}=\mathcal{M}\big(\{O^{(t)}\}\big),\ \ \Delta W_{LoRA}=U\,O_{merged}\,V^{\top},\ U\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r},\ V\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{in}\times r};\ \ \text{nothing is trained and no data enters the merge (}\beta\text{ and the rule's hyperparameters are chosen on a validation holdout)}
methods.trainable_params: 0\ \text{(training-free); the output is one rank-}r\text{ LoRA, }r(d_{in}+d_{out})\text{ per adapted matrix (e.g. }B=U\,O_{merged},\ A=V^{\top})
methods.locus: layer-wise, every LoRA-adapted matrix (\(W_q\), \(W_k\), \(W_v\), \(W_o\) in the experiments: eight rank-16 CLIP ViT-B/32 LoRAs and six LLaMA3-8B NLI LoRAs, the public KnOTS checkpoints)
methods.structure: Merging inside a shared two-sided rank-\(r\) subspace: all tasks are represented in the same frame \(U\,\mathbb{R}^{r\times r}V^{\top}\), chosen by a Tucker-2 decomposition of the norm-rebalanced task tensor with an identity task-mode factor. The base rule \(\mathcal{M}\) (TIES, DARE-TIES, Iso-C, ...) acts on the \(r\times r\) coordinates, so \(\mathrm{rank}(\Delta W_{LoRA})\le r\) by construction. For a linear rule \(\mathcal{M}=\sum_tc_t(\cdot)\), the result is \(UU^{\top}\big(\sum_tc_t\Delta W^{(t)}\big)VV^{\top}\), a two-sided orthogonal projection of the task-arithmetic sum onto subspaces fitted to the whole collection. Merge-then-compress instead takes the top-\(r\) singular subspace of the merged sum, which large-norm adapters dominate. Core Space's lossless bases \(U_B, V_A\) of the concatenated factors reduce the subspace search to \((Tr_{in})\times(Tr_{in})\) matrices without changing the optimum.
methods.mergeable_reason: The output is a single rank-\(r\) update \(U\,O_{merged}V^{\top}\) that can stay a LoRA or fold into \(W_0\).
methods.identity_at_init: Not applicable: CtM is a post-hoc, data-free merge of already trained LoRAs and has no training phase.
methods.key_idea: Impose the rank-\(r\) bottleneck before merging, not after. CtM learns shared left and right \(r\)-dimensional subspaces from the (norm-rebalanced) LoRAs, projects each LoRA to \(r\times r\) coordinates, and merges there. The result is a rank-\(r\) LoRA by construction, and the rank budget is not spent mostly on large-norm adapters or intruder directions, as truncating the merged sum would.
methods.results_note: Merging eight rank-16 CLIP ViT-B/32 LoRAs into one LoRA, CtM with DARE-TIES reaches 70.68 average normalized accuracy, against 65.91 for the best merge-then-compress baseline (DARE-TIES in Core Space) and 66.34 for the best low-rank-aware baseline (Iso-CTS); CtM with Iso-C (66.27) does not beat Iso-CTS. On six LLaMA3-8B NLI LoRAs, CtM with DARE-TIES reaches 95.63.

relations.note: Uses Core Space's lossless projection onto the bases of the concatenated factors to solve its Tucker problem in a \((Tr_{in})\times(Tr_{in})\) space. Unlike Core Space, CtM's projection is lossy by design (rank \(r\)), so no post-hoc truncation is needed.
KnOTS aligns LoRAs in a lossless joint-SVD basis, so a rank-\(r\) output still needs truncated SVD; CtM's shared basis has rank \(r\) from the start.
TIES is one of the base rules \(\mathcal{M}\) applied to the \(r\times r\) coordinates; CtM with TIES or DARE-TIES gives the best single-LoRA results.
DARE-TIES applied in CtM's \(r\times r\) coordinate space is the best configuration on both CLIP ViT-B/32 (70.68) and LLaMA3-8B NLI (95.63).

Task Arithmetic is one of the extra base rules in Appendix D.4. With \(\mathcal{M}\) a weighted sum, CtM returns \(UU^{\top}\big(\sum_tc_t\Delta W^{(t)}\big)VV^{\top}\), the task-arithmetic merge projected onto the learned shared subspaces.
Another data-free method that outputs a single rank-\(r\) LoRA (by clustering rank-1 units); it is a baseline that CtM outperforms (62.36 on CLIP ViT-B/32).

TSV is one of the extra base rules in Appendix D.4. Inside CtM's \(r\times r\) coordinates its per-task budget shrinks to about \(r/T\) directions (two for \(r=16\), \(T=8\)), and CtM gives almost no gain over merge-then-compress for TSV.

methods.name: SRR (Structured Residual Reconstruction)
methods.paper_title: Preserve-Then-Quantize: Balancing Rank Budgets for Quantization Error Reconstruction in LLMs
methods.formula_latex: W_0\approx\hat W=Q+B^{(1)}A^{(1)}+B^{(2)}A^{(2)};\ \ B^{(1)}A^{(1)}=\mathrm{SVD}_{k^\star}\big(W_0S^{\top}\big)S^{-\top},\ \ Q=\mathcal{Q}\big(W_0-B^{(1)}A^{(1)}\big),\ \ E=W_0-B^{(1)}A^{(1)}-Q,\ \ B^{(2)}A^{(2)}=\mathrm{SVD}_{r-k^\star}\big(ES^{\top}\big)S^{-\top};\ \ k^\star=\arg\min_{0\le k\le r}\rho_k\big(W_0S^{\top}\big)\,\rho_{r-k}\big(\tilde ES^{\top}\big),\ \ \rho_p(M)=1-\frac{\sum_{j\le p}\sigma_j(M)^2}{\|M\|_F^2},\ \tilde E_{ij}\sim\mathcal{U}[-1,1];\ \ S\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{in}\times d_{in}}\ \text{activation-aware scaling (e.g. QERA-exact)};\ \ \text{QPEFT: }h=\big(Q+B^{(1)}A^{(1)}+B^{(2)}A^{(2)}\big)x,\ Q\ \text{frozen},\ B^{(1)},A^{(1)},B^{(2)},A^{(2)}\ \text{trained, with the gradients of }(B^{(1)},A^{(1)})\ \text{scaled by }\gamma\in(0,1)\ (\gamma=0.1)
methods.trainable_params: r(d_{in}+d_{out})\ \ (k^\star\text{ preserved plus }r-k^\star\text{ reconstruction ranks})
methods.locus: every quantized linear layer; QPEFT runs on RoBERTa-base (GLUE, MXINT 4/3/2-bit with ranks 8/8/64) and on LLaMA-2-7B and LLaMA-3.1-8B (SlimPajama with \(r=8\), GSM8K with \(r=64\)); \(\gamma=0.1\) by default
methods.structure: A low-rank-plus-quantized split of \(W_0\) in which a rank budget \(r\) is divided, per matrix, between preserving the top-\(k^\star\) singular subspace of the activation-scaled weight in high precision and reconstructing the scaled quantization error of the remainder with the other \(r-k^\star\) ranks. \(k=0\) is ordinary quantization-error reconstruction (QERA, LQER, ZeroQuant-V2); \(k=r\) preserves structure only, as in LQ-LoRA and SVDQuant. \(k^\star\) minimizes a closed-form proxy of the scaled reconstruction error, built from the spectrum of \(W_0S^{\top}\) and a single uniform-noise probe. For QPEFT the two low-rank blocks become one rank-\(r\) adapter on a frozen \(Q\), and the high-energy preserved block is damped by gradient scaling.
methods.mergeable_reason: As with LoftQ and QLoRA, \(Q+BA\) is a plain matrix only in high precision. Keeping the model in the low-bit format requires either leaving the adapter unmerged or re-quantizing \(Q+BA\).
methods.identity_at_init: Approximate: \(Q+B^{(1)}A^{(1)}+B^{(2)}A^{(2)}\approx W_0\), with scaled error \(\|(W_0-\hat W)S^{\top}\|_F\) left by the rank-\(r\) budget. The QPEFT start is \(\hat W\), not the quantized \(Q\) alone.
methods.key_idea: Quantizing the dominant directions of an anisotropic weight creates large, high-rank error that a rank-\(r\) correction cannot undo. SRR therefore keeps the leading \(k^\star\) scaled singular directions out of the quantizer and spends only the remaining \(r-k^\star\) ranks on error reconstruction. \(k^\star\) is chosen per matrix from \(\rho_k(W_0S^{\top})\rho_{r-k}(\tilde ES^{\top})\), and the resulting \(Q+BA\) is a QPEFT starting point whose preserved block trains with damped gradients.
methods.results_note: In 2-bit MXINT QPEFT of RoBERTa-base on GLUE, SRR raises the average score by 5.9 points over QERA and by more than 10 points over LoftQ and LQ-LoRA (gains of 1.5 and 4.7 points over QERA at 4 and 3 bits).

relations.note: Both start QPEFT from \(Q+BA\) close to \(W_0\). One LoftQ iteration is SRR's \(k=0\) end with \(S=I\) (quantize, then fit the residual); further LoftQ iterations alternate quantizing \(W_0-BA\) and refitting \(BA\), with no explicit rank split. SRR splits the rank once per matrix and beats five-iteration LoftQ by more than 10 GLUE points at 2 bits.

LQ-LoRA's low-rank-plus-quantized decomposition is the paper's preservation-only end (\(k=r\)), iterated. SRR picks \(k\) per matrix and adds an error-reconstruction block; the comparison uses the same QERA-exact scaling for both.
With \(S=I\), \(k^\star=r\) and no gradient damping, SRR's QPEFT start is QPiSSA: the principal rank-\(r\) part forms the adapter and the residual is quantized.
Same QPEFT setting: a frozen low-bit backbone plus a trainable low-rank adapter. SRR changes how the adapter is initialized and how its update is scaled.

methods.name: Prompt2Effect
methods.full_name: Prompt2Effect: weight-driven hypernetwork for SVD-canonicalized LoRA prediction
methods.paper_title: Prompt2Effect: Training-Free Image-to-Video Model Specialization via LoRA Generation
methods.formula_latex: X_W^{l}=\big[\,W_0^{l}P_B^{l}\,;\,(W_0^{l})^{\top}P_A^{l}\,\big]\in\mathbb{R}^{(d_{out}+d_{in})\times d_h},\ \ Q_W^{l}=\mathrm{CrossAttn}(Q_{\text{learned}},X_W^{l},X_W^{l})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_h};\ \ X_{\mathcal{E}}=H_{\mathcal{E}}\big(\{Q_W^{l}+e_l+e_M^{l}\}_{l=1}^{L},\,E_{\text{text}}(c_{\text{eff}})\big);\ \ X_{\mathcal{D}}^{l}=\mathrm{CrossAttn}(X_W^{l},X_{\mathcal{E}}^{l},X_{\mathcal{E}}^{l});\ \ \hat B^{l}=\mathrm{Head}_B\big(X_{\mathcal{D}}^{l}[:d_{out}]\big)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r},\ \ \hat A^{l}=\mathrm{Head}_A\big(X_{\mathcal{D}}^{l}[d_{out}:]\big)^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}};\ \ h=(W_0^{l}+\hat B^{l}\hat A^{l})\,x;\ \ \text{targets: }\Delta W_{\star}^{l}=U^{l}S^{l}(V^{l})^{\top}\Rightarrow B^{\star,l}=U^{l}(S^{l})^{1/2},\ A^{\star,l}=(S^{l})^{1/2}(V^{l})^{\top};\ \ \min_{\phi}\ \frac{1}{2L}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\Big(\frac{\|\hat A^{l}-A^{\star,l}\|_F^2}{\|A^{\star,l}\|_F^2+\epsilon}+\frac{\|\hat B^{l}-B^{\star,l}\|_F^2}{\|B^{\star,l}\|_F^2+\epsilon}\Big);\ \ \text{frozen: } W_0,\ E_{\text{text}};\ \text{trained once: hypernetwork } \phi=(H_{\mathcal{E}},H_{\mathcal{D}},P_A,P_B,Q_{\text{learned}},e);\ \text{nothing trained per effect}
methods.trainable_params: |\phi|\approx 1.3\text{B (one hypernetwork, trained once by NMSE regression on the SVD-canonicalised factors of 70 per-effect LoRAs for the 11B proprietary model, }\approx12\%\text{ of its size; 49 rank-32 community LoRAs for Wan2.1)};\ \text{per new effect: } 0\ \text{trained, generated adapter } r(d_{in}+d_{out})\ \text{per adapted matrix } (r=128;\ r=32\ \text{on Wan2.1})
methods.locus: LoRA target layers (a selected set of \(L\) linear layers) of a DiT image-to-video diffusion model: Snap's proprietary 11B I2V model, with the findings reproduced on Wan2.1-I2V-14B-480P
methods.structure: Amortised LoRA generation: one 1.3B Transformer hypernetwork maps \((c_{\text{eff}},\{W_0^{l}\}_{l=1}^{L})\) to all layer-wise rank-\(r\) factor pairs \((\hat B^{l},\hat A^{l})\) in a single forward pass. The frozen base matrix is tokenised CUR-style into its \(d_{out}\) rows and \(d_{in}\) columns at full rank (truncating \(W_0\) to its top singular directions hurt in ablation). These tokens are compressed by learned-query cross-attention to \(n=256\) latents and mixed with the prompt by cross-attention. They are then decompressed by cross-attention that uses the original row and column tokens as queries, so the rows of \(\hat B^{l}\) and the columns of \(\hat A^{l}\) are indexed by the same coordinates as \(W_0^{l}\). The regression targets are SVD-canonicalised: the gauge orbit \(\{(BR,R^{-1}A):R\in GL(r)\}\) of each trained LoRA is replaced by its balanced representative \((US^{1/2},S^{1/2}V^{\top})\), which is unique up to joint sign flips of paired singular vectors (and rotations inside repeated singular values). The deployed object is an ordinary additive low-rank delta \(\Delta W^{l}=\hat B^{l}\hat A^{l}\).
methods.mergeable_reason: Each generated update \(\Delta W^{l}=\hat B^{l}\hat A^{l}\) is a plain low-rank additive delta that can be folded into \(W_0^{l}\) for a given effect. Generated deltas also blend linearly in weight space: the paper composes two effects as \(\Delta W=0.5\,\Delta W_A+0.5\,\Delta W_B\). The hypernetwork is needed only to produce new effects.
methods.identity_at_init: Not identity by design, since a non-zero \(\Delta W^{l}\) is the output. Dropping the generated LoRA recovers the frozen base. When the prediction is used to initialise LoRA fine-tuning, training starts from \(B_0=\hat B,\ A_0=\hat A\) instead of \(B_0=0\).
methods.key_idea: A LoRA delta is defined relative to \(W_0\), so the generator is conditioned on the full-rank base weights (tokenised by rows and columns) as well as the effect prompt. The factorisation gauge \((B,A)\sim(BR,R^{-1}A)\) is removed by regressing SVD-canonical factors \((US^{1/2},S^{1/2}V^{\top})\). Together these two choices make one-pass LoRA synthesis stable at video-DiT scale, where a HyperDreamBooth-style generator trains unstably and scores zero on the VLM judge.
methods.results_note: On Snap's 11B image-to-video model, the zero-shot predicted LoRAs score 56.93 overall on the VLM judge for in-distribution effects, against 57.57 for per-effect trained LoRAs and 42.57 for the base model, while replacing about 56 GPU-hours of training with 3.3 s of hypernetwork inference. Used as an initialisation, 100 fine-tuning steps reach an overall VLM score of 56.33 on out-of-distribution effects, versus 56.70 for a 1,000-step LoRA trained from scratch.

relations.note: Cited prompt-to-LoRA hypernetwork. Prompt2Effect follows the same recipe of regressing a library of trained LoRAs from a text prompt with learned layer and module-type embeddings, and adds conditioning on the base weights and SVD-canonicalised targets.
A HyperDreamBooth-style hypernetwork is the main learned baseline. Scaled to video LoRAs it trains unstably and gives near-zero VLM scores.
Cited prompt-to-weights generator for LLMs. Prompt2Effect targets video DiTs and adds base-weight conditioning.

Same amortised LoRA-generation line (not cited). D2L conditions on the frozen model's activations over a document and trains by context distillation. Prompt2Effect conditions on the frozen weights and an effect prompt and trains by regression on a LoRA library.

Two treatments of the same \(GL(r)\) symmetry of LoRA factors (not cited). Prompt2Effect picks a canonical SVD representative of each orbit; Learning on LoRAs builds GL-equivariant networks that act on whole orbits.

methods.name: GiVA
methods.paper_title: GiVA: Gradient-Informed Bases for Vector-Based Adaptation
methods.formula_latex: h=W_0x+\Gamma B\,\Lambda A\,x,\quad \Gamma=\mathrm{diag}(\gamma),\ \gamma\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}},\ \ \Lambda=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda),\ \lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{r};\ \ G=\nabla_W\mathcal{L}(W_0)\ \text{(full fine-tuning gradient on one batch)},\ G\approx U\Sigma V^{\top}\ \text{(low-rank SVD)};\ \ A=V_r^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}},\ \ B\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r}\ \text{with } B^{\top}B=I_r\ \ (\text{TopSV-B: } U_{[:,1:r]},\ \text{SecSV-B: } U_{[:,r+1:2r]},\ \text{Rand-B: QR of a Gaussian});\ \ \gamma_0=0,\ \lambda_0=\mathbf{1};\ \ \text{frozen: } W_0,\ A,\ B\ \text{(per layer)};\ \text{trained: } \gamma,\ \lambda
methods.trainable_params: d_{out}+r\ \text{per adapted matrix (plus frozen per-layer bases, } r(d_{in}+d_{out})\text{, stored once per task)}
methods.locus: any linear layer; paper: all attention and MLP projections of RoBERTa-base/large (GLUE); query, key, value, up and down projections (plus gate for Phi-3) of Qwen2-0.5B, Phi-3-3.8B and OLMo-2-7B (commonsense reasoning), OLMo-2-7B (MetaMathQA, Code-Feedback) and all attention and MLP projections of Mistral-7B (Alpaca instruction tuning); DINOv2-ViT-B/14 and CLIP-ViT-L/14 (image classification)
methods.structure: This is VeRA-type vector adaptation \(\Delta W=\Gamma B\Lambda A\): two trainable diagonals around a frozen rank-\(r\) pair. Unlike VeRA, the frozen pair is per-layer and task-informed rather than shared and random. \(A\) spans the top-\(r\) right singular subspace of the one-batch full fine-tuning gradient \(G\), and \(B\) is any matrix with orthonormal columns. Theorem 1 shows this choice minimises \(\|GA^{\top}B^{\top}BA-G\|_F\): it makes \(GA^{\top}B^{\top}BA=GV_rV_r^{\top}\) the best rank-\(r\) approximation of \(G\) (Eckart-Young). The objective comes from a first-order expansion at \(\Gamma_0=0,\Lambda_0=I\) that writes \(\nabla_\Gamma\mathcal{L}\) as the full matrix \(GA^{\top}B^{\top}\). For the diagonal \(\Gamma\) actually trained, only the diagonal of that matrix is used, so the matching is exact only for this relaxation. After training, the row space of \(\Delta W\) lies in the fixed subspace \(\mathrm{span}(V_r)\) and its column space in \(\Gamma\,\mathrm{span}(B)\). The trainable freedom is an \(r\)-vector rescaling of the frozen directions plus a \(d_{out}\)-vector rescaling of output coordinates.
methods.mergeable_reason: After training, \(\Delta W=\Gamma B\Lambda A\) is a fixed matrix of rank at most \(r\) that folds into \(W_0\), as with VeRA.
methods.identity_at_init: Exact: \(\gamma_0=0\) gives \(\Delta W_0=0\). Because \(\Gamma_0=0\), the gradient with respect to \(\lambda\) is zero at the first step, so only \(\gamma\) moves initially.
methods.key_idea: Vector-based adapters such as VeRA need very high rank (e.g. \(r=1024\)) because their frozen bases are random and carry no task information. GiVA sets the bases to the dominant right singular vectors of the first-step full fine-tuning gradient, with \(B\) orthonormal. The same \(d_{out}+r\) trainable scalars then suffice at one-eighth of VeRA's rank or less (from \(8\times\) lower on MetaMathQA and image classification to \(128\times\) lower on GLUE with RoBERTa-base), which brings training time close to LoRA's.
methods.results_note: On GLUE with RoBERTa-base, GiVA at \(r=8\) (0.08M trainable parameters, Rand-B) averages 83.8, versus 83.6 for VeRA at \(r=1024\) (0.16M) and 83.3 for LoRA at \(r=4\) (0.66M); parameter counts exclude the classification heads. Fine-tuning OLMo-2-7B on MetaMathQA takes 2h57m, versus 2h54m for LoRA and 3h26m for VeRA.

relations.note: Same \(\Gamma B\Lambda A\) parameterisation and scaling-vector initialisation. The frozen shared random bases are replaced by per-layer gradient-SVD bases.

Borrows the first-step full-gradient SVD initialisation. LoRA-GA then trains \(A\) and \(B\), whereas GiVA freezes them and trains only the two scaling vectors. The SecSV-B variant mirrors LoRA-GA's use of singular vectors \(r+1\) to \(2r\).
The TopSV-B variant uses the top left singular vectors of the gradient, as LoRA-One does for LoRA.
Cited. Also freezes gradient-initialised low-rank bases but trains a tiny \(r\times r\) core (\(r^2\) entries); GiVA trains \(d_{out}+r\) diagonal entries instead.
Compared vector-based baseline with frozen random bases and full-rank updates.
Another VeRA derivative (not cited). It keeps random bases and makes the bottleneck stochastic instead of task-informed.

methods.name: AP (Activation Prompt)
methods.full_name: Activation Prompt: universal additive perturbation of one intermediate activation map
methods.paper_title: Visual prompting reimagined: The power of the Activation Prompts
methods.formula_latex: z^{(k)}=f_{\theta^{(k)}}\big(z^{(k-1)}\big),\ z^{(0)}=x;\quad z^{(l)}\ \leftarrow\ z^{(l)}+\delta^{(l)}\ \text{at a single chosen layer } l,\ \ \delta^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{D'\times P'}\ \ (\text{channels}\times\text{spatial positions for CNNs};\ d\times\text{tokens for ViTs});\quad \min_{\delta^{(l)},\,W_{head}}\ \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{(x,y)\in\mathcal{D}}\ell\big(f_{\theta}(x,\delta^{(l)});y\big);\ \ l=0\ \text{recovers additive input-level VP};\ \ \text{frozen: backbone } \theta;\ \text{trained: } \delta^{(l)}\ \text{and the linear head}
methods.trainable_params: D'P'=|z^{(l)}|\ \text{(one activation-sized tensor, e.g. } d\times\text{tokens at a ViT block input)}+|W_{head}|;\ \text{Table 2 totals, which also count the trained head: } 0.12\text{M (ResNet-101)},\ 0.16\text{M (ViT-L/16)}\ \text{(the paper does not state the exact prompt shape; a full } 197\times1024\ \text{ViT-L/16 token map would be}\approx0.20\text{M)}
methods.locus: a single intermediate activation map: by default the input of the third-to-last residual block of ResNet-101 (CNNs prefer deep layers) and the input of the third Transformer block of ViT-L/16 (ViTs prefer shallow layers); also tested on CLIP and Swin
methods.structure: An input-independent additive offset \(z^{(l)}\mapsto z^{(l)}+\delta^{(l)}\) on the full activation tensor of one layer. Each channel and each position gets its own value, so this is a constant bias map rather than a per-channel bias. Input-level additive VP is the case \(l=0\). Proposition 1 (Appendix C.2) matches AP with shift-only normalisation tuning at the same layer under unit effective scale: for CNNs, if \(\gamma_d/\sigma_d=1\) and \(\delta^{(l)}\) is the same \(\delta_*\) at every position, AP equals BatchNorm tuning with \(\beta_d=w_d^{(l)}\delta_*+\mu_d\); for ViTs, if \(\gamma_d/\sigma_{b,p}=1\) and the LayerNorm mean \(\mu_{b,p}=\mu_p\) is the same for every sample, AP equals LayerNorm tuning with \(\beta_d=\delta^{(l)}_{p,d}+\mu_p\), i.e. \(\delta^{(l)}=\beta-\mu\). AP is therefore a position-resolved relative of a single-layer normalisation shift. Unlike VPT, it adds no tokens and touches one layer. Backpropagation only has to reach layer \(l\), so a deep \(l\) in a CNN cuts training memory and time.
methods.mergeable_reason: \(\delta^{(l)}\) is a fixed tensor added to the activations, so inference costs one addition and no extra matmuls; the paper claims no additional inference overhead but does not discuss folding. Folding into existing parameters is possible only for a position-uniform \(\delta^{(l)}\) at a point where the next operations are affine (for example the output bias of the preceding block's last linear layer in a ViT residual stream). A position-specific \(\delta^{(l)}\) needs a per-position bias, which standard layers lack, so it is stored as a constant bias map.
methods.identity_at_init: Exact when \(\delta^{(l)}=0\), because the frozen network is then unchanged. The paper does not state how \(\delta^{(l)}\) is initialised. The linear head is trained as in linear probing.
methods.key_idea: Moving the universal additive prompt from pixels to one intermediate activation turns visual prompting into a single-layer activation shift that is provably related to normalisation tuning. The best layer depends on the architecture (deep for CNNs, shallow for ViTs), which the authors tie to where global features live. Theorem 1, for a two-layer ViT on a four-pattern data model, gives zero generalisation error with \(N=\Theta(P)\) samples when AP is at the first layer and with \(N=\Theta(P^{2}\log P)\) when it is at the second, where \(P\) is the number of tokens; these are sufficient sample sizes, which the paper reads as shallow AP needing fewer samples.
methods.results_note: Across 19 datasets from FGVC, VTAB and five other benchmarks, AP beats input-level VP on every dataset for both ResNet-101 and ViT-L/16, with average gains of about 4% and 1.5%. On ResNet-101 it also nearly halves training memory relative to VP (6.3 GB vs 12.2 GB) and cuts time per epoch from 72 s to 41 s. On VTAB-1k few-shot it beats VP by 4.3 points (ResNet-101) and about 1 point (ViT-L/16).

relations.note: Additive input-level VP is AP at layer \(l=0\) (the padding-frame VP prompt is a restriction of the full-image \(\delta^{(0)}\)); the paper uses AP to explain why VP lags.

Norm-Tune (Basu et al. 2023, which trains all normalisation affine parameters, the same mechanism as LN-tuning) is a main baseline. Proposition 1 links single-layer AP to unit-scale, shift-only normalisation tuning at that layer under extra conditions, but AP does not contain multi-layer \(\gamma,\beta\) tuning, so it does not generalize LN-tuning.

VPT prepends tokens at the input or at every layer; AP adds a bias map at one chosen layer. On ViT-L/16 (Table 3) AP beats VPT-deep on the VTAB and 'Others' averages (90.25 vs 89.24, 91.09 vs 90.14) but trails it on FGVC (85.30 vs 86.34), with fewer parameters (0.16M vs 0.25M), less memory and higher throughput.

Not cited. Both edit activations without touching weights. RED applies a per-channel scale and bias, shared across positions, at every FFN output; AP is bias-only but position-specific and confined to one layer.
Not cited. LoFiT adds learned offset vectors to selected attention-head outputs; AP adds an offset to an entire activation map of one layer.
SSF's scale-and-shift feature modulation in every layer is a compared PEFT baseline (Table A8); SSF is better on FGVC and slightly worse on VTAB.

methods.name: Stable-LoRA
methods.full_name: Stable-LoRA: early-step weight shrinkage of the LoRA down-projection
methods.paper_title: Stable-LoRA: Stabilizing Feature Learning of Low-Rank Adaptation
methods.formula_latex: h=W_0x+s\,BAx,\quad B_0=0,\ \ A_0\ \text{entries sampled from } [-1/d_{in},\,1/d_{in}];\ \ \text{while not stable: if } \|A_t\|_F/d_{in}>\|B_t\|_F/d_{out}\ \text{then } A_t\leftarrow(1-\lambda)A_t\ \text{else set stable};\ \ A_{t+1}=A_t-\eta g_A^t-\eta wA_t,\ \ B_{t+1}=B_t-\eta g_B^t-\eta wB_t\ \ (g=\text{AdamW-processed gradients},\ w=\text{weight decay});\ \ \lambda\in\{5\times10^{-4},10^{-3},2\times10^{-3},5\times10^{-3}\}\ \text{(searched)};\ \ \text{frozen: } W_0;\ \text{trained: } A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}},\ B\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r}
methods.trainable_params: r(d_{in}+d_{out})\ \text{(identical to LoRA; the shrinkage is in place, so no extra memory)}
methods.locus: any LoRA-adapted linear layer; paper default q_proj and v_proj (\(r=8\)) of Qwen2-0.5B/1.5B and LLaMA-3.2-1B/3B, with ablations on qkvo and all seven projections and a Llama-3.1-8B math run (Appendix D.2)
methods.structure: The parameterisation is plain LoRA, \(\Delta W=sBA\); only the optimisation trajectory changes. During the first few steps, an in-place multiplicative decay \(A\leftarrow(1-\lambda)A\), independent of the learning rate, is applied to the down-projection only, before the AdamW update. It stops once the balance condition \(\|A\|_F/d_{in}\le\|B\|_F/d_{out}\) holds, after which training is ordinary AdamW (Algorithm 1 uses one flag; the released optimizer keeps a separate stop flag per adapted matrix). Because only \(A\) is shrunk, each shrink step rescales the current update \(\Delta W\) by \((1-\lambda)\). This differs from a gauge move \((A,B)\mapsto(cA,B/c)\), which would leave \(\Delta W\) unchanged. After \(N\) shrink steps the initialisation enters \(A_N\) only through \((1-\lambda)^{N}A_0\).
methods.mergeable_reason: The trained adapter is a standard \(sBA\) and merges like LoRA; the procedure changes only how \(A\) and \(B\) are reached.
methods.identity_at_init: Exact: \(B_0=0\) gives \(\Delta W_0=0\). Shrinking \(A\) while \(B=0\) leaves the function unchanged; later shrink steps scale \(\Delta W\) by \((1-\lambda)\).
methods.key_idea: The paper writes \(v=\Theta(n^{\gamma[v]})\) for scaling in the width \(n\) and assumes Adam-normalised gradients with \(\gamma[g_A^tZ]=1\). Under these conditions, LoRA is self-stabilised, meaning feature updates \(\Delta Y_t=\Theta(1)\) for all \(t\), when \(\gamma[s]+2\gamma[\eta]+1=0\), \(\gamma[A_0Z]\le\gamma[\eta]+1\) and \(\gamma[B_0]\le\gamma[\eta]\) (Theorem 3.1). The usual non-zero \(A_0\) violates the \(A_0\) condition at practical learning rates, and the violation persists through training. Stable-LoRA therefore keeps \(A_0\)'s early benefit (escaping the saddle at zero) but decays it geometrically until the balance condition holds.
methods.results_note: On Qwen2 (0.5B, 1.5B) and LLaMA-3.2 (1B, 3B) multiple-choice QA, Stable-LoRA has the best or tied-best accuracy on every dataset and model against AdamW-LoRA, LoRA+, Riemannian preconditioning and LoRA-RITE, with gains of up to 4 points over AdamW (average gains 0.5 to 2.1 points), at 0.6% extra training time and no extra memory. It also beats AdamW-LoRA on MetaMathQA-to-GSM8K chain-of-thought training (LLaMA-3.2-1B/3B and Llama-3.1-8B).

relations.note: Same parameterisation; only the training procedure changes.
LoRA+ restores width-stable feature learning with \(\eta_B>\eta_A\) (baseline run with \(\eta_B=4\eta_A\)). Stable-LoRA keeps one learning rate and decays \(A\) early.
Alternative route to stable LoRA feature learning (\(r\times r\) preconditioners), used as a baseline. It costs +8.3% training time versus +0.6% for Stable-LoRA in their timing (Table 5).
Transformation-invariant LoRA optimiser, used as a baseline. It costs +46% training time versus +0.6% for Stable-LoRA (Table 5).

Keeps the initialisation \(B_0=0,\ A_0\neq0\) that Hayou et al. favour. Stable-LoRA shows that this non-zero \(A_0\) breaks width-stability unless the learning rate is large enough, and removes its long-term effect by shrinkage.

methods.trainable_params: \text{training: } |\Theta|+\sum_l|\phi_l|\ (\approx(1+D_S+D_B)d_b+D_B\ \text{each})+|\mathcal{G}|+|f_{mask}|+|W_S|+|W_B|+2D_B\ \text{per backbone LayerNorm};\ \ \text{kept at inference: } 2D_B\ \text{per LayerNorm}+|W_B|
methods.locus: training: a thin side network (widths divided by a reduction factor, initialised from pretrained weights) fed by the backbone's per-layer features, plus distillation bottlenecks and a generator; deployed: the LayerNorm affine parameters of every backbone block and a new task head (ViT-B on VTAB-1K, T5-base/large on GLUE, VSE-infinity, CLIP4Clip, CLIP-ViL and MDETR for vision-language tasks)
methods.structure: A training-only ladder side network serves as scaffolding and is discarded at inference. Two distillation paths couple it to the frozen backbone. In the feature path (backbone to side), each side layer is regressed onto the backbone's features: directly through a bottleneck \(\phi(s)=sM_{down}M_{up}\) in shallow layers, and in deep layers by regenerating the teacher features from masked student tokens with a small convolutional generator \(\mathcal{G}\) (two \(3\times3\) convolutions and a ReLU). In the logit path (side to backbone), the task-trained side head teaches a new backbone head \(W_B\). The paper states that the only trainable state left in the backbone is the per-block LayerNorm \((\gamma,\beta)\) plus \(W_B\), so the deployed model is a normalisation-tuned backbone plus head; the paper does not say what is tuned in its CNN backbones (ResNeXt-101 in VSE\(\infty\), ResNet-101 in MDETR), which have no LayerNorm, and T5's LayerNorm has no shift. The side network acts as an auxiliary teacher whose task knowledge is distilled into that selective subset.
methods.mergeable_reason: The deployed model changes only normalisation affine parameters and adds a head, with no extra modules or tokens: the new \((\gamma,\beta)\) replace the pretrained values in place, and where a LayerNorm feeds only linear maps they could also be folded into those maps. The side network, the bottlenecks \(\phi\) and the generator \(\mathcal{G}\) are discarded.
methods.identity_at_init: Backbone features are unchanged at initialisation: \((\gamma_l,\beta_l)\) start at their pretrained values, and the side network does not feed back into the backbone. The task heads \(W_B,W_S\) are new, so the output layer is not identity-initialised.
methods.key_idea: Memory-efficient side-tuning keeps its side network at inference and pays for it in latency. MDPD instead uses the side network as a training-time teacher, mutually distilled with the frozen backbone. Its task knowledge ends up in the backbone's LayerNorm \((\gamma,\beta)\) and head, so it can be dropped at deployment.
methods.results_note: On vision-language tasks MDPD improves accuracy over UniPT and SHERL at almost the same training memory and cuts SHERL's inference time by at least 25.2% (the abstract's figure; the contribution list says 22.5%). On VTAB-1K with ViT-B its mean of 78.3 is the best among the compared PETL and METL methods (HST 78.1, SHERL 77.9), at 2.1 GB training memory.

relations.note: Uses an LST-style side network with ladder inputs from the backbone layers and LST's T5 layer-dropping, and is compared against LST. Unlike LST, the side network is dropped at inference.

Not cited (MDPD cites Kim et al. 2021 for normalisation tuning). The deployed model is a LayerNorm-tuned backbone plus head; MDPD learns those LayerNorm parameters through distillation from a side network instead of the task loss alone.
Res-Tuning and its memory-efficient Bypass variant are both compared baselines on VTAB-1K (means 76.3 and 72.3).

methods.structure:
The function class is LoRA's (an additive rank-\(r\) update \(\Delta W=X\)), but the optimisation variable is the point \(X\) on the fixed-rank manifold \(\mathcal{M}_r\), which is the quotient \((\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}	imes r}_*	imes\mathbb{R}^{d_{in}	imes r}_*)/GL(r)\) of full-rank factor pairs under \((B,A)\sim(BS,S^{-1}A)\); every step is therefore independent of the factorisation gauge. The Riemannian gradient \(P_X(
abla_W\mathcal{L})\) has rank \(\le 2r\) and is obtained without forming \(
abla_W\mathcal{L}\), by differentiating \(\mathcal{L}(W'+Z_1V^{	op}+UZ_2^{	op})\) at \(Z_1=0\) (a rank-\(2r\) LoRA forward and backward pass). The Muon step is the linear-minimisation-oracle direction over the spectral-norm ball restricted to the tangent space, approximated by \(P_X(\mathrm{Ortho}_{2r}(M_t))\); the singular values of this direction stayed in \((0.9,1.1)\) in their runs. Momentum is moved by projection transport and the retraction is a thin truncated SVD (Algorithm 4 also applies a decoupled weight decay \(\gamma\) inside the retraction step), so a step costs \(O((d_{in}+d_{out})r^2+r^3)\) plus one backward pass, as for factor-wise Muon. LOI chooses the starting point whose tangent space captures most of the full gradient. Theorem 5.1 parametrises all maximisers by \(S\in GL_{2r}\) acting on the top-\(2r\) gradient singular pairs (assuming \(\sigma_{2r}
eq\sigma_{2r+1}\)); the experiments use \(S=\operatorname{diag}(\alpha I_r,I_r)\), i.e. \(X_0=\alpha U_{1:r}V_{r+1:2r}^{	op}\), computed by a randomised SVD with \(2(q+1)\) extra backward passes (about 0.25% of fine-tuning time). The paper writes the orthogonalisation as \(\mathrm{Ortho}_r\) although it sets the first \(2r\) singular values to 1; the formula here calls it \(\mathrm{Ortho}_{2r}\).
methods.mergeable_reason: The trained update is a rank-\(r\) matrix in thin factored form, so \(W=W'+X_T\) (with \(W'=W_0-X_0\) under LOI) folds into one dense weight exactly as LoRA does.
methods.identity_at_init: Under LOI the frozen weight is shifted, \(W'=W_0-X_0\), so \(W'+X_0=W_0\) and the model is unchanged at step 0. \(\alpha\) is kept small, which is safe because no Gram matrix is inverted. A variant with LoRA-style zero initialisation is also reported.
methods.key_idea: Optimise the LoRA update as a point on the fixed-rank manifold \(\mathcal{M}_r\) rather than as two factors, so the step cannot depend on the \(GL(r)\) gauge \((B,A)\sim(BS,S^{-1}A)\), and take Muon's orthogonalised (spectral-norm steepest-descent) step inside the tangent space. A matching initialisation picks the rank-\(r\) point whose tangent space is best aligned with the full fine-tuning gradient.
methods.results_note: On eight commonsense-reasoning tasks with Llama-3-8B at rank 16, Riemannion averages 88.1% versus 87.1% for AdamW-trained LoRA, 86.8% for Riemannian-preconditioned AdamW, 86.6% for DoRA, 84.5% for LoRA-RITE and 83.0% for factor-wise Muon.

relations.note: Main geometry-aware baseline (RPrecAdamW, 86.8 vs 88.1). Zhang and Pilanci precondition each factor with the other factor's \(r\times r\) Gram inverse inside an Adam-style update, which keeps a dependence on the parametrisation; Riemannion works on the fixed-rank manifold itself and inverts no Gram matrix.

Both aim at transformation-invariant LoRA updates. LoRA-RITE equilibrates an adaptive update in factor space; Riemannion gets invariance by construction on the manifold. In the paper's Llama-3-8B table LoRA-RITE scores 84.5 vs 88.1.

LOI maximises tangent-space alignment with the full gradient, and the paper states the link to LoRA-GA. Substituting a block-anti-diagonal \(S\) into Theorem 5.1 gives \(U_{r,2r}\Sigma_{r,2r}S_{21}S_{12}^{-1}\Sigma_{1,r}V_{1,r}^{\top}\), which is LoRA-GA's product initialisation (proportional to \(U_{r+1:2r}V_{1:r}^{\top}\)) when \(S_{21}S_{12}^{-1}\propto(\Sigma_{r,2r}\Sigma_{1,r})^{-1}\); the paper itself uses the mirrored member \(\alpha U_{1:r}V_{r+1:2r}^{\top}\). Both shift \(W_0\) by the initial update.

The geometry of rank-\(r\) matrices, here as the \(GL(r)\) quotient of factor pairs. Riemannion does not cite this paper; it runs Muon with the embedded-manifold version of the same geometry (tangent projection, truncated-SVD retraction, projection transport; Vandereycken 2013, Absil and Oseledets 2015).

methods.name: POET-X
methods.full_name: POET-X: scalable reparameterized training by orthogonal equivalence transformation (memory-efficient POET)
methods.paper_title: POET-X: Memory-efficient LLM Training by Scaling Orthogonal Transformation
methods.formula_latex: W_{RP}=R\,W_0\,P,\ \ W_0\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\ (m=d_{in},\ n=d_{out};\ \text{fixed random initialisation, e.g. normalised Gaussian}),\ \ R\in O(m),\ P\in O(n);\ \ y=W_{RP}^{\top}x=P^{\top}W_0^{\top}R^{\top}x\ \ (\text{so in the }h=Wx\text{ convention }W=P^{\top}W_0^{\top}R^{\top}:\ R\text{ acts on the input side, }P\text{ on the output side});\ \ \text{round }k:\ R_k=\Psi_k^{\top}\operatorname{Diag}\big(\tilde G_k^{1},\dots,\tilde G_k^{\lceil m/b\rceil}\big)\Psi_k,\ P_k=\Phi_k^{\top}\operatorname{Diag}\big(\tilde H_k^{1},\dots,\tilde H_k^{\lceil n/b\rceil}\big)\Phi_k\ \ (\Psi_k,\Phi_k\text{ random permutations});\ \ \tilde G=(I+Q)(I+Q+Q^{2}+Q^{3})=I+2Q+2Q^{2}+2Q^{3}+Q^{4}\approx(I+Q)(I-Q)^{-1},\ Q=-Q^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{b\times b}\ \text{(Cayley--Neumann, }k=3\text{; only the strict upper triangle of }Q\text{ stored)};\ \ y=P_k^{\top}\big(W_{k-1}^{\top}(R_k^{\top}x)\big)\ \text{(input-centric: three matrix--vector products)};\ \ \text{every 400 steps (`POET reset gap'): }W_k=R_kW_{k-1}P_k,\ Q\leftarrow0,\ \text{new permutations};\ \ \text{frozen within a round: }W_{k-1};\ \text{trained: the skew blocks of }R_k,P_k\ (\text{embeddings, LM head and norms are trained directly})
methods.trainable_params: \big(\lceil d_{in}/b\rceil+\lceil d_{out}/b\rceil\big)\tfrac{b(b-1)}{2}=\tfrac{(b-1)(d_{in}+d_{out})}{2}\ \text{per adapted matrix per round when }b\mid d_{in},d_{out};\ \text{Llama-3B }(d=2560,\ d_{ff}=7168,\ 32\text{ layers},\ \textstyle\sum(d_{in}+d_{out})=1{,}589{,}248):\ 127.5\times1{,}589{,}248=202.6\text{M }(b=256)\text{ or }255.5\times1{,}589{,}248=406.1\text{M }(b=512)\text{ POET parameters};\ \text{adding the }164.0\text{M embedding, LM-head and norm parameters reproduces the reported }366.64\text{M and }570.06\text{M of }2764.47\text{M};\ \text{the merged }W\text{ is a full matrix}
methods.locus: Linear layers of Llama-architecture LLMs trained from scratch on C4: Llama-3B for the perplexity tables (60B tokens; 10B for POET-XQ), Llama-8B for the wall-clock curves, and 8B and 13B in the memory and throughput benchmarks. \(W_0\) is a random initialisation, not a pretrained weight. The original POET was also used to fine-tune BART-large (its App. L).
methods.structure: Two-sided orthogonal equivalence: in the paper's convention \(W_0\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{in}\times d_{out}}\) and \(y=(RW_0P)^{\top}x\), so \(R\in O(d_{in})\) acts on the input side and \(P\in O(d_{out})\) on the output side, and the weight moves on the orbit \(\{RW_0P\}\) of the \(O(d_{in})\times O(d_{out})\) action, so with exact orthogonality its singular values equal those of \(W_0\) throughout training (the Cayley--Neumann truncation makes this approximate). OFT is the one-sided case \(P=I\). Large orthogonal matrices are reached by stochastic primitive optimisation: each round trains only permutation-conjugated block-diagonal factors \(\Psi^{\top}\operatorname{Diag}(\tilde G^{j})\Psi\) with \(b\times b\) blocks, merges them into the weight after a fixed number of steps (merge-then-reinitialise; 400 steps in the reported runs) and redraws the permutations, so the accumulated transform \((R_K\cdots R_1)W_0(P_1\cdots P_K)\) can range over the full groups. POET-X keeps this algorithm and changes how it is computed: an input-centric order \(P^{\top}(W^{\top}(R^{\top}x))\), so no transformed weight is stored for backpropagation; batched per-block products instead of materialised block-diagonal matrices; permutations as index maps, with two of the four folded into the frozen weight once per round; skew blocks stored as \(b(b-1)/2\) parameters; fused Triton kernels for the Cayley--Neumann forward and backward; and a recomputation variant (POET-X\(_{\text{mem}}\)) that also allows low-bit frozen weights (POET-XQ).
methods.mergeable_reason: \(R_kW_{k-1}P_k\) is a dense matrix of the original shape. Merging into the weight happens periodically by design and at the end of training, so inference uses one ordinary matrix with no overhead.
methods.identity_at_init: \(Q=0\) gives \(\tilde G=I\), hence \(R_k=P_k=I\) and \(W=W_{k-1}\) at the start of every round (and \(W=W_0\) at the start of training).
methods.key_idea: Learn each weight as an orthogonal equivalence transform \(W=RW_0P\) of a fixed matrix, which pins its spectrum, and make this trainable at LLM scale by optimising only permuted block-diagonal orthogonal factors that are periodically merged. POET-X's contribution is the implementation: an input-centric, kernel-fused computation that brings POET's memory down to LoRA-like levels and its speed close to AdamW.
methods.results_note: Pretraining Llama-3B on 60B C4 tokens, POET-X with \(b=512\) (570M trainable parameters) reaches validation perplexity 12.05 versus 12.69 for AdamW and 11.45 for Muon, using 68.5 GB of GPU memory versus 81.0 GB and 70.9 GB.

relations.note: OFT's \(W=RW_0\) is the one-sided case \(P=I\) on a pretrained \(W_0\). POET acts from both sides on a random \(W_0\) and merges periodically; both preserve the singular values of \(W_0\) (OFT preserves hyperspherical energy as well).

BOFT builds \(R\) from butterfly products of permuted block-diagonal orthogonal factors. POET-X uses one permuted block-diagonal factor per side per round and gets coverage from redrawn permutations across merge rounds. The POET-X paper cites BOFT only as related sparse-training work.

Same group. POET-X carries OFTv2's input-centric (matrix-free) computation into the two-sided case, where the gradient for the second orthogonal factor otherwise needs the full weight. The Cayley--Neumann parameterisation comes from the original POET (arXiv 2506.08001) and is shared with OFTv2.

Both pretrain with a parameter-efficient update that is merged into the weight and re-initialised periodically. ReLoRA's update is additive and low-rank; POET-X's is multiplicative, orthogonal and spectrum-preserving.
Memory-efficient pretraining baseline: 14.88 vs 12.05 validation perplexity on Llama-3B (60B tokens).
Baseline: 12.97 vs 12.05 on Llama-3B; in the 8-bit setting Q-APOLLO reaches 20.49 vs 14.78 for POET-XQ.

methods.name: LoRA-Mixer
methods.full_name: LoRA-Mixer: mixture of LoRA experts routed into the attention/SSM projections, with a Routing Specialization Balance Loss (RSL)
methods.paper_title: LoRA-Mixer: Coordinate Modular LoRA Experts Through Serial Attention Routing
methods.formula_latex: h=W_0x+\sum_{e\in\operatorname{TopK}(p(x))}p_e(x)\,B_eA_ex,\ \ p(x)=\operatorname{softmax}\big(G(x)\big)\in\Delta^{E-1},\ B_e\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r},\ A_e\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}}\ \ (\text{soft fusion over all } E\text{ experts while training the router; sparse top-}K\text{ at inference});\ \ \mathcal{L}_{total}=\mathcal{L}_{task}+\alpha\,\mathcal{L}_{RSL}+\beta\sum_{i\in\mathcal{C}}\|\theta_i-\theta_i^{(0)}\|^{2},\ \ \mathcal{L}_{RSL}=\alpha\sum_{i}\bar p_i\bar f_i-\lambda\,\mathbb{E}_x\big[\mathcal{H}(p(x))\big];\ \ \text{frozen: } W_0\text{ (and public or pre-trained experts in the plug-and-play regime); trained: the router } G\text{ (and optionally the experts)}
methods.trainable_params: E\,r(d_{in}+d_{out})\ \text{experts}+\text{a router per adapted projection (about }0.04\%\text{ of LLaMA3-8B in total)};\ 3.88\%\text{ of LLaMA3-8B with six trained experts; router only when frozen public LoRAs are composed}
methods.locus: Linear projections that feed and read out the token mixer: the q/k/v/o attention projections of LLaMA3-8B and Mistral-7B, and the projection layers of the Falcon-Mamba-7B mixer (App. A.11 describes the in-, out-, x- and dt-projections without saying exactly which are adapted). Plug-and-play routing over public LoRAHub LoRAs is shown on Flan-T5, and the LoRA-LEGO comparison uses LLaMA2-7B. The abstract contrasts this with methods that 'primarily' target FFN blocks.
methods.structure: Token-level mixture of \(E\) low-rank deltas on a frozen projection, \(\Delta W(x)=\sum_ep_e(x)B_eA_e\), placed on the attention (or SSM) input and output projections, so the routed update passes through the token mixer in series instead of acting as a parallel branch or an FFN switch. Experts come from three sources: public LoRAs (e.g. LoRAHub modules) kept frozen, independently trained LoRAs, or experts trained jointly with deterministic hard routing by domain label. The router is then trained on a small mixed set (about 2k examples) with soft fusion; inference uses sparse top-\(K\) fusion, and accuracy rises from \(K=1\) to \(K=3\) and then falls in their ablation. RSL adds an entropy term to the Switch-style load-balancing loss. As printed, \(\mathcal{L}_{RSL}\) subtracts \(\lambda\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{H}(p)]\), which rewards high routing entropy and matches the paper's strong-convexity argument, while other passages describe the term as lowering entropy to sharpen routing. A quadratic anchor keeps selected experts near their first-stage weights. The router architecture is not specified beyond its size. The paper writes each expert as \(\Delta W^{(e)}=A^{(e)}B^{(e)}\) with \(A^{(e)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r}\); formula_latex uses \(B_eA_e\) with \(B_e\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r}\), the same product with the letters swapped.
methods.mergeable_reason: The routing weights \(p(x)\) change with every token, so \(\sum_ep_e(x)B_eA_e\) has no single static form to fold into \(W_0\); only a fixed, input-independent expert choice could be merged.
methods.identity_at_init: Not identity when composing trained LoRAs: the frozen experts act from the first step and only the router is learned. The paper does not state the initialisation of experts trained from scratch, and the official repository contains only a README.
methods.key_idea: Put a routed mixture of LoRA experts into the projections that feed and read out attention or the SSM, so expert outputs pass through the token mixer, and train the router with a load-balance-plus-entropy loss that needs little data. Off-the-shelf LoRAs can then be composed plug-and-play, on Transformers and Mamba alike.
methods.results_note: On LLaMA3-8B with six experts (3.88% trainable parameters, 48% of MixLoRA's 8.08%), LoRA-Mixer beats MixLoRA on all seven tasks of the main table, for example 65.53 vs 64.44 on GSM8K and 57.32 vs 55.49 on HumanEval.

relations.note: Main LoRA-MoE baseline: top-k LoRA experts inside the FFN. LoRA-Mixer routes on attention/SSM projections with about half the trainable parameters.
Baseline. MoLE learns gating over frozen trained LoRA layers; the paper describes it as close in inference cost but coarser-grained and weaker.
Gradient-free few-shot composition of LoRAHub modules (baseline). LoRA-Mixer reuses the same kind of public modules but learns token-level routing.
Baseline on CoLA, SST-2, MRPC and RTE with LLaMA2-7B; LoRA-Mixer is better on three of the four.
Post-hoc routing over independently trained adapters; compared in and out of distribution (QQP, RTE, MRPC).
Not cited. X-LoRA also learns token-level mixing over frozen trained LoRAs, but scales every adapter of a layer from the hidden state instead of top-K routing on the mixer projections.
