methods.name: In-Place TTT
methods.full_name: In-Place Test-Time Training: the MLP down-projection as chunk-wise fast weights with an LM-aligned target
methods.paper_title: In-Place Test-Time Training
methods.formula_latex: Z=\phi(HW_{gate}^{\top})\odot(HW_{up}^{\top})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{ff}},\ \text{split into chunks } Z_{[i]}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times d_{ff}};\ \ O_{[i]}=Z_{[i]}\big(W_{down}^{(i)}\big)^{\top};\ \ \hat V=\operatorname{Conv1D}(X_0)\,W_{target}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d};\ \ W_{down}^{(i+1)}=W_{down}^{(i)}+\eta\,\hat V_{[i]}^{\top}Z_{[i]}\ \ \big(\text{one gradient step on } -\langle Z_{[i]}W^{\top},\hat V_{[i]}\rangle_F\big);\ \ W_{down}^{(0)}=W_0\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{ff}}\ \text{(pretrained), reset at document boundaries};\ \ \text{equivalently } W_{down}^{(i)}=W_0+\eta\textstyle\sum_{j<i}\hat V_{[j]}^{\top}Z_{[j]}\ \text{(a prefix sum, so chunks run in parallel)};\ \ \text{slow weights (all, plus new } W_{target}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\text{ and a depthwise kernel-5 Conv1D) trained by continual LM training; fast weights updated in closed form at inference}
methods.trainable_params: \text{outer loop: the whole model (continual training, AdamW, lr } 5\times10^{-6}\text{) plus } d^{2}+5d\text{ new parameters per TTT layer } (W_{target},\ \text{depthwise Conv1D});\ \text{inner loop: a fast-weight state } d\times d_{ff}\text{ per TTT layer, changed by rank-}\le C\text{ increments, with no gradients stored}
methods.locus: Down-projection \(W_{down}\) of the gated MLP in a subset of layers (every sixth layer, \([0,6,\dots,36]\), in the released long-context Qwen3 config): Qwen3-4B-Base, LLaMA-3.1-8B and Qwen3-14B-Base as a drop-in, and 0.5B to 4B models trained from scratch.
methods.structure: At inference the only parameters that change are the MLP down-projections of the TTT layers. Each change is the closed-form gradient step of a linear (negative inner-product) loss, so the delta added after chunk \(i\) is the rank-\(\le C\) outer-product sum \(\eta\hat V_{[i]}^{\top}Z_{[i]}\) between the MLP's intermediate activations and an LM-aligned target. The target mixes nearby future-token embeddings through a short convolution and a learned \(d\times d\) map, so the fast weight stores associations from keys to the tokens that follow them; an induction-head argument shows that the next-token target raises the correct logit while a reconstruction target does not. Apply-then-update keeps the scheme causal: chunk \(i\) is processed with \(W_0+\eta\sum_{j<i}\Delta_j\), so the convolution may look ahead inside a chunk. The released code uses a centred depthwise kernel of size 5 confined to each chunk and, by default, the normalised MLP input rather than the token embedding as the target source. Large chunks give parallelism (\(C=512\) to \(1024\) is best in the ablation, 4096 in the released config, whose inner rate is \(\eta=3\)), and inference clips each \(\|\Delta_i\|_F\) to \(\tau\) (\(\tau=10^{-5}\) for all reported Qwen3-4B evaluations). The slow weights, including the new target modules, are learned by ordinary continual pretraining through the unrolled updates.
methods.mergeable_reason: The fast-weight delta \(\eta\sum_{j<i}\hat V_{[j]}^{\top}Z_{[j]}\) depends on the current context and is reset at every document boundary, so there is nothing static to fold; the small target modules stay as extra parameters at inference.
methods.identity_at_init: The Conv1D kernel is zero-initialised (and \(W_{target}\) is a small random diagonal), so \(\hat V=0\) and every fast-weight delta vanishes when continual training starts: the warm-started model computes exactly the pretrained function. At test time each document starts from \(W_{down}^{(0)}=W_0\).
methods.key_idea: Turn an existing MLP's down-projection into test-time-training fast weights instead of adding a new recurrent layer, update it once per large chunk with a closed-form step, and point the update at next-token information rather than a reconstruction of the current token. Test-time weight adaptation then becomes a drop-in upgrade of a pretrained LLM that is compatible with context parallelism.
methods.results_note: After identical continual training of Qwen3-4B-Base, In-Place TTT raises RULER accuracy at 64k, 128k and 256k from 74.3, 74.8 and 41.7 to 78.7, 77.0 and 43.9, with near-equal scores at 4k to 32k.

relations.note: Both let an LLM change its own weights from new information. SEAL writes self-edits and applies LoRA SFT steps inside an RL outer loop; In-Place TTT applies a closed-form update to MLP down-projections inside the forward pass, chunk by chunk, with no backpropagation at inference.

Selective-locus counterpart. Sparse Memory Finetuning updates only the memory-layer slots that a batch activates and keeps the change; In-Place TTT updates a fixed locus (\(W_{down}\) of chosen layers) transiently per context and then resets it.

Both internalise a context into weights. Doc-to-LoRA generates a persistent LoRA from a document with a hypernetwork; In-Place TTT accumulates an additive update to \(W_{down}\) online, of rank at most \(C\) per chunk, over contexts up to 128k tokens and beyond.

methods.name: FZOO
methods.full_name: FZOO: Fast Zeroth-Order Optimizer (batched one-sided Rademacher estimates with a loss-std-normalised step)
methods.paper_title: FZOO: Fast Zeroth-Order Optimizer for Fine-Tuning Large Language Models towards Adam-Scale Speed
methods.formula_latex: l_0=\mathcal{L}(\theta_t;\mathcal{B}_t),\ \ l_i=\mathcal{L}(\theta_t+\epsilon u_i;\mathcal{B}_t),\ u_i\overset{iid}{\sim}\operatorname{Unif}\{\pm1\}^{D}\ (i=1,\dots,N);\ \ g_t=\frac{1}{\epsilon N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(l_i-l_0)\,u_i;\ \ \sigma_t^{2}=\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Big(l_i-\frac1N\sum_{j}l_j\Big)^{2};\ \ \theta_{t+1}=\theta_t-\eta_t\,\frac{g_t}{\sigma_t};\ \ \mathbb{E}\sigma_t^{2}=\epsilon^{2}\|\nabla\mathcal{L}\|^{2}+O(\epsilon^{3}),\ \mathbb{E}\|g_t\|^{2}=\tfrac{N+D-1}{N}\|\nabla\mathcal{L}\|^{2}+O(\epsilon)\ \Rightarrow\ g_t/\sigma_t\approx c\,g_t/\|g_t\|;\ \ N+1\text{ forward passes per step, no backpropagation; } \theta\text{ = all } D\text{ weights or a PEFT subset}
methods.trainable_params: \text{all } D\text{ parameters (full fine-tuning) or a PEFT subset (prefix-tuning in the paper); inference-level memory, as for MeZO}
methods.locus: All parameters (full-parameter) or the parameters of a PEFT module (prefix-tuning) of RoBERTa-large, the OPT family (125M to 66B; the abstract says 350M to 66B, and OPT-125M is used for the F1 and speed experiments), Phi-2 and Llama-3 (8B)
methods.structure: A zeroth-order gradient estimate built from \(N\) one-sided finite differences that share one unperturbed loss; to first order it is the rank-\(N\) random projection \(\frac1N\sum_iu_iu_i^{\top}\nabla\mathcal{L}\). The step is divided by the empirical standard deviation of the \(N\) perturbed losses, which estimates \(\epsilon\|\nabla\mathcal{L}\|\), so the update is a zeroth-order normalised-SGD step: large in flat regions, small in steep ones. Rademacher signs turn the perturbed matrix products into additions and subtractions, so the \(N\) perturbed forward passes are fused into one batched kernel (\(1.92\times\) faster on OPT-125M with \(N=8\)). The FZOO-R variant reuses half of the previous batch's losses when estimating \(\sigma_t\).
methods.mergeable_reason: FZOO only changes how updates are computed. In full-parameter mode it edits the model's own weights in place, so there is nothing to merge; in FZOO (prefix) the trained parameters are a prefix, which stays in the input and cannot be folded into the weights.
methods.identity_at_init: Trivial: there is no reparameterisation and training starts from \(\theta_0\).
methods.key_idea: Make MeZO-style fine-tuning converge in far fewer forward passes by averaging several one-sided Rademacher probes per step and dividing the step by the spread of their losses, which turns the update into a normalised-SGD step at inference-level memory.
methods.results_note: Across RoBERTa-large, OPT (350M to 66B), Phi-2 and Llama-3 on 11 tasks, the abstract reports that FZOO beats MeZO by +3% in accuracy with 3x fewer forward passes, and by +5.6% with 18x fewer forward passes on RoBERTa-large (the unit is not stated; in Table 1, \(k=16\), the averages are 71.4 vs 67.4).

relations.note: Direct successor and main baseline. FZOO replaces MeZO's single two-sided Gaussian SPSA probe and fixed step with \(N\) one-sided Rademacher probes and a step normalised by the loss standard deviation.
FZOO (prefix) runs the zeroth-order update on prefix parameters only, for further memory savings.
Later MeZO successor in the catalogue; not compared in the FZOO paper.
Later zeroth-order optimiser (February 2026); not compared in the FZOO paper.

corrections: mergeable: yes changed to conditional. Full-parameter FZOO edits the weights in place, but FZOO (prefix), which the paper evaluates (Tables 1 and 7, Fig. 5), trains a prefix that cannot be merged into the weights.

methods.name: LD-MoLE
methods.full_name: LD-MoLE: Learnable Dynamic routing for Mixture of LoRA Experts (Sparsegen router with a predicted, token-wise sparsity factor)
methods.paper_title: LD-MoLE: Learnable Dynamic Routing for Mixture of LoRA Experts
methods.formula_latex: h_t=W_0x_t+\frac{\alpha}{r}\sum_{i=1}^{E}p_{t,i}\,B_iA_ix_t\ \ (\alpha/r=16/8=2\text{ in the released code; the paper's Eq. 7 has no scale}),\ \ B_i\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r},\ A_i\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}};\ \ u_t=W_{gate}x_t\in\mathbb{R}^{E};\ \ \lambda_t=f(x_t)<1\ \text{(an MLP shared by all modules with the same } d_{in}\text{; in the code } f(x)=\mathrm{LogSigmoid}(\mathrm{MLP}(x))+1-\epsilon,\ \epsilon=10^{-2})\text{;}\ \ p_t=\arg\min_{p\in\Delta^{E-1}}\|p-u_t\|_2^{2}-\lambda_t\|p\|_2^{2}\ \Rightarrow\ p_{t,i}=\Big[\frac{u_{t,i}-\tau_t}{1-\lambda_t}\Big]_+,\ \tau_t=\frac{U_k-1+\lambda_t}{k},\ k=\max\{k:1-\lambda_t+k\,u_{(k)}>U_k\},\ U_k=\textstyle\sum_{j\le k}u_{(j)};\ \ \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{LM}+\alpha_{lb}\,E\sum_i\mathcal{F}_i\mathcal{P}_i+\beta\,\mathrm{ReLU}\big(\lambda_{lower}(k^{\star})-\lambda_t\big),\ \lambda_{lower}(k)=1-\big(U_k-k\,u_{(k+1)}\big);\ \ \text{frozen: } W_0;\ \text{trained: the experts, } W_{gate}\text{ and } f
methods.trainable_params: E\,r(d_{in}+d_{out})+E\,d_{in}\ \text{per adapted matrix } (E=8,\ r=8)+\text{one shared }\lambda\text{-MLP per distinct } d_{in}\ (64\,d_{in}+129\text{ in the released code});\ 2.33\%\text{ to }4.23\%\text{ of the base model in the paper}
methods.locus: Every linear projection (q, k, v, o, gate, up, down) of Qwen3-1.7B, Llama-3.2-3B and an 8B Llama-3 model
methods.structure: A mixture of \(E\) LoRA deltas per projection with token-wise sparse weights, \(\Delta W(x_t)=\frac{\alpha}{r}\sum_ip_{t,i}B_iA_i\). TopK is replaced by Sparsegen: the Euclidean projection of the gate logits onto the simplex with a quadratic bonus \(\lambda\|p\|^2\), equivalently sparsemax applied to \(u/(1-\lambda)\). It is piecewise linear, differentiable almost everywhere, and always keeps at least one expert, unlike ReLU routing. A small MLP predicts \(\lambda_t\) from the token, so the number of active experts varies by token and by layer. Because \(\lambda\) fixes the support analytically, a target count \(k\) becomes the closed-form \(\lambda\)-interval of Proposition 2, enforced by a hinge on \(\lambda\) (the main results use \(\beta=0\)). In the released code \(f\) is a two-layer MLP (hidden width 64, output bias initialised to \(-2.5\)) ending in a LogSigmoid, to which \(1-\epsilon\) with \(\epsilon=10^{-2}\) is added, so \(\lambda_t\in(-\infty,0.99)\), and the denominator \(1-\lambda_t\) is clamped at \(\epsilon\); the gate has no bias; all experts are evaluated densely and then weighted; and every \(B_i\) starts at zero. The paper writes each expert as \(\Delta W_i=A_iB_i\) with \(A_i\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r}\); formula_latex uses \(B_iA_i\) with the letters swapped.
methods.mergeable_reason: \(p_t\) changes from token to token, so the mixture cannot be folded into a static \(W_0\).
methods.identity_at_init: Not discussed in the paper. The released code zero-initialises every \(B_i\), so \(\Delta W(x)=0\) and the model starts at the frozen base.
methods.key_idea: Replace TopK routing in mixture-of-LoRA fine-tuning with a closed-form, differentiable Sparsegen projection whose sparsity \(\lambda\) is predicted per token by a shared MLP, so the number of experts per token and per layer is learned rather than fixed. The closed form also yields an analytic \(\lambda\)-interval for exactly \(k\) active experts, used as a sparsity loss.
methods.results_note: On Llama-3.2-3B, LD-MoLE averages 82.05 over nine benchmarks versus 81.42 for ReLU-routed ReMoLE and 78.72 for the best TopK MoLA configuration, with eight rank-8 experts on every projection (3.28% trainable parameters).

methods.locus: LoRA-adapted linear layers of OPT-2.7B/13B and Qwen3-1.7B/32B. The mechanism diagnostics use the 28 v_proj matrices of Qwen3-1.7B; the target modules of the main runs are not listed.
methods.structure:
The stored object is an ordinary rank-\(r\) LoRA delta \(\Delta W=\alpha\sum_k b_ka_k^{	op}\). AR1-ZO changes only how a two-point zeroth-order oracle measures it. Each query perturbs one matched rank-1 atom \((b_k,a_k)\), a block of dimension \(q=d_{out}+d_{in}\). Lemma 4.1 shows that, for nonzero factors, this is the smallest complete LoRA-native block: one-sided blocks miss part of the first-order variation \(\delta b_k a_k^{	op}+b_k\delta a_k^{	op}\). The estimator's dimension term is therefore \(q\), not \(rq\). The second ingredient is scale. Under the canonical coefficient \(\gamma/r=\alpha/r\), the active finite-difference signal is \(\Theta(1/r)\). Against a rank-independent evaluation-noise floor its SNR is \(\Theta(1/r^2)\), and \(\mathbb{E}\cos(\hat
abla_k\mathcal{L},
abla_k\mathcal{L})	o0\) once \(r\gg r_c=\Theta(\alpha\mu\|g\|/\sigma_\xi)\). The paper calls this directional collapse. Setting \(\gamma=\alpha r\) gives every queried atom the rank-free coefficient \(\alpha\). In forward-map terms, the method is LoRA with scale \(\alpha\) (instead of \(\alpha/r\) or \(\alpha/\sqrt r\)) trained by cyclic block-coordinate ZO over rank-1 atoms. Rank then appears only as coverage: over a cycle the stationarity measure is \(	frac1r\sum_k\|
abla_k\mathcal{L}\|^2\). The convergence bound (Theorem 4.4(ii)) separately assumes a stable represented-adapter scale, which the paper uses to rule out output inflation. This matters because under \(\gamma=\alpha r\) the joint output scale \(\alpha\sum_kb_ka_k^{	op}\) is no longer normalised by \(r\) (this last point is the entry's reading, not the paper's wording). A rank-\(m\) block query uses \(\gamma=\alpha r/m\) and has dimension \(mq\).
methods.mergeable_reason: The trained adapter is a plain additive delta \(\Delta W=\alpha BA\) and folds into \(W_0\) exactly like LoRA. The atom schedule and \(\gamma=\alpha r\) affect training only.
methods.identity_at_init: Yes. \(B\) is initialised at zero and \(A\) at random (Appendix B.1), so \(\Delta W=\alpha\sum_k b_ka_k^{\top}=0\) at step 0.
methods.key_idea: In zeroth-order LoRA, rank should set storage and coverage, not the dimension of each query or the signal it measures. AR1-ZO perturbs one complete rank-1 atom \((b_k,a_k)\) per two-forward-pass query and gives it the coefficient \(\gamma/r=\alpha\) instead of \(\alpha/r\). This removes the \(1/r^2\) decay of the finite-difference SNR that makes naive atomwise ZO collapse at high rank.
methods.results_note: With \(r=64\) and \(\alpha=16\) on OPT-2.7B (Table 1), AR1-ZO beats MeZO-LoRA on all six tasks, e.g. SQuAD F1 77.8 vs 64.6 and DROP 27.8 vs 23.9. The same atom schedule with canonical \(\alpha/r\) scaling (ZO-Alt-naive) collapses to 19.2 and 6.3.

relations.note: Uses the same two-point SPSA/RGE oracle on paired mini-batches, restricted to one LoRA atom per query.
Keeps the rank-\(r\) LoRA parameterisation and the \(B=0\) init. Only the coefficient (\(\gamma=\alpha r\)) and the per-step update set change.

Competing rank-scaling rule. rsLoRA uses \(\alpha/\sqrt{r}\) for joint first-order updates; AR1-ZO gives each queried atom the coefficient \(\alpha\). In the paper's SQuAD ablation (Fig. 7), both \(\alpha/r\) and \(\alpha/\sqrt{r}\) stagnate under atomwise ZO (F1 about 0.17, against 0.770 for \(\gamma=\alpha r\)).

Another way to cut ZO perturbation dimension. AGZO perturbs in an activation-derived rank-\(r\) subspace of the dense weight; AR1-ZO uses the native LoRA atoms, with no auxiliary basis and no activation hooks. AGZO is cited in AR1-ZO's related work but is not a baseline.

Another 2026 low-dimensional ZO fine-tuning scheme, using a random rank-\(r\) subspace plus orthogonalisation. AR1-ZO instead exposes the stored LoRA atoms one at a time. AR1-ZO does not cite ZO-Muon, so this is a structural comparison, not a reported baseline.

methods.name: Pico
methods.full_name: Pico: Pre-merge interference calibration in output-space
methods.paper_title: Crowded in B-Space: Calibrating Shared Directions for LoRA Merging
methods.formula_latex: \text{per layer and target module, with LoRAs } \Delta W_t=B_tA_t\ (t=1,\dots,T;\ \text{scale absorbed into } B_t):\ \ B_{\text{all}}=[B_1,\dots,B_T]=U\Sigma V^{\top},\ \ s_j=\frac{\sigma_j^2}{\sum_k\sigma_k^2},\ \ \alpha_j=\frac{1}{1+(T-1)s_j},\ \ S=I_{d_{out}}+U\,\mathrm{diag}(\alpha-\mathbf{1})\,U^{\top},\ \ \tilde B_t=SB_t;\ \ \Delta W_{\text{calib}}=\mathcal{M}\big(\tilde B_1A_1,\dots,\tilde B_TA_T\big)\ \ (\mathcal{M}\in\{\text{TA},\text{TIES},\text{TSV-M},\dots\}),\ \ \Delta W_{\text{Pico}}=\gamma\,\Delta W_{\text{calib}},\ \ \gamma=\frac{\tfrac1T\sum_t\|B_tA_t\|_F}{\|\Delta W_{\text{calib}}\|_F};\ \ W=W_0+\Delta W_{\text{Pico}};\ \ \text{frozen: } W_0 \text{ and all } A_t,B_t;\ \text{nothing is trained and no data is used}
methods.trainable_params: 0\ \text{(data-free post-hoc merge); per adapted matrix: one SVD of the } d_{out}\times Tr \text{ stack plus } T \text{ left multiplications}
methods.locus: Every LoRA-adapted matrix (q_proj and v_proj in the experiments) of Llama-3.1-8B, and of Qwen3-4B-Base in an appendix. Four domain LoRAs (math, code, finance, medical) of rank 8 to 64.
methods.structure: Pico left-multiplies each output factor, before merging, by one layer-wise operator \(S=U\,\mathrm{diag}(\alpha)\,U^{\top}+(I-UU^{\top})\). \(S\) is symmetric positive definite: its eigenvalues are \(\alpha_j\in[1/T,1]\) on \(\mathrm{col}(B_{\text{all}})\) and 1 on the orthogonal complement. It therefore shrinks output directions that carry a large share of the stacked \(B\) energy. The strongest shrinkage, \(\alpha_j\to1/T\) as \(s_j\to1\), undoes the \(T\)-fold counting that a summed (Task Arithmetic) merge gives a direction used equally by all \(T\) tasks. A single scalar \(\gamma\) then restores the mean source Frobenius norm. \(A_t\) is untouched; in the ablation, calibrating \(A\) or the full \(BA\) instead lowers accuracy. Two consequences are derived here. (i) Task Arithmetic is linear, so \(\mathcal{M}(SB_tA_t)=S\,\mathcal{M}(B_tA_t)\) and Pico-TA equals the post-merge output-space reshaping \(\gamma S\Delta W_{\text{TA}}\); applying \(S\) before merging matters only for non-linear mergers such as TIES and TSV-M. (ii) \(s_j\) is a direction's share of the stacked spectrum, only a proxy for cross-task sharing, so a direction dominated by one task's energy is shrunk too. \(U\) is the left singular basis of the concatenated \(B\)'s. It is the same output basis Core Space builds (\(U_B\)). KnOTS instead takes the SVD of the stacked products \([B_1A_1,\dots,B_TA_T]\). Its left singular vectors span the same column space only when every \(A_t\) has full row rank, and they form a different basis.
methods.mergeable_reason: The output is one additive delta per layer, \(\Delta W_{\text{Pico}}=\gamma\,\mathcal{M}(\{SB_tA_t\})\), of rank at most \(Tr\) for TA. It folds into \(W_0\) like any merged LoRA.
methods.identity_at_init: Nothing is trained. With a single adapter (\(T=1\)), every \(\alpha_j=1\), so \(S=I\) and the calibration step is the identity. Under Task Arithmetic, \(\gamma\) then cancels any merge weight and \(\Delta W_{\text{Pico}}=B_1A_1\) exactly; under TIES, the merger's own trimming still changes the single adapter.
methods.key_idea: Across independently trained LoRAs, the output factors \(B_t\) reuse a few shared directions: pairwise overlap \(O_B\gg O_A\), and the effective rank of \(B\) is about 3 at LoRA rank 64. A linear merge counts these directions \(T\) times. Pico shrinks them before merging with the spectral weights \(\alpha_j=1/(1+(T-1)s_j)\) and then restores the update norm.
methods.results_note: On Llama-3.1-8B with four rank-16 domain LoRAs, Pico raises the eight-benchmark average from 0.4093 to 0.4430 under Task Arithmetic, from 0.3859 to 0.4328 under TIES and from 0.3473 to 0.4305 under TSV-M. Pico+TA (0.4430) also beats a jointly trained multi-task LoRA (0.3688).

relations.note: Plug-in calibration before TA (+3.4 points). For TA it equals left-multiplying the merged delta by \(S\) and rescaling.
Calibrated factors are then merged by TIES (+4.7 points average).
Calibrated factors are then merged by TSV-M (+8.3 points, the largest gain).

Both use a shared output basis from an SVD, but of different stacks. KnOTS factorises the stacked updates \(B_tA_t\) and merges the task-specific right factors; Pico factorises the stacked \(B_t\) and rescales the shared output directions by their energy share. KnOTS is a Table 1 baseline that Pico beats under all three mergers (overall 0.4088, 0.4207 and 0.3523, against Pico's 0.4430, 0.4328 and 0.4305).

Uses the same left singular basis of the concatenated \(B_t\) (Core Space's \(U_B\)), but calibrates in it instead of projecting to a small core. Core Space is a baseline that Pico beats in all three merger blocks of Table 1.
Sparsify-and-rescale interference reduction; a baseline in every merger block of Table 1.

LoRI reduces merge interference at training time, with frozen random (near-orthogonal) \(A_t\) and sparse \(B_t\). Pico is post-hoc and data-free on ordinary LoRAs. Pico does not cite LoRI, so this is a structural comparison.

methods.name: FrameFT
methods.full_name: FrameFT: fine-tuning with sparse coefficients in tight fusion frames
methods.paper_title: Fine-Tuning of Transformer models with Frames
methods.formula_latex: W=W_0+\Delta W,\ \ \Delta W=\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{d_{out}d_{in}}}\,P_{out}\,C\,P_{in}^{\top}=\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{d_{out}d_{in}}}\sum_{i=1}^{k}P_{out,i}\,C_i\,P_{in,i}^{\top};\ \ P_{out}=[P_{out,1},\dots,P_{out,k}]\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times k\rho_{out}},\ P_{in}=[P_{in,1},\dots,P_{in,k}]\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{in}\times k\rho_{in}}\ \ \text{(Parseval tight fusion frames from Spectral Tetris, } \textstyle\sum_iP_{\cdot,i}P_{\cdot,i}^{\top}=I\text{)};\ \ C=\mathrm{blockdiag}(C_1,\dots,C_k),\ C_i\in\mathbb{R}^{\rho_{out}\times\rho_{in}},\ \ \mathrm{supp}(C)=\Omega,\ |\Omega|=n_c \text{ random and shared by all layers};\ \ \text{(paper form; the released code sets the block size of } C \text{ independently of } \rho\text{: } 4\times4 \text{ for Llama-2-7B, } 40\times40 \text{ for Llama-2-13B, one full block for Gemma-2-2B, 128 blocks for Gemma-2-9B and Llama-3.1-8B)};\ \ \text{frozen: } W_0,\ P_{out},\ P_{in},\ \Omega;\ \text{trained: the } n_c \text{ entries } C_{\Omega} \text{ of each adapted matrix}
methods.trainable_params: n_c\ \text{per adapted matrix } (n_c=1000 \text{ for RoBERTa, } 5000 \text{ for the 2B--13B LLMs, i.e. } 320\text{K in total on Llama-2-7B } W_q,W_v);\ \text{frames and support are regenerated from } (d,\rho) \text{ and a seed, so neither is stored}
methods.locus: \(W_q\) and \(W_v\) in every Transformer block (RoBERTa-base/large, Llama-2-7B/13B, Gemma-2-2B/9B, Llama-3.1-8B, ViT-B/L)
methods.structure: A fixed two-sided frame expansion with a sparse block-diagonal core. \(\Delta W=\sum_iP_{out,i}C_iP_{in,i}^{\top}\) couples the \(i\)-th output subspace only with the \(i\)-th input subspace, and only \(n_c\) core entries are free. Rank is not capped by a small \(r\): \(\mathrm{rank}\,\Delta W\le\mathrm{rank}\,C\le n_c\). The general definition allows redundant frames (\(k\rho>d\)), but every reported experiment uses \(k\rho=d\) with Parseval normalisation. The main GLUE, instruction-tuning and ViT runs use \(\rho=2\), and the Appendix D ablation varies \(\rho\) from 2 to 256, still with \(k\rho=d\). Then \(\sum_iP_iP_i^{\top}=I\) with ranks summing to \(d\) forces the subspaces to be mutually orthogonal, so \(P_{out}\) and \(P_{in}\) are square orthogonal matrices and the frame is not redundant. Running the released construct_real_tff confirms this: the matrix is orthogonal to \(10^{-5}\) to \(10^{-4}\) (float32) for \(d=768\) to \(4096\), and its non-zero fraction is about \(2/\rho\) (99.6 to 99.9% at \(\rho=2\), about 50% at \(\rho=4\), about 25% at \(\rho=8\)). At \(\rho=2\) the Spectral Tetris unit-norm tight frame in \(\mathbb{C}^1\) is all ones, so the modulated frame is the realified \((d/2)\)-point DFT basis: each 2-D subspace is the realification of one conjugated DFT row. In this regime FrameFT is FourierFT-like: sparse coefficients in a fixed DFT-type basis on both sides. The block-sparse frames that the paper credits for throughput appear only at \(\rho\ge4\). The released code also decouples the coefficient blocks from \(\rho\). Llama-2-7B uses \(4\times4\) blocks, Llama-2-13B \(40\times40\), Gemma-2-2B one full block (no block-diagonal constraint, so a random sparse support over the whole two-sided realified-DFT basis), and Gemma-2-9B and Llama-3.1-8B 128 blocks. Four of the twelve released GLUE scripts use \(\rho=4\) (tff_l 4), although the paper states \(\rho=2\) for GLUE. Lemma 3.1: if \(f(W)\) is \(L\)-smooth, the reparameterised loss \(f(C)\) is \(LB_{out}B_{in}\)-smooth, unlike LoRA's factored \((A,B)\) landscape. Gradient descent with \(\eta\le1/\tilde L\) therefore gets the standard \(O(1/T)\) stationarity rate (Theorem 3.2).
methods.mergeable_reason: \(\Delta W\) is a dense additive matrix computed from the frames and the sparse core. The released tuner's merge() adds it to \(W_0\), so inference cost is unchanged.
methods.identity_at_init: Depends on the configuration. The released instruction-tuning scripts set init_std 0, so \(C=0\) and \(\Delta W=0\) at step 0. The GLUE scripts do not pass init_std, so the default 1.0 (GLUE/args.py and the FrameConfig default) applies: the \(n_c\) coefficients start as \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) samples and \(\Delta W\neq0\) at initialisation, as in FourierFT. The tuner's reset_frame_parameters, which would zero the coefficients, is defined but never called. The paper's Algorithm 1 only says 'Init'.
methods.key_idea: Replace LoRA's learned factor subspaces with fixed, algorithmically generated Parseval fusion frames, shared by all layers of the same width, and learn only a sparse block-diagonal coefficient matrix between them. Storage drops to \(n_c\) scalars per matrix, and the coefficient-space loss inherits the smoothness of the weight-space loss.
methods.results_note: Instruction-tuned on Alpaca with 320K trainable parameters, Llama-2-7B averages 63.62 on eight LM-eval-harness tasks, against 63.18 for LoRA (16.7M) and 63.22 for FourierFT (320K) (Table 3). LoRA stays 0.2 to 0.7 points ahead on Llama-2-13B, Gemma-2-9B and Llama-3.1-8B. On GLUE, FrameFT averages 86.1 (RoBERTa-base, 24K parameters) and 88.7 (RoBERTa-large, 48K) (Table 1).

relations.note: FourierFT is a baseline in Tables 1 to 3. Same recipe: a few trainable coefficients in a fixed basis shared across layers. In every reported setting (\(k\rho=d\), mostly \(\rho=2\)), FrameFT's basis is itself a realified DFT, so the main difference is block-diagonal rather than scattered 2D-frequency support (derived here; the paper does not present FrameFT as building on FourierFT).
Sparse coefficients under a fixed wavelet synthesis instead of fusion frames. FrameFT does not cite WaveFT, so this is a structural comparison.
Also a sparse core between fixed bases, but SVFT's bases are the singular vectors of \(W_0\), stored per layer. FrameFT's bases depend only on \((d,\rho)\). SVFT is a baseline in Tables 1 and 3.

Core between frozen SVD bases of \(W_0\). FrameFT replaces the weight-derived bases with data-independent frames. LoRA-XS is a RoBERTa-large GLUE baseline (Table 1), where the two tie on average (88.7).

FrameFT matches or beats LoRA on GLUE (12 to 17 times fewer trainable parameters) and on Alpaca for Llama-2-7B and Gemma-2-2B. On Llama-2-13B, Gemma-2-9B and Llama-3.1-8B, LoRA is 0.2 to 0.7 points ahead with about 40 to 65 times more parameters.

methods.name: PrefixMemory-Tuning
methods.full_name: PrefixMemory-Tuning (PMT; titled Prefix-Tuning+ in arXiv v1 and v2)
methods.paper_title: PrefixMemory-Tuning: Modernizing Prefix-Tuning by Decoupling the Prefix from Attention
methods.formula_latex: \text{for each layer } l \text{ and attention head } h:\ \ o_i^{\top}=\frac{\sum_{j\le i}\mathrm{sim}(q_i,k_j)\,v_j^{\top}}{\sum_{j\le i}\mathrm{sim}(q_i,k_j)}+\phi(q_i)^{\top}M,\ \ q_i=W_Qx_i,\ k_j=W_Kx_j,\ v_j=W_Vx_j,\ \ \mathrm{sim}(q,k)=\exp\!\big(q^{\top}k/\sqrt{d_K}\big),\ \ \phi\in\{\mathrm{elu},\mathrm{gelu}\}\ \text{elementwise } (d_\phi=d_K),\ \ M\in\mathbb{R}^{d_\phi\times d_V}\ (\text{per head; the paper's single-head notation writes } M\in\mathbb{R}^{d_\phi\times d});\ \ \text{derived from prefix-tuning with prefix } s_1,\dots,s_\ell \text{ by (i) taking the prefix out of the softmax with a fixed weight } \lambda,\ \text{(ii) linearising } \mathrm{sim}(\cdot,\cdot)\approx\phi(\cdot)^{\top}\phi(\cdot),\ \text{(iii) replacing } \textstyle\sum_{j\le\ell}\phi(W_Ks_j)(W_Vs_j)^{\top} \text{ by a free } M \text{, dropping the normaliser and absorbing } \lambda;\ \ \text{frozen: all base weights};\ \text{trained: } \{M_{l,h}\}
methods.trainable_params: L\cdot H\cdot d_\phi d_V\ \text{per model } (=L\,d\,d_K \text{ for multi-head attention with elementwise } \phi):\ 16.91\text{M } (0.25\%) \text{ on LLaMA2-7B-Chat, } 9.51\text{M } (0.31\%) \text{ on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct};\ \text{both reported counts exceed } LHd_Kd_V \text{ by exactly } L\cdot d\text{, consistent with one extra } d\text{-vector per layer that the text does not describe (it equals } Hd_\phi\text{, the size of one Eq.-(6) normaliser } N\in\mathbb{R}^{d_\phi} \text{ per head; suggestive, not confirmed)}
methods.locus: Every attention head of every layer: a query-conditioned branch added to each head's output before \(W_O\) (LLaMA2-7B-Chat, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-Math-7B)
methods.structure: An additive, query-conditioned bias outside the softmax: \(o_i\mapsto o_i+M^{\top}\phi(q_i)\). Unlike a prefix, it is not renormalised against the input's attention mass. Prefix-tuning gives \(o^{pt}_i=(1-\alpha_i)o_i+\sum_{j\le\ell}\alpha_{ij}W_Vs_j\), where \(\alpha_i\) depends on the input and prefix lengths; this is the paper's tradeoff argument. In PMT the input path keeps weight 1 and the memory path is independent of length. A structural reading, derived here: through the frozen output projection, each layer gains the parallel branch \(\sum_hW_O^{(h)}M_h^{\top}\phi(W_Q^{(h)}x_i)\). That is a parallel adapter whose down-projection is the frozen query projection \(W_Q\) (width \(d_K\) per head and \(Hd_K=d\) in total for both LLaMA2-7B and Qwen2.5-3B, so it is not a bottleneck), whose nonlinearity is elu or gelu, and whose trained map is block-diagonal (one \(M_h^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_V\times d_K}\) per head), read out through the frozen \(W_O\). It is the linear-kernel counterpart of He et al.'s view of prefix-tuning as a gated parallel adapter. Memory capacity scales with \(d_\phi\times d_V\) rather than with prefix length. Remark 1 notes that a trainable \(\phi_W(x)=\mathrm{ReLU}(Wx+b)\) would turn the branch into a one-hidden-layer MLP; Table 2 reports such an 'MLP Kernel' variant, better than elu on some tasks and worse on others. The paper does not say whether \(q_i\) is taken before or after RoPE; after RoPE the branch would depend on position.
methods.mergeable_reason: \(\phi(q_i)^{\top}M\) is a non-linear (elu/gelu) function of the query, so the branch cannot be folded into \(W_Q,W_K,W_V\) or \(W_O\) and stays at inference. It costs about one extra \(d_K\times d_V\) product per head per token and does not grow the KV cache.
methods.identity_at_init: Not stated, and the linked code repository is empty. With \(M=0\) the branch vanishes and \(o^{PMT}_i=o_i\) exactly. Prefix-tuning has no such parameter value: any prefix with \(\ell\ge1\) takes softmax mass \(\alpha_i>0\) from the input.
methods.key_idea: Prefix-tuning underperforms on deep LLMs because the prefix shares each head's softmax normaliser with the input, so prefix influence and input specificity trade off with sequence length. PMT moves the prefix out of the softmax, linearises it with a kernel feature map \(\phi\), and replaces the prefix key-value sum with a free memory matrix \(M\), giving \(o_i=\mathrm{Attn}_i+\phi(q_i)^{\top}M\).
methods.results_note: With one training example per class, PMT reaches 71.2% on BigBench with LLaMA2-7B-Chat and 76.6% with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, above LoRA (\(r=64\)), prefix-tuning and full fine-tuning.

relations.note: Derived from the prefix-tuning attention output by decoupling the softmax, kernel-linearising, and freeing the prefix key-value sum. With the normaliser removed, prefix-tuning is not an exact member of the PMT family, so PMT relaxes it rather than strictly generalising it.

Starts from Petrov et al.'s decomposition \(o^{pt}_i=(1-\alpha_i)o_i+\sum_j\alpha_{ij}W_Vs_j\). Argues that their explanation (prefixes cannot change the attention pattern) holds for shallow transformers but not for deep LLMs.

LLaMA-Adapter already gives adaption prompts their own softmax, separate from the token softmax, with a zero-init gate; this is PMT's step (i). PMT further linearises the prompt term and replaces it with a free matrix. The paper does not cite LLaMA-Adapter.

Derived here: through \(W_O\), the PMT branch is a parallel adapter with a frozen down-projection \(W_Q^{(h)}\) per head (total width \(d\), so not a bottleneck), an elementwise \(\phi\), and a trained block-diagonal map of per-head \(M_h^{\top}\) read out through the frozen \(W_O\).

In Table 1, PMT beats LoRA \(r=64\) (33.55M parameters on LLaMA2-7B-Chat, about twice PMT's 16.91M) on all three few-shot datasets for both models, and Table 7 shows it ahead of LoRA \(r=8\) to \(32\). It also beats a LoRA baseline in CFT math (Table 3) and in AlpacaEval 2 win-rate deltas (Table 4); the LoRA rank used in those two tables is not stated.

methods.name: FourTune
methods.full_name: FourTune: fully 4-bit (W4A4G4) LoRA post-training with a frozen low-rank numerical stabilizer
methods.paper_title: FourTune: Towards Fully 4-Bit Efficient Post-Training for Diffusion Models
methods.formula_latex: W_0\approx R+L_{\text{stab}},\ \ L_{\text{stab}}=L_1L_2\ \text{(low-rank outlier branch from the SVDQuant decomposition, kept in high precision)},\ \ R \text{ quantised offline to NVFP4 with } 16\times16 \text{ block scales};\ \ h=\mathrm{GEMM}_{4\text{bit}}\big(Q(R),Q(x)\big)+L_{\text{stab}}\,x+BA\,x;\ \ \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial x}=\mathrm{GEMM}_{4\text{bit}}\big(Q(R)^{\top},Q(g)\big)+L_{\text{stab}}^{\top}g+(BA)^{\top}g,\ \ g=\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial h}\ \text{(4-bit gradients through the backbone; block scales let } Q(R)^{\top} \text{ be used without requantising)};\ \ \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial B}=g\,(Ax)^{\top},\ \ \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial A}=B^{\top}g\,x^{\top};\ \ \text{frozen: } R,\ L_{\text{stab}};\ \text{trained: } B\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r},\ A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}}
methods.trainable_params: r(d_{in}+d_{out})\ \text{per adapted matrix } (r=64 \text{ in the experiments});\ \text{also frozen: the high-precision rank-}k \text{ stabilizer, } k(d_{in}+d_{out}) \text{ entries (} k \text{ not stated), and the 4-bit residual}
methods.locus: Linear layers (GEMMs) of the diffusion backbone: the FLUX.1-dev (12B) and Qwen-Image (20B) DiTs, plus SDXL in Appendix B. The MLP's FC1 GEMM is fused with the FC2 quantisation kernel.
methods.structure: A QLoRA-type composite with three parallel branches on each linear layer. The first is a frozen 4-bit residual GEMM (W4A4). The second is a frozen high-precision low-rank stabilizer \(L_{\text{stab}}\) that absorbs the quantisation-sensitive outlier directions of \(W_0\); this is SVDQuant's decomposition, reused here during training. The third is a trainable rank-\(r\) LoRA \(BA\). The trainable update is the ordinary additive \(BA\); what changes is the arithmetic. QLoRA dequantises and computes in W4A16G16, while FourTune runs the forward and input-gradient GEMMs in 4-bit (W4A4G4). Its \(16\times16\) block-wise scales let the transposed weight be used in the backward pass without requantisation. The LoRA down-projection, the stabilizer and activation quantisation share one fused kernel, and the 4-bit GEMM is fused with the up-projections. The block granularity is \(16\times16\) instead of the usual \(1\times16\) groups (Table 5: LPIPS 0.227 vs 0.203 for reconstruction). An INT4 variant on an RTX 4090 is reported in Appendix B. Without the stabilizer, naive W4A4G4 training shows gradient explosion in the distillation runs (Fig. 8). The stabilizer and the LoRA have the same algebraic form (high-precision low-rank maps of \(x\)), so the trained LoRA can be concatenated into the stabilizer branch: \([L_1\ B][L_2;A]\).
methods.mergeable_reason: \(BA\) can be concatenated into the high-precision low-rank branch, \(L_{\text{stab}}+BA=[L_1\ B]\,[L_2;A]\) (rank \(k+r\)), which keeps the trained function exactly in a W4A4 inference engine. Folding it into the 4-bit residual \(R\) requires requantisation. Folding it into a BF16 \(W_0\) gives \(W_0+BA\), which differs from the training-time function by the quantisation error of \(R\).
methods.identity_at_init: Not stated. Under standard LoRA initialisation (\(BA=0\)) the model starts at the quantised base \(Q(R)Q(x)+L_{\text{stab}}x\approx W_0x\), not exactly at \(W_0x\).
methods.key_idea: FourTune aims to make PEFT faster than BF16 LoRA, not only smaller, by running the whole frozen backbone in native 4-bit for weights, activations and gradients. A frozen high-precision low-rank stabilizer \(L_{\text{stab}}\) carries the outlier directions. \(16\times16\) block scales and fused LoRA and MLP kernels keep the 4-bit backward pass efficient.
methods.results_note: In end-to-end FLUX.1-dev customization training, FourTune uses 14.51 GB against 29.35 GB for BF16 LoRA. A step takes 0.86 s on an RTX 5090, 2.27x faster than BF16 LoRA and 2.79x faster than NF4 QLoRA, at matched generation quality.

relations.note: Same design of a frozen 4-bit base plus LoRA. QLoRA dequantises for compute (W4A16G16); FourTune computes in W4A4G4.
Also NVFP4 base plus LoRA (QeRL targets RL for LLMs). QeRL dequantises weights for compute; FourTune quantises activations and gradients as well.
Both handle the quantised-base mismatch with a high-precision low-rank component. LoftQ puts it into the trainable LoRA initialisation; FourTune keeps it as a separate frozen stabilizer.
Training-time acceleration baseline for LoRA (contextual channel sparsity). It underperforms FourTune on \(\pi\)-Flow distillation, even at 50% sparsity.
The trainable branch is a standard rank-64 LoRA.

methods.name: GradFix
methods.full_name: GradFix: gradient-sign masking for task-vector transport across pre-trained models
methods.paper_title: Gradient-Sign Masking for Task Vector Transport Across Pre-Trained Models
methods.formula_latex: \tau_A=\theta_A^{ft}-\theta_A\ \ (\text{per matrix } \Delta W_A=W_A^{ft}-W_A);\ \ \hat s_i=\mathrm{sign}\Big(-\sum_{(x_n,y_n)\in\mathcal{D}_s}\mathrm{sign}\big(\nabla_\theta\ell(f_{\theta_B}(x_n),y_n)\big)_i\Big)\ \ (\text{majority vote over } N=|\mathcal{D}_s| \text{ labelled target examples});\ \ m_i=\mathbb{1}\{\mathrm{sign}(\tau_{A,i})=\hat s_i\},\ \ \theta_B^{\text{trans}}=\theta_B+\alpha\,(m\odot\tau_A);\ \ \text{full-data form: } g=\nabla_\theta\mathcal{L}(\theta_B),\ \ g^{\top}\big(\alpha\,m\odot\tau_A\big)=-\alpha\textstyle\sum_im_i|g_i||\tau_{A,i}|\le0;\ \ \text{frozen: } \theta_A,\ \theta_A^{ft},\ \theta_B;\ \text{nothing is trained; } \alpha \text{ is chosen on a validation set}
methods.trainable_params: 0\ \text{(training-free); each transport builds one binary mask } m\in\{0,1\}^{|\theta|} \text{ from } N \text{ per-sample target gradients, plus the scalar } \alpha
methods.locus: All parameters covered by the source task vector: the CLIP ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/14 image encoders (text encoder frozen), and T5-base for language tasks (T5 v1.1 as source, FLAN-T5 as target).
methods.structure: A coordinatewise Hadamard filter on a task vector, in parameter coordinates. The transported delta keeps \(\tau_A\) on the sign-agreement set \(\{i:\mathrm{sign}\,\tau_{A,i}=\mathrm{sign}(-g_i)\}\) unchanged and zeros it elsewhere. This makes it a base-change map: a displacement measured at base point \(\theta_A\) is projected onto the target's local descent orthant at \(\theta_B\), with no permutation alignment and no parameter updates. The first-order descent property \(g^{\top}\delta\le0\) holds by construction for the full-data gradient, so the update lowers the loss for sufficiently small \(\alpha\). With few samples the paper's lemma is per coordinate: under an independence assumption and \(p_i>1/2\), \(\Pr[\hat s_i=\mathrm{sign}(-g_i)]\ge1-e^{-2N(p_i-1/2)^2}\) (Hoeffding). A guarantee for the whole vector would need a union bound that the paper does not state. The filter acts on coordinates, not on functions, so it depends on the basis. One consequence, derived here: for a factored adapter, \(m\odot(BA)\) is in general full-rank, so a LoRA task vector would be transported as a masked dense matrix, not as low-rank factors. The paper's experiments use full fine-tuning task vectors. For multi-task merging, merge-then-mask with a consensus target-sign mask works best; for several sources fine-tuned on one task, mask-then-merge works best. Magnitude-weighted masks underperform, which the paper reads as directions transferring across pre-trainings while magnitudes do not.
methods.mergeable_reason: The result is a single additive weight delta \(\alpha\,m\odot\tau_A\) on \(\theta_B\). It composes with Task Arithmetic and TIES (mask-then-merge or merge-then-mask) and adds no inference overhead.
methods.identity_at_init: Nothing is trained. \(\alpha=0\), or an empty mask, returns the target base \(\theta_B\) exactly.
methods.key_idea: A task vector trained on an old base \(\theta_A\) transfers to a new release \(\theta_B\) once its coordinates whose sign disagrees with the target's anti-gradient are removed. A few target gradients, combined by a majority vote of signs and with no update steps, rebase \(\tau_A\) onto \(\theta_B\) with a first-order descent guarantee \(g^{\top}\delta\le0\).
methods.results_note: With one labelled example per class, transporting a DataComp-XL CLIP ViT-B/16 EuroSAT task vector to a LAION-2B ViT-B/16 gives 61.94%. Naive task-vector addition gives 49.58%, zero-shot 49.41%, and few-shot fine-tuning on the same samples 56.61%.

relations.note: Extends task-vector addition to a different base point. Naive \(\theta_B+\tau_A\) stays near zero-shot when the bases differ.
Used with TA and TIES in multi-task merging (merge-then-mask) and multi-source merging (mask-then-merge). TIES elects signs by task-vector mass; GradFix elects them by target anti-gradient votes.

Both move fine-tuning knowledge to a new base model. Trans-LoRA re-trains the adapter by distillation on synthetic data; GradFix is training-free masking from a few labelled samples. GradFix does not cite Trans-LoRA, so this is a structural comparison.

Both are training-free cross-model transfer. LoRA-X projects onto the target's SVD subspaces; GradFix applies a coordinatewise gradient-sign mask. GradFix does not cite LoRA-X, so this is a structural comparison.

The paper frames transport against model rebasin (Ainsworth et al., cited in Sec. 3). Rebasin aligns two pre-trained models by a weight permutation; GradFix transfers a task vector between bases without any permutation, by sign masking. The paper's permutation-based baseline TransFusion is not catalogued.

methods.name: CoA-LoRA
methods.full_name: CoA-LoRA: Configuration-Aware LoRA (a hypernetwork maps each layer's quantisation configuration to an \(r\times r\) adjustment of that layer's LoRA)
methods.paper_title: On-the-Fly Adaptation to Quantization: Configuration-Aware LoRA for Efficient Fine-Tuning of Quantized LLMs
methods.formula_latex: h=\big(\widetilde W^{(i)}_{\mathbf C}+L_{1,i}\,(I_r+U_\theta(Q_i))\,L_{2,i}\big)x,\quad U_\theta(Q_i)=\gamma\cdot\mathrm{reshape}_{r\times r}\Big(\mathrm{MLP}_\theta\big(\mathrm{LN}[\,e(b_{0,i}),e(b_{1,i}),e(b_{2,i}),e(B_{0,i}),e(B_{1,i}),e(\text{module}_i),e(\text{block}_i)\,]\big)\Big)\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r};\ \ \mathbf C=\{c_i\}_{i=1}^{N},\ c_i=[b_{0,i},b_{1,i},b_{2,i},B_{0,i},B_{1,i}]\ (\text{NormalFloat bit-widths and block sizes of layer } i);\ \ W_0^{(i)}-\widetilde W^{(i)}_{\mathbf C}\approx U\Sigma V^{\top}\Rightarrow L_{1,i}=U_r\Sigma_r^{1/2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r},\ L_{2,i}=\Sigma_r^{1/2}V_r^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}};\ \ \min_\theta\ \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf C\in\mathcal C}\,\mathcal L\big(\{\widetilde W^{(i)}_{\mathbf C}+L_{1,i}(I_r+U_\theta(Q_i))L_{2,i}\}_{i=1}^{N};\mathcal D\big),\ \ \mathcal C\ \text{refined by Pareto/EHVI search};\ \ \text{frozen: quantised base } \widetilde W_{\mathbf C};\ \text{trained: mapper } \theta\ (\text{embeddings, LayerNorm, 2-layer MLP, scalar }\gamma);\ \text{the released code also trains one LoRA pair } (L_1,L_2)\ \text{shared by all configurations}
methods.trainable_params: |\theta|=129\,r^{2}+O(10^{4})\ \text{per model, shared by all } N \text{ adapted matrices and all configurations }(2{,}121{,}265\text{ to }2{,}121{,}281 \text{ at } r=128,\ 0.03\text{--}0.5\%\ \text{of the base, Table A.1};\ \approx 0.54\text{M at the main-experiment rank } r=64);\ \text{plus } r(d_{in}+d_{out})\ \text{per adapted matrix for the LoRA factors (SVD-initialised; frozen in the paper's Eq. (3), trained once and shared in the released code)}
methods.locus: Every LoRA-targeted linear layer of a NormalFloat-quantised model, each with its own per-layer configuration: query, key, value, output.dense and intermediate.dense of RoBERTa-Large; q/k/v/o/gate/up/down projections of Qwen2.5-1.5B, Qwen2.5-3B and LLaMA-2-7B
methods.structure: A family of additive rank-\(r\) updates indexed by the discrete space of per-layer NormalFloat configurations \(\mathbf C=\{c_i\}_{i=1}^{N}\), with \(c_i\in\{2,3,4,8\}^2\times\{\text{bf16},\text{fp16},\text{fp32}\}\times\{16,32,64\}\times\{16,64,256\}\) (432 choices per layer, \(432^{N}\) per model). One small hypernetwork \(\theta\) maps a layer's configuration embedding, plus its module-type and block-index embeddings, to an \(r\times r\) core \(I_r+U_\theta(Q_i)\) placed between the LoRA factors: \(\Delta W_i(\mathbf C)=L_{1,i}(I_r+U_\theta(Q_i))L_{2,i}\). The core acts only on the rank space. When it is invertible, the update keeps column space \(\mathrm{col}(L_{1,i})\) and row space \(\mathrm{row}(L_{2,i})\), so the configuration moves the update only inside a fixed \(r\times r\) coordinate window, as in LoRA-XS. In the paper's Eq. (2) the factors \(L^{(\mathbf C)}_{1,i},L^{(\mathbf C)}_{2,i}\) are the rank-\(r\) SVD of the quantisation residual \(W_0-\widetilde W_{\mathbf C}\) for that configuration, so a new configuration also needs \(W_0\) for the residual SVD. In the released GLUE code (run_glue.py, lorasync mode), one LoRA pair initialised from a single configuration's residual SVD is trained jointly with \(\theta\) and loaded into every configuration's model, so in practice one adapter is shared and only the core varies. The training set \(\mathcal C\) is itself optimised. It starts from 50 configurations of 2.25 to 7.25 average bits chosen by an integer program, then alternates training \(\theta\) with a search step: a Gaussian-process surrogate of accuracy, an expected-hypervolume-improvement acquisition maximised by finite-difference coordinate moves, and Pareto filtering inside 40 bit-width segments.
methods.mergeable_reason: For a fixed configuration \(\mathbf C\), the generated update \(L_{1,i}(I_r+U_\theta(Q_i))L_{2,i}\) is a static rank-\(r\) matrix, computed with one mapper forward pass per layer and kept beside the quantised weights. Folding it into \(\widetilde W_{\mathbf C}\) needs dequantisation, and requantising would change the configuration, as with QLoRA. The mapper \(\theta\) has to be kept to serve other configurations.
methods.identity_at_init: Not identity relative to the quantised base. In the code, the last MLP layer starts with \(\mathcal N(0,(10^{-3})^2)\) weights and zero bias, so \(I_r+U_\theta\approx I_r\). The LoRA factors start as the rank-\(r\) SVD of \(W_0-\widetilde W_{\mathbf C}\), so the initial model \(\widetilde W_{\mathbf C}+L_1L_2\) is the best rank-\(r\) correction of the quantisation error. It approximates \(W_0\), not \(\widetilde W_{\mathbf C}\).
methods.key_idea: The quantisation configuration becomes a conditioning input. A hypernetwork of about 2M parameters turns each layer's bit-width and block-size choice into an \(r\times r\) adjustment \(I_r+U_\theta(Q_i)\) of that layer's LoRA, so one training run serves any per-layer configuration instead of one QLoRA or LQ-LoRA run per configuration. The configurations used for training are chosen by a Pareto search over accuracy and average bit-width.
methods.results_note: On four GLUE tasks with RoBERTa-Large, one training run of about an hour covers 50 configurations from 2.5 to 6.25 bits, with accuracy comparable to or better than QLoRA and LQ-LoRA, which need 20-40 minutes of fine-tuning per configuration.

relations.note: Cited and used as the strongest baseline. The base LoRA factors come from the low-rank-plus-quantised (LPQ) decomposition of LQ-LoRA, and the code reuses its NF configuration space and integer-program bit allocation. LQ-LoRA needs one fine-tuning run per configuration; CoA-LoRA amortises over configurations.
Per-configuration baseline. A dedicated QLoRA adapter is fine-tuned for each bit-width, so cost grows linearly with the number of configurations.

Cited (with Flora) for the claim that most of the adaptation signal sits in one factor, which motivates adjusting only through the \(r\times r\) core. The paper places the signal in \(L_{2,i}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n}\), its input-side factor, whereas Zhu et al. find the output-side factor matters more; because the core sits between the factors, \((I+U)L_2\) and \(L_1(I+U)\) give the same update and the placement is side-neutral.

Not cited. Same shape: an \(r\times r\) core between SVD-derived factors. LoRA-XS trains one core per task from the SVD of \(W_0\); CoA-LoRA generates the core \(I+U_\theta\) per quantisation configuration, on factors from the SVD of the quantisation residual.

Not cited. Both generate adapter parameters from layer and condition embeddings with a shared hypernetwork. HyperFormer conditions on task and layer and generates adapter weights; CoA-LoRA conditions on quantisation configuration, module type and block index and generates only an \(r\times r\) LoRA core.
Cited with the asymmetry paper (Hao et al., 2024) as evidence that adaptation concentrates in one LoRA factor, the stated motivation for generating only an \(r\times r\) adjustment per layer.

methods.name: Low-Rank Ternary Adaptation
methods.full_name: Ternary multiplicative adaptation: a Kronecker-factorised ternary keep/zero/flip mask applied elementwise to ternary weights
methods.paper_title: Low-Rank Ternary Adaptation for Fine-Tuning Transformers
methods.formula_latex: W_0=\mathrm{diag}(s)\,W_{\text{tern}},\ W_{\text{tern}}\in\{-1,0,1\}^{d_{out}\times d_{in}};\ \ h=\mathrm{diag}(s)\big(W_{\text{tern}}\odot\Delta_{\text{tern}}\big)x,\quad \Delta_{\text{tern}}=A\otimes B,\ \ A=\mathrm{Tern}(\bar A)\in\{-1,0,1\}^{p_1\times q_1},\ B=\mathrm{Tern}(\bar B)\in\{-1,0,1\}^{p_2\times q_2},\ \ p_1p_2=d_{out},\ q_1q_2=d_{in};\ \ \mathrm{Tern}:\ \text{entrywise threshold set from the mean absolute value of each factor, gradients passed to the real proxies } \bar A,\bar B \text{ by a straight-through estimator};\ \ W_{\text{merged}}=W_{\text{tern}}\odot(A\otimes B)\in\{-1,0,1\}^{d_{out}\times d_{in}};\ \ \text{frozen: } W_{\text{tern}}\ \text{and its scales } s;\ \text{trained: } \bar A\in\mathbb{R}^{p_1\times q_1},\ \bar B\in\mathbb{R}^{p_2\times q_2}
methods.trainable_params: p_1q_1+p_2q_2\ \text{per adapted matrix}\ (p_1p_2=d_{out},\ q_1q_2=d_{in});\ 2d\ \text{for a square } d\times d \text{ layer only when } d \text{ is a perfect square } (p_i=q_i=\sqrt d);\ \text{Llama-3.2-1B's } 2048\times 2048 \text{ layers use } (32\times32,\ 64\times64)=5120=2.5d,\ 512\text{-wide k/v use } 2560,\ \text{MLP layers } 10240;\ \approx 7.4\times10^{5}\ \text{in total} \approx 0.06\%\ \text{of Llama-3.2-1B (Table 5)}
methods.locus: All self-attention and feed-forward linear layers of ternary Transformers, output head excluded: SpinQuant-ternarised Llama-3.2-1B/3B, the pre-trained ternary BitNet b1.58 2B4T and Falcon-E-1B/3B-Instruct, and the ternary ViT-B/16 encoder of TernaryCLIP
methods.structure: A Hadamard (entrywise) action of the multiplicative monoid \(\{-1,0,1\}\) on ternary weights. Each mask entry keeps (\(+1\)), zeroes (\(0\)) or flips (\(-1\)) the corresponding weight. \(\{-1,0,1\}\) is closed under multiplication and \(\odot\) commutes with the row scaling \(\mathrm{diag}(s)\), so adapted and merged weights stay ternary with unchanged scales. The mask is constrained to a Kronecker product \(A\otimes B\) of two small ternary factors, so \(\mathrm{rank}(A\otimes B)=\mathrm{rank}(A)\,\mathrm{rank}(B)\) is bounded by \(\min(p_1,q_1)\min(p_2,q_2)\) and reaches \(\min(d_{out},d_{in})\) for the balanced factor shapes of Table 5, with only \(p_1q_1+p_2q_2\) proxies. Despite the title, the update is neither low-rank nor additive. Written additively it is \(\Delta W=\mathrm{diag}(s)\,\big(W_{\text{tern}}\odot(A\otimes B-\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^{\top})\big)\). Because \(0\cdot\Delta_{ij}=0\), zero weights can never be reactivated (zero-locking). The weight-transition analysis confirms that no weight leaves 0 and that gains come from sign changes of nonzero weights. The 'balanced' and 'normalized' initialisations draw signed factors and pre-compensate the base, \(W_{\text{tern}}\leftarrow(\mathrm{sign}\bar A\otimes\mathrm{sign}\bar B)\odot W_{\text{tern}}\). A \(\pm1\) mask is an involution under \(\odot\), so the step-0 forward weights equal the pretrained ones.
methods.mergeable_reason: The merged weight \(W_{\text{tern}}\odot(A\otimes B)\) lies again in \(\{-1,0,1\}^{d_{out}\times d_{in}}\) with the original scales. It replaces the base layer with no dequantisation, requantisation, extra parameters or latency, and the proxies \(\bar A,\bar B\) are discarded.
methods.identity_at_init: Yes, by construction. All-ones factors give \(A\otimes B=\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^{\top}\) and \(W'_{\text{tern}}=W_{\text{tern}}\). The balanced and normalized schemes used in the main experiments have signed factors but pre-multiply the base by \(\mathrm{sign}\bar A\otimes\mathrm{sign}\bar B\), so the step-0 forward weights are again the pretrained ternary weights.
methods.key_idea: Additive LoRA updates leave the ternary domain, so the update is made multiplicative: a ternary keep/zero/flip mask applied entrywise to ternary weights. The mask is parameterised as a Kronecker product \(A\otimes B\) of two small ternary matrices, trained through real-valued proxies with a straight-through estimator. The fine-tuned model merges into a strictly ternary model with no dequantisation.
methods.results_note: On SpinQuant-ternarised Llama-3.2-3B fine-tuned on Alpaca, the merged ternary model raises the 9-task zero-shot average from 31.9 to 38.3 and cuts WikiText-2 perplexity from 45.6 to 22.3, ahead of QLoRA merged and requantised to ternary (37.5 and 22.9).

relations.note: Cited Kronecker-factorised PEFT. LoKr adds \(A\otimes B\) to the weight; here the Kronecker product is ternary and acts by Hadamard multiplication on ternary weights.
Cited Kronecker adapter, the same factorisation idea for high rank from few parameters, used additively in floating point.
Main PEFT baseline on the same ternary backbone. QLoRA's floating-point adapter must be merged and requantised to stay at 1.58 bits, which costs accuracy.
Cited. QA-LoRA merges without dequantisation by folding the low-rank update into group-wise zero points, but the merged weights cannot stay in \(\{-1,0,1\}\).

Not cited. Piggyback also thresholds real proxies with a straight-through estimator and multiplies the resulting unstructured \(\{0,1\}\) mask into frozen weights. Ternary adaptation adds sign flips and constrains the mask to a Kronecker product.

Cited (with LoKr and KronA) as a Kronecker-product adapter that preserves rank with few parameters; KAdaptation adds a floating-point Kronecker update to ViT weights, whereas here the Kronecker factors are ternary and multiply the weights entrywise.

methods.name: AdaRank
methods.full_name: AdaRank: Adaptive Rank Pruning (test-time learned binary masks on the singular components of task vectors)
methods.paper_title: AdaRank: Adaptive Rank Pruning for Enhanced Model Merging
methods.formula_latex: \tau_i^{l}=W_i^{l}-W_0^{l}=U_i^{l}\Sigma_i^{l}V_i^{l\top}\ (i=1,\dots,T);\quad W^{l}(B)=W_0^{l}+\lambda^{l}\sum_{i=1}^{T}U_i^{l}\,\mathrm{diag}(B_i^{l})\,\Sigma_i^{l}\,V_i^{l\top},\ \ B_i^{l}\in\{0,1\}^{\min(d_{out},d_{in})};\ \ B_{i,r}^{l}=\mathbf 1\{\sigma(\tilde b_{i,r}^{l}/T_{\text{temp}})\ge 0.5\}\ \ (\text{straight-through estimator},\ T_{\text{temp}}=10);\ \ \min_{\tilde b,\lambda}\ \sum_{i=1}^{T}\sum_{x\in\mathcal D_i^{\text{test}}}H\big(f(W(B),x)\big)\ \ (\text{output entropy on unlabeled test inputs});\ \ \text{frozen: } W_0 \text{ and all } (U_i,\Sigma_i,V_i);\ \text{optimised at test time: mask logits } \tilde b \text{ and layer coefficients } \lambda^{l}
methods.trainable_params: T\cdot\min(d_{out},d_{in})\ \text{mask logits per weight matrix (one per singular component per task), plus one } \lambda^{l}\ \text{per layer; all discarded after merging}
methods.locus: Every weight matrix of the task vectors of models fine-tuned from one backbone: CLIP ViT-B/32 and ViT-L/14 image encoders (8, 14 and 20 tasks), and RoBERTa and GPT-2 (7 NLP tasks)
methods.structure: Merging in the SVD basis of each task matrix with a learned 0/1 selection of singular triplets: \(\Delta W^{l}=\lambda^{l}\sum_{i}\sum_{r}B^{l}_{i,r}\sigma^{l}_{i,r}u^{l}_{i,r}v^{l\top}_{i,r}\). Each layer's mask set \(\{0,1\}^{T\times\min(d_{out},d_{in})}\) contains top-\(k\) truncation (\(B_{i,r}=\mathbf 1[r\le k]\), as in SVD merging and TSV-M) and full-rank Task Arithmetic (\(B=\mathbf 1\)) as special points. The kept rank and the kept indices can vary by task and layer, and need not be the top ones. AdaRank plugs into a base merger. With Task Arithmetic \(\tau_i=W_i-W_0\); with CART \(\tau_i=W_i-\bar W\) around the average weight; with TSV-M the concatenated \(U\) and \(V\) are whitened before masking; Iso-CTS is a fourth base merger in the experiments. Masks start at the base method's best setting and are optimised AdaMerging-style, by straight-through estimation of an entropy objective on unlabeled test batches. The motivation is that adding a top singular component of one task often raises the total multi-task loss.
methods.mergeable_reason: After test-time adaptation the masks are frozen and the output is one static weight set of the backbone's size. No masks, routers or per-task parameters are kept at inference, unlike router-based merging.
methods.identity_at_init: Not applicable as an adapter. The masks start by reproducing the base merger: \(B=\mathbf 1\) with \(\lambda=0.3\) is Task Arithmetic, the top 16\% of components for CART, and top-\(k\) for TSV-M. Setting all \(B=0\) recovers \(W_0\) (or \(\bar W\) for CART).
methods.key_idea: When merging, the top-\(k\) singular components of a task vector are not always the right ones to keep: large components of one task can raise the other tasks' losses, and the useful rank varies by task and layer. AdaRank instead learns a binary keep/prune mask on every singular component by test-time entropy minimisation, replacing the fixed top-\(k\) rule of SVD-based merging.
methods.results_note: Added to Task Arithmetic on 8-, 14- and 20-task vision merging, AdaRank raises average accuracy by 18.6% (ViT-B/32) and 11.1% (ViT-L/14), outperforming all static merging baselines.

relations.note: With all masks equal to 1, AdaRank's merge is layer-wise Task Arithmetic; it is also the default base merger.
Adopts AdaMerging's test-time entropy minimisation and learns its layer coefficients jointly with the masks; AdaRank beats AdaMerging, which tunes only the coefficients.
Plugs into TSV-M: its fixed top-\(k\) truncation of whitened task singular vectors is one mask, and AdaRank replaces it with a learned one.
Element-wise trimming and sign election, as opposed to spectral pruning; a static baseline.
Random element-wise drop-and-rescale of task vectors; cited as an element-wise alternative to spectral pruning.

methods.name: SLAO (Merge before Forget)
methods.full_name: SLAO: Single LoRA continual learning with Orthogonal initialization via continual merging
methods.paper_title: Merge before Forget: A Single LoRA Continual Learning via Continual Merging
methods.formula_latex: h=\big(W_0+B^{t}_{\text{merge}}A^{t}_{\text{merge}}\big)x,\ \ B\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r},\ A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}};\ \ \text{task }1:\ B^{1}_{\text{merge}}=B_{\text{ft},1},\ A^{1}_{\text{merge}}=A_{\text{ft},1}\ (\text{standard LoRA});\ \ \text{task } i\ge 2:\ Q_iR_i=\mathrm{QR}(A_{\text{ft},i-1}^{\top}),\ Q_i\leftarrow Q_i\,\mathrm{sign}(\mathrm{diag}R_i),\ \ A^{(0)}_{\text{ft},i}=Q_i^{\top}\ (A^{(0)}A^{(0)\top}=I_r),\ \ B^{(0)}_{\text{ft},i}=B_{\text{ft},i-1};\ \ (B_{\text{ft},i},A_{\text{ft},i})=\text{fine-tune on }\mathcal D_i;\ \ A^{i}_{\text{merge}}=A_{\text{ft},i},\ \ B^{i}_{\text{merge}}=B^{i-1}_{\text{merge}}+\lambda(i)\big(B_{\text{ft},i}-B^{i-1}_{\text{merge}}\big),\ \ \lambda(i)=1/\sqrt{i};\ \ \text{frozen: } W_0;\ \text{trained per task: one LoRA pair } (B_{\text{ft},i},A_{\text{ft},i})
methods.trainable_params: r(d_{in}+d_{out})\ \text{per adapted matrix, independent of the number of tasks } T\ (\text{storage: the merged LoRA plus the current fine-tuned LoRA, } 2r(d_{in}+d_{out}))
methods.locus: LoRA on the query and value projections of every attention layer (Appendix B), fixed rank 8: Llama-2-7B/13B-chat, Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen2.5-3B/7B; a rank ablation over 4, 8 and 16 on Llama-2-13B-chat finds 8 best on the standard CL benchmark and 4 best on the large-number-of-tasks benchmark
methods.structure: A constant-memory recursion on one LoRA pair over a task stream, in three steps. (1) \(A\) is rebased: \(A^{(0)}_{\text{ft},i}=Q_i^{\top}=R_i^{-\top}A_{\text{ft},i-1}\) with \(\mathrm{diag}R_i>0\). This moves the previous task's \(A\) inside its own row space to the representative with orthonormal rows. (2) \(B\) is warm-started from the previous fine-tuned \(B\) without the compensating factor \(R_i^{\top}\). The starting product \(B_{\text{ft},i-1}R_i^{-\top}A_{\text{ft},i-1}\) therefore differs from the previous adapter unless \(R_i=I_r\). (3) After training, \(A\) is overwritten (\(A^{i}_{\text{merge}}=A_{\text{ft},i}\)) and only \(B\) is averaged, with weight \(1/\sqrt i\) taken from the OPCM continual-merging schedule. The deployed update is \(B^{t}_{\text{merge}}A_{\text{ft},t}=\sum_{i}c^{(t)}_{i}B_{\text{ft},i}A_{\text{ft},t}\) with \(c^{(t)}_{i}=\lambda(i)\prod_{j=i+1}^{t}(1-\lambda(j))\), so every past \(B\) is paired with the latest \(A\). This is only approximately coherent: each \(A^{(0)}_{\text{ft},i}\) spans the row space of \(A_{\text{ft},i-1}\), and training moves it by the small drift bounded below. The paper's Theorem 1, a Flora-style small-step analysis with \(A^{(0)}A^{(0)\top}=I_r\), writes \(A^s=A^{(0)}+\eta A^{(0)}f_A(s)\) with \(\|f_A(s)\|_2\le\eta L^2/(1-\eta^2L^2)\), so \(A\) drifts by at most \(\eta^2L^2/(1-\eta^2L^2)\), i.e. \(O(\eta^2L^2)\), while \(\Delta B_i\approx-\eta\big(\sum_s\nabla_W\mathcal L_i^{s}\big)A^{(0)\top}_i\) accumulates each task's gradient in the current \(A\) basis. An NTK-regime forgetting/intransigence bound in \(\|B_tA_t-B_iA_i\|_F\) motivates keeping \(\|A_t-A_i\|_F\) small and merging \(B\) rather than \(A\).
methods.mergeable_reason: After any task, the deployed object is one LoRA \(B^{t}_{\text{merge}}A^{t}_{\text{merge}}\) that can be folded into \(W_0\), or kept as a side adapter while the stream continues. There are no per-task modules and no router.
methods.identity_at_init: Only for the first task (standard \(B=0\), Gaussian \(A\)). Later tasks start training from \(B_{\text{ft},i-1}R_i^{-\top}A_{\text{ft},i-1}\ne 0\), and the merged LoRA is never zero after task 1.
methods.key_idea: Continual learning becomes sequential merging inside one LoRA. Each new task starts from an orthonormal-row rebasing of the previous \(A\) together with the previous \(B\). After training, \(A\) is replaced and \(B\) is averaged with weight \(1/\sqrt i\), exploiting the asymmetry that \(B\) carries task-specific, near-orthogonal updates. Memory stays at one LoRA however many tasks arrive.
methods.results_note: On the standard CL, large-number-of-tasks and SuperNI benchmarks with Llama-2-7B-chat, the paper reports that SLAO outperforms all data-free baselines, including O-LoRA, InfLoRA, CorDA, MagMax, KnOTS, LoRA-LEGO and OPCM; its own discussion notes that MagMax is comparable on the standard CL benchmark. SAPT-LoRA, which replays generated pseudo-samples, is not data-free and is excluded from that claim.

relations.note: Baseline. O-LoRA keeps and freezes every past LoRA and constrains new ones to be orthogonal during training, so memory grows linearly in \(T\). SLAO keeps one LoRA and imposes orthogonality only through the initialisation of \(A\).
Baseline. InfLoRA stores all previous LoRAs and gradient subspaces and places each new \(A\) in an interference-free subspace. SLAO takes the new \(A\) from the QR basis of the previous \(A\).
LoRA-merging baseline, applied sequentially. It treats \(A\) and \(B\) symmetrically and has no time-aware scaling.
LoRA-merging baseline (rank-wise clustering), applied sequentially; it weights tasks equally.

Theorem 1 extends Hao et al.'s Flora dynamics (\(A\) stays near its initialisation while \(B\) accumulates gradients projected onto \(A\)) to an orthonormal \(A^{(0)}\) and a nonzero warm-started \(B^{(0)}\).
Cited (Zhu et al., 2024b) for the asymmetric roles of \(A\) and \(B\), which motivate merging only \(B\) and replacing \(A\).
Knowledge-preserving decomposition baseline, which degrades on SuperNI.

methods.name: RAIN-Merging
methods.full_name: RAIN-Merging: Reasoning-Aware Instruction-attention guided Null-space projection Merging
methods.paper_title: RAIN-Merging: A Gradient-Free Method to Enhance Instruction Following in Large Reasoning Models with Preserved Thinking Format
methods.formula_latex: \Delta_I^{k}=W_I^{k}-W_B^{k}\ (\text{instruction-model task vector of module } k\in\{Q,K,V,O,\text{FFN}\}\text{ in every layer});\ \ H_k=[h^{k}_t]_{t\in\Omega_{\text{think}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{in}\times|\Omega|}\ (\text{inputs of module } k \text{ in the reasoning model at the thinking-marker positions, 150-sample reasoning calibration set});\ \ \Delta_I^{\perp,k}=\Delta_I^{k}\big(I-H_k(H_k^{\top}H_k)^{+}H_k^{\top}\big)\ \Rightarrow\ \Delta_I^{\perp,k}h^{k}_t=0\ \ \forall t\in\Omega_{\text{think}};\ \ g^{\tilde k}=\mathbb{E}_x\big[a^{\tilde k}-\rho\,u^{\tilde k}\big],\ \tilde H^{\tilde k}=1+\mathbb{E}_x[u^{\tilde k}],\ \alpha^{\tilde k}_\star=\mathrm{clip}_{[0,1]}\big(g^{\tilde k}/\tilde H^{\tilde k}\big)\ \ (a,u:\ \text{mean attention from instruction-constrained / unconstrained response tokens to instruction tokens, 365 IFEval-style samples});\ \ \theta_\star=\theta_R+\lambda\bigoplus_{k}\alpha^{k}_\star\,\Delta_I^{\perp,k};\ \ \text{frozen: } \theta_R,\theta_I,\theta_B;\ \text{nothing is gradient-trained}
methods.trainable_params: 0\ \text{gradient-trained; computed in closed form: one coefficient } \alpha^{\tilde k} \text{ per attention head (FFN modules use the layer mean) and one global } \lambda\ (\text{grid search over } [0,1.5])
methods.locus: Q, K, V, O and FFN weight matrices of an R1-style reasoning model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B/14B/32B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B. The instruction task vector \(\theta_I-\theta_B\) comes from Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B/14B/32B-Instruct or Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and their bases. For 1.5B and 7B the reasoning model was distilled from Qwen2.5-Math, so it does not share the instruction model's base.
methods.structure: A two-stage, data-dependent but gradient-free transformation of a full task vector before it is added to a different model, the reasoning model \(\theta_R\), rather than to the base \(\theta_B\) it was computed from (for the 1.5B and 7B pairs \(\theta_R\) is not even fine-tuned from \(\theta_B\): it descends from Qwen2.5-Math). Stage 1 right-multiplies each module's task matrix by the orthogonal projector onto the complement of the span of that module's inputs at the thinking special tokens. This is the matrix form of the paper's vectorised Eq. (4), since \(\Phi=H^{\top}\otimes I\). The merged module then reproduces the reasoning model's outputs exactly on those inputs. Proposition 1 bounds the logit change at the marker tokens by \(C_1\|\Phi\,\mathrm{vec}(\Delta)\|_2+C_2\|\Delta\|_2^2\), so after projection only the second-order term remains; the paper states the resulting KL bound as \(O(\|\Delta\|_2^2)\), although its own inequalities give \(O(\|\Delta\|_2^4)\). Algorithm 1 uses the ridge version \(I-\Phi^{\top}(\Phi\Phi^{\top}+I)^{-1}\Phi\), which in matrix form is \(\Delta\mapsto\Delta(I+HH^{\top})^{-1}\). The released code (nullspace_merge_qkvo_ffn.py) uses a ridge of \(10^{-4}\) solved by conjugate gradient, on positions within 5 tokens after <think> and before </think>. It also relaxes the constraint set: Q and K are constrained through linearised attention logits between each marker and its neighbours, and V, O and the three FFN matrices through projections of the output change onto two random unit readout directions per position. The full \(\Delta h=0\) is not imposed. Stage 2 builds a diagonal quadratic model of an attention proxy (alignment minus \(\rho=10\) times leakage), with coefficients \(g\) and \(\tilde H\) measured at \(\alpha=\mathbf 1\). After dropping the \(\alpha_{(0)}\) offset, its maximiser is \(\mathrm{clip}_{[0,1]}(g/\tilde H)\), not the Newton step \(\mathbf 1+g/\tilde H\). This gives per-head scalings. The result is a block-wise rescaling of a projected task vector: the same algebraic class as task arithmetic with per-module coefficients.
methods.mergeable_reason: The output is one static weight set \(\theta_\star\) with the reasoning model's architecture. Projectors and calibration statistics are used only offline.
methods.identity_at_init: Not an adapter. With \(\lambda=0\) (or all \(\alpha=0\)) the result is the reasoning model \(\theta_R\). Stage 2 expands around \(\alpha=\mathbf 1\), the plain projected merge.
methods.key_idea: The goal is to add instruction following to a reasoning model by task arithmetic without breaking its <think>...</think> format. The instruction task vector is first projected onto the null space of the reasoning model's module inputs at the thinking-marker tokens, so those positions compute exactly as before. It is then rescaled per attention head by a closed-form score that rewards attention from instruction-constrained output tokens to the instruction span and penalises leakage.
methods.results_note: Merging Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct into DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, RAIN-Merging outperforms all merging baselines (Task Arithmetic, SLERP, Karcher, TIES, DARE, ACM, LEWIS, AIM) and SFT on the same calibration data on instruction-following, mathematical-reasoning and general-capability benchmarks, while trailing the instruction model slightly on instruction following.

relations.note: Starts from the instruction-model task vector and adds it with per-module coefficients; plain Task Arithmetic is a baseline that hurts reasoning.

Cited in the related-work appendix (Appendix D) as a null-space precedent from continual learning; the null-space step in Sec. 3 itself cites Adam-NSCL (Wang et al., 2021). GPM projects gradients off the span of stored input features; RAIN applies the same right-projector to a task vector, using features at the thinking tokens.

Cited in the related-work appendix (Appendix D). LoRA-Null puts adapters in the null space of pre-trained activations to preserve knowledge; RAIN projects a full task vector off the activations that carry the thinking format.
Cited to read the near-orthogonality of the reasoning and instruction task vectors as weak coupling (weight disentanglement), which makes lightweight merging plausible.
Data-free baseline (and the base for the DARE/ACM/LEWIS/AIM variants); it prunes from parameter statistics and ignores the output-format mismatch.
Data-free baseline (DARE-TIES).

structure: Stage 2 is not a Newton step around \(\mathbf 1\). The paper drops the \(\alpha_{(0)}\) offset, so the solution is \(\mathrm{clip}_{[0,1]}(g/\tilde H)\), not \(\mathbf 1+g/\tilde H\).

structure: the released code imposes a relaxed constraint set. Q and K get attention-logit constraints near the markers; V, O and the FFN get readout-direction projections. The full projector of Eq. (4) is not imposed.

structure: Proposition 1 restated precisely. The logit change is bounded by \(C_1\|\Phi\,\mathrm{vec}(\Delta)\|_2+C_2\|\Delta\|_2^2\). The paper's \(O(\|\Delta\|_2^2)\) KL statement is looser than its own inequalities, which give \(O(\|\Delta\|_2^4)\).

methods.name: SmartFed (MoRE + EEQA)
methods.full_name: SmartFed: Mixture of Rank-Wise Experts (MoRE) with Elastic Expert Quota Allocation (EEQA) for reusing existing LoRAs in federated fine-tuning
methods.paper_title: Elastic Mixture of Rank-Wise Experts for Knowledge Reuse in Federated Fine-Tuning
methods.formula_latex: \{(B_n,A_n)\}_{n=1}^{N}\ \text{retrieved pre-trained LoRAs (frozen)},\ \ E_m(x)=b_m a_m^{\top}x,\ \ b_m=(B_n)_{:,i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}},\ a_m^{\top}=(A_n)_{i,:}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times d_{in}},\ \ m=1,\dots,M,\ M=\sum_n r_n;\ \ g=\mathrm{softmax}(W_{\text{router}}x),\ W_{\text{router}}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times d_{in}};\ \ \tilde g=g\odot\mathbf m,\ \mathbf m=\mathrm{TopK}_{q_j}(g)\in\{0,1\}^{M};\ \ h=W_0x+\sum_{m=1}^{M}\tilde g_m\,b_m a_m^{\top}x;\ \ s_{E_m}=1-\cos(x,E_m(x)),\ S^{\text{Sum}}_j=\sum_m\tilde g_m s_{E_m},\ \alpha_j=\mathrm{softmax}_j(S^{\text{Sum}}_j),\ q_j=\mathrm{EEQA}\big(\alpha;\ \textstyle\sum_j q_j=KJ,\ q_j\le M\big);\ \ \text{frozen: } W_0 \text{ and every LoRA expert};\ \text{trained (federated, FedAvg): the routers } W_{\text{router}}
methods.trainable_params: M\,d_{in}=\big(\textstyle\sum_n r_n\big)d_{in}\ \text{per adapted matrix (router only)};\ 64\,d_{in}\ \text{in the paper's setting (two rank-32 LoRAs on } W_q,W_v)
methods.locus: Query and value projections of every attention layer, where the reused LoRAs sit, in LLaMA2-7B/13B and Qwen2-7B; one router per adapted matrix
methods.structure: A library of frozen LoRAs is split into a pool of rank-one experts \(\{b_ma_m^{\top}\}_{m=1}^{M}\) per matrix and recombined per token by a softmax router with top-\(q_j\) sparsification: \(\Delta W(x)=\sum_m\tilde g_m(x)\,b_ma_m^{\top}=\widehat B\,\mathrm{diag}(\tilde g(x))\,\widehat A\), with \(\widehat B=[B_1|\cdots|B_N]\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times M}\) and \(\widehat A=[A_1;\cdots;A_N]\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times d_{in}}\). This is an input-dependent diagonal core in the concatenated LoRA basis. It avoids the cross terms \(B_1A_2,\ B_2A_1\) that factor averaging creates (the paper's Eq. 5), and it is finer than MoLE's one gate per LoRA. The kept gates are not renormalised after top-\(K\) masking. EEQA redistributes a fixed total budget \(KJ\) of active experts over the \(J\) adapted matrices, in proportion to softmax-normalised importance (gate-weighted cosine deviation between a matrix's input and its experts' outputs), capped at \(M\) per matrix and topped up greedily. Only router weights and importance scores travel between devices and server.
methods.mergeable_reason: The gates \(\tilde g(x)\) depend on each token through a softmax and a top-\(K\) mask, so \(\Delta W(x)\) changes per token and cannot be folded into \(W_0\). The full expert pool must be kept. Fixing the gates to constants \(c\) would give a static merge \(\widehat B\,\mathrm{diag}(c)\,\widehat A\), but that is not what is trained.
methods.identity_at_init: No. The experts are pre-trained nonzero LoRAs, so at initialisation the model already applies a gated mixture of their rank-one components; it is not the bare base model.
methods.key_idea: Instead of training LoRA from scratch on each device, SmartFed reuses existing task LoRAs. Each LoRA is split into its rank-one components, and a federated-trained router sparsely mixes them per token. A budget allocator gives more active experts to the matrices whose experts change representations most.
methods.results_note: Across three skill-composition tasks on LLaMA2-7B/13B and Qwen2-7B, SmartFed reports up to 10.21% higher average performance, 3.95x faster convergence, 31.47x lower communication cost and 3.61x lower energy use than existing federated and LoRA-reuse methods.

relations.note: MoLE gates whole LoRA outputs. MoRE moves the gate down to rank-one components and adds top-\(K\) sparsity, which also bounds latency as more LoRAs are retrieved. MoLE is also a federated-adapted baseline.
Baseline. LoraHub merges retrieved LoRAs into one static composite; SmartFed routes per token instead.
Baseline: dynamic layer-wise fusion weights over whole LoRAs.
Cited as the inspiration for non-uniform, importance-driven budget allocation across matrices (EEQA); AdaLoRA is also adapted to the federated setting as a knowledge-free baseline.
Not cited. LoRA-LEGO also splits LoRAs into rank-wise units, but clusters them into one static merged LoRA rather than routing them per token.

Baseline ('Linear Arithmetic', Zhang et al., 2023a). Weighted averaging of the LoRA factors produces the cross terms \(\lambda_1\lambda_2B_1A_2\) and \(\lambda_1\lambda_2B_2A_1\) of the paper's Eq. (5), which MoRE avoids by routing rank-one components.
Knowledge-free baseline: FedIT trains a LoRA from scratch with FedAvg on each task, whereas SmartFed trains only the router over retrieved LoRAs.

methods.name: RotMoLE
methods.full_name: RotMoLE: Rotatable Mixture of Low-rank Experts (MoE-LoRA with a rotation gate)
methods.paper_title: RotMoLE: Enhancing Mixture of Low-Rank Experts through Rotational Gating Mechanism
