methods.locus: The query, key, value and output projections of only the first quarter of the layers (layers 0-6 of the 28-layer Llama-3.2-3B, 0-8 of the 36-layer Qwen-2.5-3B, 0-9 of the 40-layer GLM-4-9B); experiments use \(r\in\{2,3,4,6\}\), \(n\in\{2,3,4,5\}\) experts and top-\(k\) with \(k\in\{2,3\}\), trained with SGD (learning rate \(3\times10^{-4}\), linear decay)
methods.structure: Per-token mixture of \(n\) LoRA experts in which the router returns, for each selected expert, a scale \(g_i(x)\) and a rotation \(R_i(x)\in SO(r)\) that acts in that expert's rank space, between \(A_i\) and \(B_i\). For \(r>2\) the rotation is a single planar (Givens-type) rotation by \(\theta_i(x)\) in \(\mathrm{span}(A_ix,q_i)\). It turns the code \(A_ix\) towards or away from a learned per-expert centre \(q_i\) and preserves \(\|A_ix\|\). The printed \(R_i=[e_1\,e_2]\,\mathrm{Rot}(\theta_i)\,[e_1\,e_2]^{\top}\) is a rank-2 matrix. Because \(A_ix\) lies in that plane, it acts on \(A_ix\) exactly like the full rotation \(I_r+(\cos\theta_i-1)(e_1e_1^{\top}+e_2e_2^{\top})+\sin\theta_i(e_2e_1^{\top}-e_1e_2^{\top})\). Gauge reading (derived here): a constant \(R\) placed between \(B\) and \(A\) would be absorbed by the LoRA gauge, \((B,A)\mapsto(BR,A)\), and add nothing. RotMoLE's \(R_i\) depends on \(x\), both through \(\theta_i(x)\) and through the plane, which contains \(A_ix\). The expert map \(x\mapsto B_iR_i(x)A_ix\) is therefore a nonlinear, norm-preserving reshaping of each expert's code, and it enlarges the function class. The construction uses the Euclidean norm and Gram-Schmidt in rank space. Each expert is therefore invariant under \((B_i,A_i,q_i)\mapsto(cB_iO,\,c^{-1}O^{\top}A_i,\,O^{\top}q_i)\) for \(O\in O(r)\) and \(c>0\), with \(R_i\mapsto O^{\top}R_iO\) (the unit vector \(e_1\) does not see the scale \(c\)), but not under a general \(G\in GL(r)\): the residual gauge group of each expert shrinks from \(GL(r)\) to the similarity group \(\mathbb{R}_{>0}\times O(r)\). For \(r=2\) the fixed-basis rotation commutes with \(\mathbb{R}_{>0}\times SO(2)\); a reflection additionally needs \(W_\theta\mapsto-W_\theta\). Top-\(k\) selection uses only \(g\). The paper does not treat the degenerate case \(q_i\parallel A_ix\).
methods.mergeable_reason: The scales \(g_i(x)\), the angles \(\theta_i(x)\) and the plane \(\mathrm{span}(A_ix,q_i)\) all depend on the token. \(\sum_i g_iB_iR_i(x)A_i\) is therefore not a fixed matrix and cannot be folded into \(W_0\).
methods.identity_at_init: Yes. \(B_i=0\) (the LoRA convention, stated in Appendix B) gives \(\Delta W x=0\). \(W_\theta=0\) gives \(\theta_i=0\), so \(R_iA_ix=A_ix\) and the model starts as a conventional MoE-LoRA. The centres \(q_i\) are Kaiming-uniform initialised.
methods.key_idea: A scalar gate can only rescale an expert's output along a fixed direction. LoRA experts have an \(r\)-dimensional bottleneck, so an input-dependent rotation of the code \(A_ix\) costs only \(n\,d_{in}+n\,r\) extra parameters. Each selected expert can then also be turned, which lets a few shared experts serve several tasks differently.
methods.results_note: On a jointly trained CSQA/OBQA/SIQA mixture with Qwen-2.5-3B (\(r=6\), \(n=4\), \(k=2\)), RotMoLE averages 45.82% accuracy, against 41.42 for AdaMoLE, 35.66 for MoLA and 34.57 for MoCLE; AdaMoLE is better on CSQA (49.39 vs 43.00). Against the plain MoE-LoRA baseline on the QA mixture, RotMoLE has the higher average in all 8 configurations and the higher accuracy on every task in 7 of them (the exception is OBQA with Llama-3.2-3B, \(r=3\), \(n=4\), \(k=2\)). On the SST-2/MRPC/QNLI mixture the gains are small (75.87 to 76.03 and 73.19 to 73.42 average).

relations.note: Cited (Dou et al., 2024) as a canonical MoE-LoRA, \(h=W_0x+\sum_i g_iB_iA_ix\) with a scalar softmax gate. RotMoLE adds a rotation gate inside each expert's rank space.
Cited (Li et al., 2024) as the top-\(k\) MoE-LoRA form. RotMoLE keeps top-\(k\) selection on the scalar gate values and adds per-expert rotations.

Both put an \(r\times r\) map between \(B\) and \(A\). MoSLoRA's mixer is input-independent, so the LoRA gauge absorbs it and LoRA's function class is unchanged. RotMoLE's rotation is token-dependent and does change it. MoSLoRA is not cited.
Another way to diversify LoRA experts under a router: HydraLoRA shares \(A\) and routes over several \(B\) heads, while RotMoLE keeps full experts and rotates their codes. HydraLoRA is not cited.

methods.locus: LoRA on the query, key and value projections, output.dense and intermediate.dense of DeBERTaV3-base (GLUE, \(r=4\), scaling 8, AdaLoRA protocol); on the q, k, v, up and down projections of LLaMA2-7B and LLaMA3-8B (commonsense reasoning, \(r=8\), scaling 16, setup of Lion et al. 2025) and of Gemma-3-12B-pt (MetaMathQA, \(r=8\)). ScaLoRA-I uses \(I=10\) in the commonsense runs
methods.structure: Rebasing inside a single LoRA run. Before each step the current product is re-split as \(W_t=\tilde W_0^{(t)}+\tilde B_t\tilde A_t\) with column- and row-scaled factors. The difference \(B_t\,\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf 1-\alpha_t\circ\beta_t)\,A_t\) is merged into the frozen weight. The summed increments therefore no longer telescope to \(B_TA_T\), and \(W_T-W_0\) can reach high rank: average rank 54 at \(r=4\) on RTE, and 1,347 to 3,703 singular values above 0.005 at \(r=8\) on LLaMA2-7B across the eight commonsense tasks (ScaLoRA-I falls to 20 on ARC-e and ARC-c). Gauge reading (derived here): where \(\alpha\circ\beta>0\), write \(\alpha=c\circ s\) and \(\beta=c^{-1}\circ s\) elementwise. The move is then a diagonal (maximal-torus) gauge transformation \((B,A)\mapsto(B\,\mathrm{diag}(c),\mathrm{diag}(c)^{-1}A)\), which leaves \(W\) fixed but changes the next step because LoRA's gradient descent is not gauge-invariant. It is followed by a per-direction rescaling \(\mathrm{diag}(s^{\circ2})\) of the adapter, whose complement is merged. Only diagonal scalings are used, because they are the transformations under which Adam's moment estimates transform in closed form (Lemmas 3.3 and 3.6); a full-matrix or row-wise transform is intractable. The unrestricted optimum of the same surrogate (Theorem 3.2) takes \(\tilde B\) and \(\tilde A^{\top}\) from \(2r\) top singular vectors of \(G_t\), split into two sets of \(r\), each up to an \(O(r)\) factor. LoRA-GA's initialisation is the \(t=0\), identity-rotation case. In the paper's printed Theorem 3.7, the second block matrix lists \(\mathbf B_t\) before \(\mathbf A_t^{\top}\nabla\ell\) and needs a transpose. The pairing given in formula_latex, \(S_{in}=[G^{\top}B,\ A^{\top}]\), is the one consistent with the stated \(\lambda\) and objective (re-derived here). The paper's 'fixed subspace' remark is the telescoping identity \(\sum_t\Delta W_t=B_TA_T\), i.e. a rank-\(r\) bound on vanilla LoRA's cumulative update.
methods.mergeable_reason: The adapter is merged into the base at every re-split, and the final model is the dense \(W_T\). Because \(W_0^{(t)}\) itself changes, \(W_T-W_0\) is high-rank and cannot be shipped as a rank-\(r\) adapter. The paper states this as a limitation: ScaLoRA stores the entire merged matrix.
methods.identity_at_init: Yes. Standard LoRA initialisation has one zero factor; the paper puts the Gaussian on the \(d_{out}\times r\) factor and zeros on the \(d_{in}\) side. This gives \(W_0^{(0)}+B_0A_0=W_0\), and every later re-split preserves \(W_t\) exactly.
methods.key_idea: Vanilla LoRA's increments telescope, \(\sum_t\Delta W_t=B_TA_T\), so the cumulative update never exceeds rank \(r\). ScaLoRA merges and re-factors at every step and rescales Adam's moments to match, so it accumulates a high-rank update with no restarts. The column scaling of the current factors is chosen in closed form to minimise a smoothness upper bound on the next loss, which is the same as best matching the full fine-tuning step \(-G_t/L\).
methods.results_note: With \(r=8\), ScaLoRA-I averages 74.75 on eight commonsense tasks with LLaMA2-7B and ScaLoRA averages 77.85 with LLaMA3-8B. Both are above LoRA (73.63/76.83), ReLoRA, LoRA-GA, MoRA and HiRA, and above rank-32 LoRA (74.52/77.54). On GLUE with DeBERTaV3-base (\(r=4\)) ScaLoRA averages 88.98 against 88.13 for LoRA. On LLaMA3-8B it needs about 0.01 GB more memory than LoRA (MoRA 1.08 GB, HiRA 7.83 GB), but ScaLoRA, like MoRA and HiRA, takes 50% or more extra fine-tuning time; ScaLoRA-I is close to LoRA.

relations.note: Baseline. ReLoRA also merges low-rank increments into the base, but only rarely, with re-initialised factors, reset optimizer state and LR re-warm-up. ScaLoRA re-splits at every step, keeps scaled factors and transforms their moments.

The paper states that LoRA-GA's gradient-SVD initialisation is the \(t=0\), identity-rotation case (\(P_0=Q_0=I_r\)) of Theorem 3.2's optimal-adapter condition. LoRA-GA is also a commonsense baseline.

High-rank baseline. The paper reports that HiRA's Hadamard update has high Euclidean rank but intrinsic rank \(r\), and needs \(O(d_{out}d_{in})\) extra memory, against ScaLoRA's \(O((d_{out}+d_{in}+r)r)\).
High-rank baseline (square-matrix compress/decompress); 1.08 GB of extra memory over LoRA on LLaMA3-8B.
Another rebasing scheme: tune a LoRA, merge it, start a new one and reset optimizer state. ScaLoRA avoids such restarts. COLA is not cited.
Also feeds low-rank increments into the base weight without restarts, but by adding the product's per-step change rather than by an optimal re-split. Delta-LoRA is not cited.

methods.formula_latex: W=W_0+BA,\ B\in\mathbb{R}_*^{d_{out}\times r},\ A\in\mathbb{R}_*^{r\times d_{in}}\ (\text{paper: } M=B,\ N=A^{\top},\ X=MN^{\top});\ G_t=\nabla_W\mathcal L;\ \text{matrix-space direction } \dot X_t=-\eta\,\tilde X_t:\ \text{AdamS: } m_t=\beta_1m_{t-1}+(1-\beta_1)G_t,\ v_t=\beta_2v_{t-1}+(1-\beta_2)G_t^{\odot2},\ \tilde X_t=m_t/\sqrt{v_t};\ \text{LRACS: } \tilde X_t=\mathrm{Diag}(m_q^{t})^{-1/2}\,G_t\,\mathrm{Diag}(m_s^{t})^{-1/2}\ (\text{row and column statistics, as in RACS});\ \text{Sylvester: } (B^{\top}B)(AA^{\top})K_t+K_t(B^{\top}B)(AA^{\top})=B^{\top}\dot X_tA^{\top};\ \text{lift: } \dot B=(\dot X_tA^{\top}-BAA^{\top}K_t)(AA^{\top})^{-1},\ \ \dot A=(B^{\top}B)^{-1}(B^{\top}\dot X_t-K_tB^{\top}BA);\ \ (B,A)\leftarrow(B+\dot B,\ A+\dot A);\ \text{frozen: } W_0;\ \text{trained: } B,A\ (\text{no weight decay})

methods.locus: LoRA-adapted weights of transformer-based models. The poster reports Mix-of-Show image generation with LoRA ranks \(r=4,8,16\) and GPT-2 medium on E2E NLG (\(r=4\)); the poster does not name the base diffusion model.
methods.structure: Optimizer for plain LoRA factors, built on the quotient \((\mathbb R_*^{d_{out}\times r}\times\mathbb R_*^{r\times d_{in}})/GL(r)\cong\mathcal M_r\). The base optimizer (Adam or RACS) preconditions the full-matrix gradient in matrix space. An \(r\times r\) Sylvester equation and a horizontal lift then map the resulting direction \(\dot X\) to factor updates. Derived here from the poster's formulas: \(\dot BA+B\dot A=P_B\dot X+\dot XP_A-P_B\dot XP_A\), with \(P_B=B(B^{\top}B)^{-1}B^{\top}\) and \(P_A=A^{\top}(AA^{\top})^{-1}A\). So the first-order change of \(W\) is the orthogonal projection of \(\dot X\) onto the tangent space \(T_{BA}\mathcal M_r\). The Sylvester matrix \(K\) is exactly what removes the double-counted term \(P_B\dot XP_A\), which the \(K=0\) lift contains; that lift is scaled GD, i.e. Riemannian-preconditioned LoRA. Setting \(K=\epsilon I\) instead turns the \(K\) terms into \(-\epsilon B\) and \(-\epsilon A\), i.e. decoupled weight decay on both factors. This is the paper's reading of weight decay as a crude approximation of \(K\), and the reason it removes the decay hyperparameter. The update is equivariant under \((B,A)\mapsto(BR,R^{-1}A)\), with \(K\mapsto R^{\top}KR^{-\top}\), so the induced \(W\) update depends only on \(BA\). This is the poster's Theorem 1: transformation invariance plus the paper's 'efficient feature learning' condition. Each step costs \(\Omega(d_{out}d_{in}r)+O(r^{3}+(d_{out}+d_{in})r^{2})\).
methods.mergeable_reason: Only the optimizer changes. The trained adapter is a standard \(BA\) that folds into \(W_0\).
methods.identity_at_init: Not specified in the material available. The lift needs \((AA^{\top})^{-1}\) and \((B^{\top}B)^{-1}\), i.e. full-rank factors in \(\mathbb R_*\), so LoRA's usual \(B=0\) start lies outside its domain. The paper presumably uses a nonzero or damped start, which the poster does not show.
methods.key_idea: Precondition in matrix space, then lift. Any matrix-space optimizer becomes a gauge-invariant LoRA optimizer once its direction is lifted to the factors through the quotient geometry, with an \(r\times r\) Sylvester solve fixing the correction term. The \(\epsilon I\) weight-decay term of factor optimizers is reinterpreted as a crude approximation of that Sylvester matrix and dropped.
methods.results_note: According to the official ICLR poster, with rank-4 LoRA on GPT-2 medium (E2E NLG) LRACS reaches BLEU 70.4, against 69.3 for LoRA-RITE and 68.6 for AdamW. On Mix-of-Show image customisation, AdamS at rank 16 reaches CLIP 32.64 / FID 46.32, against 31.90 / 55.68 for LoRA-RITE.

relations.note: With \(K=0\) and \(\dot X=-\eta G\), the lift is exactly the scaled-GD step \(\dot B=-\eta GA^{\top}(AA^{\top})^{-1}\), \(\dot A=-\eta(B^{\top}B)^{-1}B^{\top}G\) of Riemannian-preconditioned LoRA, which appears as the 'Scaled GD' baseline on the poster (ScaledAdamW is cited as Zhang and Pilanci, 2024). LoRA-S adds the Sylvester correction and allows arbitrary matrix-space preconditioners (derived here).
Main transformation-invariant baseline on the poster. LoRA-RITE preconditions in orthonormal factor bases; LoRA-S preconditions in matrix space and then lifts.

Citation not checked (full paper unavailable). LoRA-Pro's equivalent gradient is also the tangent-space projection \(P_BG+GP_A-P_BGP_A\), and it fixes its free \(r\times r\) matrix with a Sylvester equation. LoRA-S applies the same projection to a preconditioned matrix-space direction (derived here).

Conceptual relation: the abstract's quotient manifold \(\mathbb R_*^{m\times r}\times\mathbb R_*^{n\times r}/\sim\) and its horizontal lifts are the fixed-rank quotient geometry developed there, which LoRA-S instantiates for LoRA. Whether the paper cites it could not be checked because the paper PDF was unavailable.

methods.verification_notes: No arXiv version exists: arXiv API searches on the title terms and on the first author returned nothing. Title and both authors (Jinyang Zheng, Tong Wu) confirmed in the official ICLR 2026 orals-posters JSON ('Accept (Poster)', poster 10010449, OpenReview Guo2XGgxZA) and on ML Anthology (zheng2026iclr-loras), whose abstract matches. OpenReview (forum, API v1 and v2, PDF and the hashed PDF link) answered every request with a challenge page, which was not bypassed, and the Internet Archive was offline. The formula was therefore re-checked against the official ICLR poster image: \(X=MN^{\top}\) with \(M\in\mathbb R_*^{m\times r}\), \(N\in\mathbb R_*^{n\times r}\); Sylvester equation \(M^{\top}\dot XN=M^{\top}MN^{\top}NK+KM^{\top}MN^{\top}N\); lifts \(\dot M=(\dot XN-MN^{\top}NK)(N^{\top}N)^{-1}\) and \(\dot N=(\dot X^{\top}M-NM^{\top}MK^{\top})(M^{\top}M)^{-1}\); the AdamS and LRACS preconditioners; cost \(\Omega(mnr)+O(r^3+mr^2+nr^2)\); optimizer memory \(O(mn)\) and \(O(m+n+1)\). With \(M=B\) and \(N=A^{\top}\) these are exactly the entry's equations. The poster writes the Adam moments in terms of \(\dot X_t\), the matrix-space gradient, which the entry calls \(G_t\). The three 'derived here' claims were checked numerically: the tangent-space projection, \(K=\epsilon I\) as decoupled weight decay, and equivariance with \(K\mapsto R^{\top}KR^{-\top}\), \(\dot B\mapsto\dot BR\), \(\dot A\mapsto R^{-1}\dot A\). Poster tables re-read. Year 2025 follows the catalogue convention for public ICLR 2026 submissions, which opened in October 2025; the exact date for this forum could not be read. The ICLR JSON has only Poster and Oral decisions, so the 'Spotlight' label of the empty GitHub repository CleverWing/lora_s (created 2026-02-23, size 0) can be neither confirmed nor excluded; venue stays 'ICLR 2026 (poster)' and code_url stays empty. Confidence stays medium because the paper body was unreadable.

methods.name: DiaBlo
methods.full_name: DiaBlo: fine-tuning only the diagonal blocks of weight matrices
methods.paper_title: DiaBlo: Diagonal Blocks Are Sufficient For Finetuning
methods.formula_latex: h=(W_0+D)\,x,\quad D=\mathrm{blockdiag}(D_1,\dots,D_N)=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{N}D_i,\ \ D_i\in\mathbb{R}^{\frac{d_{out}}{N}\times\frac{d_{in}}{N}};\ \ (Dx)_i=D_ix_i\ (\text{one batched matmul over the } N \text{ input and output slices});\ \ \nabla_{D_i}\mathcal L=\big(\nabla_W\mathcal L\big)_{ii};\ \ D=0 \text{ at init};\ \text{frozen: } W_0 \text{ (in particular every off-diagonal block)};\ \text{trained: } D_1,\dots,D_N
methods.trainable_params: \frac{d_{in}d_{out}}{N}\ \text{per adapted matrix (typically } N\in\{32,64,128\}\text{; } N=64 \text{ is about 1.04\% of Llama2-7B with } q,k,v,\mathrm{up},\mathrm{down}\text{ adapted)}
methods.locus: Linear projections of the LLM: q, k, v, up and down (FP16 commonsense and MetaMathQA runs), or q, k, v, o, gate, up and down (BF16 commonsense, code, safety, MT-Bench and, according to Appendix A.4.5, the quantized runs), on Llama2-7B/13B, Llama3-8B, LLaMA-13B, Mistral-7B and Llama-3.2-3B (block-count ablation); all linear layers except embeddings and the LM head for T5-base (GLUE). Table 4's 70M trainable parameters for Llama2-7B at \(N=64\) match q, k, v, up and down rather than all seven projections, so the paper is internally inconsistent about the quantized runs' modules
methods.structure: A fixed block-diagonal sparsity pattern on \(\Delta W\): \(N\) independent dense blocks on the diagonal. Block \(i\) maps the \(i\)-th slice of \(d_{in}/N\) input coordinates to the \(i\)-th slice of \(d_{out}/N\) output coordinates, so \(\mathrm{rank}(\Delta W)\) can reach \(\min(d_{in},d_{out})\) with \(d_{in}d_{out}/N\) parameters. The update set is a linear subspace, not a product manifold. There is therefore no \(GL(r)\) gauge, the loss restricted to it is the original loss (convex in \(D\) whenever it is convex in \(W\)), and Adam on \(D\) is Adam on the masked entries of \(W\). With decoupled weight decay (the quantized runs use decay 1.0) AdamW shrinks \(D\), i.e. pulls \(W_{ii}\) towards \(W_{0,ii}\) rather than towards 0. The block structure is tied to the coordinate basis of the hidden units: it is not invariant to permuting or rotating them. Relative to neighbouring shapes, factoring each block at rank \(r/N\) gives MELoRA, a full \(N\times N\) grid of low-rank blocks gives GraLoRA, and choosing the blocks by gradient magnitude gives SMT. Linear least squares (Theorem 1): if the inputs \(X\) are generic of rank \(r\) and \(N\le d_{in}/r\), every DiaBlo minimiser is a full fine-tuning minimiser. This uses \(d_{in}d_{out}/N\ge d_{out}r\) parameters, against LoRA's \((d_{in}+d_{out})r\). Nonlinear case (Theorem 2): if \(X\) and \(g_Y\) are generic of ranks \(r_1\) and \(r_2\) and \(N\ge\lceil r_1N/d_{in}\rceil\lceil r_2N/d_{out}\rceil\), DiaBlo's stationary points are stationary for full fine-tuning. Sizes that \(N\) does not divide use blocks of \(\lceil d/N\rceil\) with zero padding.
methods.mergeable_reason: \(D\) is a \(d_{out}\times d_{in}\) block-diagonal matrix added to \(W_0\). It can be folded in, or stored compactly as an \(N\times\frac{d_{out}}{N}\times\frac{d_{in}}{N}\) tensor. On a quantized base (the GPTQ-DiaBlo and MagR-DiaBlo runs), merging needs re-quantization.
methods.identity_at_init: Yes. \(D=0\), and since there is no product the gradient \(\nabla_{D_i}\mathcal L=(\nabla_W\mathcal L)_{ii}\) is nonzero from the first step. There is no LoRA-style zero-factor stall and no special initialisation.
methods.key_idea: Update a structured subset of the weights directly instead of a low-rank product. Training only the diagonal blocks keeps LoRA-like memory and speed, since the forward pass is one batched matmul. It removes the bilinear factorisation's sensitivity to initialisation and optimizer. Under low-rank activations and gradients it provably reaches full fine-tuning minimisers in the linear case, and full fine-tuning stationary points in general.
methods.results_note: On commonsense reasoning DiaBlo reaches an 87.3 average with Llama3-8B (\(N=64\)), against 85.2 for DoRA \(r=32\) and 80.8 for LoRA \(r=32\). The paper lists this run as 1.04% of parameters, but q, k, v, up and down blocks at \(N=64\) come to about 0.89% of Llama3-8B by our count. On MetaMathQA with Llama2-7B (\(N=32\), 2.09%) it averages 43.4 on GSM8K/MATH, against 43.2 for full fine-tuning. Training speed matches LoRA \(r=32\): 170 minutes per epoch on Commonsense-170k, against 480 for DoRA.

relations.note: MELoRA factors each diagonal block as \(B_iA_i\) of rank \(r/N\), while DiaBlo trains the same blocks at full block rank. For equal \(N\), MELoRA's update set is a subset of DiaBlo's. MELoRA is not cited.

Cited baseline. SMT selects the sub-matrices with the largest warm-up gradients; DiaBlo fixes the pattern to the diagonal blocks. DiaBlo beats SMT on commonsense reasoning with fewer parameters (83.5 at 0.52% vs 81.8 at 0.84% on Llama2-7B).
GraLoRA tiles the full \(N\times N\) block grid with low-rank adapters; DiaBlo keeps only the diagonal tiles but makes them dense. GraLoRA is not cited.

Another structured, non-product shape: MiSS replicates one small trainable shard across the matrix (rank at most \(r\)), while DiaBlo gives each diagonal block its own dense parameters. MiSS is not cited.
Strongest LoRA-family baseline on commonsense reasoning. DiaBlo exceeds it on Llama2-7B, Llama3-8B and LLaMA-13B.

Quantized-base baseline. DiaBlo fine-tunes GPTQ/MagR-quantized Llama2 models with no joint quantization and initialisation procedure, and MagR-DiaBlo matches or exceeds LoftQ and ApiQ at 4 and 2 bits.

methods.name: QZO
methods.full_name: QZO: Quantized Zeroth-order Optimization (Q-SPSA with directional-derivative clipping)
methods.paper_title: Fine-tuning Quantized Neural Networks with Zeroth-order Optimization
methods.formula_latex: \hat W=\Delta\odot\overline W,\ \ \overline W\ \text{frozen low-bit codes (GPTQ int4 with group size } g=128\text{, or AQLM 2-bit codebooks)},\ \ \Delta=S\otimes\mathbf 1_{1\times g},\ S\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{d_{out}\times d_{in}/g}\ (\text{channel-wise } S\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}} \text{ for AQLM});\ \ d=\frac{\mathcal L((\Delta+\epsilon z)\odot\overline W;\mathcal B)-\mathcal L((\Delta-\epsilon z)\odot\overline W;\mathcal B)}{2\epsilon},\ z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\ \text{on the scale entries, regenerated from a seed};\ \ d'=\mathrm{clip}(d,-C,C);\ \ S\leftarrow\max(S-\eta\,d'z,\ 0);\ \text{frozen: the integer codes};\ \text{trained: the quantization scales (in the AQLM runs, non-quantized parameters are also updated by plain SPSA)};\ \text{no backward pass and no optimizer state}
methods.trainable_params: \frac{d_{out}d_{in}}{g}\ \text{scales per quantized matrix } (g=128;\ 5.03\times10^{7}\ \text{for OPT-6.7B, about } 0.76\%);\ d_{out}\ \text{for channel-wise AQLM scales};\ \text{optimizer memory } O(1) \text{ (a seed and a scalar)}
methods.locus: Quantization scales of all quantized linear layers: GPTQ 4-bit (group size 128) OPT-6.7B, Llama-2-7B and Llama-3.1-8B; AQLM 2-bit (one 16-bit codebook) Llama-2-13B, with channel-wise scales plus the non-quantized parts trained by plain SPSA; the NF4-quantized (bitsandbytes) DiT of Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large
methods.structure: PEQA-type parametrisation trained with MeZO-style SPSA. The parametrisation is a group-wise multiplicative rescaling of frozen integer codes, \(\hat W=(S\otimes\mathbf 1_{1\times g})\odot\overline W\); per channel it is the left diagonal action \(\hat W=\mathrm{diag}(s)\,\overline W\). The gradient estimate is a rank-one random projection \(zz^{\top}\nabla_S\mathcal L\) of the scale gradient, computed from two forward passes of the quantized model. Weights are never de-quantized or re-quantized, and activations are not stored. Directional-derivative clipping caps the scalar \(d\) at \(C\) (100 in the paper), and the projection \(\max(\cdot,0)\) keeps the scales non-negative. Every code stays fixed, so the reachable set is \(\{(S\otimes\mathbf 1)\odot\overline W\}\), of dimension \(d_{out}d_{in}/g\). The paper's Theorem 1 states that the clipped estimate is unbiased. Its proof (Appendix A) passes from the clipped to the unclipped sum with only the remark that the two agree as \(\epsilon\to0\), which ignores that the clipping event depends on \(z\). In general a clipped SPSA estimate is biased. In the idealised case of a fixed batch, \(\epsilon\to0\) and Gaussian \(z\), \(\mathbb E[\mathrm{clip}(d)\,z]=c\,\nabla_S\mathcal L\) with \(c\in(0,1]\), a shrinkage along the true gradient (derived here). The second-moment bound \(\mathbb E\|d'z\|^{2}\le\mathbb E\|dz\|^{2}\) holds unconditionally. The paper's per-coordinate variance inequality is derived through Theorem 1 and is therefore not established in general.
methods.mergeable_reason: The trained parameters are the quantization scales themselves. The result is an ordinary GPTQ or AQLM model with the same codes and inference kernels.
methods.identity_at_init: No adapter is added. Training starts from the post-training-quantized model, whose GPTQ/AQLM scales approximate but do not equal \(W_0\).
methods.key_idea: Zeroth-order training removes gradients and optimizer states, and quantization shrinks the weights. The two meet in the continuous quantization scales, which SPSA can perturb and update while the discrete codes stay fixed. Clipping the directional derivative keeps the noisy estimate stable.
methods.results_note: On 4-bit GPTQ Llama-2-7B, QZO needs 5.0 GB, against 14.8 GB for 16-bit MeZO and 26.0 GB for 16-bit SGD fine-tuning, and beats MeZO on four of five tasks (for example SST-2 90.0 vs 83.5). On OPT-6.7B it trails MeZO on most tasks.

relations.note: Uses MeZO's seed-regenerated SPSA and ZO-SGD, applied to the quantization scales of a 4- or 2-bit model instead of 16-bit weights. MeZO is the main baseline.
Trains the same object as PEQA, group-wise quantization scales over frozen integer codes, but without backpropagation, by combining it with MeZO-style estimation. PEQA is not cited.

Appendix comparison on OPT-6.7B: first-order QLoRA (5.6 GB) is more accurate than QZO (4.8 GB). A two-phase QZO+QLoRA variant (zeroth-order LoRA training, then QZO on the remaining scales) closes part of the gap at 4.9 GB.

Both are zeroth-order fine-tuning methods; AGZO is not cited. AGZO reduces estimator variance by perturbing 16-bit weights only along activation subspaces; QZO perturbs quantization scales and clips the directional derivative.

methods.verification_notes: Title, all five authors (first author Sifeng Shang) and first version (v1 2025-05-19; v3 2026-02-12, 'Accepted by ICLR 2026') confirmed with the arXiv export API; Semantic Scholar agrees (2025). ICLR 2026 acceptance confirmed in the official ICLR orals-posters JSON ('Accept (Poster)', poster 10007599, OpenReview mGeeRFToaW). Formula checked against Definition 3.3, Eq. 6 and Algorithm 1 (seeded perturbation, clipping, update \(\max(\Delta_i-\eta_t d'z,0)\)) and the implementation details: GPTQ group size 128, AQLM 1x16 with channel-wise scales, \(C=100\), \(\epsilon=10^{-3}\), learning rate \(10^{-7}\). trainable_params re-derived: the OPT-6.7B linear weights total about 6.44B, and dividing by 128 gives \(5.03\times10^{7}\), matching Table 2 (0.76% of 6.65B). methods.name: PERK
methods.full_name: PERK: Parameter Efficient Reasoning over Knowledge (meta-learned test-time LoRA memory)
methods.paper_title: PERK: Long-Context Reasoning as Parameter-Efficient Test-Time Learning
methods.formula_latex: \phi^{(0)}=\theta_{\mathrm{adapter}}=\{(B_l,A_l)\},\ \ \phi^{(n+1)}=\mathrm{AdamW}_{\alpha_{l,n}}\big(\phi^{(n)},\ \nabla_{\phi}\mathcal L^{\psi}_{\mathrm{NLL}}(\phi^{(n)};\mathcal K)\big),\ n=0,\dots,N-1\ (N=4,\ \text{differentiable AdamW}),\ \ \mathcal L^{\psi}_{\mathrm{NLL}}(\phi;\mathcal K)=-\sum_{c\in\mathrm{chunks}(\mathcal K)}\sum_{t}w_\psi(c)_t\,\log p_{W_0,\phi}(c_t\mid c_{<t})\ (\approx256\text{-token chunks processed as one batch; } w_\psi \text{ a two-layer MLP token weighter}),\ \ \text{answer } q \text{ with } h=(W_0+B^{(N)}A^{(N)})x\ \text{and no context in the prompt};\ \ \min_{\theta_{\mathrm{adapter}},\{\alpha_{l,n}\},\psi}\ \mathbb{E}_{(\mathcal K,q,y)}\,\mathcal L_{\mathrm{reason}}\big(W_0,\phi^{(N)}(\theta_{\mathrm{adapter}},\mathcal K);q,y\big),\ \ \nabla_{\theta_{\mathrm{adapter}}}\mathcal L_{\mathrm{reason}}\approx\frac{\partial\mathcal L_{\mathrm{reason}}}{\partial\phi^{(N)}}\prod_{n=N-T}^{N-1}J^{(n)},\ J^{(n)}=\frac{\partial\phi^{(n+1)}}{\partial\phi^{(n)}}\ (=I-\alpha H^{(n)}\text{ for plain GD}),\ \ T\in\{1,2\}\ (\text{truncated unrolling});\ \text{frozen: } W_0;\ \text{meta-trained: the LoRA initialisation, per-layer-per-step inner learning rates } \alpha_{l,n},\ \text{token weighter } \psi;\ \text{test-time trained: the LoRA, once per context}
methods.trainable_params: r(d_{in}+d_{out})\ \text{per adapted matrix with } r=256\ (\text{rsLoRA}),\ \text{on all linear modules of every layer for models up to 1B and of the top 4 layers for 7B/8B models};\ \text{plus } L\times N \text{ meta-learned inner learning rates and a two-layer MLP token weighter. The same adapter is re-trained for every new context}
methods.locus: All linear modules (attention and MLP): every layer of GPT-2, Qwen-2.5-0.5B and LLaMA-3.2-1B; only the top 4 layers of Qwen-2.5-7B and LLaMA-3.1-8B
methods.structure: Bi-level, MAML-style meta-learning over a LoRA. The inner loop is test-time training of \(\Delta W=BA\) by \(N=4\) differentiable AdamW steps on the token-weighted NLL of the context. The context is chunked into a parallel batch, which decouples its length from the native window; chunk order is kept only through 'Document i:' tags in the text. The outer loop optimises the adapter's initial state \((B_0,A_0)\), the inner learning rates and the token-weighting network, so that the post-adaptation model answers questions without seeing the context. Meta-gradients are truncated to the last \(T\in\{1,2\}\) inner steps, so meta-training on 8K-token contexts fits on one GPU. The LoRA serves as a fast-weight memory: the context is written into parameters by gradient descent, not by a hypernetwork forward pass. Gauge remark (derived here): the inner loop is plain adaptive gradient descent on the factors, which is not invariant under \((B,A)\mapsto(BR,R^{-1}A)\). The outer loop therefore selects a particular representative of the initial adapter's orbit, and its conditioning decides what four inner steps can write. The learned object is that representative, not just the product \(B_0A_0\).
methods.mergeable_reason: After adaptation \(B^{(N)}A^{(N)}\) is an ordinary low-rank delta and could be folded into \(W_0\). It is specific to one context, however, and is regenerated by test-time training for each new one, so it is kept as a swappable module.
methods.identity_at_init: Not identity by design. Inference starts from the meta-learned adapter \(\theta_{\mathrm{adapter}}\), which is generally nonzero, so the model differs from the base even before test-time training. The base weights stay frozen, so dropping the adapter recovers the base model. The LoRA initialisation at the start of meta-training is not stated beyond 'default' PEFT settings.
methods.key_idea: Treat a LoRA as a fast-weight memory written by a few gradient steps on the context at test time. Meta-learn the adapter's starting point, step sizes and token weights, MAML-style with truncated unrolling to fit 8K-token contexts, so that the written adapter supports reasoning over long inputs rather than in-context retrieval.
methods.results_note: Trained on 8K-token contexts, PERK beats standard long-context fine-tuning (FT-ICR) on HotpotQA/TriviaQA by about 20 absolute points at the 0.5B scale and 15 at 7B. On BabiLong, PERK (Qwen-2.5-7B) leads FT-ICR by 23 points on average when extrapolating to 32K tokens.

relations.note: Same goal of internalising a context into a LoRA. Doc-to-LoRA amortises the write into one hypernetwork forward pass trained by context distillation; PERK writes it with meta-learned gradient steps at test time. D2L appeared later and is not cited.
SHINE is a single-pass in-context hypernetwork from context to LoRA; PERK is the gradient-based, test-time-training counterpart. SHINE is not cited.
Also maps a context to a parameter delta, but with a forward-pass generator instead of inner-loop optimisation. Not cited.
Cartridges compresses a corpus offline into a trained KV cache by self-study distillation, once per corpus. PERK trains a LoRA per context in four meta-learned steps. Not cited.
Uses rank-stabilised scaling for its rank-256 adapters.

methods.verification_notes: All four authors (first author Zeming Chen) and first version (v1 2025-07-08) confirmed with the arXiv export API. v1 and v2 are titled 'PERK: Long-Context Reasoning as Parameter-Efficient Test-Time Learning', the same as the ICLR listing; v3 (2026-08-31) shortened it to 'PERK: Long-Context Reasoning as Test-Time Learning'. paper_title keeps the v1/ICLR title. methods.name: VAPT
methods.paper_title: Revisit Visual Prompt Tuning: The Expressiveness of Prompt Experts
methods.formula_latex: \tilde X^{(l)}=[x^{(l)}_1,\dots,x^{(l)}_N]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d}\ \mapsto\ X^{(l)}_{\text{img}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times d};\ \ X^{(l)}_{\text{conv}}=F^{(l)}*X^{(l)}_{\text{img}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H'\times W'\times d}\ \ (F^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times K}\text{ shared by all }d\text{ channels});\ \ G^{(l)}_j=\sum_{k=1}^{H'W'}\alpha^{(l)}_{j,k}\,x^{\text{conv},(l)}_k;\ \ p^{(l)}_j(\tilde X^{(l)})=W^{(2)}\sigma\big(W^{(1)}G^{(l)}_j\big),\ j=1,\dots,\ell;\ \ \tilde h_{m}=\mathrm{Attn}\Big(\begin{bmatrix}\tilde X^{(l)}\\P^{(l)}(\tilde X^{(l)})\end{bmatrix}W^{Q}_m,\begin{bmatrix}\tilde X^{(l)}\\P^{(l)}(\tilde X^{(l)})\end{bmatrix}W^{K}_m,\begin{bmatrix}\tilde X^{(l)}\\P^{(l)}(\tilde X^{(l)})\end{bmatrix}W^{V}_m\Big)\ \text{(prompt-position outputs discarded)};\ \ \text{frozen: all ViT weights};\ \text{trained: }\alpha^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{\ell\times H'W'},\ F^{(l)},\ \text{a per-block LayerNorm},\ W^{(1)}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d},W^{(2)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r}\ (\text{one feature projector shared by all blocks}),\ \text{head}
methods.trainable_params: L\,\ell\,H'W'+L\,K^{2}+2rd\ \text{per model (token-wise projectors, channel-shared kernels, shared feature projector; paper Eq. (15)), plus per-block LayerNorm and the head; e.g. }0.36\%\text{ of ViT-B/16 on average over the 24 FGVC/VTAB tasks (VPT-Deep: }L\ell d\text{). Released code: block 1 keeps }\ell d\text{ static VPT prompts and each token-wise projector also has an }\ell\text{-vector bias}
methods.locus: input token sequence of every ViT block (VPT-Deep insertion point), with each block's prompts generated from that block's own patch tokens; paper: ViT-B/16 (supervised ImageNet-21K, MAE, MoCo v3), ViT-L/H, SETR-PUP on ADE20K, the CLIP ViT-B/32 image encoder
methods.structure: Input-conditioned deep prompts. At block \(l\) the \(N\) patch tokens are laid out as an \(H\times W\times d\) map, convolved with one \(K\times K\) kernel \(F^{(l)}\) reused across all \(d\) channels, and pooled by \(\ell\) learned token-wise weightings \(\alpha^{(l)}_{j,\cdot}\in\mathbb{R}^{H'W'}\). Each pooled vector \(G^{(l)}_j\) passes through a bottleneck MLP \(g(u)=W^{(2)}\sigma(W^{(1)}u)\) with \(r\ll d\) that is shared by all blocks. Because convolution and pooling are linear, \(G^{(l)}_j=W_jX\) for some \(W_j\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times Nd}\), so each prompt expert is \(f_{N+j}(X)=W_m^{V\top}W^{(2)}\sigma(W^{(1)}_jX)\) with \(W^{(1)}_j=W^{(1)}W_j\). It is therefore a one-hidden-layer function of the whole sequence, where VPT's expert \(W_m^{V\top}p_j\) is a constant. The prompts are re-generated at every block from \(\tilde X^{(l)}\), not from the first-layer input or a [CLS] query, and their attention outputs are dropped as in VPT-Deep. In the released code the first block keeps ordinary static VPT prompts (VPT_DEPTH=1). The token-wise projector also carries a bias and is zero-initialised, and the shared projector is residual, \(p=G+W^{(2)}\sigma(W^{(1)}G)\), a detail not in the paper's Eq. (12).
methods.mergeable_reason: The prompts are extra tokens that depend on the current input \(\tilde X^{(l)}\). They lengthen the attention sequence to \(N+\ell\) and cannot be folded into \(W^{Q},W^{K},W^{V}\). Inference keeps the generator, at most about 0.6% more FLOPs than VPT (0.08-0.59% on the five FGVC datasets, Appendix E.7).
methods.identity_at_init: No. In the released code the token-wise projectors (weight and bias) are zero-initialised and the shared projector is bias-free and residual, so the generated prompts start as zero vectors. A zero prompt token is not inert: the pre-norm ViT block maps it through LayerNorm to the LayerNorm bias, and the key and value projections (with their biases) then give it a non-zero key and value, so it still takes softmax mass from the real tokens. The first block also uses randomly initialised static prompts. The paper describes no zero-output mechanism.
methods.key_idea: In the attention-as-mixture-of-experts reading, VPT adds prompt experts \(W_m^{V\top}p_j\) that are constant in the input, while the pretrained experts \(W_m^{V\top}x_j\) are linear in it. VAPT makes each prompt a cheap nonlinear function of the current block's tokens (channel-shared convolution, then token pooling, then a shared bottleneck MLP). This uses fewer parameters than VPT because \(H'W'<d\), and least-squares prompt estimation reaches the optimal \(\mathcal{O}_P([\log n/n]^{1/2})\) rate for prompts fitted by a single atom (\([\log n/n]^{1/4}\) when several fitted atoms crowd one true prompt).
methods.results_note: On ViT-B/16 pretrained on ImageNet-21K, VAPT reaches 72.91% mean VTAB-1K and 89.58% FGVC accuracy, 7.34 and 1.04 points above full fine-tuning, while tuning 0.36% of backbone parameters.

relations.note: Same VPT-Deep insertion point and frozen backbone. The per-block static prompt matrix \(P^{(l)}\) is replaced by prompts generated from that block's own tokens, using fewer parameters (\(L\ell H'W'\) versus \(L\ell d\)). The bias-free generator in the paper cannot output a general constant prompt, so this is a successor rather than a strict generalisation.
Same group and the same attention/prompt-to-MoE correspondence. The Voronoi-loss least-squares analysis of prompt estimation is reused, here for input-dependent prompt experts.
Cited as motivation (Petrov et al.): static prompts can only add a bias to an attention block's output. VAPT's input-dependent prompt experts are meant to escape that limitation.

Instance-dependent prompt generation for NLP (not cited). IDPG generates prompts once from the input sentence. VAPT regenerates them at every block from that block's tokens, with a convolution-plus-pooling generator.
LPT generates one instance-dependent prompt from the hidden states of a single middle layer. VAPT generates prompts at every block.

Prompt-pool methods (cited as Wang et al., 2022) first forward the image through a frozen pretrained encoder and use its [CLS] feature as the query that selects prompts for the layers. The paper therefore treats their prompts as functions of the first-layer input \(X^{(0)}\). VAPT conditions each layer's prompts on that layer's input \(X^{(l)}\).

methods.name: AdaPaD
methods.paper_title: AdaPaD: Adaptive Parallel Deflation for PEFT with Self-Correcting Rank Discovery
methods.formula_latex: \Delta W_i=s\sum_{k=1}^{r_i}b_{i,k}a_{i,k}^{\top},\ \ b_{i,k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}},\ a_{i,k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{in}};\ \ \text{bilinear model (theory): } Y_{k,\ell}=Y-\sum_{k'<k}b_{k',\ell-1}a_{k',\ell-1}^{\top}X,\ \ (a_{k,\ell},b_{k,\ell})=\mathrm{Rank1}\big(Y_{k,\ell},X,T;\ \text{warm start }(a_{k,\ell-1},b_{k,\ell-1})\big)\approx\arg\min_{a,b}\|Y_{k,\ell}-ba^{\top}X\|_F^2\ \ \text{for all active }k\le\ell\text{ in parallel};\ \ \text{deep net: every }\Delta\text{ steps snapshot }\{\bar b_{i,k'},\bar a_{i,k'}\};\ \text{component }k\text{ trained on }\mathcal{L}\big(W_{0,i}+s\sum_{k'<k}\bar b_{i,k'}\bar a_{i,k'}^{\top}+s\,b_{i,k}a_{i,k}^{\top}\big);\ \ \text{growth: } r_i\leftarrow r_i+1\text{ for the top-}h\text{ modules by }\bar S_iU_i\ (r_i<r_{\max})\text{ until }\textstyle\sum_i r_i\ge B,\ \ S_i=\|\theta_i\|_2^{-1/2}\sum_{p\in\theta_i}|p\,\nabla_p\mathcal{L}|;\ \ \text{frozen: }W_0;\ \text{trained: rank-1 pairs (plus one privately warmed reserve per module)}
methods.trainable_params: r_i(d_{in}+d_{out})\ \text{per adapted matrix, plus one reserve }(d_{in}+d_{out})\text{ per module while growing};\ \ 1\le r_i\le r_{\max},\ \textstyle\sum_i r_i\le B\ \text{(GLUE, DeBERTaV3-base: }B=144\text{ over 72 modules, }r_{\max}=4\text{, }0.34\text{M trainable parameters in Table 3, against }0.32\text{-}0.47\text{M for the baselines; Qwen3-0.6B SQuAD: 196 modules, }r_{\max}=8\text{, average-rank budget }\bar r\in\{4,6\}\text{, }1.93\text{-}2.30\text{M)}
methods.locus: all linear layers: \(W_q,W_k,W_v,W_o,W_{f1},W_{f2}\) of every DeBERTaV3-base layer (72 modules); the seven attention and MLP projections \(W_q,W_k,W_v,W_o,W_{gate},W_{up},W_{down}\) of every Qwen3-0.6B layer (196 modules)
methods.structure: The deployed object is an ordinary additive update \(\Delta W_i=s\sum_{k\le r_i}b_{i,k}a_{i,k}^{\top}\) whose rank \(r_i\) differs per module. What changes is how the rank-1 terms are trained. Component \(k\) is fitted to a deflation target that removes only its predecessors, \(k'<k\), using their latest estimates. All components are refined in parallel, and each worker's target is refreshed every round. Sequential (Hotelling-style) deflation, of which the paper counts ReLoRA as an instance, freezes earlier errors into every later residual. Here the mismatch \(\|Y_{k,\ell}-Y_k^{\star}\|_F\) vanishes as rounds proceed (self-correction, Proposition 2). Activation is staggered (worker \(k\) starts at round \(k\)), and before activation a component is trained privately against its current target (advance learning). In the network the target is implicit: component \(k\) is trained with the task loss through a forward pass containing the round-start snapshot of components \(0,\dots,k-1\) and itself, with later components absent. Per-module rank grows from 1 with IncreLoRA's importance-times-uncertainty score under a shared budget, so the rank profile is an output. On CoLA it settles at 16/44/8/4 modules with rank 1/2/3/4. The theory covers a single bilinear layer \(Y=W^{\star}X+\mathcal{E}\) under a spectral-gap assumption. The total error obeys \(G_{k,\ell}\le 3\mathcal{R}_k(\ell-s_k+2)m_k^{\ell-s_k+1}\), and the weight-recovery bound splits into a vanishing algorithmic term plus a statistical floor. Two practical details depart from the analysed algorithm. The Frobenius-ball projection \(\Pi_Q\) that the theory needs is switched off (\(Q=\infty\)) in all experiments. On GLUE an optional IncreLoRA orthogonality penalty \(\lambda_{\text{orth}}(\|A^{\top}A-I\|_F+\|BB^{\top}-I\|_F)/(2n_{\text{layers}})\) is added, with \(\lambda_{\text{orth}}\) up to 0.5 per task; it is disabled on SQuAD.
methods.mergeable_reason: After training \(\Delta W_i=s\sum_k b_{i,k}a_{i,k}^{\top}\) is a fixed matrix of rank at most \(r_i\) that folds into \(W_{0,i}\), as with LoRA.
methods.identity_at_init: Not exact. Each module starts with one committed component whose \(a\) and \(b\) are both drawn from \(\mathcal{N}(0,0.02)\), so \(\Delta W_i=s\,b_{i,1}a_{i,1}^{\top}\) is small but non-zero. Components added later arrive pre-trained by advance learning, not at zero.
methods.key_idea: Treat a LoRA update as a sum of rank-1 deflation steps, but train all steps at once, each against a target rebuilt from its predecessors' current estimates. Errors in early components are then corrected over rounds instead of being frozen into later residuals. In the single-layer bilinear model, individual rank-1 directions converge nearly linearly (exponential decay with a linear prefactor). On top of this, ranks grow per module under a global budget, so the rank allocation is an output.
methods.results_note: On GLUE with DeBERTaV3-base, AdaPaD with 0.34M trainable parameters (baselines 0.32-0.47M) has the highest average (89.34), ahead of AdaLoRA (89.03) and a reproduced IncreLoRA (88.99). On Qwen3-0.6B SQuAD/SQuAD v2 it matches fixed-rank LoRA F1 with adapters 15.9-44.3% (mean 30.7%) smaller.

relations.note: Borrows IncreLoRA's importance-times-uncertainty score and reserve components (turned into advance learning) and likewise grows ranks from 1 under a shared budget. Here each new component is trained against a self-correcting deflation target.
GLUE baseline. AdaLoRA prunes from a high initial rank using SVD-triplet importance; AdaPaD grows from rank 1.
GLUE baseline. SoRA learns sparse gates on rank-1 components; AdaPaD trains rank-1 components as parallel deflation steps.
The paper calls ReLoRA's sequence of merged low-rank updates sequential deflation, whose early errors persist. AdaPaD instead trains all components in parallel with refreshed targets.
The deployed adapter is a standard LoRA update with per-module ranks. AdaPaD changes how its rank-1 terms are trained and how many each module gets.

methods.locus: any linear layer; paper: Q, K, V, O, Gate, Up, Down of LLaMA-2-7B and Q, K, V of LLaMA-2-13B (\(r=8\), \(\alpha=16\))
methods.structure: Plain LoRA with a closed-form, data-dependent starting point. The derivation is done in the frozen-\(A\) (LoRA-FA) setting with \(A\) row-orthonormal. It minimises \(\mathbb{E}\|\hat W-W_{\text{tgt}}\|_F^2\) for the constrained MLE under \(\|W_{\text{tgt}}-W_0\|_F=O(N^{-1/2})\). The bound reduces to the quadratic \(\mathrm{tr}(A\Omega A^{\top})\), whose Initialization Guidance Matrix \(\Omega\) has two parts. The variance part is the diagonal \(d_{in}\times d_{in}\) blocks of the inverse Fisher of \(\mathrm{vec}(W)\), summed over outputs, divided by \(N\). Under K-FAC this is \(\tfrac{1}{N}\mathrm{tr}(Y_F^{-1})Z_F^{-1}\). The bias part is \(-\widehat{\Delta}^{\top}\widehat{\Delta}\), with the displacement estimated by a block-diagonal natural-gradient step \(\widehat{\Delta}=-DGZ_F^{-1}\). This is not the full K-FAC step \(-Y_F^{-1}GZ_F^{-1}\), since only the diagonal of \(Y_F^{-1}\) is kept. \(A_0\) takes the \(r\) bottom eigenvectors of \(\Omega\), and \(B_0=\widehat{\Delta}A_0^{\top}\) makes \(W_0+B_0A_0\) the projection of the estimated target onto that row space. Two limits are informative. Dropping the variance term and using the raw gradient (\(\widehat{\Delta}\to-G\)) gives \(A_0=V_r^{\top}\) and \(B_0A_0=-U_rS_rV_r^{\top}\), the LoRA-One/LoRA-GA gradient-SVD choice (Remark 4.3). Keeping only the variance term gives the top eigenvectors of \(Z_F\), the principal input-activation directions an EVA-type init uses (our observation, not in the paper). The released code adds three implementation details: \(\widehat{\Delta}\) is normalised by its top singular value, the variance term is down-weighted (\(\beta=0.03\)), and both factors are scaled by \(1/\sqrt{\gamma}\) with \(\gamma=1024\). The released config also enables rsLoRA scaling (\(\alpha/\sqrt{r}\)), which the paper's hyperparameter table does not mention.
methods.mergeable_reason: Only the starting point changes. The trained \(BA\) is an ordinary rank-\(r\) delta that folds into \(W_0\).
methods.identity_at_init: No. \(B_0A_0=\widehat{\Delta}A_0^{\top}A_0\neq 0\), so training starts at a projected Fisher-gradient step from \(W_0\) (in the paper's derivation, the projection of the estimated target). Like LoRA-One, the official code does not subtract \(B_0A_0\) from \(W_0\), although it does for other init modes. With the \(1/\sqrt{\gamma}\) factor scaling the initial offset is small.
methods.key_idea: Choose the LoRA subspace to minimise the expected distance between the fine-tuned and target weights. That distance splits into a bias term, the target's distance from the subspace estimated by a Fisher-preconditioned gradient, and a variance term from sampling noise through the inverse Fisher. Both enter one symmetric matrix \(\Omega\), and \(A_0\) is its bottom-\(r\) eigenspace. Gradient-SVD inits such as LoRA-One are recovered when the variance term is dropped and the Fisher is ignored.
methods.results_note: With LLaMA-2-7B (\(r=8\)), LoRA-DA averages 84.3% on eight commonsense benchmarks against 84.0% for MiLoRA, the best baseline. After MetaMathQA-100K it reaches 55.0% GSM8K and 9.2% MATH, 1.0 point above LoRA-One on average.

relations.note: Remark 4.3: dropping the variance term and replacing the Fisher-gradient by the raw gradient makes \(A_0\) the top-\(r\) right singular vectors of \(G\) (left singular vectors in the paper's \(Y=ZW\) convention), with \(B_0A_0=-U_rS_rV_r^{\top}\). That is LoRA-One's spectral initialisation up to factor balancing and scale (initialisation only; LoRA-One's preconditioned training is not part of LoRA-DA). Like LoRA-One, the released code does not offset \(W_0\).

Gradient-based data-aware init that LoRA-DA criticises for being single-step and ignoring anisotropy. Remark 4.3 says the degenerate case 'coincides' with LoRA-GA, but only the \(A\) side does: LoRA-GA takes \(B\) from the next \(r\) left singular vectors (\(r+1\) to \(2r\)) and offsets \(W_0\).
The optimality theory is derived for frozen \(A\) (LoRA-FA); the same \(A_0\) and \(B_0\) are then used for standard LoRA, and a frozen-\(A\) experiment is reported.
Data-agnostic baseline built from the top singular directions of \(W_0\).
Data-agnostic baseline built from the minor singular directions of \(W_0\); the strongest commonsense baseline (84.0 vs 84.3).

Not cited. In the variance-only limit \(\Omega\) is proportional to \(Z_F^{-1}\), whose bottom eigenvectors are the top principal directions of the (uncentred) layer inputs. These are the directions EVA uses for \(A\), up to centring, so LoRA-DA interpolates between an activation-variance init and a gradient-SVD init (our observation, not in the paper).

methods.name: WASI
methods.paper_title: Efficient Resource-Constrained Training of Transformers via Subspace Optimization
methods.trainable_params: d_{out}d_{in}\ (+d_{out}\text{ bias})\ \text{per adapted matrix: the whole weight is updated with a dense gradient assembled from the compressed activation, but held and run as rank-}K_i\text{ factors with }K_i(d_{in}+d_{out})\text{ entries; no added parameters}
methods.locus: linear layers of the MLP blocks of ViT and Swin-T, both ImageNet-1K pretrained (the paper does not name the ViT size); all attention and MLP linear layers of ViT in an appendix ablation (Tab. 1); the last 1-5 decoder layers of TinyLlama (\(\varepsilon=0.1\)); the last 1-4 convolutions of MCUNet for the weight part (WSI) only
methods.structure: Compression-aware fine-tuning without an adapter. Each fine-tuned weight is replaced by its rank-\(K_i\) truncation, with \(K_i\) set once by an explained-variance threshold \(\varepsilon\) on \(W_0\)'s spectrum. Thereafter the factored weight \(LR\) is tracked across steps by one power/subspace-iteration step warm-started from the previous \(L\), not by fresh SVDs. This relies on the observed stability of layer ranks during fine-tuning (Fig. 3a). Forward and input-gradient passes cost \(O(K_i(d_{in}+d_{out}))\) per token. The weight gradient is formed from a Tucker/HOSVD compression of the stored input activation, whose mode factors are also warm-started by subspace iteration (the ASI method, here with a dynamic-programming rank search and 3-D/4-D activation support). The update is therefore a full-matrix step in weight space followed by re-projection onto a rank-\(K_i\) manifold, close to training a low-rank model in factored form. It is not a frozen-\(W_0\) plus \(\Delta W\) method. In the released code the dense weight remains the optimised parameter and \(L,R\) are recomputed from it at each forward pass; the paper's Eq. (11) writes the update directly on \(LR\). The method targets on-device transfer learning, where activation and weight memory dominate. Two further code-versus-paper details: the code starts from \(L=U_{K_i}\) (orthonormal) and \(R=\Sigma_{K_i}V_{K_i}^{\top}\), the reverse of Eq. (7), so \(L\) stays orthonormal as in later iterations. Eq. (11) is printed with \(+\eta\), whereas the code applies an ordinary descent step to the dense weight.
methods.mergeable_reason: There is no side branch to merge: the trained model is the factored weight \(L_iR_i\) per layer. It can be multiplied out to a dense matrix or kept factored, which is cheaper at inference (about 1.4x faster than vanilla on a Raspberry Pi 5).
methods.identity_at_init: No. From the first step the forward pass uses the truncation \(U_{K_i}\Sigma_{K_i}V_{K_i}^{\top}\) of \(W_0\), not \(W_0\), so the starting function differs unless \(\varepsilon=1\), which recovers vanilla training. Activation compression also makes the first gradients approximate.
methods.key_idea: On edge devices the memory of backpropagation, not the trainable-parameter count, is the bottleneck. WASI keeps both the weights and the saved activations in fixed low-rank subspaces and follows those subspaces with warm-started subspace iteration instead of repeated SVDs. Training memory falls by up to 62x and FLOPs by about 1.5-2x, while the low-rank weights also speed up inference.
methods.results_note: Fine-tuning Swin-T at \(\varepsilon=0.9\), WASI matches vanilla accuracy while cutting training memory by up to 62x and FLOPs by 1.5x; on a Raspberry Pi 5 it is about 1.4x faster than vanilla training for ViT on CIFAR-10.

relations.note: Not cited. Both target activation-dominated on-device training memory. TinyTL freezes weights and trains biases plus lite residual branches; WASI updates the weights inside low-rank weight and activation subspaces.

Not cited. GaLore keeps full weights and projects gradients onto a periodically refreshed SVD subspace for optimiser memory. WASI factorises the weights themselves to a fixed rank, tracks them by power iteration, and compresses the saved activations.
Not cited. Both compress the activations saved for the weight gradient: VeLoRA projects sub-tokens to rank 1, WASI uses a warm-started Tucker/HOSVD.

WASI argues that LoRA keeps the frozen dense weights and full activations in memory and loses the low-rank speed-up once merged. WASI trains and deploys a factored model instead (compared against SVD-LLM, which pairs truncated SVD with a LoRA adapter).
Cited low-intrinsic-dimension evidence (Aghajanyan et al.) motivating training inside a stable low-dimensional subspace.
Cited (Li et al., 2018) for the claim that over-parameterised models reside in low-dimensional subspaces.

methods.name: TeRA
methods.full_name: Vector-based random Tensor network for high-Rank Adaptation
methods.paper_title: TeRA: Vector-based Random Tensor Network for High-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
methods.formula_latex: \Delta\mathcal{W}(i_1,\dots,i_N)=\sum_{r_1=1}^{R_1}\cdots\sum_{r_N=1}^{R_N}\mathcal{G}(r_1,\dots,r_N)\prod_{n=1}^{N}d^{(n)}_{r_n}A^{(n)}(r_n,i_n),\ \ \Delta W=\mathrm{Unfold}_{[N;k]}(\Delta\mathcal{W})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times d_{in}},\ \prod_{n\le k}I_n=d_{out},\ \prod_{n>k}I_n=d_{in};\ \ \text{equivalently } \Delta W=L\big(\mathcal{G}_{[N;k]}\odot uv^{\top}\big)M,\ L=\big(\textstyle\bigotimes_{n\le k}A^{(n)}\big)^{\top},\ M=\textstyle\bigotimes_{n>k}A^{(n)},\ u=\textstyle\bigotimes_{n\le k}d^{(n)},\ v=\textstyle\bigotimes_{n>k}d^{(n)};\ \ h=(W_0+\Delta W)x;\ \ \text{frozen and shared by all adapted layers: random core }\mathcal{G}\in\mathbb{R}^{R_1\times\cdots\times R_N}\text{ and factors }A^{(n)}\in\mathbb{R}^{R_n\times I_n};\ \text{trained per layer: }d^{(n)}\in\mathbb{R}^{R_n},\ n=1,\dots,N
methods.trainable_params: \sum_{n=1}^{N}R_n\ \text{per adapted matrix; paper default }R_n=I_n\text{ with only one side split, e.g. a }4096\times4096\text{ matrix folded to }4096\times8\times8\times8\times8\text{ gives }4096+4\cdot8=4128\ (\approx0.0039\%\text{ of Llama-2-7B with }W_q,W_v\text{ adapted})
methods.locus: \(W_q\) and \(W_v\) of every attention layer (paper: Llama-2-7B, Llama-3-8B); any linear layer in principle, with one core and factor set sliced to each layer's shape
methods.structure: The update matrix is folded into an order-\(N\) tensor and written in Tucker form. The core and factor matrices are large, randomly initialised (the factors with Kaiming init, Appendix F), frozen and shared by every adapted layer. The trainable part is a set of \(N\) per-layer vectors \(d^{(n)}\) acting as diagonal matrices on the core's modes. After unfolding, \(\Delta W=L\,\mathrm{diag}(u)\,\mathcal{G}_{[N;k]}\,\mathrm{diag}(v)\,M\), with \(u\) and \(v\) Kronecker products of the trained vectors. This is a VeRA-type double diagonal scaling of a frozen random matrix, except that the diagonals are rank-1 tensors and the outer projections are Kronecker-structured. The rank bound is \(\mathrm{rank}(\Delta W)\le\min(\prod_{n\le k}R_n,\prod_{n>k}R_n)\), so \(R_n=I_n\) permits full rank with only \(\sum_n I_n\le d_{in}+d_{out}\) parameters (Theorems 1-2). Measured updates are near full rank in every layer. Theorem 3 bounds the approximation error by the energy of \(W^{\star}\) outside \(\mathrm{span}(L)\otimes\mathrm{span}(M^{\top})\) plus a tensor-spectral-norm term that grows with the tensor order \(N\). By our derivation (the paper does not state this reduction), VeRA is the case \(N=2\) with \(A^{(1)}=I\), core equal to VeRA's \(B\), \(R_2=r\) and \(A^{(2)}\) equal to VeRA's \(A\), which gives \(\mathrm{diag}(d^{(1)})B\,\mathrm{diag}(d^{(2)})A\). In ablations, replacing the random factors by identities (\(\text{TeRA}_{iden}\)) or using unshared per-layer cores both hurt accuracy.
methods.mergeable_reason: After training, \(\Delta W=\mathrm{Unfold}_{[N;k]}(\Delta\mathcal{W})\) is materialised once and added to \(W_0\) (\(W_{\text{final}}=W_0+\Delta W\)), so inference has no overhead. Training is slower because \(\Delta W\) is contracted from the core at every step.
methods.identity_at_init: Exact. All \(d^{(n)}\) are initialised as ones (0.1 in the released code) except one, which is zero, so \(\Delta W=0\).
methods.key_idea: Decouple rank from parameter count by putting the trainable parameters on the diagonal of a shared random Tucker tensor network. The frozen core and factors supply the high-rank directions, and each layer learns only \(\sum_n R_n\) mode-wise scalings. The result is near-full-rank updates at VeRA-level parameter counts.
methods.results_note: On Commonsense170k with \(W_q\) and \(W_v\) adapted, TeRA averages 85.31% on Llama-3-8B (0.0033% trainable). That ties HiRA (\(r=32\), 0.1695%) with about 51x fewer trainable parameters and beats the parameter-matched LoRETTA (83.58%).

relations.note: VeRA's \(\mathrm{diag}(b)B\,\mathrm{diag}(d)A\) is the \(N=2\) instance with an identity first factor and the core set to VeRA's \(B\) (our derivation; the paper only compares parameter counts with VeRA). TeRA tensorises the update so the shared frozen randomness can reach full rank with a similar number of trained scalars.
Main high-rank baseline. TeRA matches HiRA \(r=32\) with 51-64x fewer parameters and beats HiRA \(r=1\).
Tensor-train adapter with trained cores, the strongest parameter-matched baseline. TeRA trains only diagonal scalings of a frozen shared network.
Cited tensor-based adapter. LoTR trains shared bases and a per-layer \(r\times r\) core; TeRA freezes the shared core and factors and trains only per-layer mode-wise diagonals.
Not cited. RandLoRA also reaches full rank from frozen random bases with learned diagonal scalings, but sums many low-rank terms and so uses far more trainable parameters.
Cited quantum-inspired high-rank baseline. TeRA edges it out at a fraction of its parameter count (Llama-3-8B commonsense: 85.31 vs 85.27 at 0.0033% vs 0.0343%; Llama-2-7B: 78.63 vs 77.53).

methods.verification_notes: Title, authors (Yuxuan Gu, Wuyang Zhou, Giorgos Iacovides, Danilo Mandic) and first version (v1 2025-09-03, v2 2026-04-14, comment 'Accepted at ACL main conference 2026') confirmed with the arXiv export API; year 2025 correct. ACL 2026 confirmed on the ACL Anthology page 2026.acl-long.106 (Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting, Volume 1: Long Papers, pp. 2314-2329, DOI 10.18653/v1/2026.acl-long.106); no oral claim is made. Formula checked against Eq. (5) (frozen shared core \(\mathcal{G}\) and factors \(A^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{R_i\times I_i}\), trainable \(d^{(i)}\), all ones but one zero), Eq. (6) (merge), Theorems 1-2 (rank bound, \(\sum R_i\le J_1+J_2\)) and Theorem 3. The paper writes \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{J_2\times\prod R_i}\) although \(\bigotimes A^{(i)}\) is \(\prod R_i\times J_2\); the entry uses the dimensionally consistent form. Which side comes first in the unfolding is a convention. Appendix F's example (indim 4096, outdim 8, tensor 4096x8x8x8x8) leaves the input side unsplit. The parameter count is unchanged. The example count 4096+32=4128 per matrix times 64 matrices is about 0.0039% of Llama-2-7B, matching Tables 2 and 4. Code verified in peft_local/tuners/tera/layer.py: d_initial=0.1, one vector zeroed, shared Tera_core and per-mode square factors as buffers. LoTR and QuanTA are cited; RandLoRA is not, and is labelled so. Not in Hugging Face PEFT: the authors ship a local fork, and there is no tera tuner at main.

vera relation: same labelling.

methods.name: Hybrid-LoRA
methods.full_name: Hybrid-LoRA: score-based split of modules into full fine-tuning and LoRA
methods.paper_title: Hybrid-LoRA: Bridging Full Fine-Tuning and Low-Rank Adaptation for Post-Training
methods.formula_latex: \text{probe (500 warm-up steps, all }(l,m)\in\mathcal{U}=[L]\times\{W_q,W_k,W_v,W_o,W_{gate},W_{up},W_{down}\}\text{): } h=W_{0}x+b+\alpha_{l,m}B\,\mathrm{diag}(e_{l,m})A\,x;\ \ s^{(t)}_{l,m}=\tfrac{1}{r}\big\|e_{l,m}\odot\nabla_{e_{l,m}}[\mathcal{L}_{val}(\mathcal{B}_t;z^{(t)}_{-A})+\mathcal{L}_{val}(\mathcal{B}_t;z^{(t)}_{-B})]\big\|_1\ (\text{random complementary bipartition }\mathcal{U}=\mathcal{U}_A^{(t)}\cup\mathcal{U}_B^{(t)});\ \ H(l,m)=\mu_{l,m}\,\sigma_{l,m}\text{ over batches};\ \ \mathcal{S}_{fft}=\text{lowest-}H\text{ modules, added greedily while }\textstyle\sum_{\mathcal{S}_{fft}}P_{l,m}\le R_{fft}\sum_{\mathcal{U}}P_{l,m};\ \ \text{final (re-initialised from }W_0\text{): } W_{l,m}=W_{0,l,m}+\Delta W_{l,m}\ (\text{dense, trained})\ \text{for }(l,m)\in\mathcal{S}_{fft},\ \ W_{l,m}=W_{0,l,m}+BA\ (r=16)\ \text{for }(l,m)\in\mathcal{U}\setminus\mathcal{S}_{fft};\ \ \text{optimised with GRPO or GSPO}
methods.trainable_params: \sum_{(l,m)\in\mathcal{S}_{fft}}d_{out}d_{in}+\sum_{(l,m)\in\mathcal{S}_{lora}}r(d_{in}+d_{out}),\ r=16,\ R_{fft}=10\%\ (\approx105\text{M of }1{,}544\text{M on Qwen2.5-1.5B},\ 449\text{M on Qwen2.5-7B})
methods.locus: the seven attention and MLP linear projections of every decoder layer of Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B/7B-Instruct; the fully fine-tuned modules concentrate in the attention projections of later layers
methods.structure: The trainable locus is a union. A small set \(\mathcal{S}_{fft}\) of whole matrices receives dense updates, and every other candidate matrix receives a rank-\(r\) LoRA update. The partition is chosen once, before the real run. A probe attaches AdaLoRA-style SVD-form LoRA (\(B\,\mathrm{diag}(e)A\), scaled by a per-module architecture weight \(\alpha_{l,m}\)) to all modules and trains it briefly. Each module is then scored by the first-order sensitivity \(\tfrac1r\|e\odot\nabla_e\mathcal{L}_{val}\|_1\) of its LoRA coefficients. The score is measured under random complementary on/off masks of the other modules (Shapley-NAS style; \(K=20\) random partitions in the experiments) and aggregated as mean times standard deviation over batches. A low score is read as LoRA being insufficient for that module, so the lowest-scoring modules are fully fine-tuned up to the budget. Eq. (4) states the budget as a parameter fraction, while the experiments call it a 10% module ratio. The model is then re-initialised and trained with RLVR using separate learning rates (\(10^{-6}\) for dense modules, \(2.5\times10^{-5}\) for LoRA). Unlike rank-reallocation methods (AdaLoRA, AutoLoRA, SoRA), which stay inside the low-rank space, it upgrades a few whole modules to dense full-rank updates.
methods.mergeable_reason: The dense modules are simply updated in place, and each \(BA\) folds into its \(W_0\). The result is a single dense model of the original shape with no inference overhead.
methods.identity_at_init: For the final stage, fully fine-tuned modules start exactly at \(W_0\). The LoRA modules presumably use standard \(B=0\) initialisation (not stated), giving \(h=W_0x\) at the start of RL. The probe's adapters are discarded.
methods.key_idea: Modules differ in how well a low-rank update can adapt them. Hybrid-LoRA measures this with a cheap LoRA probe and spends a small full-fine-tuning budget on the modules where LoRA's coefficients show the weakest sensitivity, keeping LoRA elsewhere. The aim is to close the LoRA-to-full-fine-tuning gap in RLVR post-training while tuning roughly 6-7% of the parameters (105M of 1,544M, 6.8%, at 1.5B; 449M, about 6%, at 7B).
methods.results_note: On Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct with GRPO, Hybrid-LoRA (105M tunable of 1,544M) reaches 80.2 Math-500 pass@1, against 80.6 for full fine-tuning and 77.4 for the best module-selection baseline (AutoLoRA criterion).

relations.note: The probe reuses AdaLoRA's SVD-form LoRA (\(B\,\mathrm{diag}(e)A\)), and the mean-times-variability score echoes AdaLoRA's sensitivity-times-uncertainty importance. Here it selects whole modules for full fine-tuning rather than pruning ranks. An AdaLoRA-rank criterion is also a baseline.

AutoLoRA's learned architecture weight \(\alpha\) is the main selection baseline (bottom-10% modules by \(\alpha\) assigned to full fine-tuning). It is the best baseline on Math-500 at 1.5B and the only one reported at 3B and 7B; LoRA-Drop is higher on some 1.5B benchmarks.
Baseline criterion: modules with the smallest LoRA output contribution are assigned to full fine-tuning.

Not cited. Spectrum fully trains the matrices with the highest weight-only random-matrix SNR and freezes the rest. Hybrid-LoRA selects by LoRA-probe gradient sensitivity and puts LoRA on everything else.
Not cited. PLoP decides where LoRA should go from module-data alignment; Hybrid-LoRA decides which modules should get full-rank updates instead of LoRA.
Combines dense full fine-tuning on about 10% of modules with standard LoRA (\(r=16\)) on the rest.

methods.name: DC-Merge
methods.full_name: DC-Merge: directional-consistency model merging (energy smoothing + cover-space merging)
methods.paper_title: DC-Merge: Improving Model Merging with Directional Consistency
methods.formula_latex: \Delta_i\approx U_i\Sigma_iV_i^{\top}\ \ (\text{rank-}r\text{ truncated SVD of the task vector }\Delta_i=W_i-W_0\text{ or }\Delta_i=B_iA_i\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times d_{in}},\ i=1,\dots,T);\ \ \bar\Delta_i=U_i\bar\Sigma_iV_i^{\top},\ \text{where for LoRA inputs }\bar{\boldsymbol\sigma}_i=\Big(\tfrac1r\textstyle\sum_{j=1}^{r}\sigma_i^{j}\Big)\mathbf 1_r\ \text{(averaging) or }\bar{\boldsymbol\sigma}_i=\Big(\textstyle\sum_{j=1}^{r}\sigma_i^{j}\Big)\mathbf w,\ \mathbf w\text{ linearly decreasing},\ \textstyle\sum_j w_j=1,\ \tfrac{w_1}{w_r}=\min\!\big(\tfrac{\sigma_i^{1}}{\sigma_i^{r}},\rho\big)\ \text{(linear smoothing)},\ \text{and for full fine-tuning }\bar\Sigma_i=\Sigma_i\ \text{(truncation only)};\ \ U=[U_1,\dots,U_T]=PSQ^{\top}\ \Rightarrow\ \widetilde U=PQ^{\top}=U(U^{\top}U)^{-1/2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times k},\ \ \widetilde V\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{in}\times k}\text{ likewise from }[V_1,\dots,V_T],\ \ k=rT;\ \ M_i=\widetilde U^{\top}\bar\Delta_i\widetilde V\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times k};\ \ \widetilde M=\mathrm{Merge}(M_1,\dots,M_T)\ (\text{entry-wise; TIES after keeping the top }0.1\%\text{ of entries of each }M_i\text{ in all main experiments, TA in ablations});\ \ \Delta\widetilde W=\widetilde U\big(\widetilde M\odot\mathcal M\big)\widetilde V^{\top},\ \ \mathcal M=\mathrm{blockdiag}(\mathbf 1_{r\times r},\dots,\mathbf 1_{r\times r});\ \ W=W_0+\alpha\,\Delta\widetilde W;\ \ \text{frozen: }W_0\text{ and all task vectors; nothing is trained (}\alpha\text{ is picked on held-out validation data, fixed to }2\text{ on MM-MergeBench)}
methods.trainable_params: 0\ \text{(training-free; hyper-parameters: rank }r\ (=16=\text{LoRA rank for LoRA inputs};\ r=\lfloor\min(d_{out},d_{in})/T\rfloor\text{ for full fine-tuning}),\ \text{smoothing rule and }\rho=5\ \text{(LoRA inputs only)},\ \text{TIES trim fraction }10^{-3},\ \text{scale }\alpha)
methods.locus: Every 2-D weight matrix of \(T\) task-adapted copies of one base model: CLIP ViT-B/32, ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/14 visual encoders, either fully fine-tuned (8/14/20 tasks) or LoRA-tuned on the q, k, v and output projections at \(r=16\) (8/12/16 tasks), and LLaVA-v1.5-7B LoRA checkpoints (MM-MergeBench, 8 seen tasks plus 4 unseen). In the released full-fine-tuning code, non-matrix parameters (and the text projection) are simply averaged.
methods.structure: Training-free, layer-wise merge of \(T\) task matrices in three steps. (1) Energy smoothing: each task vector is truncated to rank \(r\), and for LoRA inputs its singular values are flattened (to their mean, or to a linear profile whose max/min ratio is at most \(\rho\)) while its singular directions \(U_i,V_i\) are kept. For full fine-tuning the paper and the released code only truncate to the top \(r=\lfloor\min(d_{out},d_{in})/T\rfloor\) components, which the paper calls implicit smoothing; explicit smoothing hurt in that setting (Appendix E.4, Fig. 10). (2) Cover space: the column-concatenated bases \(U=[U_1,\dots,U_T]\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times rT}\) and \(V\) are replaced by their polar (whitened) factors \(\widetilde U=PQ^{\top}\), \(\widetilde V\). These are the orthonormal matrices nearest to \(U\) and \(V\), the same orthogonalisation TSV-M uses. The paper motivates them as a near-optimal solution of a shared-dyadic-basis reconstruction problem (its Eqs. 7-8, 23-25). (3) Every smoothed task vector is written in the cover coordinates as a \(k\times k\) matrix \(M_i=\widetilde U^{\top}\bar\Delta_i\widetilde V\) (\(k=rT\le\min(d_{out},d_{in})\)). These matrices are combined entry-wise; all main experiments use TIES after keeping the top 0.1% of entries of each \(M_i\) (a \(10^{-3}\) fraction in both the LoRA and the full-fine-tuning code), and TA appears only in ablations. Only the \(T\) diagonal \(r\times r\) blocks are kept before mapping back, which gives one dense delta of rank at most \(rT\) per matrix. Because \(\mathrm{span}(\widetilde U)=\mathrm{span}(U)\supseteq\mathrm{col}(\bar\Delta_i)\) (and likewise for \(\widetilde V\) and the row space), the round trip \(\widetilde U M_i\widetilde V^{\top}=\bar\Delta_i\) is exact. With TA and no mask, the cover-space step therefore reduces to summing the smoothed task vectors. Its effect comes from the block-diagonal mask, which drops cross-task coordinates, and from coordinate-wise rules such as TIES applied in the cover basis. This follows from the construction and the paper does not state it. It is consistent with the ablations: for rank-16 LoRA inputs truncation is lossless, so the +6.40 points of 'TA + CSM' over vanilla TA in Table 6 can only come from the mask, and Table 5 shows the mask adding 0.3-1.4 points (LoRA) and 5.6-10.6 points (full fine-tuning) on top of TIES with smoothing. Diagnostic metric: \(\mathrm{DirSim}(\Delta_s,\Delta_t)=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{nm}}\mathbf 1_n^{\top}R(s,t)\mathbf 1_m\) with \(R_{ij}=(u_s^{i\top}u_t^{j})(v_t^{j\top}v_s^{i})\). This is cosine similarity with every singular value set equal, and its projected version correlates with post-merge per-task normalized accuracy improvement (Pearson \(R=0.64\)).
methods.mergeable_reason: The output is one static delta per matrix, \(W=W_0+\alpha\,\widetilde U(\widetilde M\odot\mathcal M)\widetilde V^{\top}\), folded into the base weights. The result is a single model with no adapters, routing or inference overhead. Merging LoRA inputs gives a dense rank-\(\le rT\) delta, not a rank-\(r\) LoRA.
methods.identity_at_init: Not applicable (training-free). \(\alpha=0\) recovers \(W_0\). For \(T=1\) with TA, \(\widetilde U=U_1\), \(\widetilde V=V_1\), \(M_1=\bar\Sigma_1\) and the mask is all ones, so the method returns \(U_1\bar\Sigma_1V_1^{\top}\). For LoRA inputs this is the energy-smoothed version of the task vector, not the task vector itself. For full fine-tuning \(r=\min(d_{out},d_{in})\) when \(T=1\) and there is no smoothing, so TA returns the task vector exactly (the default TIES step with top-0.1% trimming does not).
methods.key_idea: How much of each task survives merging depends on keeping the singular directions of its task vector, not the energy in its singular values. The paper measures this with an energy-blind directional similarity. DC-Merge therefore flattens each task's spectrum (for LoRA inputs; full fine-tuning uses truncation only) and then merges all tasks in one shared orthonormal cover basis \((\widetilde U,\widetilde V)\), keeping only the diagonal \(r\times r\) blocks so that each task's directions survive aggregation.
methods.results_note: On LoRA-tuned (\(r=16\)) CLIP ViT-B/32, DC-Merge reaches 64.17/68.40/66.27% average absolute accuracy for 8/12/16 merged tasks, against 63.01/66.28/64.61% for the strongest baseline Iso-CTS (Table 1). It is best in all 9 LoRA settings and in 7 of the 9 full-fine-tuning settings (Iso-CTS wins ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/14 at 8 tasks, Table 2).

relations.note: Cited and used as a baseline. The cover basis is TSV-M's orthogonalisation of the concatenated per-task singular vectors (\(U_\perp=PQ^{\top}\)); the released code reuses TSV-M's construction. TSV-M places each \(\Sigma_i\) in its own diagonal block. DC-Merge first smooths each spectrum, projects every smoothed task vector into the shared basis, merges with TIES (or TA) and keeps the diagonal blocks, so cross-task contributions inside each block are retained.

TIES is the rule applied entry-wise to the cover-space coefficient matrices \(M_i\) in all main experiments (TA in ablations). TIES applied in cover coordinates does better than TIES applied to raw weights (Table 6: 69.27 vs 62.09 normalized accuracy on ViT-B/32, 8 tasks).
Task vectors and the final \(W_0+\alpha\,\Delta\widetilde W\) follow Task Arithmetic, and TA is one of the two in-cover-space aggregators.

LoRA-merging baseline (KnOTS-TIES). KnOTS also aligns tasks in a shared SVD basis before applying TIES. DC-Merge beats it in all nine reported LoRA settings (Table 1) and on KnOTS's own released ViT-B/32 checkpoints (77.8 vs 68.0 normalized accuracy, Table 9).

Not cited (checked against the reference list). Core Space also maps each task's LoRA into a shared \(Tr\times Tr\) coordinate matrix, merges there with an off-the-shelf rule and maps back. Its bases come from SVDs of the stacked LoRA factors. DC-Merge uses whitened per-task singular bases, spectral smoothing and a block-diagonal mask.
