corrections: formula_latex: added standard rank-32 LoRA on the other modules, set alpha = r = 32 (App.), and quoted the exact IC prompt.
locus: the paper uses standard LoRA "elsewhere", not only the output projections.
trainable_params: added the standard LoRAs and noted the abstract's "1%" rounding.
identity_at_init: B_i = 0 is not stated in the paper; marked as presumed.
methods.verification_notes: arXiv 2504.20690 (Zhang, 2025); NeurIPS 2025 confirmed (arXiv comment). MoE equation, 4 experts, rank 32, top-1, alpha = rank, 50K training pairs and Emu Edit CLIP-I 0.907 / DINO 0.866 confirmed.

methods.name: SD-LoRA
methods.paper_title: SD-LoRA: Scalable Decoupled Low-Rank Adaptation for Class Incremental Learning
methods.formula_latex: W^{(t)}=W_0+\sum_{k=1}^{t}\alpha_k\,\frac{B_kA_k}{\|B_kA_k\|_F};\ \ \text{during task } t:\ \Big\{\tfrac{B_kA_k}{\|B_kA_k\|_F}\Big\}_{k<t} \text{ frozen},\ \{\alpha_k\}_{k\le t} \text{ and } (B_t,A_t) \text{ trained}
methods.trainable_params: \text{task } t:\ r_t(d_{in}+d_{out}) \text{ per adapted matrix} + t \text{ magnitudes (one set shared across all adapted projections)};\ r_1=10
methods.locus: query and value projections of all ViT blocks (rank 10, reduced for later tasks in SD-LoRA-RR)
methods.structure: Linear combination of frozen unit-Frobenius-norm rank-r directions with trainable scalar magnitudes (initialized to 1; one magnitude set shared across the adapted projections): each task adds one direction, while the magnitudes of all earlier directions keep being re-weighted. Variants shrink later ranks (RR) or absorb a new direction into old ones by least squares (KD).
methods.mergeable_reason: After training the sum of scaled directions is a single static matrix, and inference needs no task identity or component selection.
methods.identity_at_init: Not identity: magnitudes are initialized to 1 and each direction has unit norm, so a new task starts with a nonzero perturbation (initialization of A_t, B_t is not specified in the paper).
methods.key_idea: Decouple LoRA magnitude from direction in continual learning: freeze old directions but keep re-weighting their magnitudes. Training then follows a low-loss path into a region shared by all tasks, giving rehearsal-free, selection-free inference.
methods.results_note: ImageNet-R (20 tasks) accuracy 75.26% vs 73.59% for HiDe-Prompt (which stores samples) and 69.89% for InfLoRA; state of the art on ImageNet-A, DomainNet, CIFAR-100 and CUB-200 class-incremental benchmarks with ViT-B/16.

relations.note: Applies magnitude/direction decoupling to a growing set of LoRA components.
Rehearsal-free continual learning with prompts instead of LoRA.
Prompt-pool continual learning baseline.
Alternative PEFT-style continual learning by constraining update subspaces.

corrections: structure: "nonnegative" removed (no sign constraint in the paper); recorded that one magnitude set is shared across projections (Sec. 4 implementation details).
trainable_params: confirmed the shared magnitude set and added r_1 = 10.
results_note: added the strongest baseline at N=20 (HiDe-Prompt 73.59) so the comparison is not cherry-picked (Table 2).
methods.verification_notes: arXiv 2501.13198 (Wu, 2025); ICLR 2025 Oral confirmed (OpenReview 5U1rlpX68A). Formula h' = (W0 + sum alpha_k normalized(A_k B_k)) x, frozen old directions, magnitudes initialized to 1, q/v placement with rank 10, and the RR/KD variants confirmed.

methods.name: Sparse Memory Finetuning
methods.full_name: Continual learning via sparse memory-layer finetuning
methods.paper_title: Continual Learning via Sparse Memory Finetuning
methods.formula_latex: \mathrm{Mem}(x)=W_2^{\top}\Big[\Big(\sum_{i\in\mathrm{TopK}(K q(x))}s_i(x)\,V_i\Big)\odot\mathrm{silu}(W_1 x)\Big],\ s=\mathrm{softmax}(K_{\mathbb{I}}q(x)),\ k=32;\ \ \text{update only } \{V_i: i\in\mathcal{T}\},\ \ \mathcal{T}=\text{top-}t \text{ slots by } \frac{c(i)}{\sum_j c(j)}\cdot\log\frac{|\mathcal{B}|+1}{\sum_{b\in\mathcal{B}}\mathbb{1}[c_b(i)>0]+1};\ \text{all other parameters frozen (gradients stopped)}
methods.trainable_params: t\cdot d_v \text{ memory values per step } (d_v=1024;\ t=500 \text{ for TriviaQA}, 10^4 \text{ for SimpleQA, out of } 10^6 \text{ slots})
methods.locus: value table of a product-key memory layer that replaces one FFN (layer 12 of 22) in a 1.3B model
methods.structure: Input-dependent sparse coordinate mask over rows of the memory value table, chosen by a TF-IDF score: slot access counts c(i) on the current batch, discounted by how often the slot is used on background pretraining batches B.
methods.mergeable_reason: Updated memory values overwrite the originals in place, so the memory-layer model keeps its architecture and inference cost.
methods.identity_at_init: No new parameters; training starts exactly from the pretrained memory-layer model.
methods.key_idea: Memory layers are sparsely accessed by design; updating only the slots specifically activated by new knowledge (relative to their pretraining usage) learns new facts with much less interference than full fine-tuning or LoRA.
methods.results_note: After learning new TriviaQA facts, NaturalQuestions F1 drops 89% with full fine-tuning and 71% with LoRA but only 11% with sparse memory finetuning, at the same level of new-knowledge acquisition.

relations.note: LoRA is the main forgetting baseline it improves on.
Sparse fine-tuning, but here the sparse support is defined by memory-slot access statistics.
Alternative sparse fine-tuning method.

corrections: formula_latex: added the output projection W_2 and the silu(W_1 x) gate of the memory layer (Sec. 3, memory-layer equations).
trainable_params: value dimension d_v = 1024 made explicit, and the t values tied to their tasks.
methods.verification_notes: arXiv 2510.15103 (Lin, 2025). ICLR 2026 desk-rejected (OpenReview LGo7U1m24L); no other venue found, so arXiv. TF-IDF score, 1M-slot memory at layer 12 of 22 in a 1.3B model, and the NQ drops (89% / 71% / 11%) confirmed.

methods.name: SEAL
methods.paper_title: Self-Adapting Language Models
methods.formula_latex: SE\sim \mathrm{LM}_\theta(\cdot\mid C),\ \ \theta'=\mathrm{SFT}_{\mathrm{LoRA}}(\theta,SE)\ \ (W=W_0+\tfrac{\alpha}{r}BA;\ r=64,\alpha=128 \text{ for knowledge incorporation};\ r=128,\alpha=16 \text{ for ARC TTT});\ \ \text{outer loop: ReST}^{EM}\ \text{(SFT on self-edits with } r(SE)=1),\ r(SE)=\mathbb{1}\big[\text{adapting with } SE \text{ improves } \mathrm{LM}_\theta \text{ on } \tau\big]
methods.trainable_params: \text{inner: } r(d_{in}+d_{out}) \text{ per adapted matrix per self-edit } (r=64 \text{ or } 128);\ \text{outer: the self-edit generation policy (LoRA } r=16 \text{ in the ARC RL-SFT)}
methods.locus: inner LoRA on all attention and MLP projections (Qwen2.5-7B, knowledge incorporation) or on q/v/gate/up/down projections (Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, ARC)
methods.structure: Bi-level: the model writes its own fine-tuning data and hyperparameters ('self-edits'); a LoRA SFT step turns each self-edit into \Delta W = BA; RL (filtered behavior cloning) reinforces self-edits whose induced update improves downstream performance.
methods.mergeable_reason: Each realized update is an ordinary LoRA that can be merged into the weights.
methods.identity_at_init: Each inner LoRA update starts from B = 0.
methods.key_idea: Let the LLM learn, through RL, to generate the training data and optimization directives that best update its own weights, turning LoRA fine-tuning into an action the model can take.
methods.results_note: On SQuAD knowledge incorporation (no-context), accuracy rises from 32.7% to 47.0%, beating synthetic data written by GPT-4.1 (46.3%); ARC few-shot success 72.5% vs 20% without RL. The paper flags catastrophic forgetting under repeated self-edits.

relations.note: Self-edits are realized as LoRA SFT updates.
Context-to-weights via iterative self-generated SFT rather than an amortized generator.
SHINE amortizes the same context-to-weights step in one forward pass.

corrections: formula_latex: r=64/alpha=128 is only the SQuAD setting; ARC test-time training uses r=128, alpha=16 (App. A).
locus: split by task, following the two appendix configurations.
trainable_params: updated ranks per setting.
methods.verification_notes: arXiv 2506.10943 (Zweiger, 2025); NeurIPS 2025 poster confirmed (OpenReview JsNUE84Hxi, mlanthology). Binary ReST^EM reward (Eq. 2), SQuAD no-context 32.7 -> 47.0 vs 46.3 for GPT-4.1 data, and ARC 72.5% vs 20% confirmed.

methods.name: SparseLoRA
methods.paper_title: SparseLoRA: Accelerating LLM Fine-Tuning with Contextual Sparsity
methods.formula_latex: h=W_0\big|_{\mathcal{S}(x)}\,x+\tfrac{\alpha}{r}BAx\ \ (\text{training only}),\ \ \mathcal{S}(x)=\mathrm{TopK}\ \text{channels of the cheap proxy } (U_k\Sigma_k^{1/2})(\Sigma_k^{1/2}V_k^{\top})x\ \ \big(U_k\Sigma_kV_k^{\top}=\text{offline rank-}k \text{ SVD of } W_0\big);\ W_0 \text{ frozen},\ A,B \text{ trained}
methods.trainable_params: r(d_{in}+d_{out}) \text{ (same as LoRA)}
methods.locus: frozen main branch of attention (QKVO) and MLP projections, with non-uniform layer sparsity (deeper layers sparser); output tokens and up to the first 10% of steps stay dense. The LoRA branch (QKVO, r=32, alpha=64 in experiments) stays dense.
methods.structure: Standard LoRA update; the forward/backward pass through the frozen W_0 uses input-dependent channel sparsity, predicted by a training-free rank-k SVD sketch of W_0 (activation norms for FFN/VO, query-key norm products for QK).
methods.mergeable_reason: Sparsity is used only during training; the dense LoRA adapter merges into W_0 and inference is unchanged.
methods.identity_at_init: B = 0 as in LoRA; the sparse frozen branch only approximates W_0 x during training.
methods.key_idea: LoRA saves memory but not compute; predicting per input which channels of the frozen weights matter, with a cheap SVD proxy, lets fine-tuning skip most frozen-branch FLOPs without hurting accuracy.
methods.results_note: Up to 2.2x compute reduction and 1.6x wall-clock speedup over LoRA at matched accuracy on commonsense and arithmetic reasoning, code generation and instruction following (LLaMA-2/3).

relations.note: Adapter is unchanged; only frozen-branch computation is sparsified.
Different axis of LoRA training efficiency (compute sparsity vs weight quantization).

corrections: locus: added the LoRA configuration used (QKVO, r=32, alpha=64) and the "up to 10%" dense warm-up.
methods.verification_notes: arXiv 2506.16500 (Khaki, 2025); ICML 2025 confirmed (arXiv comment, OpenReview z83rodY0Pw). SVD estimator (rank-k sqrt(S)-split factors, Alg. 1), L2-norm metric for FFN/VO, q odot k norm metric for QK, and 2.2x FLOP / 1.6x wall-clock figures confirmed.

methods.name: LoReFT
methods.full_name: Low-rank Linear Subspace Representation Finetuning (ReFT family)
methods.paper_title: ReFT: Representation Finetuning for Language Models
methods.formula_latex: \Phi_{\text{LoReFT}}(h)=h+R^{\top}\big(Wh+b-Rh\big)=(I-R^{\top}R)\,h+R^{\top}(Wh+b),\quad R\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d}\ (RR^{\top}=I_r),\ W\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d},\ b\in\mathbb{R}^{r};\ \text{applied to the residual-stream vector } h^{(l)}_i \text{ at the first } p \text{ and last } s \text{ prompt positions of the chosen layers } l\in\mathcal{L};\ \text{LM frozen},\ \{R,W,b\}\ \text{trained};\ \text{DiReFT ablation: } \Phi(h)=h+W_2^{\top}(W_1h+b),\ W_1,W_2\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d}
methods.trainable_params: (2rd+r)\ \text{per intervention } (R,W\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d},\ b\in\mathbb{R}^{r});\ |\mathcal{L}|\,(2rd+r)\ \text{with prefix and suffix weights tied},\ 2|\mathcal{L}|\,(2rd+r)\ \text{untied (one intervention for the prefix and one for the suffix positions in each layer)}
methods.locus: residual-stream hidden states (Transformer block outputs) at a fixed number of prefix and suffix prompt positions in selected layers; generated tokens are not intervened on
methods.structure: Low-rank affine edit of hidden states confined to an r-dimensional subspace. With the orthogonal projector P = R^T R, Phi(h) = (I - P)h + R^T(Wh + b): the component of h in row(R) is replaced by a learned affine function of h, and the orthogonal complement is untouched. The edit is sparse in both positions (prompt prefix and suffix) and layers. DiReFT drops the orthonormality and the difference term, giving a LoRA-shaped map h -> h + W_2^T(W_1 h + b) on activations.
methods.mergeable_reason: The edit acts on the residual stream, including the skip path, at specific token positions, so it cannot be folded into any weight matrix; its cost is a small constant per prompt rather than per generated token.
methods.identity_at_init: Not identity-preserving. In pyreft R gets a random orthogonal initialization (torch orthogonal parametrization) and W, b use the default nn.Linear initialization, so Phi(h) != h at step 0; the identity is recovered only when W = R and b = 0.
methods.key_idea: Learn task-specific interventions on hidden representations instead of changing weights. LoReFT adapts the distributed interchange intervention from causal-abstraction interpretability (DAS): it rewrites the hidden state only inside a learned low-rank orthonormal subspace and only at a few prompt positions, using 15x-65x fewer parameters than LoRA.
methods.results_note: With 0.031% trainable parameters on LLaMA-7B it averages 80.2 on eight commonsense-reasoning tasks, the best among the compared PEFTs. On Llama-2 7B instruction tuning it reaches an 85.60 AlpacaEval win rate with 0.0039% of parameters (LoRA: 81.48). It trails LoRA and adapters on arithmetic reasoning.

relations.note: both edit representations; RED applies a diagonal affine map to FFN outputs at all positions, LoReFT a low-rank subspace edit at selected positions
both are framed as representation interventions; RoAd's is an element-wise 2D rotation that can be merged
DiReFT is essentially LoRA applied to hidden states at chosen positions; LoReFT reports 15x-65x fewer parameters than LoRA
main weight-based baseline on commonsense and arithmetic reasoning
both act only on activations at token positions and leave the weights untouched; prefix-tuning adds key/value states, LoReFT edits existing states

corrections: trainable_params: spelled out that 'untied' means one prefix and one suffix intervention per layer (pyreft share_weights semantics, which reproduces the reported 0.031% and 0.0039% budgets). The paper's formal I_untied, read literally, has one intervention per position.
methods.verification_notes: arXiv 2404.03592 (Wu et al., 2024) matches. NeurIPS 2024 spotlight confirmed on OpenReview (NeurIPS.cc/2024/Conference). Phi_LoReFT and Phi_DiReFT checked against eqs. 2-3 of the arXiv HTML. Init checked in pyreft interventions.py: orthogonal R, default nn.Linear W and b, so the map is not the identity at init. Parameter budgets re-derived: LLaMA-7B, r=8, 32 layers tied gives 32*(2*8*4096+8)=2.10M (0.031%); Llama-2 7B, r=4, 4 layers untied gives 8*(2*4*4096+4)=0.26M (0.0039%). Results (80.2 commonsense average, 85.60 vs 81.48 AlpacaEval) checked against Tables 1 and 3. Not in HF PEFT main (no reft tuner); it ships in pyreft.

methods.name: LongLoRA
methods.full_name: LongLoRA (LoRA with trainable embeddings and norms, plus Shifted Sparse Attention)
methods.paper_title: LongLoRA: Efficient Fine-tuning of Long-Context Large Language Models
methods.formula_latex: W_{\{q,k,v,o\}}=W_0+\tfrac{\alpha}{r}BA\ \ (B\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r},\ A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}});\ \ E=E_0+\Delta E\ \text{(input embedding, dense)};\ \ \gamma_{\text{norm}}\ \text{(all RMSNorm gains) trained};\ \ \text{training-time attention } \mathrm{S^2\text{-}Attn}:\ \text{tokens split into groups of size } G,\ \text{half of the heads attend within groups, the other half within groups shifted by } G/2;\ \ \text{inference: standard full attention};\ \ \text{RoPE positions rescaled by Position Interpolation};\ \ \text{MLP weights frozen}
methods.trainable_params: r(d_{in}+d_{out})\ \text{per adapted attention matrix } (4L \text{ matrices}) \;+\; |\mathcal{V}|\,d\ \text{(input embedding)} \;+\; (2L+1)\,d\ \text{(norm gains)}
methods.locus: W_q, W_k, W_v, W_o of every attention layer (LoRA, r = 8, alpha = 16 in the official code), plus the input token-embedding matrix and all normalization layers (trained densely); S2-Attn changes only the training-time attention pattern
methods.structure: Composite of three factors. (i) Rank-r additive updates Delta W = BA on the attention projections. (ii) Dense, selective updates of the input-embedding table and the norm gains, which together are under 2% of Llama2-7B's parameters. (iii) A training-only sparsification of the attention graph into block-diagonal token groups, with a G/2 shift on half of the heads so that information flows between neighbouring groups (Swin-style). The paper calls (i)+(ii) 'LoRA+', which is unrelated to LoRA+ by Hayou et al.
methods.mergeable_reason: The LoRA factors merge into W_0, the trained embedding and norm tensors replace the originals, and S2-Attn is used only in training, so inference runs the original dense-attention architecture (with Position-Interpolation RoPE scaling) at the original cost.
methods.identity_at_init: Standard LoRA init (B = 0) and the pretrained embedding and norm values, so the weights are unchanged at step 0. The training-time function still differs from the base model, because attention is restricted to shifted local groups and positions are interpolated.
methods.key_idea: Plain LoRA fails at context extension at any rank, but also training the cheap embedding and normalization layers closes almost all of the gap to full fine-tuning. Training can use shifted sparse local attention, which approximates full attention and takes two lines of code, while inference keeps dense attention.
methods.results_note: Extends Llama2 7B, 13B and 70B to 100k, 64k and 32k tokens on a single 8xA100 machine. At 32k context on PG19, LoRA with trainable norms and embeddings reaches perplexity 8.12, versus 8.08 for full fine-tuning and 11.44 for plain rank-8 LoRA.

relations.note: LoRA on W_q, W_k, W_v, W_o, extended with dense updates of the embeddings and norms
trains all normalization gains alongside LoRA; the norms account for the largest single perplexity gain per parameter
both cut fine-tuning compute with training-only sparsity and keep dense inference; LongLoRA sparsifies attention over tokens, SparseLoRA sparsifies channels of the frozen weights

methods.verification_notes: arXiv 2309.12307 (Chen et al., 2023) matches. ICLR 2024 oral confirmed on OpenReview (6PmJoRfdaK) and in the ICLR 2024 accepted list. LoRA on W_q, W_k, W_v, W_o plus trainable embeddings and norms, S2-Attn used only in training (G/2 shift on half the heads) and Position Interpolation all checked against Sec. 3 and the official fine-tune.py (LoraConfig r=8, lora_alpha=16; trainable_params='embed,norm'). PG19 32k numbers checked against Table 2: full FT 8.08, LoRA r=8 11.44, LoRA+norm+embed 8.12. 100k/65536/32768 limits checked against Table 4. Not a native HF PEFT method.

methods.name: O-LoRA
methods.full_name: Orthogonal Low-Rank Adaptation (orthogonal subspace learning for continual learning)
methods.paper_title: Orthogonal Subspace Learning for Language Model Continual Learning
methods.formula_latex: W^{(t)}=W_0+\sum_{i<t}B_iA_i+B_tA_t,\quad A_i\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}},\ B_i\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r};\quad \text{paper: }\min_{A_t,B_t}\ \mathcal{L}_{\text{task}}(\mathcal{D}_t)+\lambda_1\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\big\|B_i^{\top}B_t\big\|_F^2\ \ (\mathcal{U}_t=\operatorname{col}(B_t)\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}};\ \text{the paper writes }\Delta W=AB\text{ with its }A\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r}\text{ the output-side factor});\quad \text{official code: }\lambda_1\sum_{i<t}\big\|A_iA_t^{\top}\big\|_{1}\ (\text{entry-wise, on PEFT lora\_A})+\lambda_2\big(\|A_t\|_F+\|B_t\|_F\big);\quad W_0\ \text{and}\ \{A_i,B_i\}_{i<t}\ \text{frozen; after task } t:\ W_0\leftarrow W_0+\textstyle\sum_{i\le t}B_iA_i
methods.trainable_params: r(d_{in}+d_{out})\ \text{per adapted matrix per task (after } t \text{ tasks } t\,r(d_{in}+d_{out}) \text{ are stored unless merged)}
methods.locus: W_q and W_v of every attention layer (T5-large, LLaMA-7B)
methods.structure: Sum of per-task rank-r updates. A soft penalty on an r x r cross-Gram matrix, which vanishes exactly when two tasks' subspaces are orthogonal, pushes each new task's subspace away from all earlier ones. Delta W is therefore close to a direct sum of mutually orthogonal rank-r pieces; orthogonality is a regularizer, not a hard constraint. The paper defines each task's subspace as the column span of the output-side factor (catalog B_t, in R^{d_out}) and squares the entries of B_i^T B_t. The official trainer instead penalizes the input-side rows (PEFT lora_A) with an entry-wise absolute value and adds an L2 term (lambda_2).
methods.mergeable_reason: Each task's BA is a static low-rank matrix that can be merged into W_0 after training, and inference needs no task ID.
methods.identity_at_init: Each new task's LoRA uses the standard init (B_t = 0), so the model function is unchanged at the start of every task.
methods.key_idea: Use each finished task's LoRA subspace as a cheap stand-in for its gradient subspace, instead of storing gradients as OGD does, and learn the next task's LoRA in a subspace orthogonal to all earlier ones. This gives continual learning without rehearsal or task IDs and preserves instruction-following generalization.
methods.results_note: On the standard 5-task continual-learning benchmark with T5-large, O-LoRA averages 75.8% over three task orders, against 72.7% for LFPT5 (the paper's previous state of the art) and 80.0% for multi-task training. On the 15-task benchmark it averages 69.6% against 69.2% for LFPT5. ProgPrompt, which needs task IDs at inference, scores 75.1% and 77.9%.

relations.note: one LoRA per task, with earlier LoRAs frozen
O-LoRA uses a soft orthogonality penalty between learned subspaces; InfLoRA uses a hard, data-designed frozen down-projection
both enforce orthogonality to the update subspaces of earlier tasks; OSF does so inside full-rank SVD components

both grow per-task LoRA components for rehearsal-free continual learning without task IDs; SD-LoRA decouples magnitude and direction instead of enforcing orthogonality (SD-LoRA does not benchmark O-LoRA)
both make per-task or per-concept LoRAs orthogonal so their sum does not interfere; O-LoRA uses a penalty during sequential training, Orthogonal Adaptation fixed orthogonal bases for later merging
rehearsal-free continual-learning baseline that uses a prompt pool

corrections: formula_latex: the old formula mixed the code's factor (A_i A_t^T on the down-projections) with the paper's squared-Frobenius penalty, so it matched neither source. Rewritten to give both explicitly: the paper penalizes ||B_i^T B_t||_F^2 on the output-side factors (the paper's A in Delta W = AB, A in R^{d x r}); the official code penalizes sum |A_i A_t^T| entry-wise on PEFT lora_A, plus lambda_2(||A_t||_F + ||B_t||_F).
structure: updated to state which factor each version penalizes (paper: column spaces of the up-projection; code: rows of the down-projection), consistent with the corrected formula.

results_note: 'previous best (LFPT5)' qualified. ProgPrompt scores higher (75.1 on 5 tasks, 77.9 on 15 tasks) in the same Table 2, but it requires task IDs at inference; the paper excludes it from the state-of-the-art comparison for that reason.

relations: sd-lora note corrected. The old note said SD-LoRA compares against O-LoRA, but the SD-LoRA paper (arXiv 2501.13198) never mentions O-LoRA. The competes-with edge is kept on structural grounds.
methods.verification_notes: arXiv 2310.14152 (Wang et al., 2023) matches. Findings of EMNLP 2023 confirmed by the arXiv comment and ACL Anthology 2023.findings-emnlp.715. Paper objective (eqs. 6-9: Delta W = AB with A in R^{d x r}, O_{i,t} = A_i^T A_t, squared entries) compared with the official uie_trainer_lora.py (|lora_A @ loranew_A^T|.sum() plus lambda_2 times the norms of the new A and B); the two penalize different factors. LoRA is placed on W_q and W_v as stated in Sec. 3; the related-work section loosely says 'key and value'. Results checked against Table 2. Not in HF PEFT (PEFT's OSF is a different method).

methods.name: InfLoRA
methods.paper_title: InfLoRA: Interference-Free Low-Rank Adaptation for Continual Learning
methods.formula_latex: W_t=W_{t-1}+B_tA_t,\quad A_t=(U_t)_{[1:r]}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}}\ \text{frozen, from the SVD } \hat H_t^{\top}=V_t\Sigma_tU_t,\ \ \hat H_t=(I-M_tM_t^{\top})H_t\ \ \text{or}\ \ M_t^{\perp}M_t^{\perp\top}H_t;\quad B_t\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r}\ \text{trained, init } 0;\quad \Rightarrow\ \Delta_{B_t}W_t=(\Delta_{W}W_t)\,A_t^{\top}A_t,\ \ (B_tA_t)\,M_t=0
methods.trainable_params: r\,d_{out}\ \text{per adapted matrix per task (}A_t\text{ is designed, not trained; one } r(d_{in}+d_{out}) \text{ branch is kept at a time, earlier branches are merged)}
methods.locus: key and value projections of every ViT-B/16 attention block (variant InfLoRA-b5: bottom 5 blocks only)
methods.structure: Rank-r additive update with a frozen, data-designed down-projection A_t. Its orthonormal rows are the top principal directions of the current task's layer inputs H_t after projection onto the orthogonal complement of the old tasks' input subspace span(M_t), which DualGPM maintains; they therefore lie in N_t intersected with M_t-perp. Training B_t alone equals full fine-tuning projected onto row(A_t), Delta W = G A_t^T A_t, so Delta W annihilates old-task inputs. Notation is swapped relative to the paper, which calls the up-projection A_t and the down-projection B_t.
methods.mergeable_reason: After each task the branch B_t A_t is merged into W_{t-1}, and inference uses a single weight matrix without task identity.
methods.identity_at_init: B_t = 0 (zero-initialized up-projection), so the function is unchanged at the start of each task. A_t is set before training by an SVD of the projected current-task activations.
methods.key_idea: Fine-tuning only the up-projection of a LoRA branch is exactly full fine-tuning restricted to the row space of the frozen down-projection. Choosing that row space inside the new task's input span but orthogonal to the old tasks' input space removes interference by construction.
methods.results_note: With an ImageNet-21K ViT-B/16, InfLoRA reaches final accuracies of 75.65% on 10-task ImageNet-R (77.52% with 5 tasks, 71.01% with 20), 86.51% on 10-task CIFAR-100 and 74.53% on 5-task DomainNet. It leads L2P, DualPrompt, CODA-P, C-LoRA and LAE on ImageNet-R and DomainNet. On CIFAR-100, CODA-P has a slightly higher final accuracy (86.62%), while InfLoRA has the best averaged accuracy (91.70% vs 91.08%).

relations.note: one LoRA-like branch per task, merged after training
per task it is structurally LoRA-FA (frozen down-projection, trained up-projection), with a designed rather than random down-projection
hard, data-designed subspace versus O-LoRA's soft orthogonality penalty
SD-LoRA reports 75.26% vs InfLoRA's 69.89% on 20-task ImageNet-R
both restrict continual-learning updates to subspaces orthogonal to what earlier tasks use
prompt-based rehearsal-free class-incremental baseline
prompt-pool baseline

corrections: results_note: the claim that InfLoRA is 'ahead of ... CODA-P' was false for CIFAR-100 final accuracy (CODA-P 86.62 vs InfLoRA 86.51 in Table 2); qualified the claim and added the 5- and 20-task ImageNet-R numbers.
methods.verification_notes: arXiv 2404.00228 (Liang & Li, 2024) matches. CVPR 2024 confirmed by the arXiv comment, the CVF open-access page and DOI 10.1109/CVPR52733.2024.02231. Formula checked against eqs. 1-8 and Proposition 1, with the paper's letters swapped into catalog notation (paper A_t = trained up-projection, initialized at 0; paper B_t = designed and frozen down-projection). Rows of the designed factor are principal directions of the projected inputs H-hat_t, which lie in M_t-perp, so (B_tA_t)M_t = 0. Placement in K and V and merging of old branches confirmed (expanded parameters 4ldr). The SD-LoRA numbers on 20-task ImageNet-R (75.26 vs 69.89) were confirmed in SD-LoRA Table 2. Not in HF PEFT.

methods.name: Textual Inversion
methods.paper_title: An Image is Worth One Word: Personalizing Text-to-Image Generation using Textual Inversion
methods.formula_latex: v_*=\arg\min_{v\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\ \mathbb{E}_{z\sim\mathcal{E}(x),\,y,\,\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I),\,t}\Big[\big\|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta\big(z_t,t,c_\theta(y)\big)\big\|_2^2\Big],\quad y=\text{neutral template (e.g. ``A photo of } S_*\text{'') whose token } S_* \text{ is embedded as } v;\quad c_\theta,\ \epsilon_\theta,\ \mathcal{E}\ \text{and all existing token embeddings frozen}
methods.trainable_params: d\ \ \text{(one token embedding; } k\,d \text{ for a } k\text{-vector pseudo-word)}
methods.locus: token-embedding table of the frozen text encoder (one new row for the pseudo-word S_*); the pseudo-word can appear anywhere in a prompt
methods.structure: Extends the frozen vocabulary with one learned point v_* in input-embedding space. The update is a single new row of the embedding matrix, used compositionally inside arbitrary natural-language prompts rather than as a fixed task prefix.
methods.mergeable_reason: The learned vector is just a new vocabulary entry: inference runs the unchanged text encoder and diffusion model at the same cost, with one token standing in for a word.
methods.identity_at_init: The model itself is untouched. v is initialized to the embedding of a single-word coarse descriptor (e.g. 'cat', 'sculpture'), so prompts without S_* behave exactly as before and S_* starts out as that word.
methods.key_idea: Personalize a frozen text-to-image model by inverting 3-5 images into a new word in its text-embedding space, trained with the ordinary denoising loss. One word embedding is enough to capture an object or style, which can then be composed into new prompts.
methods.results_note: On LDM a single learned embedding reproduces object and style concepts from 3-5 images more faithfully than human-written captions or DALL-E 2 image prompts. CLIP-based and user-study evaluations place it at a favourable point on the reconstruction-editability trade-off, which the learning rate can shift.

relations.note: same frozen-model soft-token principle; a single reusable pseudo-word placed anywhere in a prompt instead of a fixed task prefix
equivalent to training only the embedding row of one newly added token in the text encoder
Custom Diffusion also trains a new token (V*), together with the cross-attention K/V weights
alternative personalization of text-to-image models

methods.verification_notes: arXiv 2208.01618 (Gal et al., 2022) matches. ICLR 2023 confirmed in the ICLR 2023 virtual-site paper list. Objective checked against eq. 2 of the paper (the paper writes epsilon ~ N(0,1)). Initialization from a single-word coarse descriptor, 3-5 images and the CLIP-ImageNet templates checked against Sec. 3 and Sec. 4. Not in HF PEFT (diffusers provides textual_inversion.py and load_textual_inversion). PEFT TrainableTokensConfig on one newly added token index reproduces the parametrization, which justifies the special-case-of edge.

methods.name: Custom Diffusion
methods.full_name: Custom Diffusion (cross-attention K/V fine-tuning for multi-concept customization)
methods.paper_title: Multi-Concept Customization of Text-to-Image Diffusion
methods.formula_latex: K=W^{k}c,\ V=W^{v}c\ \text{in every U-Net cross-attention layer};\quad W^{k}=W^{k}_0+\Delta W^{k},\ W^{v}=W^{v}_0+\Delta W^{v}\ \text{(dense)},\ \text{plus a new modifier-token embedding } V^{*};\ \text{all other weights frozen; loss: denoising loss on the target images plus 200 retrieved real regularization images};\quad \text{merging } N \text{ concepts: } \hat W=\arg\min_W\|WC_{\text{reg}}^{\top}-W_0C_{\text{reg}}^{\top}\|_F\ \ \text{s.t.}\ \ WC^{\top}=V_{\text{tgt}},\ \ \hat W=W_0+\mathbf{v}^{\top}\mathbf{d},\ \ \mathbf{d}=C(C_{\text{reg}}^{\top}C_{\text{reg}})^{-1},\ \ \mathbf{v}^{\top}=(V_{\text{tgt}}-W_0C^{\top})(\mathbf{d}C^{\top})^{-1}
methods.trainable_params: 2\,d_{out}\,d_{text}\ \text{per cross-attention layer } (W^{k},W^{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times d_{text}}) \;+\; d_{text}\ \text{per modifier token}
methods.locus: key and value projections of the text features in all cross-attention layers of the diffusion U-Net (Stable Diffusion), plus the modifier-token embedding
methods.structure: Block mask over the parameter tensors: only the two matrices that read the text condition (W^k, W^v) are updated, densely. Multi-concept merging is a closed-form, equality-constrained least-squares projection: it maps each concept's target-word features to the fine-tuned values while staying close to W_0 on about 1000 regularization captions.
methods.mergeable_reason: The fine-tuned W^k and W^v replace the originals and V^* is one extra vocabulary row, so inference runs the original architecture at the original cost; the closed-form merge folds several concepts into a single pair of matrices.
methods.identity_at_init: Training starts from the pretrained W^k, W^v (Delta W = 0), and V^* is initialized to a rarely occurring token's embedding, so the model is initially unchanged on ordinary prompts.
methods.key_idea: Fine-tuning moves the cross-attention weights much more than any others, so update only the K/V projections that map text into latent features, together with a learned modifier token and retrieved real images as regularization. The method is fast, small and resists language drift, and concepts can be combined by joint training or a closed-form constrained merge.
methods.results_note: On Stable Diffusion it beats Textual Inversion and matches or beats DreamBooth on text/image alignment and human preference, while training about 5x faster (~6 minutes) and storing 75MB instead of 3GB per concept. The closed-form multi-concept merge takes about 2 seconds.

relations.note: also trains a new token embedding V* jointly with W^k and W^v
both merge linear layers in closed form by least squares on input features; Custom Diffusion adds hard equality constraints on the concepts' target-word features
the paper reports that the K/V updates are effectively low-rank (5x SVD compression with similar quality), though training them as low-rank directly was worse
compact diffusion personalization that also supports multi-concept generation
multi-concept customization by merging per-concept adapters
merging independently trained subject and style adapters

methods.verification_notes: arXiv 2212.04488 (Kumari et al., 2022) matches. CVPR 2023 confirmed on the CVF open-access page and by DOI 10.1109/CVPR52729.2023.00192. Only W^k and W^v of the cross-attention layers plus V* are trained (Sec. 3.1). 200 LAION regularization images were retrieved at CLIP-text similarity > 0.85. The constrained least-squares merge (eqs. 4-5, about 1000 regularization captions) was checked character by character. V* is initialized from a rare token (id 42170). Claims checked: 5x faster than DreamBooth and 75MB vs 3GB of storage (Sec. 4.1), a merge of about 2 seconds, 5x SVD compression at the top 60% of singular values, and low-rank training being sub-optimal (App. C). Not in HF PEFT (diffusers examples/custom_diffusion).

methods.name: ESFT
methods.paper_title: Let the Expert Stick to His Last: Expert-Specialized Fine-Tuning for Sparse Architectural Large Language Models
methods.formula_latex: g_i^{l}=\frac{1}{N_s}\sum_{j=1}^{N_s}\frac{1}{L_j}\sum_{k=1}^{L_j}g_{i,k}^{l}\ \ (\text{ESFT-Gate})\quad\text{or}\quad r_i^{l}=\frac{1}{N_s}\sum_{j=1}^{N_s}\frac{1}{L_j}\sum_{k=1}^{L_j}\frac{\mathbb{1}(g_{i,k}^{l}>0)}{K}\ \ (\text{ESFT-Token});\quad E_s^{l}=\text{top-scored experts with }\textstyle\sum_{i\in E_s^{l}}R_i^{l}\ge p;\quad \theta_e\ (e\in E_s^{l})\ \text{trained; all other routed experts, shared experts, attention, router and embeddings frozen}
methods.trainable_params: \sum_{l=1}^{L}|E_s^{l}|\cdot 3\,d\,d_{ff}^{(e)}\ \ (\text{gate/up/down projections of each selected routed expert; on average 2-15 of 66 experts per layer})
methods.locus: the routed (non-shared) FFN experts in each MoE layer that are most relevant to the task; attention, router, shared experts and embeddings stay frozen
methods.structure: Data-dependent block mask over experts. In each layer the selected set is the smallest group of top-scored routed experts whose cumulative relevance (average gate score or token-selection ratio on sampled task data) reaches p. Selected experts are updated densely, everything else is frozen, and routing stays free during training and inference.
methods.mergeable_reason: The updated experts simply replace the originals, so the architecture, routing and inference cost are unchanged.
methods.identity_at_init: Training starts from the pretrained weights (Delta W = 0); expert selection is computed from router statistics on a task sample.
methods.key_idea: In fine-grained MoE LLMs, each task activates a concentrated and distinct set of experts, so fine-tune only the experts most relevant to the task. This nearly matches full fine-tuning on the target task, forgets less, and cuts storage by up to 90%.
methods.results_note: On DeepSeek-V2-Lite, ESFT-Gate averages 50.2 on downstream tasks (FFT 51.0, LoRA 44.9) while keeping more general ability (ESFT-Token 61.5 vs FFT 58.8 and LoRA 59.1), with 2.57-3.20 GB of trained parameters versus 28.6 GB for FFT.

relations.note: main PEFT baseline (rank 8); ESFT beats it on both task performance and general-ability retention
block-level selective tuning placed where the task lives; ESFT chooses experts from router statistics instead of choosing layers
selective full-parameter tuning of a subset of blocks (layers rather than experts)

methods.verification_notes: arXiv 2407.01906 (Wang et al., 2024) matches. EMNLP 2024 main confirmed in ACL Anthology 2024.emnlp-main.46. The ESFT-Gate and ESFT-Token scores and the cumulative-threshold selection rule match eqs. 6-8, and the selected experts are trained with all other experts and modules frozen while routing stays free. DeepSeek-V2-Lite has 66 experts per layer, 2-15 of them selected on average (Sec. 6.1), with p = 0.1 for Gate and 0.2 for Token. Numbers checked: 50.2/49.4 vs FFT 51.0 and LoRA 44.9, general ability 61.5/60.6 vs 58.8/59.1, and 2.57/3.20 GB vs 28.6 GB. Not in HF PEFT.

methods.name: Intruder-dimension reduction
methods.full_name: Intruder Dimension Reduction (post-hoc spectral surgery on LoRA adapters)
methods.paper_title: LoRA vs Full Fine-tuning: An Illusion of Equivalence
methods.hf_peft_config: from peft.tuners.lora.intruders import reduce_intruder_dimension; reduce_intruder_dimension(peft_model, old_adapter_name='default', new_adapter_name='intruder_reduced', top_k=10, threshold_epsilon=0.5, mitigation_lambda=0.75)  # adds and activates a new LoRA adapter
methods.formula_latex: W_0+\Delta W=U\Sigma V^{\top},\ \ W_0=U^{0}\Sigma^{0}V^{0\top};\quad \mathcal{I}=\{\,j\le k:\ \max_i|\langle u_j,u^{0}_i\rangle|<\epsilon\,\};\quad W'=W_0+\Delta W+(\lambda-1)\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}}\sigma_j\,u_jv_j^{\top};\quad (B',A')=\text{rank-}r\ \text{truncated SVD of } (W'-W_0)/s,\ \ s=\tfrac{\alpha}{r}\ (\tfrac{\alpha}{\sqrt r}\text{ with rsLoRA}),\ \ B'=U_r\Sigma_r^{1/2},\ A'=\Sigma_r^{1/2}V_r^{\top};\quad \text{no training: } W_0 \text{ frozen, the trained } (B,A) \text{ replaced by } (B',A')\ \ (\text{paper: only the top-ranked } j\in\mathcal{I}\text{ is scaled, no re-factorization})
methods.trainable_params: 0\ \ (\text{training-free; the output is again a rank-}r\text{ adapter with } r(d_{in}+d_{out}) \text{ parameters per matrix})
methods.locus: every LoRA-adapted linear (or embedding) layer of an already trained adapter
methods.structure: Spectral endomorphism on the space of trained adapters. Among the top-k singular directions of the merged matrix, those nearly orthogonal to every pretrained left singular vector (the intruders) are shrunk by lambda, and the edited Delta W is projected back to rank r. The paper scales only the top intruder per matrix and does not re-project; HF PEFT scales every detected intruder and re-factorizes to rank r.
methods.mergeable_reason: The result is an ordinary LoRA adapter (B', A') that merges into W_0 like any other LoRA.
methods.identity_at_init: Not applicable (post-hoc edit). lambda = 1 leaves the adapter unchanged up to rank-r truncation, lambda = 0 removes the intruder components, and lambda > 1 amplifies them.
methods.key_idea: LoRA creates high-ranking intruder singular vectors that are nearly orthogonal to the pretrained spectrum; full fine-tuning does not. These directions drive most of the forgetting, so shrinking them after training recovers pretrained behaviour at little cost in task accuracy.
methods.results_note: Scaling the top intruder dimension of each matrix with lambda = 0.7 (RoBERTa-base on QQP, LoRA r = 8) left test accuracy unchanged and cut fine-tuning-induced forgetting (pre-training loss) by 33.2%. For LLaMA2-7B on MetaMath (r = 256), lambda = 0.3 cost 0.1% accuracy and cut forgetting by 33.3%.

relations.note: post-hoc edit of a trained LoRA adapter, returning a LoRA adapter of the same rank
a preventive alternative: train in the minor singular directions so the principal spectrum is not disturbed; intruder reduction is a post-hoc repair
knowledge-preserving initialization versus post-hoc removal of the components that cause forgetting
the paper finds that PiSSA, which edits principal singular vectors, also produces many intruder dimensions

corrections: formula_latex: the LoRA scaling divided out before re-factorization is PEFT's layer.scaling (alpha/r, or alpha/sqrt(r) with rsLoRA), not always alpha/r. Added the symmetric sqrt(Sigma) split used for B' and A', and the paper-vs-PEFT difference (the paper scales only the top intruder).

hf_peft_config: added the import path and the old_adapter_name/new_adapter_name arguments. The utility writes the edited factors into a new adapter (default 'intruder_reduced') and activates it, leaving the original adapter in place.
methods.verification_notes: arXiv 2410.21228 (Shuttleworth et al., 2024) matches. OpenReview shows NeurIPS 2025 poster (xp7B8rkh7L) after rejection at ICLR 2025. Definition 3.1 / Algorithm 1 and the scaling rule W = W0 + dW + (lambda-1) u_i sigma_i v_i^T (top intruder only) checked in Sec. 5; the paper uses cos without abs, PEFT uses |cos|. PEFT main src/peft/tuners/lora/intruders.py was read in full: abs cosine of the merged vs base left singular vectors over the top_k, all detected intruders scaled, then (W'-W0)/scaling re-factorized to rank r. The utility is documented in the PEFT LoRA developer guide and announced in the v0.19.0 release (2026-04-14). The PEFT docstring for mitigation_lambda says 'higher = more subtracted', but the code computes (lambda-1), so a higher lambda subtracts less; the formula follows the code. No author code is linked from the paper. Results (QQP 33.2%, MetaMath 33.3%) checked.

methods.name: CODA-Prompt
methods.paper_title: CODA-Prompt: COntinual Decomposed Attention-based Prompting for Rehearsal-Free Continual Learning
methods.formula_latex: p(x)=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\alpha_m(x)\,P_m,\quad \alpha_m(x)=\gamma\big(q(x)\odot A_m,\;K_m\big),\quad q(x)=\theta(x)_{[\mathrm{CLS}]}\ \text{(frozen ViT pass)},\ \gamma=\cos;\quad p=[p_K;p_V],\ p_K,p_V\in\mathbb{R}^{\frac{\ell}{2}\times d}:\ \mathrm{MSA}\big(h_Q,[p_K;h_K],[p_V;h_V]\big)\ \text{at each prompted layer};\quad \min_{P^{n},K^{n},A^{n},\phi_n}\ \mathcal{L}\big(f_\phi(f_{\theta,P,K,A}(x)),y\big)+\lambda\big(\|PP^{\top}-I\|_2+\|KK^{\top}-I\|_2+\|AA^{\top}-I\|_2\big);\ \ \theta\ \text{frozen},\ \text{components of earlier tasks frozen}
methods.trainable_params: n_p\,M\,(\ell d+2d)+\text{head}\quad(n_p=\text{prompted layers, 5 in the paper};\ M/N\ \text{new components trained per task})
methods.locus: keys/values (prefix form) of MSA layers 1-5 of a frozen ViT-B/16; the query comes from a separate frozen forward pass ([CLS] output)
methods.structure: Input-conditioned linear combination of a growing dictionary of prefix components, p(x) = sum_m alpha_m(x) P_m. The weights are unnormalized cosine similarities between a feature-gated query q(x) ⊙ A_m and a key K_m. Each task adds M/N components, and the components, keys and attention vectors of earlier tasks are frozen, so the trainable space is an increasing chain of component sets with soft orthogonality penalties.
methods.mergeable_reason: The prompt depends on the input through the query pass, and its prefix slots lengthen the key/value sequence, so nothing folds into W_0.
methods.identity_at_init: No identity: prefix slots change attention from the first step. P, K and A are orthogonally initialized.
methods.key_idea: L2P and DualPrompt select prompts from a pool by hard key-query matching. CODA-Prompt replaces that with an attention-weighted sum of prompt components, so the selection mechanism is trained end to end with the task loss. Capacity grows by adding components rather than lengthening prompts, and freezing past components plus orthogonality limits forgetting.
methods.results_note: Rehearsal-free class-incremental ImageNet-R with ViT-B/16: 75.45% average final accuracy on 10 tasks vs 71.32% for DualPrompt (up to +4.5% across the 5/10/20-task splits). It is also ahead on CIFAR-100, DomainNet and a dual-shift ImageNet-R benchmark.

relations.note: Replaces hard top-N retrieval from a prompt pool, whose keys are trained by a separate matching loss, with a continuous, end-to-end-trained weighted sum of components.
Keeps DualPrompt's prefix attachment at layers 1-5 of ViT-B/16 and changes only how the prompt is formed; outperforms it by up to 4.5% A_N on ImageNet-R.
The prompt is split into p_K, p_V and prepended to the keys and values (prefix-tuning attachment).

Both build instance-conditioned prompts as attention-weighted mixtures of prompt components. ATTEMPT mixes pre-trained source prompts for multi-task NLP; CODA mixes continually grown components for continual vision learning.

methods.verification_notes: arXiv 2211.13218 (Smith, 2022-11) matches; CVPR 2023 confirmed on CVF open access. Formula checked against Eqs. 2-7 (p = sum alpha_m P_m, alpha = cos(q(x) ⊙ A_m, K_m), prefix split p_K/p_V of length L_p/2, ortho penalty ||BB^T - I||). Param count re-derived: 5 layers x 100 components x (8*768 + 2*768) = 3.84M, matching the paper's 4.6% of ViT-B. ImageNet-R 10-task 75.45 vs 71.32 (DualPrompt) and max gain +4.50 (20-task) confirmed in Table 1. Not in HF PEFT (main @85be3f3).

methods.name: Trans-LoRA
methods.full_name: Trans-LoRA (nearly data-free transfer of PEFT modules across base models by distillation on filtered synthetic data)
methods.paper_title: Trans-LoRA: towards data-free Transferable Parameter Efficient Finetuning
methods.formula_latex: \phi^\ast=\arg\max_\phi\ \mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\log p_{\phi}(\text{yes}\mid t(x))+\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{M}_s}\log p_{\phi}(\text{no}\mid t(x));\quad \mathcal{D}_{syn}=\{x\sim\mathcal{M}_{gen}(\cdot\mid\bar{\mathcal{D}}):\ p_{\phi^\ast}(\text{yes}\mid t(x))>p_{\phi^\ast}(\text{no}\mid t(x))\},\ |\bar{\mathcal{D}}|=5,\ |\mathcal{D}_{syn}|=|\mathcal{D}|;\quad \theta_t=\arg\min_{\theta}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{syn}}H\big((\mathcal{M}_t+\theta)(x),\,(\mathcal{M}_s+\theta_s)(x)\big);\ \ \mathcal{M}_s,\mathcal{M}_t,\theta_s\ \text{frozen};\ \theta_t\ \text{trained (e.g. } W_t=W_{t,0}+B_tA_t)
methods.trainable_params: r\,(d^{t}_{in}+d^{t}_{out})\ \text{per adapted target matrix (whatever the target PEFT needs)}\ +\ \text{a one-off LoRA discriminator on }\mathcal{M}_s
methods.locus: the target model's adapter locations (default LoRA on W_q, W_v). The transfer acts on the model's input-output behavior, not on weights.
methods.structure: Function-level transport of an adapter along a change of base model. The source pair (M_s, theta_s) acts as a teacher, and the target adapter is fitted by knowledge distillation on synthetic inputs that a discriminator has filtered to imitate the distribution of the original training inputs. No weight correspondence between source and target is needed, so they may differ in family, size and even PEFT type (LoRA, DoRA, prompt tuning).
methods.mergeable_reason: The output is an ordinary adapter of the chosen target type: a transferred LoRA or DoRA merges into the target weights, a transferred soft prompt does not.
methods.identity_at_init: The target adapter starts from the standard initialization of its type (for LoRA, B = 0, so M_t + theta_t = M_t at the start). Algorithm 1 only says 'Initialize theta_t'.
methods.key_idea: When a base model is retired, its LoRAs can be retrained on the new base without the client's data. An LLM seeded with 5 examples synthesizes task inputs. A discriminator, trained once alongside the source LoRA, keeps only samples that look like the real training inputs. The target LoRA is then distilled from the source model plus LoRA on those samples.
methods.results_note: Across 86 BBH, MMLU, MBPP and GSM8K tasks with Llama-2 and Gemma (within and across families), the transferred LoRA matches or beats both the source LoRA and the unadapted target. For example, BBH Gemma-2b to Gemma-7b: 43.61 vs 31.84 (source LoRA) and 37.75 (target base). It also transfers LoRA<->DoRA and prompt tuning, and survives two consecutive transfers.

relations.note: The default transported object is a LoRA, retrained on the target as a LoRA.

Same base-model-change problem. Trans-LoRA transports behavior by distillation, which needs synthetic data and training; LoRA-X transports weights by subspace projection, with no data and no training.
The same pipeline transfers DoRA adapters and converts between LoRA and DoRA (Table 6).
Also transfers soft prompts, showing that the transport lives in function space and is independent of the adapter's parametrization.

methods.verification_notes: arXiv 2405.17258 (Wang, 2024-05) and NeurIPS 2024 proceedings page confirmed. Eq. 1 (discriminator), the D_syn rejection rule, |D-bar| = 5, |D_syn| = |D|, M_gen = M_t, and Algorithm 1's cross-entropy distillation all match. Default LoRA on q,v confirmed (Sec. 4.1). BBH Gemma-2b->Gemma-7b 43.61/31.84/37.75 (Table 1), LoRA/DoRA/PT transfer (Table 6) and two-step 45.04 (Table 7) confirmed. github.com/raywang4/TransLoRA still contains only a placeholder README, so code_url stays empty. Not in HF PEFT.

methods.name: LoRA-X
methods.paper_title: LoRA-X: Bridging Foundation Models with Training-Free Cross-Model Adaptation
methods.formula_latex: W_0=U\Sigma V^{\top}\ \text{(SVD, cached)},\quad W=W_0+\tilde U_r\,\Delta\Sigma\,\tilde V_r^{\top},\ \ \tilde U_r\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r},\ \tilde V_r\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{in}\times r}\ \text{(top-}r\text{ singular vectors, frozen)},\ \ \Delta\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\delta\sigma_1,\dots,\delta\sigma_r)\ \text{(or a full } r\times r\text{ core) trained},\ \sigma_i+\delta\sigma_i\ge 0;\quad \text{transfer (no training): }\Delta W_{t\leftarrow s}=U_tU_t^{\top}\,\Delta W_s\,V_tV_t^{\top}=U_t\big(U_t^{\top}\tilde U_s\,\Delta\Sigma_s\,\tilde V_s^{\top}V_t\big)V_t^{\top}
methods.trainable_params: r\ \ (\text{diagonal }\Delta\Sigma)\quad\text{or}\quad r^{2}\ \ (\text{full core})
methods.locus: attention projections (to_q, to_k, to_v, to_out) of diffusion UNets: SDXL family (UNet only) and SD-v1.5 family (UNet and text-encoder attention); TinyLlama in an appendix. Transfer skips 'filter blocks' with low source-target subspace similarity and re-matches some blocks to a more similar source block.
methods.structure: The update lives in span(U_r) ⊗ span(V_r) of W_0, i.e. a spectral core between frozen top-r SVD bases. Cross-model transfer is a two-sided orthogonal projection onto the target weight's column and row spaces (Eq. 3). Layers are matched by subspace similarity (Eq. 4); for mismatched sizes a least-squares map replaces the source bases (Sec. 4.2.2). Across architectures, an optimal-transport cost over the layer-similarity matrix (the Adapter Transferability Cost) scores how hard a transfer is; it is a metric, not the transfer map itself. Caveat (derived): the released pseudocode uses a thin SVD, so for square full-rank layers the projection is the identity and transfer copies Delta W_s unchanged.
methods.mergeable_reason: Both the trained and the transferred adapter are plain additive matrices that fold into the source or target W_0.
methods.identity_at_init: Not stated in the paper. The natural choice Delta Sigma = 0 (inferred) gives Delta W = 0.
methods.key_idea: An adapter becomes portable if it may not create new feature directions. LoRA-X trains only a rescaling or mixing of the base weight's top singular directions, then moves it to a new base model (an updated, distilled or fine-tuned version) by projecting onto that model's singular subspaces, with no data and no training.
methods.results_note: Training-free transfer of LoRA-X style adapters, from SD-v1.5 to SD Eff-v1.0/RV-v3.0 and from SDXL to SSD-1B/RVXL-v3.0, gives HPSv2, LPIPS-diversity and DINOv2 scores close to adapters trained directly on the target, whereas projected plain LoRA degrades markedly. A TinyLlama 3T to 2.5T text experiment shows the same.

relations.note: The diagonal variant (the one used in all experiments, r = 320) is SVDiff restricted to the top-r singular values: W = U diag(s) V^T with s_i = sigma_i + delta sigma_i >= 0 for i <= r and s_i = sigma_i otherwise. The paper calls SVDiff 'a similar adapter structure' and differs by truncation, by touching only attention layers, and by targeting transferability.

With a full r x r core, Delta W = U_r Delta Sigma V_r^T has the same reachable set as LoRA-XS (U_r R Sigma_r V_r^T, where R Sigma_r ranges over all r x r matrices). Derived here, not stated in either paper.
The diagonal variant is SVFT with the fixed sparsity pattern Omega = {(i,i): i <= r} in W_0's singular basis. Derived here.
Weight-space, training-free transport vs. function-space transport by distillation on synthetic data.
Projecting a plain LoRA onto the target subspaces transfers much worse (Table 2), which motivates the subspace constraint.

corrections: locus: added the SD-v1.5 text-encoder attention layers (App. B.2) and the filter-block / block re-matching detail (App. B.1.1, App. F).
structure: the Adapter Transferability Cost is an optimal-transport transferability metric (Sec. 4.2.4), not an assignment used to perform the transfer; reworded and added the thin-SVD caveat.

relation svdiff: builds-on -> special-case-of; the diagonal LoRA-X update is exactly SVDiff with delta_i = 0 for i > r (same non-negativity constraint), which the paper describes as a similar structure rather than a base it builds on.
methods.verification_notes: arXiv 2501.16559 (Farhadzadeh, 2025-01) and ICLR 2025 proceedings confirmed. Formula matches Eqs. 1-3 (diagonal Delta Sigma with sigma_i + delta sigma_i >= 0; full core allowed in the text). r = 320 parameters per module (App. B) is consistent with trainable_params. Table 2 (projected LoRA -27.8% HPSv2 at r = 32) and Table 13 (TinyLlama) confirmed. Identity at init not stated. No official code. Not in HF PEFT.

methods.name: LoFiT
methods.paper_title: LoFiT: Localized Fine-tuning on LLM Representations
methods.formula_latex: \text{Step 1 (localize): } z^{(l,i)}\leftarrow(1+A_l^{i})\odot z^{(l,i)},\ \ \min_{A}\ \mathcal{L}_{CE}+\lambda\textstyle\sum_{l,i}\|A_l^{i}\|_1,\ \ T=\operatorname{top\text{-}K}_{(l,i)}\|A_l^{i}\|;\quad \text{Step 2 (tune): } z^{(l,i)}\leftarrow z^{(l,i)}+v_l^{i}\ \ \text{for }(l,i)\in T,\ \ \mathrm{MultiHead}(h)=\operatorname{concat}\big(z^{(l,1)},\dots,z^{(l,H)}\big)W^{O};\ \ \text{all } W_0\ \text{frozen},\ v_l^{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{head}}\ \text{trained}
methods.trainable_params: K\,d_{head}\ \ (\text{final; }K=48,96,160\ \text{for Gemma-7B, Llama 2-7B, Llama 2-13B}\Rightarrow 48\cdot256=96\cdot128\approx12\text{K},\ 160\cdot128\approx20\text{K});\ \text{the discarded selection step trains }L\,H\,d_{head}\ \text{scalings }(=L\,d\ \text{when }H\,d_{head}=d,\ \text{e.g. Llama 2})
methods.locus: outputs of a learned sparse set of attention heads (3-10% of all heads), before the output projection W^O
methods.structure: Input-independent translation of selected head-output coordinates, z -> z + v, on a support T chosen by an L1-regularized multiplicative probe. Because z enters W^O linearly, the edit equals a bias Delta b_O = sum_{i in T_l} W^O_(i) v_l^i on the attention output projection (derived here). It is therefore sparse, localized bias tuning in representation space, spanning at most K d_head directions.
methods.mergeable_reason: The offset is constant and passes through the linear W^O, so it folds into an output-projection bias. Llama and Gemma o_proj layers have no bias, so one bias vector per edited layer must be added (derived from the paper's equations).
methods.identity_at_init: Approximate only: v ~ N(0, sigma_v) and, in the selection step, A ~ N(0, sigma_A), with sigma_A = sigma_v = 0.001 in all experiments (App. D), so the model starts near the base model but not exactly at it.
methods.key_idea: LoFiT borrows localization from interpretability. It first learns per-head scaling factors with an L1 penalty to find which attention heads matter for the task, then fine-tunes only additive offset vectors on those heads. Task-specific localization beats random head sets and head sets chosen for other tasks.
methods.results_note: With 10% of heads (about 12K-20K parameters) on Gemma-7B and Llama 2-7B/13B, LoFiT beats ReFT on average and is comparable to LoRA (about 200x more parameters) and RED (about 20x more) on TruthfulQA, MQuAKE and CLUTRR. It is slightly below them on SIQA, ARC-c, BoolQ and SVAMP, and it outperforms ITI.

relations.note: Both learn interventions on hidden representations. LoReFT edits a low-rank subspace of the residual stream at chosen layers without localization; LoFiT adds offsets at learned heads.
RED learns a scaling plus a bias on every layer's representations, roughly LoFiT's Step 1 and Step 2 combined but without localization; LoFiT uses about 20x fewer parameters.
Step 2 is bias tuning, as in BitFit, restricted to the head outputs of a learned sparse set of heads.
Comparable accuracy with about 200x fewer parameters in the paper's low-data settings.

corrections: trainable_params: L H d_head equals L d only when H d_head = d (true for Llama 2, false for Gemma-7B, where 16 x 256 = 4096 != 3072); added the paper's per-model K values (Sec. 6) and the resulting 12K/12K/20K counts.
identity_at_init: added the initialization scale sigma_A = sigma_v = 0.001 used in all experiments.
methods.verification_notes: arXiv 2406.01563 (Yin, 2024-06) and NeurIPS 2024 proceedings confirmed. Step 1 ((1 + A) ⊙ z with L1 penalty, top-K by ||A||) and Step 2 (z <- z + v) match Sec. 3. Table 3 numbers (12K/12K/20K params; LoRA 200x, RED 20x more) confirmed. The o_proj-bias folding is derived (z enters W^O linearly). Not in HF PEFT.

methods.name: MoSLoRA
methods.paper_title: Mixture-of-Subspaces in Low-Rank Adaptation
methods.formula_latex: W=W_0+s\,B\,M\,A,\quad s=\alpha/r\ \text{(LoRA scaling, used in the official code; Eq. 7 omits it)},\quad B\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r},\ M\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r},\ A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}};\quad \Delta W=s\textstyle\sum_{i,j=1}^{r}m_{ij}\,b_i\,a_j^{\top};\ \ W_0\ \text{frozen};\ A,M,B\ \text{trained}\quad\big(M=I_r:\ \text{LoRA};\ M=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}I&I\\ I&I\end{smallmatrix}\right]:\ \text{two-subspace mixing}\big)
methods.locus: any linear layer; q, k, v, up and down projections in the LLaMA-3 8B commonsense experiments (Table 7); q, k, v, o, up, down and gate for LLaVA visual instruction tuning (Table 8); also used for SDXL subject-driven generation
methods.structure: Three-factor low-rank update B M A, in which a learnable r x r mixer weights all r^2 rank-one 'subspaces' b_i a_j^T. The reachable set is still {rank <= r}, the same as LoRA's, so the mixer changes the parametrization and the optimization, not the expressivity. The gauge symmetry grows from GL(r) to GL(r) x GL(r): (B, M, A) ~ (BG, G^{-1}MH, H^{-1}A) (derived here).
methods.mergeable_reason: BMA is a single d_out x d_in matrix that folds into W_0.
methods.identity_at_init: B = 0 (A Kaiming-uniform; mixer Kaiming-uniform or orthogonal), so Delta W = 0. A zero-initialized mixer gives all three factors zero gradient and training stalls (paper, Appendix C).
methods.key_idea: Splitting LoRA into rank-one subspaces and mixing them improves results. MoSLoRA generalizes the fixed identity between A and B (LoRA), or the fixed butterfly (two-subspace mixing), to a learnable r x r mixer, at negligible extra parameters and compute.
methods.results_note: On LLaMA-3 8B commonsense reasoning (8 tasks) it averages 85.6, vs 82.8 for LoRA, 85.0 for DoRA and 84.2 for FLoRA, at about the same parameter count and LoRA-level training time. It also improves LLaVA visual instruction tuning and DreamBooth-style subject-driven generation.

relations.note: M = I_r recovers LoRA.

On 2-D weights FLoRA uses the same three-factor form A G B^T, with a possibly rectangular core. The two methods differ in initialization: FLoRA zero-inits the core, MoSLoRA zero-inits B and Kaiming/orthogonal-inits M (84.2 vs 85.6 in MoSLoRA's Table 4).
LoRA-XS is B M A with B and A frozen at the truncated SVD of W_0 and only the mixer trained.
LoRA-SB is B M A with B and A frozen at the SVD of an estimated first full fine-tuning step and only the mixer trained.
AdaLoRA uses a diagonal, pruned middle factor (P Lambda Q); MoSLoRA's core is dense and unpruned.
Higher commonsense average at lower training time and memory (Table 4).

corrections: formula_latex: added the LoRA scaling s = alpha/r; the paper's Eq. 7 omits it, but App. B sets alpha (32 for r = 16) and the official code multiplies BMA by lora_alpha / r.
locus: the commonsense experiments adapt q, k, v, up, down only (Table 7), not 'all attention and FFN projections'; o and gate are added only in the visual-instruction-tuning runs (Table 8).
methods.verification_notes: arXiv 2406.11909 (Wu, 2024-06; comment 'EMNLP 2024 Main, Oral') and ACL Anthology 2024.emnlp-main.450 confirmed. Eqs. 5-7 (xAWB, identity and butterfly mixers), init (A Kaiming-uniform, B zero, mixer Kaiming/orthogonal; zero mixer does not converge, App. C) and Table 4 (85.6 vs 82.8/85.0/84.2; 28.4M vs 28.3M params) confirmed. Reachable-set and GL(r)xGL(r) gauge statements are derived and correct. Not in HF PEFT.

methods.name: NOAH
methods.paper_title: Neural Prompt Search
methods.formula_latex: \text{block } l:\ \ x\leftarrow[\mathrm{CLS},P_l,E]\ (P_l\in\mathbb{R}^{\ell_l\times d},\ l<D_V);\ \ Q=W_qx+s\,B^{l}_{q}A^{l}_{q}x,\ K=W_kx+s\,B^{l}_{k}A^{l}_{k}x\ \ (\text{rank } r^{L}_l,\ l<D_L);\ \ h\leftarrow h+W^{l}_{up}\,\phi\big(W^{l}_{down}h\big)\ \ (\text{width } r^{A}_l,\ l<D_A);\quad a=\big(D_V,D_L,D_A,\{\ell_l,r^{L}_l,r^{A}_l\}\big),\ \ \ell_l,r_l\in\{5,10,50,100\}\ \text{or}\ \{1,5,10\},\ D\in\{3,6,9,12\};\ \text{one-shot supernet (AutoFormer weight entanglement), then evolutionary search under a parameter cap};\ \text{backbone frozen}
methods.trainable_params: \textstyle\sum_{l<D_V}\ell_l\,d+\sum_{l<D_L}4d\,r^{L}_l+\sum_{l<D_A}2d\,r^{A}_l\ (+\text{biases, head});\ \text{capped at }0.64\text{M on ViT-B/16 (found subnets average }0.43\text{M)}
methods.locus: every ViT-B/16 block up to each module's searched depth: VPT-Deep tokens at the block input, LoRA on W_q and W_k as written in Eq. 3 (the official code instead attaches one rank-r LoRA to the fused qkv projection, d -> 3d, with no scaling; it has the same 4dr parameter count), and a bottleneck adapter applied residually to the MLP output
methods.structure: Per-dataset architecture search over a product design space. Each point combines three PEFT modules, each truncated in depth and in width. With weight entanglement, every candidate is a coordinate restriction (a prefix slice) of one supernet's maximal-width modules. The found subnet is a sum of an additive part (LoRA), a serial insertion (adapter) and an input augmentation (VPT).
methods.mergeable_reason: Only the LoRA part folds into W_q and W_k; the adapter and prompt parts remain at inference unless the search gives them zero depth.
methods.identity_at_init: No identity at init. LoRA starts at zero (LoRA_b = 0, LoRA_a Kaiming-uniform in the official code), but the adapter's down- and up-projections are both Xavier-uniform initialized (model/module/adapter_super.py), so its output is not near zero, and VPT tokens (also Xavier-uniform) change attention from the first step. The paper does not discuss this.
methods.key_idea: NOAH treats Adapter, LoRA and VPT as interchangeable 'prompt modules' and lets neural architecture search decide, per downstream dataset, which modules to use, at what depth and with what width, instead of hand-designing a PEFT recipe.
methods.results_note: On VTAB-1k with ViT-B/16 (ImageNet-22K) it averages 75.5% with 0.43M parameters, vs 74.5 for LoRA, 73.9 for Adapter, 72.0 for VPT and 68.9 for full fine-tuning. It is also stronger in few-shot learning and ImageNet domain generalization.

relations.note: LoRA (on W_q, W_k) is one of the three searched modules.
VPT-Deep tokens are one of the three searched modules; depth and token count are searched.
A bottleneck adapter after the MLP is one of the three searched modules.
GLoRA also trains a one-shot supernet and runs an evolutionary search per layer, but over a merge-friendly unified affine space.
Both search a combined PEFT design space. NOAH uses a weight-shared supernet with evolutionary search on vision; AutoPEFT uses multi-objective Bayesian optimization on NLP.
UniPELT combines modules with learned input-dependent gates instead of searching over them.

corrections: url: arXiv abs -> TPAMI DOI (10.1109/TPAMI.2024.3435939, vol. 47, no. 7, pp. 5268-5280, July 2025, confirmed via Crossref) so the url matches the venue.
locus: noted that the official code (model/module/qkv_super_prompt.py) puts a single LoRA on the fused qkv weight rather than separate q/k LoRAs; parameter count 4dr is unchanged.
identity_at_init: 'near-zero adapters' is wrong for NOAH; the official AdapterSuper initializes both linear layers with Xavier-uniform, so the adapter output is non-zero at init.
results_note: pre-training set is ImageNet-22K as stated in the paper (Sec. 3, Implementation Details), not 'ImageNet-21K'.
methods.verification_notes: arXiv 2206.04673 (Zhang, 2022-06) confirmed; venue IEEE TPAMI 47(7):5268-5280 (2025) confirmed via Crossref DOI 10.1109/TPAMI.2024.3435939. Eqs. 2-4, search space ({5,10,50,100} or {1,5,10} widths, depths {3,6,9,12}), AutoFormer weight entanglement, 0.64M cap and the 0.43M / 75.5 VTAB result confirmed. Repo redirects from Davidzhangyuanhan/NOAH to ZhangYuanhan-AI/NOAH. Not in HF PEFT.

methods.name: AutoPEFT
methods.full_name: AutoPEFT (automatic, multi-objective configuration search for PEFT)
methods.paper_title: AutoPEFT: Automatic Configuration Search for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
methods.formula_latex: \text{layer } l\ (m_l=1):\ \ h\leftarrow F(x)+W^{up}_{SA}\,\mathrm{ReLU}\big(W^{down}_{SA}F(x)\big)+W^{up}_{PA}\,\mathrm{ReLU}\big(W^{down}_{PA}x\big),\ \ K'=[P_k;K],\ V'=[P_v;V],\ P_k,P_v\in\mathbb{R}^{L_{PT}\times d};\quad a=\big(m\in\{0,1\}^{L},\,D_{SA},\,D_{PA},\,L_{PT}\big)\in\mathcal{A};\quad \max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\big(f(a,W^\ast(a)),\,-g(a)\big)\ \ \text{s.t.}\ W^\ast(a)=\arg\min_W\mathcal{L}_{train}(a,W)\ \ \text{(SAAS-GP surrogate, NEHVI acquisition, low-fidelity inner loop)};\ \text{PLM frozen}
methods.trainable_params: \textstyle\sum_{l}m_l\,\big(2d\,D_{SA}+2d\,D_{PA}+2L_{PT}\,d\big)\ (+\text{biases})
methods.locus: in each selected Transformer layer: a serial adapter after the FFN, a parallel adapter around the FFN, and prefixes on the attention keys/values
methods.structure: Bi-level, bi-objective search (performance vs parameter count) over a discrete product space: a layer mask times three module sizes on a log scale, where 0 means the module is absent. The answer is a Pareto front of configurations, not a single PEFT. Each configuration is a sum of serial and parallel bottleneck insertions plus key/value prefixes.
methods.mergeable_reason: ReLU bottleneck adapters and prefix slots cannot be folded into the frozen weights.
methods.identity_at_init: Not addressed. Modules use AdapterHub defaults (near-zero adapter outputs), while prefixes change attention from the first step.
methods.key_idea: Instead of hand-picking a PEFT recipe, AutoPEFT searches jointly over which layers get modules and how large the serial adapter, parallel adapter and prefix are. It uses multi-objective Bayesian optimization with cheap low-fidelity evaluations, and the discovered configurations transfer across tasks and models.
methods.results_note: On GLUE with BERT-base, a configuration searched on RTE (0.76% parameters) averages 83.17 vs 83.15 for full fine-tuning, beating serial and parallel adapters, prefix-tuning, LoRA, UniPELT, MAM and AdaMix; per-task search reaches 83.49. Gains are similar on SuperGLUE, RoBERTa-large and T5, where it is compared with S3PET.

relations.note: The serial adapter (SA) after the FFN is one of the three building blocks.
The parallel adapter (PA) around the FFN is a building block; the paper treats LoRA as a scaled variant of PA and leaves it out.
The prefix module (PT) on attention keys and values is a building block.

MAM is a Table 1 baseline (80.25 GLUE avg at 6.97% params vs 83.17 at 0.76%). Its module types (parallel FFN adapter plus key/value prefix) are a subset of AutoPEFT's, but MAM itself is not a point of the search space: its sizes (prefix length 30, adapter width 512) and fixed scaling s = 4 are not in AutoPEFT's per-module grid {0,1,3,6,12,24,48,96,192,384,768} (11 values, inferred from 5,451,776 = 2^12 x 11^3 on BERT-base and the reported 12/96/1 values).
UniPELT also combines adapter, prefix and LoRA, but through learned gates rather than a search.
Both search a combined PEFT design space; NOAH uses a weight-shared supernet with evolutionary search on ViTs.
A baseline mixture of homogeneous adapters; AutoPEFT beats it at similar parameter cost.

corrections: relation mam-adapter: generalizes -> competes-with; MAM's prefix length 30, adapter width 512 and scaling s = 4 lie outside AutoPEFT's discrete size grid, so AutoPEFT's space does not contain MAM.
methods.verification_notes: arXiv 2301.12132 (Zhou, 2023-01; comment 'Accepted to TACL') and ACL Anthology 2024.tacl-1.29 confirmed. Eqs. 1-4 (SA, PA, SAPA composition, prefix P_k,P_v, bi-level bi-objective max), SAAS-GP + NEHVI and the 2^|l| x |D_SA| x |D_PA| x |L_PT| count confirmed. Param formula re-derived on the RTE config (layers 3,4,8,9,10; 12/96/1; d = 768): 837K = 0.76% of BERT-base, matching Table 2. Table 1 (83.17 vs 83.15 FFT; per-task 83.49) confirmed. Serial = Pfeiffer adapter (App.). Not in HF PEFT.

methods.name: Laplace-LoRA
methods.full_name: Laplace-LoRA (Bayesian low-rank adaptation via a post-hoc Laplace approximation over LoRA parameters)
methods.paper_title: Bayesian Low-rank Adaptation for Large Language Models
methods.formula_latex: W=W_0+BA,\ \ \theta=\{A,B\}\ \text{fit by standard LoRA}\to\theta_{MAP};\quad p(\theta\mid\mathcal{D})\approx\mathcal{N}(\theta_{MAP},\Sigma),\ \ \Sigma^{-1}=\textstyle\sum_{n}\mathbb{E}\big[(a\,a^{\top})\otimes(g\,g^{\top})\big]+\lambda I\ \ \text{(K-FAC per factor, large Kronecker factor stored at rank } n_{kfac});\quad f(x_\ast)\sim\mathcal{N}\big(f_{\theta_{MAP}}(x_\ast),\,J_\ast\Sigma J_\ast^{\top}\big),\ \ J_\ast=\nabla_\theta f_\theta(x_\ast)\big|_{\theta_{MAP}};\ \ \lambda\ \text{maximizes the Laplace marginal likelihood};\ \ W_0\ \text{frozen}
methods.trainable_params: r\,(d_{in}+d_{out})\ \text{(MAP, as LoRA)}\ +\ \text{post-hoc K-FAC statistics (not trained)}\approx n_{kfac}(d_{in}+d_{out})+2r^{2}\ \text{per matrix}\ +\ \text{one prior precision }\lambda
methods.locus: LoRA factors on W_q, W_v and the output (LM-head) layer in the paper; the LLLA variant uses only the output-layer LoRA
methods.structure: A Gaussian (Laplace) posterior over the LoRA factors, treated as two separate linear layers with Kronecker-factored precision (the d x d factor kept low-rank). Prediction integrates the linearized network over this posterior: a Bayesian model average over adapter parameters with the base weights fixed.
methods.mergeable_reason: The posterior mean BA merges into W_0, but the calibrated predictive needs the Jacobian with respect to the LoRA factors and the stored covariance at test time.
methods.identity_at_init: Standard LoRA initialization (B = 0) for the MAP fit. The Laplace step is post-hoc and leaves the mean unchanged.
methods.key_idea: Fine-tuned LLMs are overconfident on small datasets. After ordinary LoRA training, Laplace-LoRA fits a Laplace approximation over the LoRA parameters only, with low-rank K-FAC so memory stays LoRA-sized, and predicts with the linearized model. This calibrates the model without a validation set.
methods.results_note: On six commonsense reasoning tasks with LLaMA2-7B, full Laplace-LoRA keeps accuracy while greatly reducing ECE and NLL relative to MAP, MC dropout, checkpoint ensembles and LoRA ensembles. This holds under distribution shift too, at about 1-5% extra memory.

relations.note: Uses an unchanged LoRA fit as the MAP point; the Bayesian layer is post-hoc.
Both put a distribution on LoRA parameters. MonteCLoRA learns a Gaussian-mixture posterior during training; Laplace-LoRA fits a Gaussian after training.
BLoB (NeurIPS 2024) learns a variational posterior over LoRA during training, as an alternative to post-hoc Laplace.

Both put a distribution over LoRA adapters and average predictions at test time: LoRA Dropout (Lin et al., 2024, later work) samples sparsified adapters, Laplace-LoRA uses a Gaussian posterior. Laplace-LoRA's own baseline is standard MC dropout on a LoRA fine-tune (rate 0.1, 10 samples), which it beats on ECE/NLL; that baseline is not the LoRA Dropout method itself.

corrections: trainable_params: marked the K-FAC factors as post-hoc statistics rather than trained parameters and added the single prior precision lambda tuned by marginal likelihood.
relation lora-dropout: note no longer equates the paper's MC-dropout baseline (Gal & Ghahramani, 2016) with the catalog's LoRA Dropout method (arXiv 2404.09610, which postdates this paper).
methods.verification_notes: arXiv 2308.13111 (Yang, 2023-08) and ICLR 2024 proceedings confirmed. Eqs. 1-15 (MAP, K-FAC Fisher, low-rank large factor of rank n_kfac, linearized predictive, marginal-likelihood lambda) match. LoRA on q, v and the output layer (Sec. 5), LLLA = output layer only, six commonsense datasets and 1-5% memory overhead (Sec. 5.3) confirmed. Not in HF PEFT.

methods.name: BLoB
methods.paper_title: BLoB: Bayesian Low-Rank Adaptation by Backpropagation for Large Language Models
methods.formula_latex: h = W_0x + B A x,\quad A\sim q(A\mid M,\Omega)=\prod_{ij}\mathcal{N}(A_{ij}\mid M_{ij},\Omega_{ij}^2),\ \Omega_{ij}=G_{ij}^2,\ B\ \text{deterministic};\quad \min_{M,G,B}\ -\mathbb{E}_{q(A)}\big[\log P(\mathcal{D}\mid A,B)\big]+\mathrm{KL}\big[q(A)\,\Vert\,\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_p^2 I)\big];\quad \text{equivalently } q(\mathrm{vec}\,W)=\mathcal{N}\big(\mathrm{vec}(W_0+BM),\,(I_{d_{in}}\otimes B)\,\mathrm{diag}(\mathrm{vec}\,\Omega)^2\,(I_{d_{in}}\otimes B^{\top})\big);\ W_0\ \text{frozen}; M,G,B\ \text{trained}
methods.locus: LoRA-targeted linear layers (paper: W_q, W_v of every attention layer plus the output layer of Llama2-7B; RoBERTa for classification)
methods.structure: Stochastic low-rank update \Delta W = BA in which only the down-projection A is a random matrix with a mean-field Gaussian posterior (mean M, std \Omega = G^{\circ 2}); B is a point estimate. The induced full-weight posterior is a degenerate Gaussian centred at W_0 + BM whose covariance (I\otimes B)\,\mathrm{diag}(\Omega)^2(I\otimes B^\top) has rank at most r\,d_{in}. The prior is a matching low-rank Gaussian, so the full-weight KL reduces exactly to the KL on A. Sampling uses Flipout restricted to A.
methods.mergeable_reason: The posterior mean W_0 + BM can be merged into W_0 (BLoB with N=0 samples), but the Bayesian predictive that gives the calibration gains averages N (default 10) sampled A matrices, and this cannot be folded into one weight.
methods.identity_at_init: B = 0, as in LoRA. The mean M of A is uniform-Kaiming and G \sim \mathcal{U}(\epsilon/\sqrt2,\epsilon). The sampled update B A is therefore exactly zero at initialization. The authors fix the variance of B to 0 for this reason: a stochastic B would make the early forward passes noisy.
methods.key_idea: BLoB does variational Bayes inside the LoRA subspace and trains the posterior mean and variance jointly during fine-tuning, instead of adding a Laplace approximation afterwards. Only A is made stochastic (asymmetric Bayesianization), and the prior is designed so that the full-weight ELBO equals a cheap ELBO on A. The posterior std is parameterized as G squared for fast KL convergence, and LoRA-Flipout decorrelates the samples within a mini-batch.
methods.results_note: On Llama2-7B over six commonsense tasks, BLoB (N=10 samples) keeps accuracy close to MLE-LoRA while cutting ECE sharply (e.g. WG-S 29.8% to 9.4%, ARC-C 29.0% to 9.6%); it also improves NLL over MC-dropout, ensembles, BBB and Laplace-LoRA on most datasets, and the gains extend to OOD shifts.

relations.note: same W_0 + BA parameterization; the A factor is replaced by a Gaussian variational distribution
Laplace-LoRA (Yang et al., ICLR 2024) fits a post-hoc Kronecker-factored Laplace posterior over LoRA weights; BLoB learns the mean and covariance jointly during training
both put distributions on low-rank adapter parameters; MonteCLoRA targets robustness to hyperparameters, BLoB targets calibrated uncertainty

corrections: Removed relation blob -> asylora (builds-on): BLoB does not cite AsyLoRA (Zhu et al., 2402.16842); its asymmetry argument is about LoRA's B=0 init making a stochastic B noisy early in training, not AsyLoRA's finding that B matters more than A.
methods.verification_notes: arXiv API: title, first author Yibin Wang, v1 2024-06-17 match; NeurIPS 2024 confirmed by arXiv comment and Semantic Scholar. Checked against arXiv HTML (v5): Thm 3.1 covariance [I_n⊗B]diag(vec Ω)^2[I_n⊗B^T], Thm 3.2 low-rank prior, KL (1/2σ_p^2)(||M||^2+||Ω||^2)-Σlog Ω, Ω=G^2, Alg. 1 init G~U(ε/√2,ε), M Kaiming-uniform, B=0, LoRA-Flipout on A only, N=10 at test. Trainable count r d_out + 2 r d_in (M, G, B) re-derived. Table 1 ECE values (MLE 29.83/29.00 -> BLoB N=10 9.35/9.59 on WG-S/ARC-C) confirmed. Not in HF PEFT v0.21.1 (PEFT has MonteCLoRA, not BLoB).

methods.name: LoRAPrune
methods.paper_title: LoRAPrune: Structured Pruning Meets Low-Rank Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
methods.trainable_params: r(d_{in}+d_{out})
methods.locus: all LoRA-adapted linear layers of LLaMA-family LLMs; pruning acts on dependency groups (attention heads, MLP channels) across coupled layers
methods.structure:
Additive rank-r update \Delta W = BA composed with a structured 0/1 mask on output channels or heads (a coordinate projection onto a sub-network). Mask importance is a first-order Taylor score in which the full-weight gradient \partial\mathcal{L}/\partial W is replaced by the LoRA proxy \partial\mathcal{L}/\partial(BA) \approx 
abla_B\mathcal{L}\,A + B\,
abla_A\mathcal{L} - 
abla_B\mathcal{L}\,
abla_A\mathcal{L}, which is derived from one SGD step on B and A.
